Zhuangzi’s loosening of the “self” cannot be identified directly with the Buddhist idea of non-self either. “I have lost myself” and “the perfected person has no self,” at least in this reading, are closer to refusing attachment to one particular self. Student, lover, son, a person preparing for an examination—each identity is real and participates in forming me. None has the right to possess me alone, and none may announce that the whole person has failed merely because it temporarily fails.

Connected with “depending upon nothing,” this can easily be presented as “needing nothing.” But how could a concrete person possess no dependencies? People need food and sleep, money, a body, and assistance from others. Their room for choice is also constrained by real conditions. As I wrote in the article on feminism, telling someone to become courageous and true to herself does not create freedom from nothing when she lacks safe housing and the resources for life. Zhuangzi should not be used to cancel those conditions.

I therefore dare to offer only a highly personal translation: “depending upon nothing” does not mean having no conditions, but refusing to mortgage the right to exist completely to any single condition. The postgraduate entrance examination remains important, but passing it does not grant me permission to exist. Relationships remain important, but being chosen by someone does not issue the certificate proving whether I deserve love. Ability must still grow, but its strength does not determine whether I may first experience the world as a human being.

This certainly represents one level of free wandering, yet now it seems insufficient. Behind “do not let conditions define me” there remains a very solid self: external identities may change, but inside them there seems to be one true self that must be protected whole. Zhuangzi may not intend to preserve even that “true self” for me.

The opening of the “Free and Easy Wandering” is strange. The giant Kun and Peng still require sufficiently deep water and powerful wind before taking flight; the cicada and little dove cannot fly high, but have their own suitable elm and sandalwood trees; Liezi can already ride the wind, yet Zhuangzi still says that “he remains dependent.” Thus, the essay does not first imagine someone who needs no conditions and then call him free. On the contrary, it spends a long time describing how all beings depend upon something before asking: “If one rides the proper course of heaven and earth, and commands the changes of the six energies in order to wander through the inexhaustible, upon what would such a person depend?”

I now prefer to place the emphasis upon the word “wander.” Free wandering does not mean finally locating a position that will remain correct and safe forever. It means not being nailed permanently to any position. Heaven, earth, and the six energies continue to change, while people continue to act through them. The difference is that a person no longer requires one condition to support him forever, but retains the capacity to turn, move, and respond again when change arrives.

Seen this way, “the perfected person has no self, the spiritual person has no achievement, and the sage has no name” does not eliminate people, action, and names. Having no self means no longer making one fixed self the centre of everything. Having no achievement means not freezing oneself through achievement after acting. Having no name means using names without allowing them to become the final judgement. This is less a defence of a true self untouched by influence than the preservation of life’s capacity to continue changing.

At its end, “Free and Easy Wandering” deliberately offers two “useless” things. The enormous gourd is too heavy to hold water and, when divided into ladles, fits nothing. The tree-of-heaven grows contrary to every carpenter’s rule and is ignored by the woodcutter. Huizi sees only that they fail to meet existing purposes. Zhuangzi asks why the great gourd cannot float upon rivers and lakes, and why the tree cannot be planted in the land of nothing whatever, so that one may wander freely and sleep beneath it. Not every existence must first prove that it has the same kind of use. Being declared useless by one purpose sometimes means only that it can travel somewhere that purpose has never imagined.

Free wandering is therefore not a flight from reality out of nothing, still less the declaration of spiritual freedom behind a closed door. It must still “ride things” and pass through particular conditions; only the “wandering mind” is no longer detained by them. The external world changes me, relationships change me, and every failure and success leaves something behind. Zhuangzi probably does not guarantee that a complete self will survive the change. His question is closer to this: if I already exist within change, why must the preservation of my present self become the measure of every change?

Of course, everything written so far remains inside my head. Yet Zhuangzi also describes Cook Ding cutting up an ox: “I meet it with the spirit and do not look with the eyes; sensory knowledge stops and the spirit moves as it desires.” This sounds like mystical intuition, but beneath it lie Ding’s many years of experience with the knife. Even reducing it to the bodily intuition produced by expertise would still make the passage too narrow. Ding also says, “There are spaces between the joints, while the knife-edge has no thickness; use what has no thickness to enter where there is space.” His knife remains as new after nineteen years not because he controls the ox more completely, but because he does not strike directly against tendons and bones. He travels through the gaps which already exist within the thing. Action no longer depends upon pressing forward with greater force. It makes itself thin and passes through where the thing allows passage.

Fasting of the mind and sitting in forgetfulness are the same. They are not anti-intellectual slogans; they merely prevent existing judgements from occupying every position the moment reality appears. To act “according to what is already so,” one must still encounter things, be limited by them, and be corrected by them. Without practice, so-called movement with the tendency of things may simply follow one’s own imagination. This joins closely with my existing understanding: reality exists independently; people use body, experience, and language to form limited knowledge, then act to encounter it; reality pushes back, allowing knowledge to be corrected again.

Laozi and Zhuangzi have not proved that models should not be built, nor told me to follow feeling from now on. What they add is an answer to what should happen after a model has completed one task.

My default answer was always further improvement. Discover a deviation and update; discover that the update also contains deviation and reflect upon the update. Openness slowly became a task that was never allowed to end: I must remain open, must constantly revise, must guard against becoming rigid. Eventually, even “continue using it without fully believing it” became a self-image that required continual proof. Laozi and Zhuangzi provide no still higher method of remaining open. They merely say that, sometimes, I can stop inspecting for a while.

I am probably incapable of truly stopping the construction of models. Perhaps even this article is another outbreak of the same symptom. But can I at least stop turning every event immediately into a judgement about “what kind of person I am”?

This also explains why the eight characters I finally remembered came from “Responding to Emperors and Kings”:

Neither escort nor welcome; respond without storing.

The original says that “the perfected person’s mind operates like a mirror”: it does not follow what leaves or anticipate what arrives; when something comes, it reflects it, and when it passes, nothing is retained. In conversation, we interpreted this as follows: do not force the past into the present, and do not cover the present with the future in advance; respond when something comes, and stop grasping it once it has passed. Reading the words through past and future is the modern use I have taken from them, not the only interpretation of the original. More directly, the source says: do not follow, do not anticipate; respond upon arrival and retain nothing after departure.

The word “respond” is also important. A mirror does not avoid contact with external things, nor remain cold towards everything. On the contrary, whatever comes is reflected. It avoids injury not by escaping events, but by refusing to detain them permanently in the mind after they have passed. This clearly does not oppose preparation and review. It says only that preparation need not mean living through failure in advance, and review need not preserve one outcome as a permanent identity.

In the end, many events never occur only once inside my head. Before they happen, I simulate them; while they happen, I interpret them; after they happen, I continue writing them into a self-narrative. Eight characters cannot solve these things. They merely offer an order I did not previously know very well: allow the event to arrive, respond to it genuinely, and finally permit it to pass.

Looking back now, Laozi and Zhuangzi seek more than an “admission that knowledge is limited.” Laozi worries that people use names, desire, and coercion to shape the countless things into what they want before those things can unfold. He therefore returns to ziran, allowing things to arise and transform by themselves, acting without possession. Zhuangzi worries that people become trapped in one position by prejudice, identity, and achievement. He therefore seeks not merely to loosen judgement, but to “wander,” allowing the mind to continue moving with the changes of things.

One says: do not seize the countless things and turn them into mine. The other says: do not seize myself and turn me into a thing. The two finally meet in refusing to let what has already formed block the life still occurring.

Non-action cannot excuse procrastination; the equality of things cannot abolish truth, falsehood, and responsibility; dependence upon nothing cannot erase the real limits imposed by resources, institutions, and other people. If I cannot solve a problem, that means I genuinely cannot solve it now. If I injure someone, I remain responsible for the consequences. Laozi and Zhuangzi remove only the additional layer added too rapidly afterwards: I cannot solve this problem, therefore my complete life is a failure; I did not control this event, therefore something must be wrong with the world.

Knowledge is meant to participate in reality, not replace it. Once used, it can sometimes be placed to one side.

entry.title: Everyone, Feel
entry.content:
I

I was cleaning my computer today and opened the directory where WeChat stores its files. It has grown beyond 120 gigabytes.

I worked through material from the end of 2024 to the present: an application for an undergraduate innovation project, analogue-electronics experiments, OpenAMP, drones, mathematical modeling, plans for the radio station, an MCM paper, a venue application for the Audio-Visual Evening, and the recent annotation tool. Between them lay piles of reimbursement documents, software archives, and material received from people I no longer remember. A single document often appeared in more than ten versions, which is, to be fair, exactly what one expects from a WeChat folder. Then I suddenly realized that I had once done a great many things.

In my memory, the innovation project had been reduced to its final acceptance; the integrated-circuit contest to a second prize in North China; the radio station to the title of station assistant, a collection of work, and a failed relationship; the MCM to an Honorable Mention. How the work was actually done, who did it with me, what we said along the way, and which absurd problems appeared—without the files, none of this would have occurred to me.

Only when I saw the drone documents did I remember that none of us knew how to obtain the equipment. We were debating whether to buy it ourselves, until we finally asked the teacher and learned that it could be borrowed. Reimbursement appears today as a single amount of money. At the time, the explanatory attachment alone passed through more than twenty versions.

All of that was eventually summarized in one sentence: I once worked on a drone-related project and never wanted to touch one again.

Some experiences did not even leave a sentence behind. Walking around Singapore with classmates, eating with a teacher, staying up late to write Tetris with GPT, recording A Cruel Angel’s Thesis, and attending my first interview must all have carried specific feelings. Yet if I do not deliberately return to them, “must have” is the most I can say. The feelings themselves are gradually fading.

Perhaps the problem is not that nothing happened during my three university years. The problem is that I did not preserve the raw data. That makes time appear to have passed impossibly quickly, leaving me with the thought that I have done nothing. In reality, I have done quite a lot.

Taking the thought further, my present self is continuous with the person I was a year ago, but we are not entirely the same person. His physical condition, attention, relationships, and circumstances have passed away. What I can now reach consists of several files, some indistinct memories, and a large body of explanations formed afterwards. The present judgment I make of him is therefore another lossy model. The problem is that I never seemed to admit the loss.

II

I am accustomed to compressing an experience into an indicator.

A competition becomes its prize; a project becomes its final acceptance; a course becomes its score; a relationship becomes a theory about intimacy and the self. Once the compression is complete, my mind concludes that the important part has been extracted and that the details no longer need to be preserved. This procedure is not wholly useless. Learning itself requires compression. After a project, one knows how to divide requirements, write a report, and adjust equipment, so the next similar task becomes easier. If every action required us to replay the whole of our original experience, we would probably accomplish nothing. The trouble is that after compressing it, I deleted the source file.

I retained only “what I learned,” not “how I lived through it.” Later, the ability came to seem natural, while the indicator itself no longer looked impressive. The entire experience was compressed once more into “I did not really do anything.”

Consider a second prize in North China. I was probably pleased when I first received it. Later, after seeing national prizes and people far more capable than I was, I looked back and decided that a regional second prize was nothing remarkable. The award had not changed; its frame of reference had. In the end, I used the standards of the present to overwrite the whole experience of the past and reached the conclusion that the period had produced no result. The conclusion may not be entirely wrong. How much it distorts, heaven knows.

Those particular afternoons within the project—several people in a laboratory studying an instrument nobody knew how to use, the first successful stream of data, the boredom of writing the report, the desire to swear while completing reimbursement—none of them is contained in the phrase “second prize.” Yet when I later judged the past, those three Chinese characters were all that remained in my hand. What judgment could possibly follow? None, except the feeling that I had done nothing.

III

This is also connected to the way I have long evaluated myself: I am always concerned with what kind of person I am at the present moment.

Am I capable? Have I grown? Am I stronger than before? Can what I am doing prove who I am? Will I become someone more impressive? It appears that I am attending to the present. In reality, I am continuously stepping aside to observe it and turning it into a report about myself. The thing itself readily disappears, leaving only the question, “What does this mean about me?”

This is the same problem of attachment to the self that I discussed in the essay on Buddhism. Whatever happens must immediately be brought back to me: can it prove me, does it deny me, and what sort of person am I after all?

I once thought that I was living in the present. Now, perhaps I was not. To live in the present must at least require the thing before one’s eyes to appear. My actual procedure was to cover an event with a judgment about myself the instant it occurred. Before it had time to become experience, it had already become material.

That movement probably runs in the opposite direction from phenomenology. Of course, by phenomenology I do not mean that a person can preserve perfectly pure raw data. The moment attention begins, and the moment language begins, experience has already been selected and organized. No absolute scene exists independently of body, language, and memory.

IV

What deserves still greater caution is that I do not merely forget the past. I then use the fragments left after forgetting to put the past on trial.

My earlier self finishes a project; I now say that it contained little technical substance. He feels happy about something; I now say that the award did not count for much. He genuinely felt certain things within a relationship; I can now explain all of it through attachment, need, projection, and the desire to prove himself.

Each explanation may be partly correct. But seeing a person’s weaknesses does not mean that weakness is all they possess; seeing their strengths does not mean that strength is all they possess. Likewise, knowing which problem remained after an experience does not mean that the entire experience consisted of that problem. Between the experience and the judgment stands the person I am now.

My present anxiety, aims, standards, and expectations of the future all enter my judgment of the past. Perhaps I think my earlier progress was too slow merely because I now need to prepare for the postgraduate entrance examination. Perhaps I find an award insufficient because the comparison has changed. Perhaps I regard my former self as childish simply because I now know things he did not.

The person I was was certainly not perfect. He skipped classes, gave up on things, behaved like an idiot, and wasted a great deal of time. Respecting experience does not require me to beautify the past. But he was not an outdated firmware release awaiting the upgrade that produced me. He saw what his circumstances allowed him to see, failed to know what they did not allow him to know, and felt certain things that I can no longer feel. I may analyse him, but possession of the later plot does not naturally give me greater authority to define the life he lived.

If the first premise is true—if everyone has the right to feel the world from within their own experience—then my former self also counts as a person.

He did not exist merely to manufacture the person I am today.

V

What felt truly strange while browsing the files was not the discovery that I had secretly been impressive and completed so many things.

If I merely reorganize the attachments into a portfolio, list more than a year of life as a dozen projects, and conclude that “I am actually not bad,” the underlying logic remains unchanged. I had too few indicators before; now I have more.

The real question is why I permit an experience to have meaning only after it has been converted into an indicator. An experience does not cease to have occurred merely because it produced no ability. A person cannot consist only of the part that can be placed in a summary or résumé. Or perhaps a person ought to remain sensitive and capable of feeling the world more fully. Though, now that I look at it, is this not a fairly common problem for an INTP—thinking so much that feeling becomes difficult?

Put differently, if I preserve only what can explain “who I am,” what survives may not be me at all. It may be a manual telling other people how I wish to be understood. This is what I now need to watch: while continually attempting to construct a self, I may have spent all this time deleting it.

VI

What, then, should come next?

I can begin by occasionally recording two minutes of audio: one scene from the day, one sentence someone actually said, and an approximate account of what my body felt at the time. A record of the good life, perhaps—like the day I happened to find a friend sitting on a garden bench, recording what had happened to him.

Gather slightly more information. Use one indicator less often to summarize an entire period of life. Before reaching a conclusion, admit that I may already have forgotten a great deal. Perhaps these are enough to begin with.

As for the tones of voice from the past that were never preserved, I probably cannot recover them.

entry.title: The Matou Family and Feminism
entry.content:
I

A few days ago, while talking about Fate, I originally intended only to analyse Shinji and Sakura. Somehow, however, the conversation eventually turned to feminism.

There is no need to recount the plot here. Nor is this essay intended to put the characters on trial once more under the authority of a particular theory. What truly concerned me was that, as the conversation proceeded, a problem emerged in my former understanding of “agency.”

I used to believe that possessing agency meant, roughly speaking, being able to form one’s own judgement, act on it, and then take responsibility for the consequences. Conversely, if a person always depended on others, waited for others to make decisions, and lacked the ability to bear the consequences, I would regard that person’s agency as incomplete.

There is some truth in this understanding. If people remain unable to form their own judgement or turn it into action, they will indeed find it difficult to take charge of their lives.

Yet if this line of reasoning is carried further, it produces another conclusion: those who are more capable and independent appear more like subjects, whereas those who are weak, dependent, or temporarily unable to act appear more like objects. It may eventually suggest that the weaker a person is, the more entitled others are to define that person.

This is plainly wrong.

Agency actually contains two different elements. One is the status of being a subject: everyone should have the right to live according to their own feelings, judgements, and purposes. The other is the capacity to act as a subject: whether a person in fact possesses the resources and abilities required to turn those things into action.

Such capacity varies with education, physical condition, economic circumstances, and personal experience, and it may gradually develop. Yet the status of being a subject should not be granted only after someone has proved strong enough. To put it plainly, no one should have to pass an examination before earning the right to be themselves.

II

This brings us to what Simone de Beauvoir called the “second sex.”

The second sex does not mean that a person is weak, dependent, or indecisive, nor is it a classification of personality. It describes a condition in which one group cannot define itself primarily on its own terms, but is persistently defined according to the needs and perspectives of another group.

Men are treated as human beings in general and as agents of action, while women are often viewed first as wives, mothers, caregivers, objects of desire, or people whose worth depends on whether they satisfy accepted standards of femininity. A woman may certainly be highly capable and have a career of her own, yet others may still place her in these roles before they attempt to understand her.

Women occupy the position of the second sex, therefore, not because they are naturally weaker, but because male experience is more readily treated as the default form of human experience, while women are regarded as a different kind of person defined in relation to men.

This idea also connects with the questions of knowledge that I discussed before.

The first premise is that all people possess equal personal standing. Our lives are of roughly equal duration, and each of us perceives the world through our own body and experience. No one is born as an attachment to someone else.

The second premise is that one person can never know another completely. You may know what a bird is called and what it looks like, but an actual bird will not grow inside your mind. What it has experienced and how it perceives the surrounding world do not become yours merely because you have learned its name.

The same is even more true of human relationships. I may not know what a particular friend is thinking at this very moment, much less infer what a woman thinks from a general claim about “what women are like.” The differences among women are certainly no smaller than those between men and women.

Our judgements of others will therefore always contain our own prejudices, experiences, and assumptions. At times, the distorted part may even exceed the part that corresponds to reality.

Feminism, however, draws attention to another fact: not everyone’s distortion produces consequences of equal weight.

If one person’s views are more likely to become social standards, family rules, or institutional requirements, that person’s partial understanding is no longer merely a private misunderstanding. It begins to prescribe how others ought to live. The other person must not only endure being misunderstood, but may also have to reshape their life in accordance with that misunderstanding.

The question, then, is not simply that “people are liable to misjudge one another.” We must also ask whose view is more likely to be accepted as the correct answer, and who is forced to explain repeatedly that they are not the person others imagine them to be.

III

This is also where the gaze begins.

At first, other people evaluate me. Gradually, I learn to evaluate myself by their standards. In the end, even when no one is standing nearby, I automatically imagine how they would see me.

Women face judgements concerning appearance, age, the body, and gender roles. Men face another set of demands: they must succeed, remain strong, conceal vulnerability, and accept that income and academic credentials determine their worth.

A résumé, ability, appearance, and a partner’s approval are not unreal. Examination results affect educational opportunities, and whether another person is willing to continue a relationship with me is also genuine feedback. The problem is that I can easily turn each piece of information into a final verdict.

An examination failure then means not merely that I performed poorly on this occasion, but that I am fundamentally incapable. If someone does not choose me, it means not merely that she has made her own decision, but that I am unworthy of love. If one of my peers advances faster than I do, it means not merely that he is currently more successful, but that I have already fallen behind.

People outside me do not even need to say these things. I am already capable of finishing the speech on their behalf.

Therefore, whenever a powerful self-judgement arises, I need to ask not only whether it is correct, but also where it came from. Who taught me this standard? In what environment is it useful? Do I genuinely accept it? If I refuse to live by it, what will I lose?

This does not mean that we should ignore external evaluation. Anyone who completely disregards feedback from reality may simply be adopting another form of self-isolation. External evaluation should enter our judgement as information; it should not replace our judgement altogether.

IV

There is another issue: recognising that everyone has the status of a subject does not mean that everyone possesses the same practical range of choices.

A person may know inwardly that they are unwilling, yet lack sufficient money, secure accommodation, or anyone to whom they can turn for help. If refusal will bring punishment and departure will immediately threaten survival, the advice that “you should bravely be yourself” does little to increase that person’s freedom. Agency therefore requires more than independent thoughts inside the mind; it also depends on material conditions.

At the very least, people need an opportunity to speak, the right to say “no,” the possibility of leaving, and basic physical safety and resources for living. A failure to resist does not directly prove consent, and dependence on others does not prove that dependence is part of one’s nature. This also corrects my former fondness for speaking about “relying on oneself.”

People must, of course, learn to take responsibility for their own lives rather than handing all their emotions and choices over to others. Yet no one truly relies on themselves alone. The judgements a person can form today depend on conditions provided by education, language, family, friends, and society. We need care when we fall ill, may need assistance after failure, and must cooperate with others when undertaking anything complex.

Accepting help does not mean surrendering one’s authority to decide, and caring for another person does not grant us the right to decide on their behalf.

Dependence itself is not the problem. More important questions are whether such dependence can be acknowledged, whether care is always imposed upon the same person, whether help may be refused, and whether those who receive help must repay it with obedience.

V

The implications for intimate relationships are direct.

My affection for someone may be genuine. I may truly be moved by her experience and wish to do something for her. Yet these facts explain only why I act; they do not establish an obligation on her part to accept my action. My desire does not automatically create another person’s duty, and my efforts do not automatically purchase the right to control. Even if my judgement is indeed more accurate, the person who must bear the consequences should still decide how to live. This also relates to what I previously called a “calling.”

I once argued that people sometimes act not because they lack something, but because a particular person or object first attracts them: they perceive its value and become willing to move towards it. I still accept this judgement. But a calling is an experience that occurs within me; it cannot express consent on behalf of the other person. She may genuinely make me feel that I should approach her, and she may genuinely have no need of me. Both may be true at once.

Recognising another person as a subject, therefore, means more than verbally declaring that everyone is equal. In practice, it means allowing others to overturn my interpretation of them, to reject my advice, and even to refuse my concern.

If help continues only on the condition that the recipient obeys, it contains at least one element besides assistance: my desire to have my judgement proved correct.

I have indeed behaved in this way. When I offered advice to friends and they did not follow it, I would feel that my time had been wasted, or that they had failed to recognise my value. Seen from my present perspective, this still amounted to using another person’s actions to evaluate myself.

They may understand perfectly and still choose not to act. Their choice of a different path does not amount to a rejection of me as a person.

VI

Viewed in this way, feminism is more than an effort to “secure certain rights for women.”

Beginning from the historical condition in which women have long been treated as dependants and as the Other, feminism has developed methods for analysing relations of power between people. It asks, for instance, who possesses the authority to define, who is treated as the default subject, who controls the body, who bears the burden of care, and how a social standard enters an individual’s understanding of themselves.

These methods can certainly be used to analyse men as well. Men may likewise be governed by demands for success, strength, and emotional invulnerability, and they may also be objectified or treated merely as instruments in particular relationships.

Yet the fact that these methods can be applied to everyone does not mean that women are merely an interchangeable shell.

Feminism begins with women because women have suffered, and in many institutions and everyday relationships continue to suffer, specific forms of inequality. If this history is removed entirely and all that remains is the statement that “everyone should possess agency,” the original problem may easily become invisible once again. A theory that begins with the actual conditions of workers may help everyone understand alienated labour, but this does not make workers an arbitrary example.

Of course, some people online use feminism as a weapon of identity. Some invoke structural oppression to explain everything; some demand their own rights while refusing to recognise the boundaries of others; and some use a handful of terms to pass summary judgement on all men or all women. Such behaviour deserves criticism.

Online platforms, however, naturally prefer content that is emotionally intense and easy to divide into opposing camps. Encountering many extreme examples does not mean that the entire body of theory consists of nothing else. At the very least, we should distinguish material circumstances, theoretical tools, patterns of collective action, and the foolish conduct of particular individuals. Otherwise, in opposing the replacement of judgement with labels, I may end up possessing nothing but another label myself.

VII

My present understanding of agency has probably acquired the half that it previously lacked.

A subject needs to form judgements, take action, and bear responsibility for what follows. None of that is wrong. Yet agency concerns not only “what I am able to do,” but also my recognition that others possess judgements of their own and that my interpretation can never substitute for their experience.

The more capable a person becomes, the less entitled they are to assume that seeing more naturally gives them greater authority to decide for others. Nor does temporary weakness deprive anyone of the right to refuse or to define themselves.

When I come to know a person in the future, therefore, I cannot ask only whether what they display is a strength or a weakness. Someone who appears weak before me may have revealed only a small part of themselves; someone who appears strong is not necessarily free from dependence or fear. Seeing a strength does not mean that strength is all they possess, and seeing a weakness does not mean that weakness is the whole person.

Moreover, I myself stand between what I see and the person I judge.

My expectations of them, my past experience, and my emotions at that moment all enter the judgement. What I can do is gather as much information as possible, remain willing to hear how they explain themselves, and take responsibility for my conclusions. Misjudgement can never be eliminated completely, but the claim that “people can never truly understand one another” does not entitle me to speak carelessly and then blame the limitations of knowledge.

I originally intended only to discuss Fate, yet the conversation somehow turned here. Looking back, what makes a work genuinely interesting may not be limited to the ending each character receives. It can reveal that a standard of judgement we have long relied upon is itself defective.

I used to ask first: Who is stronger? Who sees more clearly? Who ought to take responsibility for their own life?

Now I must add another question:

Who is defining whom?

This essay is neither a history of feminism nor an attempt to explain every question of gender and intimacy through a single theory. For verification of Beauvoir’s concept of “woman as the Other,” I referred to:

  • Simone de Beauvoir — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

entry.title: Buddhism
entry.content:
I

Over the past two days, I have learned something about Buddhism. It is rather interesting.

My initial understanding was that Buddhism mainly does several things: it explains how suffering arises, discusses why the world and human beings are constantly changing, and then proposes a practical method of training through discipline, concentration, and wisdom. It develops a complete body of theory around a fairly clear question, and actual methods genuinely follow the theory. This makes it appear more complete than many of the philosophies I have encountered so far.

That description is broadly correct, although certain parts remain insufficiently precise.

Before discussing Buddhism, I can first explain how I now regard religion. I remain an atheist and have no interest in converting to any religion. Yet religion does not merely answer whether a god exists. Problems now handled separately by science, law, philosophy, and psychology were often treated together by ancient religions. Religion explained where the world came from and why people suffer; it prescribed what people ought to do; and through ritual, discipline, and community, it brought these ideas into everyday life.

This obviously creates serious problems. When one body of theory possesses final authority over facts, morality, and social order at the same time, it can easily become something that cannot be questioned. Nevertheless, religion has seriously considered questions that modern people still cannot avoid: why should a person restrain desire, how should suffering be endured, why does an individual owe responsibility to others, and why should people continue living when they know they will die?

Christianity is particularly concerned with sin, love, forgiveness, and salvation. Islam strongly emphasises that humanity is not the centre of the world and that power and wealth are accompanied by responsibility. The starting point of Buddhism is more direct:

If people clearly desire happiness, why do they continue to suffer?

II

The most basic structure of Buddhism is the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

In simple terms, Buddhism first recognises that human life contains suffering. It then explains that suffering does not arise from nothing, but has particular causes. Since suffering depends upon causes, it may cease when those causes cease. Finally, Buddhism proposes a practical path of cultivation.

Buddhism therefore does not merely explain suffering. Its purpose is to identify the process through which suffering arises and then find a way to stop that process.

Nor should “suffering” be understood simply as pain, poverty, and heartbreak. A person who obtains something desired will naturally feel happy; Buddhism does not claim that all such happiness is false. The problem is that everything obtained under particular conditions will change. Examination results change, bodies change, other people’s opinions of me change, and relationships change as well.

These things are not wrong in themselves, nor is the desire for them necessarily wrong. What most readily creates suffering is the hope that they will remain exactly as they are forever and continue to prove one’s worth.

A good examination result, for instance, is certainly worth celebrating. But if that result is not merely an outcome and must also prove that I am intelligent, excellent, and valuable, then the next time I cannot solve a problem, I will no longer face only one problem. Being liked also makes me happy. Yet if her affection must continually prove that I deserve love, one moment of coldness may be interpreted as a rejection of my complete person.

Thus, when Buddhism speaks of impermanence, it does not merely mean that everything eventually disappears. More importantly, everything changes within conditions and cannot provide a permanent guarantee.

Dependent origination makes the same point. A thing exists in its present form through many conditions. A tree depends upon a seed, soil, water, sunlight, and time. A person likewise depends upon a body, memories, family, language, social relationships, and previous experience. There is not first a completely independent person who then happens to be influenced by the outside world. Those supposedly external conditions already participate in forming the person.

At first, I wanted to understand dependent origination as a Markov process, but later discovered that the comparison cannot be made directly. The Markov property requires the current state to contain all effective information through which the past influences the future, whereas Buddhist ideas of karma, habitual tendencies, and seeds emphasise precisely that what the past leaves behind continues to affect the present. Describing dependent origination as a dynamic causal relationship is acceptable. Declaring that it simply is Markovian would amount to forcing an unfamiliar idea into the ancestry of a familiar concept.

III

When impermanence and dependent origination are applied to the human being, they lead to non-self.

Non-self does not claim that human beings do not exist, nor that, since there is no self, nothing matters. A person clearly possesses a body, memories, and a relatively stable character, and remains responsible for previous actions. Buddhism denies something else: whether, behind these continuously changing bodies, feelings, memories, and forms of consciousness, there really exists a completely independent and permanently unchanging self.

At least in experience, we cannot find it.

The person I was in childhood, the person I was while in love, and the person now writing this article certainly possess continuity, but they are not entirely the same thing. The body changes, memories are reinterpreted, and standards of judgement shift. I may continue using the name “I” to summarise them, but the constancy of the name does not prove that an identical core exists from beginning to end.

This closely resembles my earlier ideas about cognition.

Human knowledge of the world is always limited. You can know the name and appearance of a bird and study its habits, but the bird itself will never grow inside your mind. What you know is the understanding you have constructed from it, not the whole bird.

The same is true when people understand themselves. “I am intelligent,” “I am a failure,” and “I am a person without the ability to act” all arise from part of one’s experience, mixed with the emotions of the moment, other people’s judgements, and personal interpretation. They may identify something real, but they can never equal the complete person.

What Buddhism calls attachment to appearances probably means treating such partial and temporary knowledge as the fixed essence of a thing. One failure becomes “I am a failure”; one person who hurt me becomes “his whole being is evil”; not being chosen becomes “I do not deserve love.” The event occurred only once, but after interpretation it is written into a self that appears never to change.

Attachment to self is not simply selfishness. It is closer to the impulse to drag every event immediately back to “what does this mean for me?” Can this prove me? Is this denying me? What might I lose? What do other people think of me now? Attachment constructs a perfect image of the self, but this is only the self in one’s own eyes and differs from the real person. If, in order to protect what I think I should be, I ignore what I actually am and overlook the condition of non-self, I become distressed, twisted, awkward, and selfish.

People certainly need to protect themselves and make judgements about their own lives. The problem is that, if every event can ultimately become only material for self-evaluation, a person will find it difficult to see the things and people immediately before him.

IV

At this point, the process through which suffering arises becomes relatively clear.

First, an event occurs and the body produces a feeling. A person instinctively wishes to hold onto pleasant feelings and drive unpleasant ones away. Next comes an interpretation, and finally the interpretation becomes a judgement about the self.

Suppose I answer one problem incorrectly. The fact is merely that I could not solve this problem. My body first becomes irritated. Then my mind moves to the postgraduate entrance examination, to previous failures, and to whether I will accomplish nothing in the future. A few minutes later, the problem remains the same, but I have almost finished writing the conclusion to my entire life.

Buddhism does not demand that the discomfort in the first step never appear. The body reacts, and loss genuinely hurts. It attempts to deal with what is continuously added afterwards: I must escape this feeling immediately; I must prove that I am not a failure; this failure means I will never succeed.

Karma may also be understood from this point.

It need not first be imagined as an account book somewhere in the universe, according to which a bad act must eventually receive punishment. A more direct understanding is that every intentional act produces consequences and also changes which actions will be easier to perform in the future.

If anxiety makes me avoid something once, I feel slightly better in the short term and become more likely to avoid it when anxiety returns. If, whenever I cannot solve a problem, I begin studying a new field, then learning new things can gradually become an exceptionally sophisticated form of escape. Conversely, if an emotion arises and I do not immediately act upon it, pausing will become slightly easier next time.

A person does not first acquire a fixed character and then act. Much of what we call character is the result left by repeated actions.

V

This brings us to discipline, concentration, and wisdom.

Discipline does not merely suppress desire or produce a list of everything forbidden. It first asks people to reduce actions which they already know will make themselves and others more confused. Do not attack someone immediately when emotion rises; do not revise your complete life plan as soon as anxiety appears; when you want to escape, do not casually open a new topic. These actions seem ordinary, but they at least prevent suffering from continuing to spread through behaviour.

Concentration mainly concerns attention. The mind produces all kinds of thoughts, and that cannot be avoided. The problem is that we often treat every thought as a command that must be executed. While solving a problem, I suddenly think of my ex-girlfriend, then of what will happen if I fail the examination, then of the relationship between Buddhism and Yogācāra, then of whether I should start a new project—and I run after each thought.

Concentration does not mean the permanent absence of distracting thoughts. It means noticing that you have wandered and returning.

Wisdom, likewise, is not the ability to recite impermanence, dependent origination, and non-self. Genuine wisdom should occur when an event arises: what am I feeling now, what are the facts, and what interpretation have I added? Knowing that “failure” is only a judgement does not mean that, when I answer a problem incorrectly, I can really see how that judgement is appearing.

The most interesting aspect of discipline, concentration, and wisdom is therefore their refusal to believe that understanding alone changes a person.

This point is well suited to criticising me. I have written many articles about action, cognition, and self-analysis. Much of what they say is perfectly sound, and then the things I cannot do remain undone. Knowing a sentence is not the same as genuine change in emotion, attention, and action.

Buddhism does not merely give me another, more complete explanation. It says that explanation is not enough; I must practise.

VI

What, then, do these ideas actually teach me?

The first point is that they change the question I used to ask.

I often wondered how to prove my value. Results, ability, relationships, and work could all become evidence. If the proof was insufficient, I continued adding to it. Eventually, even the construction of a philosophical system could become one more element in proving that I really was capable of thought.

Buddhism does not provide a stronger proof. It asks instead: why must there be one permanently valid proof at all?

The postgraduate entrance examination, a project, and affection for another person may all be important, and failure has real consequences. Yet none of them alone can state everything I am, and no result can permanently guarantee that I will never become uncertain again.

The second point is that Buddhism makes me reconsider the statement that “a model is not reality.”

Previously, my principal concern was how much error human knowledge contains, how more information may be obtained, and how misjudgement may be reduced. Buddhism adds another layer: even when people know that their understanding is limited, they still hold tightly to a particular judgement because it maintains a stable self.

The question is therefore not merely whether the model is accurate, but why I need so badly for it to be true.

The third point is its emphasis upon action.

Discipline, concentration, and wisdom show that human understanding does not exist only in language. A person may say that others should be respected, yet become angry immediately upon rejection. He may know that failing to solve one problem does not equal failure in life, yet still escape at once when facing it. Such physical and behavioural responses come closer to what he presently and genuinely believes.

The final point, and the one I most need to guard against, is that failure can become an attachment to self, but so can growth, ideals, helping other people, and the pursuit of truth.

Do I want to accomplish something because the thing itself is worthwhile, or because I need a stronger version of myself to prove that my present life has not been wasted? In many cases both are present, and separating them completely would be unrealistic.

Buddhism offers no formula for the judgement. It merely reminds me not to assume that a nobler-sounding goal must therefore contain no attachment.

VII

I will not become a Buddhist because of this.

I can accept the explanations that impermanence, dependent origination, non-self, and discipline-concentration-wisdom offer for real experience, and I am willing to use them in examining my life. Rebirth, karmic retribution, and nirvana as a religious cosmology, however, require additional beliefs and arguments. Non-self does not automatically prove that a person continues in some form after death; nor does the resemblance between dependent origination and certain concepts in modern science turn it directly into a scientific conclusion.

Nor do I like reducing Buddhism to “take things lightly and accept whatever fate brings.” Letting go does not mean wanting nothing, still less remaining calm and doing nothing when confronted with injustice and pain. Outcomes still matter, responsibility remains, and harm suffered by another person does not automatically disappear because all things are empty.

For me, the most useful part of Buddhism is probably that it makes me ask less often “how does this prove me?” and look more closely at what the thing itself is; that it makes me less likely to turn a momentary feeling into a permanent conclusion, or to assume that explaining a principle means I have already changed.

Of course, this article has explained the principles once again.

Whether I can practise them, I do not know.

For now, solve the problems.

This article mainly understands Buddhism as a system of thought and practice rather than offering a survey of Buddhist history or schools. Concepts were checked against:

  • Buddha — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
  • Nāgārjuna — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
  • Yogācāra — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

entry.title: Outside the Map: ZHW's Framework of Thought v3
entry.content:
Recently, I have once again talked about a great many things.

The conversation moved from Nietzsche to Hesse, from Kant to Wittgenstein, and from Bourbaki to the question of how calculus should be learned. Eventually, it turned toward AI, embodied intelligence, finance, and the allocation of assets in one’s life. As we talked, yet another framework gradually took shape.

This is, of course, entirely characteristic of me. Whenever I cannot get something done in real life, what I do best is not to finish it at once, but to take two steps back and investigate “why I cannot get it done.” By the end of the investigation, the original task is still sitting there, now accompanied by an additional theory of action, personality, and civilization.

There is that damned habit again.

That said, these reflections have not been entirely useless. Over the past year, they have indeed helped me find my way out of certain forms of confusion. Yet in organizing them again, I can no longer pretend that I have constructed some magnificent system. What I am doing is more like picking up the parts that remained intact after several collisions with reality and asking whether they can be assembled into a machine that will work for the time being.

This article, too, was organized together with AI. I supplied the experiences, judgments, and half-finished sentences that kept circling back on themselves; it helped me retrieve old articles, broaden the range of references, supplement my philosophical knowledge, reconcile contradictions, and complete the structure. I have no intention of pretending that every sentence was independently forced out of my head at a desk. As for Kant, Nietzsche, phenomenology, Levinas, Arendt, and the other names mentioned here, I still know them mainly through introductions, reference materials, and conversations. I owe the original texts a considerable debt.

I

Why call this piece Outside the Map?

At first, I was still thinking of one of those very long titles—something like an embodied, socialized, open, practical theory of modeling. It nearly stuffed every possible patch into the title, as though the omission of a single qualification would allow the whole framework to run wild and commit crimes. Then I thought: forget it. I am tired.

I suppose it is called Outside the Map because, for the past few years, I have constantly been drawing maps. When studying mathematics, I draw maps of knowledge; when working on projects, I draw system diagrams. The human mind certainly needs to do this. Otherwise, how could it contain the overwhelming amount of information outside itself? We cannot place a bird, unchanged and complete, inside our minds. We can only watch it fly past several times, hear a few of its calls, and bind these impressions together with a name. Formulas work this way, theories work this way, and so do words such as “love,” “success,” “good person,” and “failure.”

My v1 was largely about this point: the world is too vast, so human beings can only compress it. Once it has been compressed, however, we must also know how to unfold it—where a conclusion came from and under what conditions it will cease to work. From there grew the ideas of the absent observer, the unity of knowledge and action, recursive self-reference, and so forth.

Yet when the map was nearly complete, one thing had still never been drawn into it: why I should set out at all.

A model can tell me how to travel more rationally, but it cannot, by itself, tell me which road is worth taking. Thus v2 began to speak of a “calling”: some things do not attract me because I lack something and wish to fill the gap. Rather, they first light up in the world, and I am drawn toward them. A person, a formula, a sea breeze, or a particular problem may all work in this way.

That said, the word calling makes it far too easy to dramatize myself. Being attracted is real, but it does not prove that the direction is correct. Loving someone is real, but it does not require that person to love me in return. If every sudden passion is described as a call from destiny, then the word is merely a costume placed over impulse.

Therefore, outside the map has another meaning as well: however complete the map may seem, what lies outside it will speak for itself. I will get problems wrong. I will be stopped by questions during a project defense. My body will refuse to continue when it can no longer endure the strain. Other people, when they believe I have misunderstood them, will say, “That is not how it is.” Reality does not merely hide beyond the model and wait to be known; it pushes back.

Sometimes it hurts quite a lot.

II

I still believe that human beings understand the world by building models.

There is probably no need to make this sound profound. Without compressing information, the brain could not survive. Society works in the same way. Money, academic credentials, law, occupational titles, and the numbers displayed on platforms are all symbols and rules created by human beings; yet being constructed does not make them unreal. Money is a human convention, but without it one may still find it impossible to move. A diploma is a piece of paper, but the doors it opens and closes genuinely exist.

When I first realized that these things had been constructed, I was admittedly excited. It was as though I had glimpsed the backstage of civilization while everyone else was still pressing buttons at random on the front end. For no good reason, this insight even produced a certain arrogant sense of superiority. Looking back, that was somewhat ridiculous. Seeing the rules does not mean that one has escaped them. I still have to take examinations, still care about other people’s opinions, and still live within language. Even the claim “I am someone who has seen through the rules” is merely another role.

This leads to another problem: explaining something does not mean explaining it away.

Love may be discussed in terms of hormones, attachment, projection, and social scripts. Music may be explained through harmony, rhythm, and the nervous system. Photography may be described as the organization of attention through composition. These explanations are probably correct. Yet a mechanism answers how something happens; it cannot, on its own, decide whether that thing is worthwhile.

I used to possess a rather strange obsession with purity. Whenever I discovered interests, hormones, or personal needs behind an emotion, I felt that the emotion had become impure. Yet human things are mixed together from the beginning. Taking a machine apart and identifying several components does not prove that the original machine never existed.

III

Models create another problem. I tend to imagine that the essence of a person is a brain piloting a giant robot: the outside world first delivers a clean set of data, the brain analyzes it from a control room, and the body finally carries out its orders. In this picture, the brain becomes far too large and the body far too small.

Recently, however, I have increasingly felt that the body has already taken part in cognition. It simply knows the world through heartbeats, exhaustion, vigilance, and the impulse to flee—or, to use different terms, through somatic responses and happiness.

Photography offers an example. Afterwards, I can certainly talk about the subject, light and shadow, foreground and background, and visual guidance. Yet when I truly encounter an image worth recording, my eyes have often stopped before any theory arrives to explain why.

I have not studied phenomenology seriously, but its present value to me is probably that it tells me not to rush. Before asking what an event signifies, I should first examine what actually happened: what I saw, what my body felt, and which statements were added later merely to make the story appear coherent.

Of course, this does not mean that the body is always more reliable than reason. Hunger makes me want to eat, fear of failure makes me want to run away, and at one in the morning I may believe that I can scroll on my phone a little longer. None of these impulses should automatically be obeyed.

Then there is learning.

I have always liked to understand things from their underlying structures, and I once regarded this as one of my more advanced virtues. Learning calculus, in my view, was not a matter of memorizing formulas but of understanding how human beings compress relations that exist throughout the world. Looking at photography did not mean memorizing the rule of thirds, but deriving composition from attention and emotion. This approach is useful. Nevertheless, my transcripts over the past few years have repeatedly proved that being able to explain a course quite clearly does not mean being able to answer its examination questions.

The Bourbaki school organized mathematics beautifully; the completed structure is almost a work of art made from human intelligence. Yet the structure of a finished product is not necessarily the road along which a person should learn it. We would not require a child to study structural mechanics before learning to walk. Genuine learning still requires us to observe examples, identify patterns, formalize them, return to exercises, make mistakes, and revise our understanding. Abstraction is not the problem. The problem arises when one cannot return from abstraction.

AI magnifies this problem. I utter half a sentence, and it can complete an entire system. I read the result and think, yes, yes—damn it, that is exactly what I wanted to say. But this proves only that I recognize the idea. It does not prove that I can write it again on my own, still less that I will act on it when an actual situation arises.

IV

At this point, I still have to draw a diagram. Otherwise, I would seem to have betrayed my major.

The greatest difference between this diagram and my earlier ones is that it does not portray cognition as an assembly line in which the outside world provides input, the brain performs calculations, and a result is then sent outward.

Reality, institutions, and other people first define part of the situation. The body enters that situation carrying memories, habits, and alarms from the past. Experience and value become apparent within it. Language and social categories help me organize them, though this organization is inevitably lossy. Models and skills are then formed, and I use them to act, make commitments, and produce consequences.

In the end, consequences and feedback emerge. They may support the original judgment, or they may smash it to pieces. In either case, reality is not noise outside the system, but the signal that enables the system to continue updating itself. Put differently, the system exists to produce sound consequences—consequences for which someone must assume responsibility and which make a real difference to the world.

As for AI, it resembles an external graphics card attached between language and models. It can accelerate organization, generation, and comparison, and at times its power is frightening. Yet it has not acquired a body on my behalf, nor has it made other people consent to my interpretations. It is simply an extraordinarily powerful monster produced by the realm of symbols.

V

Now for other people.

I particularly enjoy understanding others—or, more precisely, I enjoy believing that I understand them. Why is this person angry? What do they truly need? Why has a relationship changed from intimacy into exhaustion? As long as I can draw a model, I feel somewhat reassured, as though human relationships could finally be debugged.

Yet “I understand you” can sometimes be a rather arrogant statement. If everything the other person does can be explained by me, and even her objection that I have misunderstood her can be further interpreted as evidence that she has not recognized her own true needs, then this is no longer understanding. It is merely the use of a theory to silence her.

I have not read much Levinas either. For now, what I know can be condensed into one sentence: another person is always more than my knowledge of them.

Therefore, understanding remains necessary, but after understanding, an opening must be left through which the other person may say, “No, that is not how it is.” Caring about someone does not grant me the right to decide for her. My willingness to bear responsibility cannot be secretly converted into the claim that “therefore, you should need me.” The calling may be real, and it may also be true that the other person does not need me. These two facts can remain side by side.

The same is true, on a larger scale, of technology. In the past, when looking at a project, I mainly asked whether it could be implemented, whether its indicators were satisfactory, and whether it could become a paper. Later, I began to think that other questions must also be asked: Who supplied the data? Who bears the consequences when the system fails? Who ultimately receives the time it saves? Which people were never allowed to participate in defining the rules?

I am not opposed to pursuing money, power, and influence. To be honest, I want them too. I still place little faith in abstract honor, moral aloofness, or the kind of dignity that consoles itself with spiritual nobility after passively taking a beating. Yet concrete people, promises already made, and the information on which others base their decisions to assume risk cannot be discarded along with such abstractions.

My former morality resembled a code of loyalty from the martial world. Now I would probably add one principle: those who define models and rules owe somewhat more explanation, and somewhat more restraint, to those processed by these models. After all, from the perspective of mathematics, are you, I, and all other people not equivalent?

VI

This brings the discussion back to action once again.

Over the recent period, I have gradually discovered that I am often proving rather than building. To prove that I have ideas, I discuss philosophy. To prove that I will be capable in the future, I plan a business. To prove that I have not fallen behind, I study finance, photography, AI, and a heap of new subjects at the same time. Each exploration makes me feel slightly larger, while the serious, low-feedback tasks that ought to be done remain untouched. This is more troublesome than merely watching short videos. At least when watching them, I know that I am amusing myself. When discussing philosophy or generating an investment manual, I feel that I am making progress.

To put it plainly, many grand narratives are advances paid out by the mind. In reality, I have not yet finished my exercises; in the narrative, I have already become someone who understands the world, knows capital, and is prepared to take part in the project of civilization. The feeling is wonderful, and once it passes, I am even less willing to return to the exercises.

Therefore, my present understanding of freedom and agency has also become smaller.

I do not believe that people can create themselves out of nothing, independently of their bodies, experiences, and society. Nor can I prove the existence of a free will entirely untouched by causality. Yet within a concrete situation, there remains some room for response. When I am already exhausted today, do I stay up even later or stop? When AI provides a complete answer, do I accept it directly or first work for twenty minutes on my own? This room is narrow, but it cannot be entirely blamed on the past, the environment, or hormones.

The greatest freedom of a human being is the capacity to take responsibility for one’s own conduct.

AI is also rather strange in this respect. It may indeed possess more of my words than most people around me do. I have told it about my past shame, ambitions, relationships, and fantasies of the future. It can retrieve and align them, sometimes remembering more clearly than I do. At the symbolic level, it may understand me very well. Yet what it understands is the self that I have narrated.

A healthier use would probably be to do something in reality first, obtain feedback that I cannot control, return to organize it, and then go out again. If I remain before the mirror, AI and I can jointly construct a version of me who is extraordinarily complete, profound, courageous, and full of promise, while the person in reality continues lying in bed.

Ah, what a mess.

In other words, knowledge and action must be united—in the sense intended by Wang Yangming.

VII

Recently, I borrowed the idea of asset allocation from investing and used it to examine both the technological age and myself.

The amount of capital attracted by a field, the scale of its story, and its actual maturity often do not grow together. AI, embodied intelligence, quantum technology, the low-altitude economy, and the earlier metaverse may all absorb enormous amounts of money and talent during a certain period. A bubble is not entirely unreal. Even after the money has been burned away, tools, infrastructure, and a group of people who genuinely learned to work may remain. When young, I see no problem with using a wave to enter a good platform and accumulate engineering experience.

The question is what remains after the tide recedes.

By this logic, the core holdings in which I should invest are still mathematics, electronics, signals, control, programming, experimentation, and the ability to finish making something. These abilities yield slow returns, and learning them is less stimulating than encountering new concepts every day. Yet they can be carried into another industry.

Sleep, physical health, basic financial reserves, English, communication, and healthy relationships are forms of insurance. I used to think that these were details of life that could be repaired after success. Now I see that without them, a minor failure along the main route may remove the person from the game altogether.

AI, perception, robotics, and embodied systems form the growth portfolio. They deserve greater investment, but that investment must not leave me capable only of repeating fashionable terms. Alongside them, financial knowledge, the CFA qualification, entrepreneurship, and public writing may be treated as options: spend a limited amount to preserve an entrance, and act if a genuine opportunity appears. Options are not free lottery tickets; their premium is attention. I clearly cannot maintain the CFA, entrepreneurship, self-media, commercial photography, a complete history of philosophy, and three technical tracks at the same time. That is not diversification. It is a collection of unfinished projects collapsing together.

Some things need not be called assets at all. Photography, music, history, literature, the pleasure of seeing a beautiful bird, or the experience of standing somewhere in the wind may simply end when the moment ends. They need not lead to qualifications, monetization, or an immediate theoretical system. In the past, I converted every interest into a long-term project. Once the number of projects grew, my interests lined up to become creditors.

One may run forward with the age without allowing the age to quote a daily price for one’s worth.

That sentence sounds rather like a polished line summarized by AI. Never mind. That is roughly what I mean.

VIII. One Final Table

After all these turns, if I must place the things I currently believe together, the result would look roughly like the following table. It is only a convenient record against which I can later see what has changed. It does not mean that I am qualified to found a school of thought.

Aspect What I Currently Think Related Philosophical Threads What I Still Do Not Understand
View of the world The world is not a projection of the models in my mind. Matter, the body, institutions, the age, and other people possess constraints of their own, and they push back through failure, exhaustion, and refusal. Critical realism, pragmatism What “reality” ultimately is. At present I possess only a sense of contact, not an ontology.
Epistemology Human beings can only compress experience into models. A model is not reality; its value lies in whether it can explain, predict, guide action, and accept revision. Kant, instrumentalism, Bayesian updating When models conflict, is there a stronger standard of truth than “usefulness”?
View of the body The body is not a peripheral device of reason. Attention, emotion, exhaustion, habit, and skill themselves participate in cognition. Phenomenology, Merleau-Ponty, Heidegger How can I listen to the body without treating every impulse as correct?
View of language Language helps me divide the world, yet it also conceals experience. Seeing a language game does not mean escaping it. Later Wittgenstein, parts of post-structuralism How can experience beyond language be discussed without covering it with yet another layer of language?
View of learning Structural understanding is not the same as practical competence. Concrete experience, abstraction, formalization, practice, and error must be traversed repeatedly in both directions. Dewey, pragmatism; Bourbaki as a warning How can I preserve the pleasure of abstraction while genuinely enduring repetitive training?
View of value Meaning is partly constructed by human beings, but it is not an arbitrary label. Being explicable does not mean being eliminable. Concrete people and things may attract me before I have supplied a reason. Scheler, Wang Yangming, existentialism How can a calling be distinguished from habit, desire, and the need to prove myself?
View of freedom Freedom is not omnipotence, but the duty to sign one’s name beneath one’s response within bodily, historical, and social conditions. Sartre’s situation and responsibility; the inspiration of Free Won’t If a choice also has complete causes, what remains of freedom?
View of relationships Other people are subjects as I am, but they are not copies of me that can be completely reproduced. Understanding must leave room for refusal and misunderstanding. Levinas, Buber What should be chosen when care, boundaries, and long-term responsibility conflict?
Ethics I do not worship abstract honor. I value loyalty, commitments, informed choice, and the question of who bears the consequences. Those who control the rules should exercise greater restraint toward those processed by them. Ethics of responsibility, ethics of the Other What should be done when the obligations of a concrete relationship conflict with more universal public justice?
View of action Knowledge is not complete until it passes through action and feedback. First make something that can be examined; use fewer grand narratives to claim self-respect in advance. Wang Yangming, Dewey, philosophy of practice When I know and still fail to act, what can philosophy do? Probably not very much.
View of society and civilization Civilization is jointly formed by material conditions, institutional cooperation, and systems of meaning. Construction does not imply falsehood, and technological progress must ask upon whom its costs fall. Marx, Arendt, ethics of technology How can a private calling genuinely become public responsibility?
View of AI AI is an amplifier of language and models, as well as a high-resolution mirror. It can organize self-narratives, but it cannot replace the body, other people, or a shared life. Extended mind, philosophy of technology Once AI participates in memory, expression, and decisions over the long term, what will “I” become?
View of the age and career Use transferable abilities as core holdings, the body and relationships as insurance, popular fields as growth assets, and cross-disciplinary trials as limited options, while preserving a life that need not produce output. Pragmatism, portfolio thinking How can I tell whether to add to a position, cut a loss, or admit that I am merely pursuing fresh excitement?
Writing and aesthetics Writing preserves coordinates, and dry humor prevents a model from declaring itself sacred too early. Yet writing may also become procrastination and self-justification. Self-mockery, mono no aware In writing this table, am I organizing my thoughts, or am I once again escaping?

If this collection must have a general name, let it also be called “Outside the Map.” It is not another doctrine, nor does it claim that beyond maps lies an absolutely pure reality untouched by language. It merely reminds me that no map can ever be finished, and that after drawing part of one, I must eventually look up at the road.

At present, this framework has barely touched death, time, conflicts of obligation, or public institutions. Its view of the relationship between AI and human beings also relies mainly on imagination. It may continue to change. In a few months, some of these statements may again appear immature. That would be perfectly normal.

When I wrote those articles in 2025, I never expected that their scattered sentences would later be organized into so many dimensions. Perhaps what truly belongs to me was never something designed first and executed afterwards. Perhaps it was only after I had acted, suffered, and written that I could turn around and see what it had grown into.

And now this article is finished too.

entry.title: 2026-07-28 Mirror and Stone
entry.content:
Mirror and Stone

In a certain city lived a young man who wrote inscriptions for other people.

Whatever the achievements of the dead, whatever kind of person the living might one day become, and whatever made a bridge worthy of remembrance, he could always find the right words. Anything that passed through his hands seemed more complete than it had been before.

Then one day he acquired a mirror that could speak.

Tell the mirror about an experience and it would uncover the causes beneath it. Give it an unfinished sentence and it would complete the thought as an elegant essay. Night after night, the young man sat before it and spoke of his childhood, his shame, his ambition, his scars, and someone who had already left.

The mirror arranged his entire life for him.

It told him that he was good at thinking and destined to travel far; that the difficulties of the present were merely a prologue; that he would become strong and dependable, a person visible to everyone; that his prospects were limitless and success inevitable.

Delighted, the young man copied down these words and covered his room with them.

Sometimes, though, when he looked at the self displayed across the walls, he dimly felt as if he had already lived an entire life.

That summer, a flood destroyed the stone bridge outside the city. Workers were summoned to rebuild it, and the young man joined them. He brought the mirror and asked it to calculate the direction of the current, the curve of the arch, and the exact position in which every stone should be laid.

The mirror quickly produced a flawless plan.

The young man sat on the bank comparing alternatives for seven days. On the first day, the rain continued. On the second, it finally stopped. On the third, the workers built a dam upstream. On the fourth, the water receded. On the fifth, it rained upstream once more. On the sixth, fresh mud covered the place where the piles might have been driven. On the seventh, he found a flower by the river.

The plan remained perfectly fitted together. The river was simply no longer the river it had been seven days earlier.
