After forging, the part is normalized or annealed to homogenize the structure, lower hardness, and relieve residual stress, leaving some margin for subsequent machining. Then come turning, drilling, hobbing, and shaping. Gears under high load are then carburized, quenched, and tempered at low temperature, so that the surface is hard and wear-resistant while the core retains toughness. Finally, grinding, shot peening, and inspection are done before a gear counts as ready to run for long periods inside a machine.

Behind the most ordinary-looking gear stands an entire row of disciplines: metallurgy, materials science, thermodynamics, solid-state physics, plastic forming, mechanical design, manufacturing processes, and quality inspection.

I found that rather striking at the time.

Of course, the feeling was a bit like opening a computer for the first time and discovering that the inside is not a green board labeled “computer.” An engineering student had come into contact with another slice of engineering and started making a fuss.

But if you keep pushing along that question, things begin to get out of hand.

1. Where Modern Industry Grows From

Machinery, electronics, chips, automobiles, and aerospace look like several completely different majors. Universities do indeed place them in different schools, the curricula have nothing in common, and students in one field cannot understand those in another.

Yet they are not isolated islands.

Mathematics provides a language for describing change, structure, and uncertainty. Calculus handles continuous change, linear algebra handles multivariate structure, probability and statistics study uncertainty, differential equations describe dynamical systems, and numerical analysis makes it possible to approximate problems that have no neat closed-form solutions on a computer.

Physics studies matter, energy, motion, electromagnetism, heat, light, and the microscopic world. Chemistry studies the composition and transformation of matter. Biology studies how life exists, inherits, and evolves.

On top of these basic sciences grow the engineering fundamentals: materials, mechanics, thermodynamics, electronics, information, and control. Above those come the professional fields: mechanical, electrical, civil, chemical, metallurgical, computer, communication, and integrated circuit engineering, which finally flow into specific industries such as automobiles, energy, medicine, the Internet, artificial intelligence, and aerospace.

If we suppress precision and crush it into a single chain, it looks roughly like this:

In the past, I saw majors as a row of separate course catalogs. Materials was materials, mechanics was mechanics, electronics was electronics, and computer science was computer science.

Now I see things differently. Some disciplines are responsible for understanding the world, some for transforming matter, some for controlling energy, and some for processing information. Each of them takes root downward, only to reconverge in complex systems such as automobiles, robots, chip-making equipment, industrial automation, and aerospace.

So I said at the start that modern industry resembles a vast tree of knowledge.

That is how I put it, but in reality it is not truly a unidirectionally growing tree. Humanity did not first study thermodynamics and then, turning to the exercises at the end of the chapter, invent the steam engine; nor did it establish materials science before first learning how to smelt iron. Far more often, craft collides with something first, machines break in the real world, and theory lumbers up afterward to explain why they broke. Theory improves tools, tools create new observations, and new observations in turn break theory.

The tree of knowledge is merely a compressing diagram that is convenient for understanding. If you actually unfolded it, it would be a network with feedback running everywhere.

Still, a person needs some map to begin with. In the appendix, I have drawn this “tree that is not really a tree.” I will post the accuracy disclaimer here first, so it does not go around pretending to be the truth later.

2. The Industrial Tree of Knowledge Is Not Yet Civilization

Industry and the natural sciences still make up only one part of civilization.

Human beings must not only produce material goods; they must also organize society, distribute resources, preserve memory, express feeling, and establish meaning.

Economics studies how scarce resources are produced, exchanged, and distributed. Finance studies how resources flow across time and how risk is priced and shared. Political science studies how power arises, operates, and is constrained. Law studies how rules are made explicit and enforced. Sociology studies how institutions, classes, groups, and organizations shape individuals.

Psychology studies human cognition, emotion, and behavior. History studies how today grew out of yesterday. Philosophy asks what the world is, how knowledge is possible, and how one ought to live. Religion deals with life and death, suffering, belonging, and transcendence. Literature preserves the inner experience of human beings.

Science can record how many people died in a war, and history can explain why the war happened, but literature preserves how an ordinary person, living inside that war, felt fear and hesitation and loss, and how that person still got up the next morning and went about the day.

History records what happened in an era. Literature records what it felt like to live in that era.

Seen this way, human civilization contains at least three interacting systems:

The material system includes agriculture, industry, energy, transportation, medicine, construction, and communication. The institutional system includes the state, law, markets, finance, enterprises, education, and bureaucracy. The meaning system includes language, religion, philosophy, literature, art, history, and morality.

Losing any one of the three spells trouble.

With material alone and no meaning, a person might live as a device with decent specifications that does not know why it was switched on. With meaning alone and no material, civilization would not last several days. With material and meaning but no institutions, large-scale cooperation would dissolve into disputes over distribution, trust, and violence.

If you compress further, what human civilization repeatedly answers amounts to four questions:

  1. What is the world?
  2. How do we live together?
  3. What can we create?
  4. What does any of this mean?

These four questions are, admittedly, shamelessly large.

And at the time, I had only been listening to a friend talk about heat treatment.

3. This Made Me Rethink the Postgraduate Entrance Exam

Once I placed mathematics back on this map, the flavor of the postgraduate entrance exam changed a little.

Limits, derivatives, integrals, matrices, and probability have the most obvious use in passing an exam half a year away. But they are also, genuinely, not merely exam content. Mathematics is the language humans use to describe change, structure, and uncertainty; it props up physics, engineering, economics, finance, computer science, and artificial intelligence above it.

So I kept asking: Why am I taking this exam? Why do I study? Why do I keep wanting to connect different disciplines?

In the end, it seems to reduce to a sentence that is not exactly fresh:

I want to know how this world actually works, and I also want to know what I can do inside it.

What I truly long for may not be the two characters “graduate school.” What I want is a relatively complete stretch of time in which I can study systematically, do research, write, and work on projects; enter deeply into some specialty while still keeping the ability to reach into materials, computer science, economics, philosophy, literature, and society.

That sounds rather like a recruitment video.

Worse, this grand thirst for knowledge very easily turns into an advanced form of procrastination. You skip integral problems and instead study the place of mathematics in human civilization; you do not organize your wrong-answer notebook and instead start building a knowledge tree of civilization covering every discipline. You feel you have grasped the essence of learning, while the one thing you were actually supposed to do today has not moved a single word.

A map can serve as a compass; it cannot substitute for walking.

Even though I have become highly skilled at using compass-drawing to avoid walking.

4. Does a Person Really Need to Learn All This?

Pushing further, several rather practical questions surface.

First, learning all this demands enormous energy. Second, what is the use of learning so much. Third, no single person can truly master all human knowledge, so what am I drawing this map for?

It is already difficult for a person, in a lifetime, to reach the frontier of a single field. A sensible knowledge structure should therefore not be “go deep in every discipline” but rather consist of at least three layers.

The first layer is knowing it exists. Knowing what questions a discipline studies and what function it serves within civilization.

The second layer is understanding the basic framework. Being able to grasp its core concepts and methods, and being able to talk normally with people in that field when needed, without revealing ignorance the moment you open your mouth.

The third layer is forming professional competence. Being able to read papers, run experiments, solve problems, and eventually produce something that others can use or verify.

Only a very small number of fields can truly be pursued in depth. A more reasonable shape might be:

Take root in one or two fields, build competence in a few neighboring fields, and keep a map-like awareness of a large number of peripheral fields.

As for “usefulness,” it should not be read as merely whether something immediately raises income or exam scores.

Some knowledge has direct instrumental value: you can apply it immediately to a task. Some has transfer value: it changes how a person approaches problems. Economics makes you notice incentives, history makes you notice path dependence, psychology makes you wary of cognitive biases, and literature forces you to admit that concrete human beings are usually far messier than models.

Some knowledge has defensive value.

If you know only technology, you tend to read every problem as a technical problem; if you know only markets, you tend to see every relationship as a transaction; if you know only power, you tend to mistake every kindness for disguise. Interdisciplinary knowledge may not give direct answers, but at least it stops one model from monopolizing your mind and then declaring that it explains everything.

The remaining knowledge may have no value beyond existence itself.

Understanding the universe, life, history, and literature is not necessarily a means to something else. A thing that has become aware of the world may simply want to know what kind of world it is in.

That sounds like a platitude.

But it took humanity a long time before it could afford to produce such platitudes seriously.

5. Is Reality Like a Game?

From a certain angle, reality does resemble a game.

It has underlying rules, finite resources, competition and cooperation, feedback mechanisms, and constraints that an individual will cannot bypass. A person cannot live without food through willpower alone, nor bypass the laws of physics through ideals. Individuals, firms, and nations likewise cannot violate for long the laws of resources, incentives, and information.

Being able to see the rules means a person has begun to move from the surface of events to the inside of the system.

But reality is not like an ordinary game, because it has no explicit designer and no single standard of victory or defeat.

Wealth, reproduction, power, happiness, truth, creation, and morality constantly conflict with one another. A person can succeed in a biological sense and fail in a moral one; can be eminent in a social sense and miserable in a subjective one.

Reality has no single scoreboard. Even the question of what “winning” means has not been settled after several thousand years of discussion.

Moreover, a person is not merely a player inside the rules, but something that can reflect on those rules and modify them locally. Because disease kills, we developed medicine; because violence begets violence, we established law; because desires can be manipulated, we began studying how to manage desire—though in the end this usually means downloading a time-management app and then continuing to watch videos.

Human beings cannot leave nature, yet within the scope nature permits, they can redesign their own lives.

The conversation keeps bending further. If you keep pressing with first principles, what lies at the very bottom of this game?

6. Survival, Reproduction, and Then a Little Something Extra

Many behaviors can indeed be traced back to survival and reproduction.

High-calorie food means energy; status means allocation rights; reputation affects cooperative opportunities; love and intimacy are linked to reproduction; the state and the group provide security; education raises the competitive ability of individuals and their offspring.

If you keep dismantling along these lines, love becomes hormones and attachment, altruism becomes reciprocity and reputation, ideals become reward circuits, and research becomes evaluation systems and status competition. Everything looks like a different interface for the same underlying command: stay alive, leave offspring, keep iterating.

This explanation is extremely powerful. So powerful that it is a little frightening.

But it is precisely here that the problem emerges.

If everything serves survival and reproduction, why do people like sunsets?

A sunset cannot fill the stomach, mountains do not help reproduction, and a beautiful mathematical proof usually does not improve the odds of escaping a predator. A wine glass does not solve hunger, and a musical instrument creates no wealth, yet they do make an ordinary evening worth staying for and give an empty room a bit of warmth.

When I first saw certain physics formulas in high school, I genuinely thought, “This is goddamn beautiful.” That beauty did not come from how many points it could earn on an exam. I did not first compute the marginal benefit of appreciating a formula for my future employment. It simply lit up.

I came up with a term that may not be rigorous but serves well enough for now: cognitive surplus.

To survive, humans evolved perception, memory, prediction, pattern recognition, spatial judgment, social reasoning, and information compression. The brain had to find patterns in messy environments, judge whether a shadow in the grass was dangerous, remember where food and water were, read the intentions of others, and take as few computational steps as possible in a complex world without calculating itself to death.

But once these tools grew out, they did not restrict themselves to the original tasks.

Pattern recognition can be applied to mathematics, sound discrimination can grow into music, spatial and color judgment can become painting, and the simulation of others’ intentions can enter fiction. Capabilities originally formed for survival have a range of application that exceeds immediate survival tasks, so the mind begins to take an interest in things that confer no direct survival benefit.

A patch is needed here. “After survival is satisfied” must not be read as a strict sequence of eating first, then singing. People write poetry while hungry, at war, and in bereavement; some works are written precisely when survival looks impossible.

Surplus here does not necessarily mean an idle CPU core in the brain. It means more like this: the usable range of a capacity exceeds the specific task that originally shaped it.

Put bluntly, survival wrote the drivers for the brain, and the brain began running unauthorized programs with those drivers.

The beauty of a formula may also come from this overstepping. A formula compresses a vast range of phenomena into a very small number of symbols; things that were scattered suddenly cohere under a single understanding, and the mind says “so that’s how it is.” What is truly beautiful is often not absolute simplicity but the sudden appearance of compressible structure amid complexity.

Chase first principles all the way down, and there is still a flower left on the ground.

Then I thought of emergence.

7. Why Does Quantity Turn into Quality

A single neuron only receives, integrates, and transmits signals. It does not enjoy sunsets, nor does it find formulas beautiful. Yet when roughly eighty-six billion neurons connect in complex ways, consciousness, memory, the self-model, and aesthetic experience appear.

Likewise, no single water molecule is “wet,” no single individual has a market price, and no single character is literature. But once organized, the whole possesses properties that cannot be found in any of the parts.

Because I happened to be studying differential calculus at the time, what came to mind first was:

$$
\Delta y=f’(x)\Delta x+o(\Delta x)
$$

The linear part describes the main change, and higher-order infinitesimals can be neglected locally. So could “qualitative change” be precisely those usually-neglected higher-order terms accumulating until they suddenly overturn the table?

That intuition grazed the edge of the truth, but it was not accurate enough.

When a slender rod is subject to a small compressive load, it stays straight; as the load increases, it may deform slightly. But past a certain critical value, the straight state becomes unstable, and the rod suddenly buckles sideways. It is not that small prior bends finally filled up a progress bar; rather, the restoring mechanism maintaining the original state fails, and the new bent state becomes stable instead.

Avalanches are similar. The last snowflake does not possess the energy to push the whole slope; it only lands on a system that was already close to instability.

So “quantity changes into quality” cannot be understood merely as “more of the same.” What matters more is that a change in quantity or parameters alters the relationships, feedback, and stability structure among the parts.

Eighty-six billion neurons completely isolated from one another would not automatically produce consciousness. Several billion people entirely incapable of transmitting experience to one another would not automatically produce civilization.

What matters is connection. Synapses organize signals into dynamic networks; language lets one person’s experience enter another’s mind; writing detaches memory from the body; education and institutions allow knowledge to be preserved across generations.

Thus descendants need not restart from rubbing sticks to make fire every time. What one person stumbles into can be caught, modified, and built upon by another.

Civilization is not a simple sum of population size. It is what slowly grows once memory ceases to be zeroed out with the death of each individual.

Of course, not every instance of emergence has a sharp critical point like an avalanche. Some structures form gradually, and it is hard to point to which particular neuron, which word, or which generation suddenly made it consciousness, language, or culture.

The common thread is roughly this: macroscopic properties do not hide inside any single component; they live in the relationships that persist among components.

8. Civilization Begins to Redesign Survival in Return

At this point in the conversation, the chain curved back around.

Pattern recognition may have originally helped people read the environment, but it later grew into mathematics. Mathematics entered physics and engineering; physics and engineering produced machines, drugs, communications, and computers, which in turn changed how people produce, how they die, how they love, and how they remember one another.

A tool that originally served survival, having overflowed survival, turns around and redefines survival itself.

So “by-products” are not irrelevant scraps either. Aesthetic appreciation made people preserve murals, music, and cities; the thirst for knowledge made people study mathematics of no immediate use; the novel lets people of different eras share a kind of inner experience. These things enter education, institutions, and technology, and end up as part of civilization maintaining itself.

Look back at that gear. It, too, was not deduced by some genius from first principles all the way down to an assembly line.

Countless people observed, tried, erred, recorded, and taught; theory and craft pushed back against each other; thousands of years of experience were compressed into material grades, processing standards, tooth-profile parameters, and inspection procedures. When today’s worker presses a button, many long-dead people are still working alongside through that process.

Industry is solidified collective memory.

Civilization is a group of mortal animals that found a way to keep their experience from dying along with them.

9. Once the Mechanism Is Known, Does the Warmth Remain?

Knowing that aesthetics may borrow from pattern recognition and information compression does not make a sunset any less real. Knowing that love involves hormones, attachment, and self-interest does not make the hand one person reaches out at a particular moment an illusion.

Mechanism answers how something happens; it does not automatically answer whether it is worth anything.

I used to feel that explaining something clearly was equivalent to dissolving it. Love has a mechanism, so love is fake; ideals have reward circuits, so ideals are just self-indulgence; the beauty of formulas has a cognitive basis, so it is just neurons amusing themselves.

But if the self-amusement of neurons ends up producing calculus, symphonies, and a letter that genuinely makes someone cry, then the phrase “just” is carrying far too much weight.

Yet explanation is not dissolution. Knowing the mechanism does not make the warmth fake.

First principles can tell me what a high-level structure stands on, but it cannot live that high-level structure’s life for it. A novel is made of atoms, yet atomism is not literary criticism; consciousness arises from neural activity, yet no single voltage change can be written down as “I”; civilization is bound by energy, resources, and reproduction, yet it still produces things that are temporarily useless and even turn around to interrogate survival itself.

Perhaps what we call meaning is simply this: when natural law runs up to a certain scale, the system begins to see itself and develops preferences, doubts, and intentions to modify its own operation.

Perhaps not. That is a rather large claim, and I cannot say for certain.

10. In the End, It Is Still a Limit

The conversation began with a gear, wandered over to the industrial tree of knowledge, then from civilization to the postgraduate exam, and from first principles all the way down to survival and reproduction. In the end, because the sunset and the formula were still lying in the ruins, untouched by dismantling, I had to drag out cognitive surplus, quantity-into-quality, and emergence.

Looking back now, it seems it was always asking the same thing:

A group of animals that only needed to survive—why, in the course of surviving, did they build gears, calculus, novels, and symphonies, and stop in the evening to find the horizon beautiful?

I do not know.

But I quite like “cognitive surplus” as a provisional answer. Survival put a set of tools into human hands, and humans did not follow the manual exactly. The tools kept interconnecting, memory accumulated, local interactions grew new structures, and civilization appeared. Civilization then turned around and made new tools, letting the next generation keep overstepping.

A gear does not enjoy sunsets.

But the people who make gears write poetry after work.

As for what this has to do with my exam tomorrow.

Probably nothing direct.

First, let me finish that limit.

Appendix: A Knowledge Map of Industrial Civilization

Let me first explain what this map is actually depicting.

Between the formal sciences, natural sciences, engineering, manufacturing, and industry, knowledge dependencies do exist; but a knowledge dependency is not a historical sequence, nor is it a hierarchy of value. The steam engine preceded a complete thermodynamics; smelting practice preceded modern materials science; engineering failures in turn force theory to catch up.

So this is not a tree growing unidirectionally from root to crown. More precisely, it is a cycle of “understand the world—transform the world—receive feedback—understand again.” Institutions are what allow the cycle to run stably; values and public purposes determine where it should be directed.

B. The Formal Sciences: First, How to Describe and Reason

The formal sciences do not study any particular material or machine; they study relations, structures, proofs, and computation themselves. They provide other disciplines with a language that can be reused across different objects.

Branch Core Object Main Content and Methods What It Solves Once It Enters Industry
Mathematical Logic Propositions, proofs, axioms, and computable processes Propositional logic, predicate logic, set theory, model theory, proof theory, recursion and computability Checking whether reasoning is self-consistent; supporting programming languages, database queries, digital logic, formal verification, and security protocols
Geometry Shape, position, distance, and curvature Euclidean geometry, analytic geometry, differential geometry, computational geometry Describing part geometry, surfaces, and motion trajectories; used in mechanical drawing, robot path planning, computer graphics, and surveying
Topology Structures invariant under continuous deformation Connectedness, boundaries, homeomorphism, manifolds, and topological invariants Handling complex spaces, networks, and continuous deformation; entering robot configuration spaces, material defects, data analysis, and field theory
Calculus Continuous change and accumulation Limits, continuity, derivatives, integrals, series, multivariable functions, and calculus of variations Describing velocity, temperature, stress, current, and similar changes; computing global results from local laws
Linear Algebra Vector spaces and linear transformations Matrices, linear systems, eigenvalues, orthogonal decomposition, tensor basics Handling multivariate coupling; used in structural computation, control, signals, imaging, machine learning, and engineering simulation
Probability Theory Random events and uncertainty Random variables, probability distributions, stochastic processes, Markov chains, laws of large numbers Describing noise, load fluctuation, life scatter, and communication bit errors; giving “uncertainty” a computable model
Mathematical Statistics Inferring populations from finite data Parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, ANOVA, Bayesian inference, and experimental design Judging whether processes are stable, whether improvements work, whether measurements are credible; supporting quality control and clinical trials
Ordinary Differential Equations How states change over time Initial-value problems, stability, linear and nonlinear dynamical systems Describing circuits, mechanical vibration, reaction processes, controlled objects, and population dynamics as time-evolving systems
Partial Differential Equations How states change in both time and space Elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic equations, boundary and initial conditions Describing heat transfer, fluids, elastic bodies, electromagnetic fields, diffusion, and waves; the core of continuum simulation
Discrete Mathematics Finite or countable discrete structures Graph theory, combinatorics, sets, relations, recurrence, Boolean algebra Supporting algorithms, network routing, production scheduling, chip logic, coding, and supply chain connectivity analysis
Numerical Analysis Finite-precision approximation of mathematical problems Discretization, interpolation, iteration, error estimation, condition numbers, and numerical stability Turning large equations without closed-form solutions over to computers; forming the basis of finite elements, finite differences, and computational fluid dynamics
Optimization and Operations Research Choices with objectives and constraints Linear and nonlinear programming, convex optimization, integer programming, dynamic programming, queueing theory, game theory, and search Solving design, scheduling, routing, and resource allocation problems across cost, weight, efficiency, safety, and delivery time
Information Theory and Coding Quantity of information, channels, and recoverability Entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, source coding, error-correcting codes, rate distortion Setting theoretical bounds on compression and communication; guiding storage, wireless communication, sensing, and data fusion

Take the gear: the involute tooth profile is described with geometry and calculus; tooth-contact stress requires solving mechanical models; machining error and life scatter require probability and statistics; gearbox vibration enters differential equations and frequency-domain analysis. Mathematics does not directly make gears, but without it, much experience stalls at “roughly usable.”

Here one should distinguish four easily conflated activities. Mathematics first writes the object as a model; analysis studies what properties the model has; numerical methods turn the model into finite steps a computer can solve; statistics then checks the model against real data. Once engineering software packages all four steps behind a single button, people easily believe that simulation images grow out of the computer by themselves. In fact, if the boundary conditions are wrong, the colorful contours merely render the error in higher resolution.

C. The Natural Sciences: Studying How the World Itself Runs

The formal sciences guarantee “how to infer”; the natural sciences must also face whether reality is actually like that. They must accept external validation through observation, experiment, and measurement.

If one slices more finely, the natural sciences are not four tidy boxes but a set of research traditions growing crosswise by scale and object:

This table will still miss the crossover zones. Materials physics belongs to both physics and materials science; biochemistry straddles life and chemistry; geochemistry carries chemical methods into rocks and water. Disciplinary boundaries serve education, organization, and communication; nature was not cut into pieces along faculty signs.

Physics

Classical mechanics studies force, motion, energy, momentum, and rigid bodies; it is the underlying language of mechanical design and structural analysis. Vibration and waves study how systems respond to disturbance, and they concern gearbox noise, bridge resonance, acoustics, and signal propagation.

Thermodynamics studies energy conversion, temperature, entropy, and equilibrium conditions; it answers why heat treatment requires specific temperatures and holding times and sets the efficiency boundaries that engines, refrigerators, and power plants cannot exceed. Statistical physics explains temperature, pressure, diffusion, and phase transitions from the motion of vast numbers of microscopic particles.

Electromagnetism studies electric fields, magnetic fields, currents, and electromagnetic waves; above it grow motors, power grids, wireless communication, radar, and optoelectronics. Quantum mechanics and solid-state physics study atoms, electron energy levels, lattices, and energy bands; they are the foundation of semiconductors, magnetic materials, lasers, and modern material properties.

Chemistry

Chemistry studies what matter is made of, how atoms combine, why reactions occur, and what controls reaction rate and direction.

Inorganic chemistry concerns metals, ceramics, minerals, and catalysts; organic chemistry handles carbon-based molecules and underlies fuels, drugs, plastics, and coatings; physical chemistry applies thermodynamics, kinetics, and quantum theory to chemical processes; electrochemistry supports batteries, electroplating, corrosion, and protection; analytical chemistry confirms what a material actually contains and how much.

When a gear is carburized, how carbon atoms diffuse from the surface inward, how the surface oxidizes, and how the lubricant ages are all chemical questions. Chemistry determines not just the “formula” but also reaction pathways, rates, interfaces, and stability.

Biology

Biology studies how life maintains, replicates, regulates, and evolves itself. Molecular and cellular biology handles genes, proteins, cellular metabolism, and signaling; physiology studies organs and whole-organism function; genetics and evolution study how information is preserved across generations and modified by selection; ecology studies the network relationships between species and environments.

Above it grow medicine, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, biomaterials, fermentation, public health, and ecological governance. The objects modern engineering faces increasingly involve living systems: a medical device must satisfy not only mechanical strength but also biocompatibility, immune response, and variation among human bodies.

Earth and Environmental Sciences

Geology studies rocks, minerals, and the evolution of the Earth, and it determines where industrial raw materials come from; hydrology, meteorology, and oceanography study how water, air, and energy circulate in the Earth system; environmental science studies how pollutants spread, accumulate, and affect ecosystems and human health.

Industry does not float outside the Earth. Ore grade, fresh water, climate, land, and ecological carrying capacity all become hard constraints on production. Engineering converts natural resources into products, but it must also face waste heat, wastewater, carbon emissions, and the question of where materials eventually go.

D. Engineering Fundamentals: Turning “Knowing the Laws” into “Being Able to Design”

The natural sciences care about general laws; engineering fundamentals care more about how to calculate, choose, and control under real constraints.

The gear falls most directly at the junction of materials science and engineering mechanics. Materials determine its potential; heat treatment tunes that potential out; tooth-profile design determines how load is distributed; lubrication determines how the contact interface behaves; reliability analysis then asks when it will fail under random loading.

E. Engineering Disciplines: Building Complete Responsibility Around a Class of Real Objects

An engineering discipline is not a re-sorting of basic knowledge; it is a closed loop around a class of objects, connecting analysis, design, manufacturing, operation, and maintenance.

The true boundary of a discipline is often not “which courses I took” but “which layer I am responsible for when something goes wrong.” A materials engineer must explain structure and properties; a mechanical engineer, load and structure; a control engineer, stability; a software engineer, logic and data. Complex systems do not run because everyone knows everything; they run because responsibility can be traced along interfaces.

F. Manufacturing and System Integration: How Knowledge Gets Compressed into an Object

A design drawing is not yet a product. Manufacturing must organize materials, energy, equipment, processes, and people to reproduce the same thing repeatedly within allowable error.

Raw materials and material preparation include mining, smelting, petrochemicals, alloy melting, wafer growth, ceramic sintering, and polymer synthesis. It determines “what to make it from.”

Forming processes include casting, forging, rolling, stamping, extrusion, and additive manufacturing. They give material its initial geometry while altering internal structure, defects, and residual stress.

Machining includes turning, milling, planing, grinding, drilling, and tooth generation. It turns rough stock into parts satisfying dimensional, shape, and surface-accuracy requirements. Higher precision generally costs more, so engineering does not seek maximum precision but adequate precision that is stable.

Heat treatment and surface engineering change structure and surface state through annealing, normalizing, quenching, tempering, carburizing, nitriding, coating, and shot peening. They barely change the visible shape of a part, yet they can completely change its life.

Assembly joins parts into equipment; embedded systems and software give equipment the ability to sense and control; inspection and metrology confirm whether dimensions, composition, defects, and performance meet specifications; quality management ensures that a part made good by accident becomes a batch made good on purpose.

System integration handles a different kind of trouble: every part passes individually, yet assembled together they still may not work well. Interfaces, timing, thermal management, electromagnetic compatibility, fault propagation, human-machine interaction, and cost are problems that only emerge at the system level.

This small diagram is closer to reality than “mathematics grows downward into a gear.” Physics and chemistry provide mechanisms; materials science handles composition, process, structure, and properties; mechanical engineering imposes geometric, load, and life requirements; the manufacturing process presses these requirements into the billet; and failures in service send information back.

Take tooth-surface pitting. It may be related simultaneously to contact stress, material hardness, residual stress, lubrication, and surface roughness. It is not a single course being done wrong; it is conditions at several levels converging in the actual contact region. Failure analysis works backward along this chain.

H. The Industrial System: Engineering Branches Reconverge in Large-Scale Production

A patch first: the following is not a verbatim transcription of national economic industry codes, nor does it claim that real firms must sit in a single box. It is a functional tree of industrial civilization—what task each layer performs in the whole production system. Semiconductors belong to electronics manufacturing, yet they also supply intermediate goods to automobiles, medicine, power grids, and communications; chemicals produce final consumer goods and also supply materials to nearly all manufacturing. The tree is for locating positions; real industry is a network of mutual supply.

The material flow is fairly intuitive: iron ore becomes steel, steel becomes a gear, the gear enters a reducer, and the reducer enters a fan or a machine tool. The energy flow tends to be hidden by drawings, but mining, steelmaking, transport, machining, and data centers alike depend on electricity, fuel, steam, and cooling. The information flow includes drawings, material grades, tolerances, programs, orders, inspection results, and failure reports. Without it, material arriving at a factory does not know what it is supposed to become. The organizational flow is even less visible: contracts determine who delivers, finance bears the time gap, standards define interfaces, law assigns responsibility, and education ensures the next generation still knows what is actually happening behind the button.

Equipment manufacturing holds a very special position in this system. It is both a branch of the industrial tree and the producer of production tools for all other branches. Machine tools make the parts of machine tools; semiconductor equipment uses chips to control the manufacture of the next generation of chips; the power industry supplies electricity to the factories that build power-generation equipment. Industry is therefore not a one-way assembly line but a recursive system that produces the conditions of its own production.

The energy industry handles coal, oil, gas, nuclear power, solar, wind, and storage; its core task is to convert, transmit, and dispatch the energy of nature stably. It simultaneously requires thermodynamics, materials, electrical engineering, control, environmental science, and economic systems.

The transportation industry covers automobiles, railways, ships, aviation, and logistics. It is not merely building vehicles; it includes roads, stations, maintenance, dispatch, regulation, and energy supply. A gear enters a gearbox, the gearbox enters a vehicle, and the vehicle finally enters the entire transport system.

The information industry includes communication networks, satellites, the Internet, data centers, and software services. It combines chips, optical fiber, radio, protocols, algorithms, and energy infrastructure so that information can be copied and moved at scale.

The medical industry contains drugs, devices, imaging, surgery, hospitals, and public health. Its object is a highly individualized living system, so it pursues not just performance but also ethics, clinical evidence, regulation, and risk.

The building and urban system packs materials, structures, energy, water supply, transportation, communication, and governance into a single space. The agriculture and food system connects biology, machinery, chemicals, soil and water, logistics, and public health. Industrial automation connects machine tools, sensors, controllers, robots, and software on the production floor.

A complex industry is not a magnified version of one discipline. It is many disciplines achieving temporary cooperation through standards, interfaces, supply chains, and organization. Break any one interface, and the grand system stops, quite honestly.

I. Institutional Support: Why Correct Formulas Are Not Enough

For modern industry to operate stably, it needs not only correct knowledge but also the ability to transmit, collaborate, compare, finance, and take responsibility.

Education hands acquired knowledge to the next generation; research explores problems that do not yet have stable answers; open publication, databases, and the patent system handle how knowledge spreads, is protected, and is reused.

Standards define dimensions, interfaces, materials, tests, and safety requirements, allowing components made by different firms to be interchangeable. Metrology ensures that a millimeter, a volt, a kilogram still mean the same quantity across different laboratories and factories. Without metrology, precision industry cannot even say clearly whether “what we measure is the same thing.”

Enterprises and project management organize people from different disciplines into the same delivery process. Markets and finance allocate resources to equipment, factories, and long-term research, and they also determine which demands are easier to see. Law and regulation pursue liability for accidents, pollution, monopoly, and evaded responsibility. Logistics and supply chains allow raw materials, parts, and products to actually move across regions.

These institutions do not compute tooth-contact stress for the engineer, but they determine whether engineers are trained at all, whether inspection reports can be trusted, whether defects can be hidden, and who answers when something goes wrong.

J. The Humanities and Values: What Industry Ought to Be For

Industry can answer how to produce more, faster, and more stably, but it cannot by itself decide what should be produced, who bears the risk, where pollution lands, and who finally owns the time saved by higher efficiency.

Discipline Main Object of Study Common Questions and Methods What It Adds to Industrial Civilization
Economics Scarce resources, production, exchange, distribution, and incentives How prices form, how externalities are handled; using models, statistics, causal identification, and institutional comparison Explaining why technologies are adopted, where costs and benefits fall, and when markets fail
Finance The allocation of funds across time and the pricing of risk Investment, financing, interest rates, asset portfolios, insurance, and corporate governance Providing capital for factories and infrastructure with long construction periods and huge upfront costs; also exposing leverage and short-termism risks
Management and Organization Studies Firms, teams, processes, strategy, and decision-making How organizations divide labor, coordinate, learn, and process information; using case studies, surveys, behavioral experiments, and operations research Organizing dispersed professional capabilities into projects that can be delivered, maintained, and held accountable
Political Science Power, the state, public policy, and collective action Who makes the rules, how interests contend, how policy is implemented and constrained Explaining why energy, transportation, defense, platforms, and environmental protection are never purely technical choices
Law Rights, obligations, procedures, and enforceable rules Contracts, torts, property, labor, environment, competition, and administrative regulation Defining responsibility beyond interfaces: who pays for defects, who owns data, who cleans up pollution, how monopolies are limited
Sociology Groups, classes, organizations, institutions, and social networks How technology changes occupations, families, communities, and inequality; using surveys, interviews, statistics, and fieldwork Showing that “efficiency gains” do not produce identical consequences in different populations; preventing evaluation of a factory only from inside the factory
Anthropology Ways of life, technology use, and meaning systems across cultures Fieldwork, participant observation, thick description, and cross-cultural comparison Discovering that the same technology is reinterpreted and used differently in different communities; products do not run only as designers imagine
Psychology and Cognitive Science Perception, attention, memory, emotion, decision-making, and behavior Experiments, measurement, modeling, clinical and behavioral observation Supporting human-computer interaction, safety design, training, consumer behavior, and organizational decision-making; also reminding us that the “rational user” does not exist
History How institutions, technologies, and societies form over time Documents, archives, artifacts, oral history, and causal narrative Revealing path dependence: today’s railway standards, urban layouts, and industrial division of labor cannot be reset to zero by redesign
Philosophy Existence, knowledge, language, value, and the boundaries of reasoning Conceptual analysis, argument, thought experiments, and intellectual history Distinguishing “can do,” “know what will happen,” and “ought to do”; examining the premises smuggled into models
Ethics The value principles that actions, institutions, and technologies should obey Duty, consequences, virtue, justice, care, and concrete case analysis Addressing judgments in automation, medical trials, artificial intelligence, environmental costs, and intergenerational responsibility that efficiency cannot replace
Linguistics and Communication Studies Language structure, symbols, media, and public communication Semantics, pragmatics, discourse, communication networks, and media effects Making standards, manuals, risk disclosures, and public discussion understandable; also studying how information is amplified or distorted by platforms
Literature and the Arts Concrete experience, structures of feeling, form, and aesthetics Narrative, imagery, style, performance, criticism, and creation Preserving inner experience outside metrics; reminding us that an engineering project changes not only output but also how people feel and live

Economics studies scarce resources, incentives, exchange, and distribution, helping to explain why technologies get adopted and how costs transmit. Political science studies power and collective decision-making; law writes the permitted and the forbidden into enforceable rules; sociology studies how organizations, classes, and institutions reshape individual circumstances; psychology studies how real people perceive, choose, and err.

History leaves a record of where technologies and institutions succeeded before and where they produced catastrophe. Philosophy asks about the boundaries of knowledge, about value, about responsibility. Ethics discusses what may be done and what should not be done. Literature and the arts preserve what system-level perspectives most easily crush: how a specific human being actually lives inside a grand project, a war, a migration, or an industrial transformation.

So the more complete division of labor is roughly this:

Only here does industrial civilization barely close into a loop.

Of course, this appendix itself remains a large-scale compression. It helps with orientation; it cannot replace actually entering any discipline. When a concrete problem arises, one must jump down from the map, read sources, calculate, run experiments, and let reality push back.

This map can show that “connections exist between disciplines.” It cannot teach me any discipline automatically.

Including how to review the mathematics I have to take tomorrow.

entry.title: After a Thousand Sails
entry.content:
Something rather irritating keeps happening when I work through exercises. My mind remains quiet while I eat, sleep, or scroll through videos. The moment I begin serious mathematics—especially when I cannot solve a question—my former partner, the stupid things I once did, and the possibility of failing the postgraduate entrance examination all arrive together. It begins with an unsolved limit and soon accelerates into the question of whether my entire life is finished. Not one additional symbol appears on the page.

Today I came across an explanation. The human brain, it seems, is not nearly as modern as we imagine. A tiger attempting to eat you is obviously a danger. To the brain, however, an action that may fail, cause humiliation, or prove one’s inadequacy is dangerous too. This is especially true of the postgraduate entrance examination, into which I have placed far too many other things. It is no longer a collection of mathematics problems; it is connected to education, the future, and the question of whether I am an idiot.

When I cannot solve something, uncertainty and the fear of being classified as a failure rise together. The sympathetic nervous system starts first. Adrenaline and noradrenaline prepare the body for conflict; the slower HPA axis and cortisol response follow. The heart accelerates, attention narrows, and the body assumes that I am about to fight or flee. In reality, I am calculating a limit.

To be precise, cortisol does not carry a loudspeaker through the brain ordering it to “begin searching the archive of shame.” The process is closer to this: once stress rises, working memory and quiet reasoning are impaired, while attention tilts toward danger. The feeling that “I may fail again” becomes a retrieval cue in its own right. Memory is recovered through association, so earlier failures, embarrassments, and moments of shame become easier to call up, as though old surveillance footage had suddenly begun playing on a loop.

But the system is probably not attacking me.

It has merely detected a scent resembling an earlier danger and is trying to prevent me from falling into the same trap. The program was written a long time ago, when rejection by the group or a mistake during a hunt might genuinely have been fatal. In the twenty-first century, it still cannot reliably distinguish “I cannot solve this question” from “the tribe is about to cast me out.”

Damn it. The firmware needs an update.

Once I understood this, the experience became slightly easier to interpret. The reason old memories return whenever a question defeats me may not be that those events urgently need to be discussed. The present state of “perhaps I am incapable” simply points toward earlier moments in which “I genuinely failed to do well.” The memories are not appearing without cause. The mind is searching for like terms.

Love is among them. I think I understand a little better why she may once have liked me, although this is only a model I have fitted to the past from one side; I do not know what she actually thought. Perhaps the person I was then genuinely did think about many things and, after all that thought, remained willing to love something. Later, as the models multiplied and I learned more unpleasant facts, I grew colder. Love was a transaction, friendship an exchange of needs, dreams a release of dopamine, and research an evaluation system. Everything could be explained. Nothing remained interesting.

Love, however, is only one example. What truly concerns me is the person I want eventually to become.

I do not think I want to return to the self who knew nothing. Innocence untouched by experience is beautiful, but part of its beauty comes merely from not having seen. Once it encounters interest, failure, departure, and helplessness, it can break at once. Then a person begins to call himself mature: everyone is selfish; love is false; ideals cannot purchase food; look after yourself first.

None of these statements is entirely wrong. Yet if maturity ends by seeing an interest behind every person and a fraud behind every object, has one not merely travelled from one kind of childishness to another?

What I want may be one step farther on. I want to see something of the world: to know how society operates, how to speak, how to handle affairs, how to keep accounts, and how to make something real. I want to have been rejected and defeated, to have watched relationships dissolve, and to understand that effort does not always produce a result. After passing through all of that, I do not want to pickle myself into a smooth old cynic. I want to remain capable of believing in something again.

To believe that love can exist; that a formula can truly be beautiful; that a problem may deserve investigation for reasons beyond papers and employment; that one person sometimes reaches out simply because another person is in pain. Not because I remain ignorant of the mechanisms, interests, and hormones beneath these events, but because knowledge of a mechanism does not make the event false.

This is probably what I meant by those earlier sentences: idealism at its furthest point becomes inseparable from realism; complete maturity from complete innocence; a genuine dream from the power to act. If an ideal is real, it must understand how reality operates. If maturity is real, it cannot stop at “I have seen through everything and therefore believe in nothing.” If a dream is real, it must eventually become the number of exercises completed today.

The innocence that remains after a thousand sails is not the innocence present at the beginning. The first believes because it does not yet know. The second knows and remains willing. It is not a return to the point of origin. It is arriving there after a long circle, carrying both the wounds and the abilities acquired along the way.

As Romain Rolland is so often quoted that the sentence has nearly worn smooth: true heroism consists in loving life after recognising its truth. I used to regard that as another correctly phrased piece of nonsense. Now I can feel a little of its weight.

What I should do next, then, has two sides. I must learn the operations of reality, become shrewder, acquire the ability to act, earn money, and assume responsibility. At the same time, I must avoid pickling myself entirely into an old cynic. I would like to become someone who can still be delighted by a flower, a formula, or a particular person.

An innocent person who has passed a thousand sails.

Or, to put it differently, a father who has retained the spirit of a boy.

That phrase is rather good.

Of course, this entire essay emerged while I was supposed to be solving problems. Once again, I have successfully explained why I was not working and substituted the explanation for the work itself. How the hell is it still the same recursion?

At least this version can be shorter.

Let the alarm sound. Its sounding does not mean that a tiger is present, nor that the old events must be resolved now. If I cannot solve the question, then I cannot. Read the solution, cover it, and write the answer again. If the brain insists on playing old footage, it may do so in the background. I will finish the next line first.

entry.title: The Beast's Method of Studying
entry.content:
Original version:

Recently I have been thinking about a kind of beast’s method of studying. The idea is to treat myself as a beast: stop thinking about everything, stop applying a whole moral code in order to condemn myself, and regard myself as an idiot. I am simply too stupid for this question, so I have to study it more. I am a beast that must pile up enough hours before these things can be learned properly. If I think of myself as a work animal and get on with the labour, there seems to be much less internal friction. Different parts of the brain also need to take turns; I cannot study the same subject without interruption. I have done mathematics for two days in a row and now feel close to vomiting. I need some English, politics, or a major course in the middle to slow down and recover. Sometimes philosophy should remain philosophy. Too much thought, philosophising, and summarising of methods delays actual study, just as listening to lesson after lesson without producing any output interferes with progress.

GPT-organised version:

I have recently been considering a beast’s method of studying. That means, first of all, ceasing to treat myself as a defendant before a moral court and treating myself as a beast instead.

If I cannot solve the question, it is not because my life has failed, my soul is inferior, I lack the mentality of the strong, or I have not discovered some ultimate method of learning.

I am simply bad at it.

If you are bad, practise. If you are slow, look again. If you do not know, put in the hours.

I am an idiot. I cannot solve this question, and this concept has not yet grown inside my brain. What can be done? Nothing particularly clever. Read it again. Write it again. Get it wrong tomorrow, then crawl back the day after that.

It sounds unpleasant, but the statement has a peculiar advantage: it produces much less internal friction.

Once I admit that “I am simply slow,” a great deal of additional judgment disappears. Previously, the process after a wrong answer looked something like this: get the question wrong; ask why I got it wrong again; wonder whether I am unsuited to mathematics; wonder whether I will fail the postgraduate entrance examination; and eventually arrive at existentialism, family structure, the education system, and the limitations of human civilisation.

The question remains uncorrected.

Good grief. Why am I writing a sociological elegy for another wrong answer?

Here is a rougher model:

flowchart TD
    A[做错题] --> B[我不会]
    B --> C[看答案]
    C --> D[遮住重做]
    D --> E[明天再做]

The process is not elegant. It contains no epistemological beauty and no philosophical depth. It is effective. Or perhaps it is effective precisely because it is not elegant. It leaves the brain too little room for performance and prevents my overdeveloped analytical mind from calling another meeting.

The second thing I have felt very clearly is that different parts of the brain really do need to take turns.

After two consecutive days of mathematics, I feel close to vomiting. This is not the ordinary “oh, I do not feel like working hard” kind of nausea. A particular region of the brain genuinely feels as though it has been rubbed with sandpaper. Show me another limit, derivative, or integral and I want to throw both the book and myself out of the room.

The book cannot be thrown away, of course. It was rather expensive.

So the same task cannot remain at full load indefinitely. When mathematics makes me sick, I switch to English. When English vocabulary turns numb, I switch to politics. When politics makes me feel that I am memorising a pile of correctly phrased nonsense, I switch to a major course. When that material begins to scatter, I return to basic mathematics problems.

This is not avoidance.

Avoidance means opening Bilibili and announcing, “I am taking a short break.”

Switching mental gears is still study. It simply stops one part of the brain from being squeezed to death. Even a work animal cannot pull the same cart without pause; a beast occasionally needs a different trough. The language is crude, but the fact is real.

The third rule is that philosophy should shut up for a while.

The sentence makes even me laugh. One of my strongest abilities is turning a specific problem into an abstract one. If I merely failed to review vocabulary today, I can transform the matter into the question of “whether language acquisition is essentially the subject’s domestication of a symbolic system.” It sounds cultured.

The vocabulary remains unlearned.

If I merely failed to produce solutions in mathematics, I can diagnose a “knowledge–action gap between input and output.”

The questions remain unwritten.

That is idiotic.

I am not saying that the analyses are wrong. On the contrary, most of them may be correct. That is precisely the problem. A correct idea can still delay the work, and its correctness may make the delay even easier to defend.

The same applies to lessons. The teacher explains everything smoothly; you follow without difficulty; the notes fill page after page in several carefully distinguished colours. The brain develops the illusion that the knowledge has already been mastered.

Then the video ends and the exercise sheet comes out.

Oh dear.

Who was the person who had mastered the subject a minute ago? Has he logged off?

I may therefore need a brutal rule: input that is not received by output counts only as passing traffic.

A lesson without exercises is passing traffic. A book that cannot be restated is passing traffic. Vocabulary that cannot be recalled is passing traffic. Understanding a worked solution without covering it and solving the question again is also passing traffic.

Knowledge entered through the eyes and ears, took a tourist photograph at the gate of the brain, and left. You cannot claim that it moved in merely because it once visited.

In plain language:

I am a beast.

I am a work animal.

I am a slow creature that can be built only through time and repetition.

The sentence sounds insulting, yet it contains a certain kindness. A beast does not question the meaning of life because it cannot differentiate today. A work animal does not write an existentialist essay because it pulled the mill poorly.

It continues pulling.

I do not literally want to become a beast. A human being must still think; without thought, one merely reaches a different form of numbness. At this stage, however, excessive thought is not the ability in short supply.

For me, what is scarce is the ability not to think.

At least during these hours at the desk, think a little less.

Write a little more.

If you do not know, admit that you do not know.

If one subject makes you sick, change subjects.

After input, produce output.

When you want to summarise another methodology, ask one question first: have today’s exercises been completed?

If not, this essay should not become too long either.

It is already long.

Damn it.

Sleep.

entry.title: Chapter One: Functions, Limits, and Continuity—The First Foundation of Calculus Viewed Through Epistemology
entry.content:
This is the single-chapter version of Chapter One. The same epistemological thread was later expanded into Advanced Mathematics: An Epistemological Map from Functions to Fields.

Wang Yangming said that before you looked at a flower, it and your mind both returned to silence; when you came to look at it, its colours became clear at once. The rough meaning is that the world does not enter the mind in a completely naked form. When you find a flower beautiful, the beauty does not arise merely because the flower is “objectively beautiful.” Its colour, form, light, and shadow produce an image in your mind, and your mind brightens with it.

Epistemologically speaking, human beings are continually compressing, abstracting, and modeling the objective world. We do not know the world itself directly. Instead, we compress its enormous, confused, and complicated information into models that can be understood, used, and transmitted. This is particularly evident in natural science: physics compresses motion and force into formulas; chemistry compresses changes in matter into structures; mathematics uses still more abstract symbols to compress relations themselves.

A good model cannot be excessively bulky. Ideally, it consumes little energy, remains concise and elegant, and is nevertheless useful. As for beauty, I currently suspect that it may be whatever reduces information entropy. Symmetry, unity, and the sudden appearance of a simple structure beneath a complicated phenomenon all have this quality. Upon seeing such a structure, one thinks, “So that is how it works.” This is a kind of cognitive pleasure. At a more fundamental level, perhaps the pleasure arose from the pressure for survival written into human genes?

Consider the first chapter of advanced mathematics. Calculus studies change, but before studying change we must identify the object that changes. We therefore begin with functions.

A function is a model of material, quantitative, and changing relations, represented through algebra and graphs. Reality contains many complicated relations: time and position, temperature and time, voltage and current, cost and profit. Mathematics abstracts them into a correspondence between an independent and a dependent variable: y=f(x). A complicated relation in reality is thereby compressed into a model that algebra and a graph can describe together.

We consequently study a function’s domain and range; inverse, implicit, and composite functions; and such properties as monotonicity, parity, periodicity, and boundedness. These topics are all asking what the model looks like. Over what range does it hold? Can it be understood in reverse? Can several simpler relations be composed to produce it? Does it contain symmetry, repetition, boundaries, or order?

At this point, the model called a function has been provisionally established.

A function alone, however, is insufficient. It describes a correspondence but does not adequately answer questions about approach. Often, what concerns us is not an isolated point, but the tendency shown by f(x) as (x) gradually approaches a value or travels towards infinity.

We therefore introduce the limit.

A limit enables us to study stability within a process. It is concerned not with the static result at one point, but with the destination approached by one variable while another continually draws nearer. Infinitesimals and infinities enter mathematical language in the same way. An infinitesimal is not simply a very small ordinary number; it is a quantity tending towards zero within a process. Infinity is not a number that can literally be held in one’s hand, but a tendency for function values to increase without bound.

Within the rigorous system used for postgraduate mathematics, limits are normally defined over the real numbers through the language of $\varepsilon-\delta$. For purposes of understanding, however, I find it illuminating to imagine extending the reals into the hyperreals. Hyperreal numbers offer a more intuitive picture: beyond ordinary real numbers, there seem actually to exist infinitesimal quantities “infinitely close to zero without being zero,” as well as infinite quantities greater than every ordinary real number.

As a proof, 1=3/3=3*1/3=0.33333333*3=0.99999999 is of course valid. The real-number system is continuous and complete and contains no infinitesimal gaps; infinitesimals belong to the hyperreal system. In other words, there is no gap between 0.999999999 and 1 among the reals.

This does not mean that a postgraduate examination will test hyperreal numbers. Rather, they provide a cognitive model for understanding limits. “Approach” ceases to be merely a formal definition and becomes something that can almost be handled in imagination. Standard analysis constrains approach rigorously with $\varepsilon-\delta$, whereas non-standard analysis seems to place infinitesimals directly inside the number system. The former is more rigorous and the latter more intuitive. At different levels, both help us understand the same thing.

The limit thus adds a sense of process to the model of a function. A function states what a relation is; a limit states what happens to it at a boundary, during an approach, or at infinity.

We then study the definition and properties of limits and the methods by which they are calculated. Arithmetic operations on limits, the squeeze theorem, the two important limits, and equivalent infinitesimals are all devices for treating relations of approach more effectively.

L’Hôpital’s rule and the Taylor formula can be regarded as more advanced instruments for calculating limits.

L’Hôpital’s rule is particularly interesting. Many limits are difficult because they appear in an indeterminate form such as $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$. Looking directly at the function values tells us little. L’Hôpital’s rule says that we may instead examine the rates of change of numerator and denominator. When both quantities tend towards zero or both towards infinity, we compare not the quantities themselves but the speeds at which they change.

This, too, is a form of modeling. When the original model is difficult to interpret or calculate, we change perspective from the “size of a quantity” to its “rate of change.” If two runners are both standing at the starting line at one instant, their positions do not reveal who is faster. Their velocities do.

The Taylor formula is an extreme form of model compression. A complicated function may be difficult to understand near a point, but Taylor tells us that a polynomial can approximate it:

$$f(x)\approx f(a)+f’(a)(x-a)+\frac{f’’(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2+\cdots $$

This is remarkably beautiful. Polynomials are among the most familiar and easily calculated objects in mathematics, yet near a point a complicated function can be decomposed into a constant term, a linear term, a quadratic term, a cubic term, and so on. It is as though an intricate curve were opened near one point and revealed as an ordered sequence. Adding more terms makes the model more precise; retaining only the first few makes it simpler. The aesthetic force is strong: complexity is compressed into simplicity, a curve into a polynomial, and local variation into information carried by derivatives.

L’Hôpital and Taylor are therefore more than techniques for solving examination questions. Both have an epistemological meaning. When a model is difficult to handle in its original form, we replace it with a more workable model that approaches the same object. L’Hôpital compares change through rates of change; Taylor approximates a complicated function locally through a polynomial.

Continuity and discontinuity then appear as natural applications.

If a limit studies the tendency of a function near a point, continuity asks whether that tendency meets the function’s actual value at the point. If, as $x$ approaches $x_0$, the limit of $f(x)$ equals $f(x_0)$, the function is continuous there.

Continuity means that the model does not break locally. Its tendency and value connect. A discontinuity means that the connection has failed: perhaps a removable point has not been filled; perhaps the left and right sides move towards different values; perhaps the function rushes towards infinity; or perhaps it oscillates without settling.

Seen in this way, the first chapter of advanced mathematics does not merely pile functions, limits, and continuity together. It establishes the most basic cognitive model of calculus. First, functions compress relations found in reality. Limits then describe the tendencies of those relations during a process of approach. Infinitesimals, infinities, and the intuitive picture of hyperreal numbers help us imagine such tendencies. Methods of calculation allow us to handle them, and continuity finally judges whether the local model remains stable and joined together.

This is my present understanding: mathematics does not move away from the world. It recompresses the world in a form that consumes less energy and is more concise and beautiful. A function models a relation; a limit models a tendency; L’Hôpital models comparison through rates of change; Taylor models local approximation; and continuity models stability. The whole structure of calculus begins here.

entry.title: Fitness Research Report
entry.content:
This is a comprehensive research report on natural fitness, ranging from exercise physiology and standards of lean-muscular aesthetics to physical assessment, training systems, and nutritional strategies. The main text remains available as a Markdown version for online reading, while a compiled PDF can be downloaded below and at the end of the article.

Source note: The material comes from a personal fitness research project, and the PDF is a compiled product.

PDF Download

  • Click to Download the PDF

Reading Guide

This report consists of eleven chapters and an appendix, covering the complete chain from basic physiology to practical training. Chapters One to Three establish the theoretical and conceptual foundations; Chapters Four and Five define aesthetic standards and methods of assessment; Chapters Six to Eight move into practical training; Chapters Nine to Eleven discuss nutrition, integration with daily life, and advanced development.

Fitness Research Report

Fitness Research Report

From Physiology to Aesthetics · From Assessment to Training · From Nutrition to Life

July 2026

Chapter One: Exercise Physiology and Medical Foundations

Before formally beginning a fitness journey, understanding how the body’s precise machinery operates is far more important than lifting weights blindly.

1.1 Anatomy of the Musculoskeletal System

The seven major muscle groups are the chest (pectoralis major), back (latissimus dorsi and trapezius), shoulders (the anterior, lateral, and posterior heads of the deltoid), arms (biceps and triceps), legs (quadriceps, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus), core (rectus abdominis and external obliques), and forearms.

Types of Muscle Fibre

Type Contraction Speed Resistance to Fatigue Suitable Training
Type I (slow-twitch) Slow High Endurance training
Type IIa (intermediate) Fast Medium Combined strength and endurance
Type IIx (explosive) Extremely fast Low Heavy strength work and explosive power

1.2 Molecular Mechanisms of Muscle Growth

The Three Principal Drivers of Hypertrophy

  1. Mechanical tension—the strongest signal: heavy compound movements directly activate mechanoreceptors
  2. Metabolic stress—the science behind the pump: high-repetition training accumulates metabolic waste and triggers a cellular-swelling response
  3. Muscle damage—reconstruction produces growth: training creates microscopic tears; after supercompensation, the muscle fibres become thicker and stronger

1.3 Energy Metabolism Systems

Energy System Duration Typical Application
ATP-CP system 6-10 seconds Maximum loads and sprinting
Glycolytic system 30-90 seconds Strength training at 8-15RM
Aerobic oxidative system Several minutes to several hours Low-intensity aerobic exercise

1.4 The Endocrine System

  • Testosterone: the king of anabolic hormones. It rises briefly after heavy compound movements
  • Growth hormone and IGF-1: promote fat breakdown and tissue repair
  • Cortisol: a double-edged sword. A persistently high level → muscle breakdown and fat accumulation
  • Insulin: the manager of nutrient distribution. Greater sensitivity means a lower tendency to store fat

1.5 Adaptation of the Nervous System

During the first month of strength gains, the muscles have not yet grown larger, but have already become stronger—this is neural adaptation.

The mind-muscle connection has a scientific basis—when attention is concentrated upon the target muscle, activation measured by EMG may rise by 10-20%.

Chapter Two: The Underlying Logic of the Lean-Muscular Male Physique

2.1 Definition and Measurement

Body-Fat Range: 10-14%

Body-Fat Range Visual Appearance
10-12% Abdominal definition is visible; facial contours are clear
12-14% Abdominal muscles are faintly visible; clothes produce the best appearance
15-18% Abdominal definition is unclear, but the body looks generally solid

A body-fat percentage below 10% carries costs including reduced testosterone and weaker immunity.

Reference Muscle Mass for a 175 cm Man

A fat-free mass index, or FFMI, of approximately 19-20; upper-arm circumference of 35-38 cm; chest circumference of 95-100 cm.

2.2 Aesthetics of Key Proportions

The V-shaped physique and shoulder-to-waist ratio: a ratio above 1.6 produces an obvious inverted triangle. Increasing shoulder width by 4-5 cm while keeping the waist between 72 and 76 cm is sufficient to reach this standard.

The ideal head-to-shoulder ratio is 2.5-3.0:1. East Asian men commonly measure 2.1-2.4, so shoulder training offers an exceptionally high return.

2.3 Nature versus Training

The skeleton and the shape of muscle bellies are genetically determined, but most people remain far below their limits.

Body-fat percentage, muscular circumference, posture, flexibility, and neuromuscular efficiency can all be changed.

2.4 Metabolic Advantages

A lean-muscular physique possesses greater insulin sensitivity, so carbohydrates enter muscle glycogen stores in preference to fat storage.

Chapter Three: Self-Assessment of Constitution, Body Type, and Posture

3.1 Classification of Body Types

Body Type Characteristics Difficulty of Gaining Muscle
Ectomorph (long and lean) Narrow shoulders and rapid metabolism Difficult
Mesomorph (well proportioned) Broad shoulders and narrow waist Easy
Endomorph (rounded) Broad hips and a tendency to store fat Easy to gain muscle but difficult to lose fat

3.2 Estimating Body-Fat Percentage

Visual comparison + skinfold callipers + bioelectrical impedance—cross-check the result through several methods.

3.3 Postural Assessment

Upper crossed syndrome (rounded shoulders, forward head, and hunched back): stretch the chest and strengthen the upper back.

Lower crossed syndrome (anterior/posterior pelvic tilt): for anterior tilt, stretch the iliopsoas and strengthen the glutes and abdominal muscles; for posterior tilt, stretch the hamstrings and strengthen the iliopsoas.

Order of priority in postural correction: breathing pattern → pelvic position → thoracic mobility → scapular stability.

Chapter Four: Aesthetic Standards for a Lean-Muscular Male Physique—A Detailed Guide by Body Part

4.1 Shoulders—Three-Dimensional Capped Deltoids

The ideal ratio among the anterior, lateral, and posterior heads of the deltoid is 1:1.5:1. The lateral head determines shoulder width, while the posterior head must not be neglected.

4.2 Chest—Square Rather than Rounded

The upper chest is the first priority: it determines the visual effect around the collar of a T-shirt. Avoid excessive development of the lower chest.

4.3 Back—The V-Shaped Inverted Triangle
