01 — A Detailed Guide to the Transmission Protocol: Framing Messages in a TCP Stream

Intended readers: Electronic Information Engineering students with basic Python knowledge.
This section centers on network_protocol.py and network_transfer.py.

I. Why Do We Need a Custom Protocol?

1.1 TCP Is a Stream, Not a Sequence of Messages

TCP is a stream protocol: it guarantees that bytes arrive in order, but does not guarantee that one call to recv() returns exactly one complete message.

For example, suppose the sender calls send() twice:

The receiver may obtain 'HelloWorld' in one call to recv(), or it may receive 'Hel', 'loW', and 'orld' in three separate calls.

These phenomena are commonly called packet sticking and packet splitting. To handle them, we define an application-layer protocol above TCP that tells the receiver where each message begins and ends.

1.2 Our System’s Solution

Our system addresses TCP framing in two ways:

Technique Description
Fixed-length header + variable-length body Send a fixed-size header containing the subsequent data length, then send the data
Special terminator Append \r\n to control messages as a boundary

Both methods are classic techniques in network programming.

II. Protocol Constants and Magic Numbers

2.1 The Magic Number 0xDEAD

A magic number is a fixed identifying value. The sender writes 0xDEAD into the file header, and the receiver checks it first. A mismatch indicates that the data is corrupted or does not belong to this protocol, so an error is raised immediately.

The design principle is to choose an uncommon value—0xDEAD is not an ordinary ASCII character—as a gatekeeper that filters out irrelevant data.

2.2 Chunk Size: CHUNK_SIZE

Each transmission contains 64 KB. Why not use larger chunks?

  • Too large: consumes excessive memory and forces substantial retransmission after even a small packet loss.
  • Too small: frequent send and recv calls increase system-call overhead.
  • 64 KB is a practical choice that balances throughput against latency.

2.3 Control Messages

Control messages are fixed four-byte codes:

Constant Bytes Meaning
MSG_READY REDY The server is ready to receive
MSG_ACCEPT ACPT The server accepts the file metadata
MSG_REJECT RJCT The server rejects the transfer, followed by a reason
MSG_ACK ACK\x00 Acknowledges receipt of one chunk
MSG_DONE DONE The entire transfer is complete

Why four bytes? That is exactly the size of a 32-bit integer, making the codes convenient to pack with struct.

III. Packing and Unpacking Data

3.1 A Quick Look at the struct Module

struct is a built-in Python module that converts between Python values and C-style binary bytes.

Quick reference for format characters:

Character C Type Python Type Size
I unsigned int int 4 bytes
B unsigned char int 1 byte
H unsigned short int 2 bytes
s char[] bytes Variable

Big-endian order places the most significant byte first. Network protocols generally use big-endian, also called network byte order, so that different CPU architectures interpret data consistently.

3.2 File Header: pack_header / unpack_header

Packing (Sender)

Field-by-field interpretation:

Field Format Bytes Description
PROTO_MAGIC >I 4 Magic number for validation
file_type B 1 0x01 = ordinary file; 0x02 = image
len(name_bytes) I 4 Byte length of the filename
total_size I 4 Total file size in bytes
name_bytes {N}s N Filename
ext_bytes 256s 256 Extension in a fixed 256-byte field

Why reserve a fixed 256 bytes for the extension? It allows the receiver to parse the field directly without knowing the filename length in advance. This is a typical use of a fixed-length field.

Unpacking (Receiver)

Line-by-line interpretation:

  1. HEADER_FIXED_SIZE = 4 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 13 — total bytes occupied by the first four fixed-length fields.
  2. Unpack the fixed portion first to obtain the magic number, file type, filename length, and total size.
  3. Validate the magic number; a mismatch raises an error as the protocol’s first line of defense.
  4. Read the name dynamically according to name_len, the variable-length portion.
  5. Read the extension as a fixed 256-byte field, then strip trailing \x00 padding with .rstrip(b"\x00").
  6. Return a dictionary so callers can access values by field name.

3.3 Data Chunks: pack_chunk / unpack_chunk

A large file is divided into 64 KB chunks and sent sequentially, with each chunk carrying its own header.

Format: >I I {N}s

Field Bytes Description
seq (sequence number) 4 Chunk number, starting from 0
len(data) (data length) 4 Actual length of this chunk
data (payload) N The data itself

Unpacking:

The receiver first reads the 8-byte header (CHUNK_HEADER_SIZE = 8) to obtain chunk_len, and then reads a payload of exactly chunk_len bytes.

3.4 Control Messages: pack_control / unpack_control

Control messages use the format “length prefix + message body + terminator”:

Three components:

  1. Four-byte length prefix: the total body length packed with >I.
  2. Message body (4 + N bytes): a four-byte message code such as REDY, followed by an optional payload.
  3. Terminator \r\n: two bytes indicating the end of the message.

Why include a terminator? It provides a second safeguard for message boundaries. Even if the length prefix is corrupted, the receiver can attempt to resynchronize at \r\n.

IV. Transfer Engine: The TransferProgress Class

Core functions:

  • Track the number of bytes transferred.
  • Calculate the percentage (pct).
  • Calculate the instantaneous rate (rate = transferred bytes / elapsed time).
  • Estimate the remaining time (remaining = untransferred bytes / rate).
  • Send progress information to the UI through a callback.

Progress-callback type signature:

V. Complete Sending Workflow: send_file

Sequence Diagram

Step-by-Step Interpretation

Internally, _recv_control calls _recv_exact to ensure that one complete control message is received. Anything other than REDY indicates an abnormal server state and raises an error.

Use sendall rather than send: send may transmit only part of the data, while sendall ensures that all of it is sent.

The server may accept or reject the file based on its name, type, and other metadata. A rejection includes explanatory text.

Key points:

  • Send 64 KB (CHUNK_SIZE) at a time.
  • Wait for an ACK after every chunk, a classic Stop-and-Wait protocol.
  • Update progress after receiving the ACK.
  • Increment seq from zero to detect loss or reordering.

Send an empty chunk with a data length of zero as the end marker, a common technique in TCP transmission.

VI. Complete Receiving Workflow: receive_file

Step-by-Step Interpretation

First read the 13-byte fixed portion (4+1+4+4) and validate the magic number.

Then read the filename dynamically according to name_len, followed by the fixed 256-byte extension field.

Core Receiver Logic

  1. Send REDY to indicate readiness.
  2. Parse the header to obtain file metadata.
  3. Reply with ACCEPT to accept the file.
  4. Receive chunks in a loop, replying with ACK to each.
  5. Exit the loop upon an empty chunk (chunk_len == 0).
  6. Calculate the SHA256 hash of the received data and include it in the DONE message.

VII. Helper Function: _recv_exact

This is the most fundamental function in the entire protocol. TCP’s recv(n) does not guarantee that it will return n bytes in one call, so the function must loop until all bytes have arrived.

Imagine that the receiver expects 100 bytes but TCP delivers only 40. _recv_exact continues waiting until the complete 100 bytes have been accumulated.

VIII. Summary

Concept Implementation in This System

Fixed-length header First 13 bytes of header fixed; extension fixed at 256 bytes
Length prefix Control messages begin with a four-byte length
Chunked transmission 64 KB per chunk, each with a sequence number
Stop-and-Wait acknowledgment Wait for ACK before sending the next chunk
Terminator Control messages end in \r\n

Integrity check DONE message includes SHA256

02 — A Detailed Guide to C/S Architecture: Server–Client Handshake and Encrypted Transmission

Intended readers: Electronic Information Engineering students with basic Python knowledge.

I. What Is C/S Architecture?

Client–Server (C/S) architecture is the most common model for network applications:

  • The server runs continuously, waits for connections, and provides a service.
  • The client initiates a connection and requests that service.

Architecture Diagram

II. The Server

2.1 Class Structure Overview

The server’s core responsibilities are to:

  1. manage RSA keys through generation, import, and export;
  2. create a TCP server and listen on a port;
  3. accept client connections;
  4. receive encrypted data, decrypt it automatically, and save it.

2.2 Standard Socket-Server Workflow

These five steps form the standard workflow of every TCP server:

Step API Description
① socket() Create a socket
② setsockopt() Set SO_REUSEADDR to avoid address-in-use errors
③ bind() Bind to an IP address and port
④ listen() Begin listening and waiting for connections
⑤ accept() Accept a client connection (blocking)

Key parameters:

  • AF_INET: use IPv4 addresses.
  • SOCK_STREAM: use TCP, a reliable connection-oriented protocol.
  • "0.0.0.0": bind to every network interface so that any device on the LAN can connect.
  • SO_REUSEADDR: allow rapid restarts without being blocked by an “address already in use” error.

2.3 Accepting Connections with Multiple Threads

Why set a timeout on accept()?

  • Without a timeout, accept() blocks forever and cannot respond to the “Stop Service” button.
  • A one-second timeout wakes it once per second to check the _running flag.

Why handle accepted connections with threads?

  • Run the accept loop in a separate thread.
  • After each new connection is accepted, use root.after(0, ...) to process it on the main thread.
  • This prevents the GUI from freezing.

The client needs only three steps: create a socket → connect → configure the timeout.

Why cancel the timeout after a successful connection?

  • The connection timeout also affects later recv calls; without cancellation, a long interval without incoming data could terminate the connection.

Principles of Diffusion Models

Intended readers: EE students with no prior background

Prerequisites: deep-learning fundamentals, including neural networks and basic PyTorch concepts

1. What Is a Diffusion Model?

An Analogy: Carving a Statue from Marble

Imagine that you have a block of pure white marble (pure noise) and want to carve it into an exquisite statue (a generated image).

A traditional generative model tries to teach you how to carve the statue stroke by stroke. This is extremely difficult because every cut must be planned precisely.

A diffusion model takes the opposite approach:

  1. Begin with an existing statue and keep covering it with clay until its shape disappears into an unrecognizable block.
  2. Then learn how to remove the added clay one step at a time and recover the statue.

You may ask, “Why destroy it before restoring it? Isn’t that needlessly complicated?”

The answer is that learning to remove clay is much easier than learning to carve directly. How much clay to remove and where to remove it follow learnable patterns. The model only needs to estimate how much “clay” separates the current state from the final statue.

Core Intuition

Concept Everyday Analogy
Original image An exquisite statue
Forward process (adding noise) Cover the statue with increasingly thick clay
Pure noise A marble block whose shape is entirely hidden
Reverse process (denoising) Remove clay layer by layer to recover the statue
Training Observe the full “add clay → remove clay” process and learn to judge the current state
Generation (inference) Begin with a plain block and remove imaginary “clay” step by step

2. Forward Process: Adding Noise Step by Step

The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to an image until it becomes pure noise.

Mathematical Description (Intense, but Do Not Worry)

Suppose we have an original image $x_0$, such as a photograph of a kitten.

At each step $t$, we add a small amount of Gaussian noise and obtain $x_t$:

$$x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t} \cdot x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t} \cdot \epsilon$$

where:

  • $x_t$ is the image after noise has been added at step $t$;
  • $\beta_t$ is a small number such as 0.0001 that controls the amount of noise added at each step;
  • $\epsilon$ is random noise sampled from the standard Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$;
  • $t$ ranges from 1 to $T$, usually with $T = 1000$.

For EE students: this is essentially a process of low-pass filtering plus noise injection. Each step slightly lowers the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). After 1,000 steps, the SNR approaches zero and the image is completely overwhelmed by noise.

An Important Property

Because each step adds only a small amount of noise and Gaussian noise is additive—the sum of Gaussian variables is still Gaussian—we can calculate the result at any step $t$ directly:

$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \cdot x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \cdot \epsilon$$

Here, $\bar{\alpha}_t$ is the cumulative product of coefficients over the first $t$ steps. As $t$ grows, $\bar{\alpha}_t$ approaches zero and $x_t$ approaches pure noise.

3. Reverse Process: Denoising Step by Step (The Core)

The forward process is simple: repeatedly add noise.

The reverse process is the soul of a diffusion model. We train a neural network to recover the original image from noise.

Mathematical Description

The central formula of the reverse process is:

$$x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \left( x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t}} \cdot \epsilon\theta(x_t, t) \right) + \sigma_t \cdot z$$

Does it look complicated? Let us break it down:

Symbol Meaning Intuitive Interpretation
$x_t$ Current noisy image The statue currently covered in clay
$\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ Noise predicted by the neural network The network says, “This is what the current clay layer looks like”
$\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}}$ Denoising scale factor “How thick a layer should be removed this time”
$\sigma_t \cdot z$ Random perturbation term Add slight randomness during denoising to avoid rigidity
$x_{t-1}$ Denoised image The statue after one layer of clay is removed

What Does the Neural Network Do?

The neural network $\epsilon_\theta$, usually a UNet, receives two inputs:

  1. the current noisy image $x_t$, such as a 512×512×3 noisy image;
  2. the current time step $t$, which tells the network where it is in the process because different steps require different denoising strengths.

Its output is the predicted noise $\epsilon$, with the same dimensions as the input image.

The denoising formula for each layer can be understood as:

$$\text{去噪后图像} = \text{当前图像} - \text{预测噪声} \times \text{缩放系数}$$

4. Training Process

Preparing the Training Data

Suppose we have one million cat images.

For each image $x_0$:

  1. randomly select a time step $t$ from 1 to 1000;
  2. use the forward-process formula to calculate $x_t$ directly from $x_0$, without traversing every intermediate step;
  3. record the actual noise $\epsilon$ that was added.

Training Objective

Make the network’s predicted noise $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ as close as possible to the actual noise $\epsilon$:

$$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}{x_0, \epsilon, t} \left[ |\epsilon - \epsilon\theta(x_t, t)|^2 \right]$$

In plain language: minimize the average squared difference between the noise predicted by the network and the noise actually added.

For EE students: this is essentially a minimum mean-square error (MMSE) estimation problem. The neural network is learning to become an optimal noise estimator.

Training Pseudocode

5. Inference (Generation) Process

After training, a new image is generated as follows:

Moving from $T=1000$ down to $t=0$, each step removes a small amount of predicted noise until a clear image emerges.

6. DDPM vs DDIM: Trading Speed Against Slowness

DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models)

  • The original diffusion model, requiring 1,000 steps.
  • Every step includes the random perturbation $\sigma_t \cdot z$.
  • Generation quality is high, but the method is very slow, requiring 1,000 neural-network evaluations for one image.
  • Analogy: carve carefully, one cut at a time, with caution at every step.

DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models)

  • Supports skipping sampling steps, perhaps using only 20–50 steps.
  • Removes the random perturbation term and becomes a deterministic generation process.
  • Runs 20–50 times faster with almost no loss in quality.
  • Analogy: an experienced sculptor can make bolder cuts, removing more at every step.

Comparison

Property DDPM DDIM
Steps 1000 20–100 (configurable)
Speed Slow Fast
Quality High Nearly as high
Deterministic No Yes
Practical use Training Inference

In practical Stable Diffusion inference, a DDIM sampler commonly generates a high-quality image in 25–50 steps.

7. Quick Reference for Key Mathematical Concepts (EE-Friendly)

Concept Mathematical Expression EE Analogy
Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ The most common noise model; thermal noise is Gaussian
Markov chain $P(x_t x_{t-1}, …, x_0) = P(x_t
SNR $\frac{\bar{\alpha}_t}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}$ Signal power/noise power; SNR falls as $t$ increases
MSE loss $|\epsilon - \hat{\epsilon}|^2$ Minimization of error energy
Reparameterization trick $x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon$ Turn random sampling into a differentiable deterministic operation

8. Summary

Question Answer
What is the core idea of a diffusion model? First learn to add noise, then learn to remove it; generate through denoising
Why can a diffusion model generate images? It learns to recover meaningful image structure gradually from pure noise
Is the forward process difficult? No; it repeatedly adds Gaussian noise, and any step can be calculated directly
Who performs the reverse process? A UNet neural network predicts the noise at each step
Are 1,000 steps necessary? During training, yes; during inference, DDIM can skip steps and needs only 20–50
What advantage do EE students have? Gaussian noise, SNR, Markov chains, and MMSE estimation already appear in undergraduate EE courses

Next Step

After understanding the basic principles of diffusion models, we turn to Stable Diffusion and examine how this enormous model can run with limited computational resources.

A Detailed Guide to Stable Diffusion

Intended readers: EE students with no prior background

Prerequisites: principles of diffusion models and Python fundamentals

Reference code: txsc/backend/pipeline.py and txsc/backend/main.py

1. Why Do We Need Stable Diffusion?

The previous section explained how diffusion models generate images by progressively removing noise.

However, there is a practical problem: original diffusion models operate directly in pixel space, such as a 512×512×3 RGB image. Consequently:

  • every denoising step must process 786,432 pixel values (512×512×3);
  • 1,000 steps require enormous computation;
  • an ordinary consumer GPU cannot handle the workload efficiently.

Stable Diffusion, or SD, solves this problem through its core innovation: first compress the image into latent space with a VAE, perform diffusion there, and then decode the result back into an image.

An Analogy: Shipping a Package

Imagine shipping an entire encyclopedia set, representing the original image.

  • An ordinary diffusion model moves the entire set directly: heavy and slow.
  • Stable Diffusion scans the books, compresses them into a ZIP archive (encoding into latent space), transfers the ZIP (latent-space diffusion), then extracts and prints it at the destination (decoding back to an image).

The ZIP file is far smaller than the original books and much faster to transfer. This is SD’s central idea.

2. Overall Architecture: Three Main Components

Stable Diffusion consists of three core components:

Component 1: VAE (Variational Autoencoder) — Image Compression and Decompression

Role Function Intuitive Interpretation
VAE encoder Compress a 512×512×3 image into a 64×64×4 latent representation Compress a high-resolution photo into a “thumbnail + detail description”
VAE decoder Restore a 64×64×4 latent representation to a 512×512×3 image Reconstruct a high-resolution photo from the “thumbnail + detail description”

Key figure: the compression ratio is approximately 48:1 (512×512×3 ÷ 64×64×4 = 48).

For EE students: a VAE resembles a lossy codec, such as JPEG compression. The encoder extracts the image’s principal features and discards unimportant details, while the decoder reconstructs the image from those features. The lost information is largely imperceptible visually.

Component 2: UNet — The Latent-Space Denoising Engine

UNet is the neural network that actually performs denoising. Its structural features include:

  • an encoder–decoder architecture that first downsamples to extract features and then upsamples to restore dimensions;
  • skip connections that pass encoder features directly to corresponding decoder layers, preserving detail;
  • cross-attention layers that receive CLIP text embeddings, telling the network what noise to remove and what content to retain.

In SD, both the input and output of UNet are 64×64×4, the latent-space dimensions, and the network has roughly 860 million parameters.

Component 3: CLIP Text Encoder — Understanding Text Prompts

CLIP, or Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training, is a contrastive text–image learning model.

It converts user text such as “a cute cat” into a 77×768 vector containing the text’s semantic information.

For EE students: CLIP resembles an encoder that maps text into semantic space. Just as a Fourier transform maps a time-domain signal into the frequency domain, CLIP maps text into a “semantic domain.” “Cat” lies closer to “dog” than to “car” in that space.

During SD generation, CLIP’s output is injected into UNet through cross-attention, telling it that the noise being removed should reveal the shape of a cat.

3. Module-by-Module Code Analysis

We now turn to the actual code in pipeline.py.

3.1 Device Detection: detect_device()

Line-by-line explanation:

Line Purpose
torch.cuda.is_available() Check whether an NVIDIA GPU is available; CUDA is NVIDIA’s GPU computing platform
torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0) Obtain properties of the first GPU, such as model and memory
total / 1e9 Convert bytes to GB (1e9 ≈ 1 GB)
Return "cuda" or "cpu" Tell subsequent code where to run

Why do this? SD requires enormous computation. A GPU is 10–50 times faster than a CPU. If an NVIDIA GPU is available, use it; otherwise, fall back to the much slower CPU.

3.2 Loading the Model: load_pipeline()

Key concepts:

Concept Explanation
torch.float16 Half-precision floats: halve VRAM usage and run faster; available on GPUs
torch.float32 Single-precision floats: higher precision but more memory; used on CPUs
AutoPipelineForText2Image An automatic pipeline class in Hugging Face diffusers that detects the model type
model_id A string containing either a local path or a Hugging Face repository name
use_safetensors=True Use the safer and faster safetensors model format rather than traditional pickle
safety_checker=None Disable the NSFW safety checker to save memory
enable_model_cpu_offload() GPU-memory optimization: move inactive modules to CPU memory and return them to the GPU when needed
enable_attention_slicing() Memory optimization: compute attention in slices to reduce peak VRAM usage

Model source: _resolve_model() in main.py defines the loading order:

  1. Prefer the path specified by the SD_MODEL environment variable.
  2. Next, check the local models/AI-ModelScope/stable-diffusion-v1-5 directory.
  3. Finally, fall back to the Hugging Face repository runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5.

3.3 Core Generation: generate()

Parameters in detail:

Parameter Description Typical Value
prompt Positive prompt: content you want "a cute cat"
negative_prompt Negative prompt: content you do not want "blurry, low quality"
num_inference_steps Number of denoising steps 20–50 with DDIM, far fewer than DDPM
guidance_scale Guidance strength, the CFG (Classifier-Free Guidance) scale 7.5
width/height Image dimensions, each a multiple of 8 512×512
seed Random seed; fixing it makes results reproducible 42

Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) scale:

$$ \text{预测噪声} = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing) + g \cdot (\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \text{prompt}) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing)) $$

  • At $g=1$: follow the text prompt without extra guidance.
  • At $g=7.5$, the typical value: substantially strengthen the prompt’s influence.
  • At $g>15$: oversaturation and image distortion may appear.

Intuitive interpretation: CFG controls how obedient the model is. At $g=7.5$, the model works harder to match the text description. Mathematically, this pushes conditional generation toward high-probability regions of the distribution.

Random-seed mechanism:

  • Same seed + same prompt = exactly the same output.
  • Different seed = different random-noise initialization = different output.
  • The seed controls the initial noise, or starting point; the model determines the subsequent denoising path.

For EE students: a seed is the initial value of a pseudorandom number generator. The same seed produces the same noise sequence and therefore exactly the same generated result under identical prompts, steps, and parameters. This is valuable in controlled experiments.

torch.inference_mode():

This context manager is crucial for faster inference. It:

  • disables gradient computation, which inference does not need, saving memory;
  • prevents construction of the Autograd graph;
  • enables faster implementations for certain operations.

For EE students: this resembles turning off unnecessary measuring instruments while debugging a circuit, reducing load and allowing the system to run faster.

3.4 Callback Wrapper: Adapting to Different diffusers Versions

Why wrap the callback?

The diffusers library changed its callback signature across versions:

Version Callback Signature
Older (< 0.32) callback(step, timestep, latents)
Newer (>= 0.32) callback(pipeline, step, timestep, callback_kwargs)

The newer callback must return the callback_kwargs dictionary and receives the pipeline object itself. The wrapper therefore:

  1. accepts all parameters in the new callback format;
  2. extracts step and timestep for the external callback;
  3. returns callback_kwargs, without which the pipeline raises an error.

4. REST API Architecture (from main.py)

API Endpoint Overview

Method Path Function Returns
GET /health Health check Model status and device information
POST /generate Submit a generation task task_id
GET /status/{task_id} Query task progress Status + progress percentage
GET /result/{task_id} Obtain the generated result Status + Base64 image

Request and Response Formats

POST /generate request body:

GET /result/{task_id} response:

Pydantic Model: Input Validation

Pydantic automatically handles:

  • type checking, ensuring that steps is an integer and guidance a float;
  • default values, allowing the user to supply only prompt;
  • input validation, automatically returning a 422 error for invalid data.

5. Asynchronous Task Processing: Why Not Return Directly?

Problem: Model Inference Is Slow

Generating one 512×512 image takes:

  • about 5–10 seconds on an RTX 3060 GPU;
  • about 2–5 minutes on a CPU.

If the server waits for generation to finish before responding, the front end remains stuck on a loading indicator, producing a poor user experience.

Solution: An Asynchronous Task Queue

Thread Safety: tasks_lock

Why is a lock necessary?

The main FastAPI request thread and background thread may read and write the tasks dictionary simultaneously. Without a lock:

  • a data race may occur when two threads write the same key, corrupting data;
  • a dirty read may occur when one thread reads incomplete data while another is writing.

threading.Lock ensures that only one thread can access tasks at a time.

For EE students: this resembles bus arbitration. Multiple devices—CPU cores or threads—share the same RAM and need mutual exclusion to prevent conflicting simultaneous writes.

Progress-Reporting Mechanism

Data flow:

Result Storage

After generation, the result is stored in memory as a Base64-encoded string:

What is Base64? It encodes binary data such as an image as plain ASCII text. The image can then be embedded directly in a JSON response for convenient front-end/back-end transmission.

6. Architectural Issues in Progress Callbacks

Current Approach: Synchronous Multithreading + Polling

Problem Analysis

Problem Description Impact
Polling delay The front end queries once per second, causing up to one second of delay Progress is not fully real-time
Unnecessary traffic Requests repeat even when progress is unchanged Wasted bandwidth
Memory growth Every result remains in tasks and is never cleaned up Long-running service may exhaust memory
Single point of failure Every task is lost when the service restarts In-progress generations become invalid

A Better Approach: WebSocket

WebSocket is a full-duplex communication protocol that allows the server to push progress proactively to the front end:

Advantages: real-time updates, lower traffic, and server-side control.

Why does the current system not use WebSocket? Simplicity is the priority. REST API + polling is easier to understand and implement, while WebSocket adds deployment complexity through additional connection management.

7. Overall Workflow Summary

8. Quick Reference for EE Students

Concept Explanation
Latent space A low-dimensional representation resembling compressed sensing—the compressed “essence” of an image
VAE Similar to a lossy image codec such as JPEG, but differentiable and trainable
CLIP An encoder from text to semantic vectors, as though text were “modulated” onto a semantic carrier
Cross-attention Similar to beamforming in wireless communication, directing textual information into specific image regions
CFG A gain factor controlling obedience to the prompt, like gain in a feedback-control system
Seed A pseudorandom seed that ensures reproducibility
DDIM step skipping Downsampling in the spatiotemporal domain, making large jumps rather than taking every step
Base64 encoding Encode binary images as text for transport in JSON

Next Step

After understanding SD’s architecture and code, proceed to the FastAPI back end and examine the complete design and deployment of a web back end.

A Detailed Guide to the FastAPI Back End

Starts from first principles and is suitable for EE students with no prior web-back-end experience

1. What Is a Web Back End?

In One Sentence

A web back end is “a program running on a server that waits for requests and returns data.”

Analogy

The back end resembles a restaurant kitchen: the front end is the waiter who presents the menu, the back end is the chef who prepares the food, and the API is the menu specifying what can be ordered.

2. Our Back-End Architecture

Why Use Asynchronous Tasks?

SD takes several seconds to generate an image. Rather than making the user wait idly, the server returns a task_id first and the front end polls for progress.

3. Core Code Analysis

3.1 Creating the Application

3.2 Loading the Model at Startup

@app.on_event("startup") runs automatically when the server starts. It loads the model once and reuses it for subsequent requests.

3.3 Request Format

Pydantic automatically performs type checking, supplies defaults, and generates API documentation.

3.4 Task-Submission API

The key is to return the task ID immediately while actual inference runs in a background thread.

3.5 Progress and Result Queries

3.6 Background Inference

4. Key Design Decisions

Problem Solution Reason
Avoid blocking during long inference threading.Thread Run in the background and return immediately
Thread safety threading.Lock Protect the shared tasks dictionary
Progress feedback Polling at 500 ms intervals Simpler than WebSocket
Image transmission Base64 data URL No separate file server required

5. Starting the Server

Visit http://localhost:8000/docs to view the automatically generated API documentation.

Next Step

After studying the back end, read the React Front-End Fundamentals section to understand how the front end interacts with it.

React Front-End Fundamentals

Starts from first principles and is suitable for EE students with no prior front-end-development experience

1. What Is a Front End?

The front end is “the interface that users see directly, click, and operate.”

Page Layout

The control panel for parameter input appears on the left, while the generated result appears on the right.

2. Core React Concepts

2.1 Components

A page is assembled from components like a Lego model:

A component is a function that returns HTML:

2.2 State

State is data that changes over time.

2.3 Props

Props are data passed from a parent component to a child component:

3. The Main App.tsx Component

result && (...) displays the right-hand panel only when result is not empty.

4. ImageGenerator and Control Parameters

State for Every Parameter

Calling the Back End

Progress Bar

5. API Client (client.ts)

Complete interaction flow:

6. Front-End Technology Stack

Technology Purpose
React 19 Component-based UI framework
TypeScript Type-safe JavaScript
Vite Development server and build tool
Tailwind CSS Styling written directly through className="..."
lucide-react Icon library

Next Step

You now understand the complete AIGC system from back end to front end. You can return to the Stable Diffusion section and revisit the discussion of model inference.

entry.title: Signals and Systems: A First-Principles Primer
entry.content:
This is a curated tutorial for absolute beginners to quickly grasp the overall structure of the subject. The main text is kept as a Markdown web-reading version, with a compiled PDF available for download below and at the end.

Source note: Derived from the Markdown of the Signals and Systems First-Principles Primer; the PDF is the compiled output.

PDF Download

  • Click to download PDF

How to Read This

The goal of this kind of tutorial is not to replace a textbook, nor to write out every proof in maximum detail. It is first to build the backbone of a course or a field: what it studies, how the common concepts connect, roughly what problems the formulas are solving, and where you should fill in the gaps afterwards.

Signals and Systems: A First-Principles Primer

Starting from zero, using the most basic ideas, to build the entire knowledge system of signals and systems.

How This Primer Is Written

Traditional textbooks start from definitions. This primer starts from problems.

Each chapter tackles one core problem. It begins with “why do we need this thing” and gradually derives the whole theory from there. No calculus background is required (each step is explained). All you need is the most basic logical thinking.

A Five-Step Intellectual Journey

Contents

Part Core Question Approach
Part 1 What is a signal? What is a system? Start with everyday examples like thermometers and speakers
Part 2 How do you see the “ingredients” of a signal? Fourier: break a signal into sine waves of different frequencies
Part 3 How do you analyze the “character” of a system? Laplace: turn differential equations into algebraic equations
Part 4 How does a computer process signals? Sampling + difference equations + the Z-transform
Part 5 How does it all fit together? A comparison and unification of the four transforms

Reading Advice

  • First pass: read only the “core idea” (bold text) and the “one-sentence summary” in each part
  • Second pass: read the “why” sections
  • Third pass: work through the derivations and examples

Output Files

File Contents
part1_信号是什么.md Signals & Systems basic concepts
part2_分解的魔法.md Fourier series -> Fourier transform
part3_推广变换.md Laplace transform
part4_离散世界.md Discrete time + Z-transform
part5_统一视角.md Comparison of the four transforms + summary

Part 1: What Is a Signal? What Is a System?

Core question: The world is full of change. How do we describe it? How do we use it?

Goal: Build an intuitive worldview of signals and systems — no calculus required, only curiosity.

Before We Begin: Why Are You Taking This Course?

Imagine you are listening to music on your phone — the electrical signal in the phone becomes sound and reaches your ear; you say “Hey Siri,” and the sound becomes an electrical signal that the phone understands. You send a photo on WeChat; it is compressed, transmitted, decompressed, and finally displayed on your friend’s phone. You get an electrocardiogram; the electrical signal of your heart is amplified and filtered, and the doctor judges your health from it.

Behind all of this is “signals and systems.”

This course is not teaching you a pile of mathematical formulas. It is teaching you a framework for viewing the world: anything that “changes” can be described as a signal; any device that “processes information” can be analyzed as a system.

Ready? Let’s start from the most basic thing.

1. A Signal Is “Something That Changes”

❓ Question: How do you describe a changing world?

The water cup on the table does not change — it sits there, motionless. But your body temperature changes (lower in the morning, higher in the afternoon), the sound outside the window changes (loud when a car passes, quiet when it is still), the brightness of your phone screen changes (with auto-brightness).

The essence of the world is not stillness; it is change.

So the question becomes: How do we “record” these changes and “describe them to others”?

💡 Core Idea

A signal = the process of a physical quantity changing over time (or space)

Put more plainly:

  • Put a thermometer at the window, and record a number every minute -> you have a “temperature signal”
  • Record with a microphone, capturing air vibrations -> you have a “sound signal”
  • Take a photo with your phone, recording the brightness at each point -> you have an “image signal”

As long as something is changing, and those changes carry information, it is a signal.

🔍 Intuitive Understanding: The Three Most Common Signals

(1) Temperature Signal — the Easiest to Understand

You have a fever, and your temperature changes:

What this figure shows is: temperature changes with time. The horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is temperature. That is a signal.

You need no mathematics to have understood what a signal is. A signal is a record of “how something changes.”

(2) Sound Signal — Air Is “Shaking”

When you speak, your vocal cords vibrate and compress the surrounding air. These vibrations reach someone else’s ear, and that person hears your voice.

The air pressure is changing rapidly:

This up-and-down wobbling curve is a sound signal. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch; the larger the amplitude, the louder the volume.

You do not need to learn the Fourier transform to understand sound — you process sound signals with your ears every day.

(3) Image Signal — Adding “Space” to the Picture

Temperature signals and sound signals both change with time. But what about a photograph?

A photograph does not change with time (unless it is a video), but it changes across space:

Each point has a different brightness: bright areas have large values, and dark areas have small values.

So an image is a signal that varies with position. More precisely, an image is a function of two spatial variables: $f(x, y)$ denotes the brightness at position $(x, y)$.

Signals are everywhere. They are “the changes of the world.”

🔍 Classifying Signals: Continuous vs. Discrete

This is an important classification, but it is simple to understand.

Continuous-Time Signals: A Value at Every Instant

Like water flowing from a tap — there is a flow rate at every single moment.

Mathematically this is written as $x(t)$, meaning “the value at time $t$.” $t$ can take any value — 1 second, 1.5 seconds, 1.578423 seconds, any of them.

Discrete-Time Signals: A Value Only at Specified Moments

Like the daily closing price of a stock — there is a price only at each day’s close; between those moments, nothing is recorded.

Mathematically this is written as $x[n]$, meaning “the value at the $n$-th instant.” $n$ can only be an integer — day 1, day 2, day 3 …

Why Does This Distinction Matter?

Type Example Mathematical Representation Corresponding Tool
Continuous signal Analog tape, real-world sound $x(t)$ Fourier transform, Laplace transform
Discrete signal MP3, digital photos, stock data $x[n]$ Z-transform, digital signal processing

The real world is continuous (sound vibrates continuously), but computers can only handle discrete data (digital recordings). Continuous -> discrete -> process -> back to continuous — that is the entire pipeline of modern signal processing.

You will understand this conversion deeply in Part 4. For now, just know: continuous is “at every instant,” discrete is “record once every interval.”

📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Change is a signal.

2. A System Is “Something That Transforms a Signal”

❓ Question: Once you have a signal, then what?

A signal alone is not enough. You have a sound signal with echo (recorded at a concert), and you want to remove the echo. You have a dim photo, and you want to brighten it. You have a recording of someone speaking, and you want to recognize what they are saying.

These “things that process signals” are systems.

💡 Core Idea

A system = input a signal -> perform some transformation -> output another signal

This is the single most important mental model for understanding the entire course:

Signals are raw materials; systems are processing plants.

🔍 Intuitive Understanding: Three Examples from Daily Life

(1) Speaker System: An Amplifier

The sound signal picked up by a microphone is very weak. After amplification by the speaker system, it becomes a large signal that can drive the loudspeaker.

What the speaker does is simple: output = input × amplification factor.

Mathematically: $y(t) = A \cdot x(t)$, where $A$ is the amplification factor.

(2) Phone Filters: An Image Processor

The input is an original photo signal. The filter does two things:

  • Makes the skin smoother (a kind of “filtering”)
  • Makes the colors more vivid (a kind of “transformation”)

The output is a better-looking photo.

(3) Echo Cancellation: What Your Headphones Are Doing

You are speaking in a Zoom meeting, and the other person hears an echo. The echo-cancellation system analyzes: which part is the original voice? Which part is the echo (a delayed, attenuated version)? Then it removes the echo.

This is far more complex than amplification — the system needs to know “how much delay” and “how much attenuation.”

What these examples share: each has an input signal, some processing, and an output signal.

🔍 What Determines a System’s “Character”?

Different systems react to the same input in different ways. Give the same sound signal to:

  • A subwoofer: keeps the bass, reduces the treble (low-pass filter)
  • A tweeter: keeps the treble, reduces the bass (high-pass filter)
  • An equalizer: boosts some frequency bands, cuts others

A system’s “character” is the way it transforms the input signal.

Later in the course, we will learn how to describe this “character” precisely.

📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

A system turns a signal from one form into another.

3. Why Analyze Systems?

❓ Question: After knowing what a system is, then what?

All right, now you know what a signal is and what a system is. But is that enough?

Imagine you are designing a hearing aid. You place a microphone at the ear, and you need to: amplify certain frequencies (human speech), attenuate other frequencies (noise), while making sure a sudden blast of sound does not damage the user’s ear.

You need to predict: given an input, what is the output of the system?

💡 Core Idea

The goal of system analysis: prediction, stability, design.

After finishing this course, you should be able to answer three questions:

  1. Prediction: given an input, what will the output be?
  2. Stability: will the system run out of control? (Will the output become unbounded?)
  3. Design: how do we design a system so that it does what we want?

🔍 The Core Example Throughout the Book: The RC Circuit

This is the most important simple circuit in a signals and systems course. Why? Because it is so simple, yet it contains all the core ideas.

![RC circuit diagram]

What Is It?

An RC circuit is simply a resistor $R$ and a capacitor $C$ in series.

  • Input $x(t)$: the voltage applied across the circuit (varying with time)
  • Output $y(t)$: the voltage across the capacitor (this is what we measure)

What Does It Do?

The RC circuit can be understood as a “smoother”:

  • If the input voltage jumps suddenly (from 0V to 5V), the output does not jump immediately — it rises slowly, until it approaches 5V.
  • If the input voltage fluctuates rapidly, the output “ignores” these fast changes and follows only the slow ones.

This is like a system with “inertia” — it rejects rapid changes and follows only slow ones.

Why Use It Throughout the Book?

Because of this circuit:

Method of analysis What it tells us
Part 1 (intuition) “This system smooths the input”
Part 2 (Fourier) “It attenuates high frequencies and preserves low frequencies” -> low-pass filter
Part 3 (Laplace) “Its differential equation can be turned into an algebraic one and solved”
Part 4 (discrete) “This behavior can be simulated with digital circuits”

One circuit, four perspectives. That is the essence of this course.

The Three Core Questions as Applied to the RC Circuit

  1. Prediction: if the input is a square wave (0V->5V->0V->5V…), what does the output look like?

    • Answer: the output becomes a “rounded square wave” — the capacitor takes time to charge and discharge.

  2. Stability: if the input is a sine wave, will the output grow larger and larger until it explodes?

    • Answer: no. The RC circuit is inherently stable. However large the input is, the output is at most about that large; it never runs out of control.

  3. Design: I want the RC circuit to let only frequencies below 20 Hz pass (low-pass filter). How should $R$ and $C$ be chosen?

    • Answer: choose the $RC$ product so that the cutoff frequency $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} = 20\text{Hz}$ gives the desired value.

🔍 A Broader View of the Three Core Questions

The intuition of stability:

Stable = finite input implies finite output.
You give a swing a push (a finite input), and the swing sways a few times, then stops (a stable system).
You give a swing a push, and it sways higher and higher until it flips over (an unstable system).

The intuition of design:

Design = choosing the right parameters so that the system does what you want.
It is like adjusting the equalizer on a speaker system — if you want heavier bass, turn up the low-frequency knob.

📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Analyzing a system = predicting it + confirming it is stable + designing it.

4. The Most Important Class of Systems: LTI (Linear Time-Invariant)

❓ Question: There are all kinds of systems in the world. Where do we start?

Some systems are terrifyingly complex — the human brain is a system, with sensory signals as input and thoughts and actions as output. Such a system currently cannot be described completely by mathematics.

We need to start with the simplest and most useful class of systems.

That is the LTI system — and a large number of real-world systems (including the RC circuit) belong to this class.

💡 Core Idea

LTI = Linear + Time-Invariant

Linearity: scaling the input scales the output proportionally; adding inputs adds outputs.
Time-invariance: doing it today and doing it tomorrow give the same effect.

Together, these two properties make the system extraordinarily simple — if you know its response to one “impulse,” you know its response to any input.

🔍 Intuitive Understanding: Linearity (Linear)

(1) Homogeneity (Proportional Scaling)

If the input is scaled by k, the output is also scaled by k.

Examples from life:

  • A speaker system is linear (ideally): if you turn the volume knob up by a factor of two, the sound is also twice as loud.
  • A mirror is linear: if you step twice as far away, the image shrinks by a factor of two (approximately).

Counter-example:

  • Microphone overload: if you shout too loudly, the sound becomes distorted and broken — the output no longer scales with the input. This is not linear.

(2) Additivity (Superposition)

The sum of two inputs = the sum of their respective outputs.

This is the superposition principle. It is one of the most important concepts in signals and systems.

Examples from life:

  • When two people speak at the same time, what you hear is the two voices superimposed.
  • If you play back the two recordings separately, then play both simultaneously, it is the same as the two people speaking at once.

The power of superposition: if you know the system’s response to “basic signals,” you can combine those basic signals to obtain the response to any input. It is like:

  • You know how to stack building blocks (the processed results of basic signals)
  • So you can build any shape (the processed result of any signal)

The Mathematical Expression of Linearity (No Need to Fear It — It Is Intuitive)

If the system maps input $x_1(t)$ to output $y_1(t)$, and input $x_2(t)$ to output $y_2(t)$, then for input $a \cdot x_1(t) + b \cdot x_2(t)$ (where $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary constants), the output must be:

$$y(t) = a \cdot y_1(t) + b \cdot y_2(t)$$

In plain language: if you mix two inputs in some proportion, the output is the two corresponding outputs mixed in the same proportion.

🔍 Intuitive Understanding: Time-Invariance (Time-Invariant)

Core Idea: Delaying the Input = Delaying the Output

Doing it now and doing it later have the same effect.

Mathematically: if input $x(t)$ produces output $y(t)$, then input $x(t-t_0)$ (delayed by $t_0$) produces output $y(t-t_0)$ (the output is delayed by the same amount).

Examples from Life

  • A doorbell: time-invariant. Pressing it in the morning and pressing it in the evening produce the same sound (apart from the time difference).
  • A speaker system: time-invariant (ideally). Playing a song today and playing it tomorrow produce the same sound from the system.
  • An RC circuit: time-invariant. Giving it a square wave today and giving it a square wave tomorrow produce exactly the same output waveform (only the time differs).

Counter-examples:

  • Running a bath: time-varying. Running the water in the morning and running it in the evening can produce different water temperatures (because the water heater may have been used by someone else).
  • Aging electronic components: time-varying. A speaker system sounds different this year than last year, because the components have aged.

Why Is Time-Invariance So Important?

Because it makes prediction feasible! If a system is time-varying, you have to relearn and retest it every day. If it is time-invariant, you learn it once — the rules of today still apply tomorrow.

🔍 Why Is LTI the “Holy Grail” of Signals and Systems?

Given linearity and time-invariance, a striking result appears:

An LTI system is completely described by its “impulse response.”

What is the impulse response?

  • You give the system a very short, very sharp input (like banging on a table once)
  • The system “shudders” for a moment, then recovers
  • The waveform of that “shudder” is the impulse response

The remarkable thing about LTI systems is: once you know that “shudder” waveform, you know the system’s response to any input.

Why? Because you can view any input signal as the superposition of “countless table-bangs” at different times and with different amplitudes. Using linearity (superposition) and time-invariance (same delay), you can piece together the final output from countless “bang responses.”

This is the idea of convolution. You will learn it in the second chapter of this course.

Formula: $y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) h(t-\tau) d\tau$

Do not be afraid of that integral for now — Parts 2 and 3 will turn it into simple multiplication. That is exactly what the Fourier transform and the Laplace transform do!

🔍 Examples of Non-LTI Systems — To Deepen Your Understanding

System Why is it not LTI?
Squarer: $y(t) = [x(t)]^2$ Nonlinear. Input doubled gives output quadrupled (not doubled).
Time compressor: $y(t) = x(2t)$ Time-varying. A delayed input does not produce an equally delayed output.
Threshold detector: $y = 1$ if $x > 0$, otherwise $y = 0$ Nonlinear. Two small signals added together may cross the threshold, although neither does alone.
Human ear Approximately linear but time-invariant? If you listen to the same song in a different mood, you feel it differently.

📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

LTI = scaling the input by n scales the output by n + doing it today is the same as doing it tomorrow.

5. Preview of the Core Idea: The Power of Decomposition

❓ Question: How do you solve a supremely complex problem?

Imagine a highly intricate LEGO model in front of you. How do you understand it?

You could break it into individual LEGO bricks. Understand each brick, and you understand the whole model.

This is the most important idea in the entire signals and systems course — bar none.

💡 Core Idea

Complex problem -> break into simple problems -> solve each -> combine the answers.

In programming this is called “divide and conquer”; in signals and systems it is called “decomposition.”

🔍 The LTI System’s “Decomposition” Strategy

We have already learned that an LTI system can be completely described by its impulse response. But convolution is awkward to compute (there is an integral).

Every later chapter in this course is essentially answering the question: how do we break a “complex signal” into a superposition of “basic signals” so that the computation becomes simple?

🔍 A Survey of the Various “Ways of Breaking Apart”

Method Breaks the signal into… What is it for?
Impulse decomposition Impulses at different times Prelude to Part 2: leading to convolution
Fourier decomposition Sine waves of different frequencies Main course of Part 2: seeing the “frequency content” of a signal
Laplace decomposition Sine waves that grow/decay exponentially Part 3: analyzing unstable systems
Z-transform The “Laplace” of the discrete world Part 4: computer signal processing

Each decomposition method is a concrete realization of this same “breaking apart” idea.

🔍 Preview: How Did Fourier Break Things Apart?

Fourier proposed a wild idea:

Any signal (however complex) can be written as a superposition of sine waves of different frequencies, amplitudes, and phases.

Just as white light is split by a prism into a rainbow — the light of seven colors adds back into white light.

Can you guess why sine waves are so special?

Because when a sine wave passes through an LTI system, it is still a sine wave — only its amplitude and phase change!

This means that if you break the input into sine waves, you know the result for each sine wave passing through the system (amplitude changed, phase changed), and adding them together gives the final output.

That is the magic of the Fourier transform. Part 2 will explain this in detail.

📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Any signal can be decomposed into a superposition of simple signals.

Part 2 Preview

By now we know:

  • Signals are things that change
  • Systems are machines that transform signals
  • LTI systems are the most important class of systems

But one fatal problem remains unsolved:

The convolution operation $y(t) = x(t) * h(t)$ is too hard to compute! Every time you have to evaluate an integral. So tedious!

What can be done?

In Part 2, we will encounter a brilliant solution:

Change the point of view. Look at the signal in “frequency” instead of “time.”

It is like putting on special glasses: things that look terribly complicated in the time domain become almost unbelievably simple in the frequency domain — convolution becomes multiplication.

You do not need to know how to compute integrals. You only need to know:

  • Any signal can be decomposed into sine waves of different frequencies
  • A sine wave passing through an LTI system is still a sine wave (only amplitude and phase change)
  • So if you know how the system treats each frequency, you know how it treats every signal

That is 《Part 2: The Magic of Decomposition — From Fourier Series to the Fourier Transform》.

“All science is the refinement of everyday thinking.” — Albert Einstein

Part 2: The Magic of Decomposition — The Fourier Idea

Core question: How do we break a complex signal apart and see its “ingredients”?

Knowledge Map

1. The Problem: How Do We Analyze a Complex Signal?

1.1 ❓ A Cup of Mixed Juice

Imagine a cup of juice in front of you. You take a sip; the taste is complex — a bit sweet, a bit sour, a bit astringent. How do you know what is in it?

You might think: this juice = orange juice + apple juice + watermelon juice.

In other words — you imagine the complex thing as a combination of simple things. Then you can analyze it:

  • Sweetness -> from the apple juice
  • Sourness -> from the orange juice
  • Freshness -> from the watermelon juice

Signal analysis is the same. We have a complex signal and want to know “what is inside it.”

1.2 ❓ A Piece of Music

You hear a piece of music. It is many kinds of sounds mixed together:

  • The singer’s voice
  • The guitar
  • The drums
  • The bass

Your ear manages a remarkable feat: extracting the one you care about from the mixture. At a noisy party, you can still hear your friend speaking — this is called the “cocktail party effect.”

Your brain performs “signal decomposition” natively. But our brain cannot say exactly how it does it. The role of mathematics is: turn this instinct into a precise tool.

1.3 💡 Core Idea

A complex thing = a combination of simple things.

That is all.

This idea is everywhere in life:

  • Matter is made of elements (the periodic table)
  • Colors are made of three primaries (RGB)
  • Music is made of notes (Do Re Mi Fa So La Ti)
  • Sentences are made of words
  • Programs are made of functions

The same holds for signals. Any complex signal can be written as a weighted sum of simple signals.

The key question is: what do we choose as the “simple signals”?

1.4 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

A complex signal is a superposition of simple components. Analyzing a signal means finding its “ingredient list.”

2. Finding the “Basic Building Block”: The Sine Wave

2.1 ❓ What Bricks Do We Use to Build a House?

If we want to decompose any signal, the first question is: what do we use as the basic brick?

You could use many kinds of bricks:

  • Use an impulse (a sharp spike) — that is the convolution approach (mentioned in Part 1)
  • Use steps
  • Use parabolas

But none of these is perfect. Because once you choose them, analyzing system behavior is still hard.

We need a brick that satisfies a key property:

If a system is LTI (linear time-invariant), then when a sine wave goes in, a sine wave still comes out.

2.2 💡 This Is the Most Important Insight

This is also the most important sentence in all of Part 2:

The sine wave is an “eigenfunction” of LTI systems.

What does that mean? Imagine a particular function $f(t)$. You throw it into an LTI system, and what comes out is a “scaled version” (amplitude changed) and “shifted version” (phase changed) of $f(t)$, but its shape is completely unchanged.

In mathematics:

$$\cos(\omega t) \xrightarrow{\text{LTI系统}} |H(j\omega)| \cdot \cos(\omega t + \angle H(j\omega))$$

In plain language:

  • Input: a cosine wave with a specific frequency $\omega$
  • Output: a cosine wave with the same frequency $\omega$
  • Amplitude changed (multiplied by $|H(j\omega)|$)
  • Time position changed (shifted by $\angle H(j\omega)$)

The frequency did not change! That is the key.

2.3 🔍 Analogy: A Prism and White Light

If you have a beam of white light (complex) and send it through a prism, what happens?

White light -> prism -> rainbow (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet)

The prism decomposes the “complex” white light into “simple” lights of different colors.

In the world of signals, Fourier analysis is that prism:

  • Input: a complex signal
  • Output: the components at each frequency

White light is made of different colors <-> A signal is made of sine waves at different frequencies

Different frequencies are like different colors. Low frequencies are like red; high frequencies are like violet.

2.4 🔍 Why Are Sine Waves So Special?

This gets into differential equations — but do not fear; we will use intuition.

Many physical systems can be described by differential equations. A sine wave has a wonderful property: if you differentiate it (or integrate it), you still get a sine wave.

  • $\frac{d}{dt}\sin(\omega t) = \omega\cos(\omega t)$ — still a sine wave (just changed into a cosine)
  • $\frac{d}{dt}\cos(\omega t) = -\omega\sin(\omega t)$ — still a sine wave (with a minus sign)

What an LTI system does, at bottom, is: add, multiply by constants, differentiate, integrate. None of these operations changes the frequency of a sine wave.

That explains why a sine wave passing through an LTI system keeps its frequency.

2.5 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

The sine wave is the “native language” of LTI systems — the system has “nothing to say” against it; it can only adjust the size and the position, but cannot change what it fundamentally is.

3. Step One: Decomposing Periodic Signals (The Fourier Series)

3.1 ❓ What Is “Periodic”?

A periodic signal is one that repeats.

For example:

  • A heartbeat: endlessly repeating “lub-dub, lub-dub…”
  • A pendulum: swinging back and forth
  • Mains electricity: 50 Hz, repeating 50 times per second
  • A musical note: the vibration of a string is periodic

Mathematically, a periodic signal satisfies:
$$x(t + T) = x(t)$$

where $T$ is the period. For 50 Hz mains, $T = 1/50 = 0.02$ is 1/50 second.

3.2 💡 Core Idea: Any Periodic Signal Can Be Decomposed into Sine Waves

This is the discovery that made Fourier immortal:

Any periodic signal (as long as it is not too “outlandish”) can be written as the weighted sum of infinitely many sine waves at different frequencies.

Mathematical form:

$$x(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[ a_n\cos(n\omega_0 t) + b_n\sin(n\omega_0 t) \right]$$

Wait — do not be scared off by the formula. Let us translate it:

  • $\omega_0$ — the fundamental frequency (the basic rate at which the signal repeats, $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$)
  • $n\omega_0$ — the harmonics ($2\omega_0$ is the 2nd harmonic, $3\omega_0$ the 3rd, …)
  • $a_0$ — the DC component (the average value)
  • $a_n, b_n$ — the weights (how much of each frequency is present)

In plain words: a periodic signal = fundamental + 2nd harmonic + 3rd harmonic + … all added together.

3.3 🔍 Example: A Square Wave = A “Human Pyramid” of Sine Waves

Imagine a square wave (jumping back and forth between -1 and +1).

Fourier tells us:

Let us see how cool this is:

We can draw it in ASCII to see the effect of adding terms:

That is the magic of the Fourier series: using sine waves to “assemble” any shape!

3.4 🔍 What Do the Coefficients $a_n, b_n$ Mean?

Each coefficient represents “how much of this frequency is in the signal.”

  • $a_n$ large -> there is a lot of cosine component at this frequency
  • $b_n$ large -> there is a lot of sine component at this frequency
  • A coefficient of 0 for some $n$ -> the signal has no component at that frequency

This is like asking: how much orange juice is in this cup? How much apple juice? The coefficients are the “amount of each ingredient.”

3.5 🔍 A More Elegant Form: Exponential Notation

Engineers prefer another notation (do not fear — it is the same thing in disguise):

$$x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n e^{jn\omega_0 t}$$

This uses Euler’s formula: $e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta$.

It is essentially the same as the first form, just more compact. $c_n$ is “how much of the component at frequency $n\omega_0$ is present.”

You do not need to memorize this. Just know: $c_n$ tells us how much “energy” the signal has at the $n$-th frequency.

3.6 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

A periodic signal = fundamental + integer multiples of the fundamental, all sine waves added together. A square wave looks “square” because countless sine waves are “stacked” together.

4. Step Two: Decomposing Non-Periodic Signals (The Fourier Transform)

4.1 ❓ Most Signals Are Not Periodic

Very few signals in the real world are perfectly periodic:

  • A sentence you speak (not repetitive)
  • A song (it has a beginning and an end)
  • The waveform of an earthquake
  • An image

These signals do not repeat. How can we use the Fourier series?

Answer: treat them as signals with an infinitely long period.

4.2 💡 Core Idea: From Discrete Frequencies to Continuous Frequencies

The frequencies of a periodic signal are “discrete”: only $\omega_0, 2\omega_0, 3\omega_0, …$

What about a non-periodic signal? Every frequency may exist.

Imagine looking at a comb from far away:

  • A periodic signal -> the teeth of the comb (discrete points, spaced at intervals)
  • A non-periodic signal -> the teeth are so close together that they merge into a continuous band

That is the Fourier transform:

$$X(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt$$

The formula looks intimidating. But what it means is:

For every frequency $\omega$, compute how much of that frequency is “contained” in the signal $x(t)$.

The output $X(j\omega)$ is a function that tells you: how large a component the signal has at each frequency $\omega$.

4.3 🔍 The “Intellectual Leap” from Series to Transform

Fourier series Fourier transform
Applies only to periodic signals Applies to any signal
Frequencies are discrete (stepping) Frequencies are continuous
Output is a set of coefficients $c_n$ Output is a continuous function $X(j\omega)$
Like an ingredient list Like a continuous curve

Do not obsess over how to compute the integral. The meaning of the Fourier transform matters more than its computation. It is like driving a car without knowing how the engine is built.

4.4 🔍 Getting Back to the Essence: What Does $X(j\omega)$ Look Like?

It is usually shown as a spectrum plot — horizontal axis is frequency $\omega$, vertical axis is “magnitude” (how large the component is at that frequency).

Many low-frequency components -> high on the left
Many high-frequency components -> high on the right

For example:

  • A double bass -> high in the low-frequency region
  • A violin -> high in the high-frequency region
  • White noise -> present at all frequencies

4.5 🔍 The Inverse Fourier Transform: Back from Frequency Domain to Time Domain

If the Fourier transform is “extracting the components,” then the inverse transform is “assembling them back”:

$$x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(j\omega) e^{j\omega t}d\omega$$

In other words: add up the components at every frequency, and you recover the original signal.

It is like recombining the rainbow into white light after using the prism.

4.6 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

The Fourier transform: open up a signal and read its “frequency ingredient list” — how much of each frequency is present, all laid out clearly.

5. Understanding the Frequency Domain Intuitively

5.1 ❓ What Is the Relationship Between the Time Domain and the Frequency Domain?

You can look at a signal in two ways:

Time domain: horizontal axis is time; look at how the signal “changes.”
Frequency domain: horizontal axis is frequency; look at what “components” the signal has.

The same signal, two ways of viewing it.

5.2 🔍 Analogy: Recipe vs. Ingredient List

Imagine making a dish (say, braised pork):

Time-domain view (the recipe):

  1. Cut the meat (minutes 0-5)
  2. Blanch in water (minutes 5-8)
  3. Caramelize the sugar (minutes 8-12)
  4. Add seasoning and stew (minutes 12-60)
  5. Reduce the sauce (minutes 60-65)

This is a description of process — how it changes over time.

Frequency-domain view (ingredient list):

  • Pork belly 500g
  • Soy sauce 3 tablespoons
  • Rock sugar 20g
  • Star anise 2 pieces
  • Cinnamon bark 1 piece
  • Cooking wine 2 tablespoons

This is a description of composition — regardless of order, only “what is in it.”

The time domain and the frequency domain describe the same thing, just in different ways.

5.3 🔍 More Vivid Analogies

Scenario Time domain (how it changes over time) Frequency domain (what components it has)
Music The melody unfolding over time The chord structure of the notes
Food The steps in a recipe The list of ingredients
Color The order of applying paint The RGB values
Speech A sentence The vocabulary you used
Photo The arrangement of pixels The distribution of color frequencies

5.4 🔍 The Cost of Converting

The time domain and frequency domain can be converted into each other. But — perfect time-domain information means complete ignorance of the frequency domain, and vice versa.

Imagine a signal: a single impulse at one instant. In the time domain, it is “very clear” (it is right there). In the frequency domain, it contains all frequencies (present at every frequency).

Conversely: a pure sine wave (only one frequency) -> it repeats forever in time (no time localization at all).

This is the mathematical root of the uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics!

A signal cannot be simultaneously localized precisely in both the time domain and the frequency domain.

5.5 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Time domain = “how it is made”; frequency domain = “what it is made of.” The same dish, two perspectives.

6. Why Is Frequency-Domain Analysis So Useful?

6.1 ❓ Convolution Is a Hassle

In Part 1 we said that the output of an LTI system is the convolution of the input and the impulse response:

$$y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) h(t-\tau) d\tau$$

The integral has functions nested inside it, and you have to flip, shift… Computing convolution by hand is painful, and it is not intuitive either.

6.2 💡 The Magic of the Frequency Domain: Convolution Becomes Multiplication

This is perhaps the most useful property in all of signals and systems:

Convolution in the time domain = multiplication in the frequency domain

In mathematics:
$$x(t) * h(t) \xrightarrow{\text{傅里叶变换}} X(j\omega) \cdot H(j\omega)$$

Don’t believe it? It is true.

What does this mean?

  • To analyze a system in the time domain: you must do the hard work of convolution
  • To analyze a system in the frequency domain: you only do simple multiplication

Multiply here, and you are done! No integrals needed!

6.3 🔍 A System’s “Character”: The Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$

$H(j\omega)$ is called the frequency response. It tells you what “attitude” the system has toward each frequency.

$$H(j\omega) = |H(j\omega)| e^{j\angle H(j\omega)}$$

Two parts:

  • $|H(j\omega)|$ — the magnitude response: the “amplification factor” of the system at each frequency
  • $\angle H(j\omega)$ — the phase response: the “time delay” the system applies at each frequency

$H(j\omega)$ is the system’s “signature.” Every system has its own unique frequency response.

6.4 🔍 Filters: A System’s “Attitude” toward Different Frequencies

Low-pass filter: lets low frequencies through, blocks high frequencies

High-pass filter: lets high frequencies through, blocks low frequencies

Band-pass filter: lets only a certain range of frequencies through

6.5 🔍 Real-World Analogy: A Sieve

Low-pass filter = a flour sifter

  • Low frequencies (small particles) -> pass through ✅
  • High frequencies (large particles) -> blocked ❌

High-pass filter = a sieve that only lets large particles through (used in reverse)

  • Low frequencies (small particles) -> fall through ❌
  • High frequencies (large particles) -> retained ✅

Band-pass filter = a sieve with holes of a specific size

  • Too small or too large -> cannot pass
  • Just right -> passes

6.6 🔍 Real-World Applications

Sound EQ (equalizer):

  • Bass (low frequencies) -> makes the sound “thick”
  • Midrange (middle frequencies) -> makes vocals clear
  • Treble (high frequencies) -> makes the sound “bright”

EQ adjusts the “weights” of different frequencies — essentially it is modifying the frequency response of a filter.

Image processing:

  • Images can also undergo a Fourier transform (two-dimensional)
  • “Low frequencies” of an image = smooth regions (sky, skin)
  • “High frequencies” of an image = edges, details, noise
  • Low-pass filtering -> blur (removing detail)
  • High-pass filtering -> edge detection

Communication systems:

  • Different radio stations use different frequencies
  • Your radio receiver is a band-pass filter: tune to a frequency, and it “opens” the channel for that signal
  • This is the basis of frequency-division multiple access (FDMA)

6.7 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Frequency-domain analysis turns convolution, which the human brain handles poorly, into multiplication, which it handles well. A filter is a “frequency sieve.”

7. The Sampling Theorem (Intuitive Version)

7.1 ❓ How Do We Store Signals in the Digital Age?

Signals in the real world are continuous (analog). But computers can only handle discrete (digital) data.

To turn an analog signal into a digital signal, we must sample — record a value at regular intervals.

The question is: how fast is fast enough?

7.2 💡 The Sampling Theorem (Nyquist’s Theorem)

Shannon and Nyquist told us:

The sampling frequency must be greater than 2 times the highest frequency in the signal.

$$f_s > 2f_{max}$$

where:

  • $f_s$ — the sampling frequency (how many samples per second)
  • $f_{max}$ — the highest frequency in the signal

If this condition is satisfied, the original signal can be perfectly recovered from the samples.

If this condition is violated… problems arise.

7.3 🔍 If Sampling Is Too Slow: Aliasing

What happens when sampling is too slow? High-frequency signals masquerade as low-frequency signals.

The classic example: the backward-spinning wheel

Imagine watching the wheel of a car (assume the wheel has spokes). If the wheel spins very fast, and the video frame rate (say 24 frames per second) cannot keep up:

Reality: the wheel spins clockwise, 10 revolutions per second
Sampling: only 24 photos per second

Result: in the video, the wheel appears to be spinning backward!

Why? Because the sampling rate is insufficient; the high-frequency rotation has been “aliased” into a low frequency.

This is aliasing.

7.4 🔍 More Examples of Aliasing

Wagon wheels in old movies:

  • The wheel spokes appear to spin backward
  • They even appear to stop (when the rotation speed is an exact integer multiple of the frame rate)

Moiré patterns:

  • When two fine grids are overlaid, strange large ripples appear
  • This is essentially “aliasing” in the spatial domain

Audio sampling aliasing:

  • When recording high-frequency sounds with an insufficient sampling rate
  • High frequencies get “folded” into the audible range, becoming unpleasant noise
  • CDs use a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz — more than twice the highest frequency a human ear can hear (about 20 kHz)

7.5 🔍 How Do Real Engineers Handle This?

In real systems, one thing must be done before sampling:

Before sampling, use a low-pass filter to remove all frequencies above $f_s/2$.

This filter is called an anti-aliasing filter.

Why? Because real signals always contain all sorts of high-frequency noise. If they are not filtered out in advance, after sampling they will “masquerade” as low-frequency signals and sneak in — and once they are in, they cannot be removed!

7.6 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Sampling is like taking photos: to capture something changing rapidly, the shutter must be fast enough. Otherwise, high frequencies will “masquerade” as low frequencies and fool you.

8. The Limits of the Fourier Idea

8.1 ❓ The Fourier Transform Is Not Omnipotent

The Fourier transform is powerful, but it has a precondition:

The Fourier transform assumes the signal is absolutely integrable: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)| dt < \infty$

In plain language: the signal’s energy is finite; it cannot grow without bound.

But many real signals do not satisfy this:

  • $e^{at}$ (when $a > 0$, a signal that grows larger with time)
  • A ramp signal that keeps growing
  • The output of unstable systems

8.2 🔍 What Is an Unstable System?

The Fourier transform cannot analyze unstable systems, because the system’s response grows to infinity and has no finite “spectrum.”

8.3 💡 This Is Where Laplace Comes In

The Laplace transform is an “enhanced version” of the Fourier transform.

It adds a “decay factor” $e^{-\sigma t}$ in front of $e^{-j\omega t}$:

$$e^{-j\omega t} \rightarrow e^{-(\sigma + j\omega)t} = e^{-st}$$

This $\sigma$ (decay factor) is like a “tranquilizer,” allowing even signals that grow too fast to be analyzed.

The Fourier transform is a special case of the Laplace transform (when $\sigma = 0$).

8.4 📌 One-Sentence Memory Hook

Fourier only handles “well-behaved” signals. When a system “blows up,” Laplace comes to the rescue.

  • The Fourier series = the “ingredient list” of a periodic signal.
  • The Fourier transform = the “ingredient list” of a non-periodic signal.

  • Convolution in the time domain = multiplication in the frequency domain.
  • What “attitude” each of low-pass/high-pass/band-pass has.
