Most complaints about “inefficient learning” do not have slow learning as their root cause, but rather that the learning path stops after Stage Two, always lacking the closed loop of compression and reconstruction.

5. Underlying Logic: Abstraction and Switching

Let us take an overview of the previous layers:

Level Core Question Key Concept
Trigger Why do formulas become more complex? Compression, omission, precision hierarchy
Epistemology What does it mean to truly understand a system? The dual ability of compression and expansion
Theory of knowledge How is knowledge organized in the mind? Fractal structure, multi-scale models
Interpersonal What do understanding a person and understanding a formula have in common? Implicit modeling, recursive loops, generative paths
Methodology How to learn efficiently? Skeleton → derivation → compression → reconstruction from zero

What runs through all levels is not any single concrete conclusion, but one repeatedly appearing pattern:

Faced with an infinitely complex input — whether the physical world, a disciplinary system, or another person — extract a limited set of key variables, establish the relational structure among them, and then move freely between different levels of abstraction.

6. Extension: Why Can Mathematics Describe the World?

All of the above, in turn, makes me think of another question: why can mathematics be used to describe the world at all?

Mathematics is not a product of nature. It is a symbolic system invented by humans. Natural numbers come from counting; the equals sign comes from the concept of conservation; calculus comes from an abstraction of motion and change — every branch can be traced back to some primal human impulse to understand and predict the environment. But the question is: why would an artificial language be so particularly good at describing nature?

This is not a question that modeling experience alone can answer. Historically, several major explanations have been offered. Let me examine each, and compare it with the foregoing reflections.

1. Platonism: Mathematics Was Always There

This position holds that circles, pi, and exponential functions “existed” before humans — not as physical entities, but as abstract forms independent of matter. The physical world merely happens to instantiate these mathematical structures. Planetary orbits are elliptical not because you invented the ellipse equation, but because the ellipse already existed in a Platonic world, and nature chose to use it.

The appeal of this view lies in its directness; it requires no further explanation. But its weakness is equally obvious: why would nature choose these structures rather than others? And further, branches of mathematics developed purely out of human interest (group theory, number theory) later found uses in physics — if they exist independently, is this “pre-installation” too coincidental?

Relation to the preceding reflections: The farthest. Everything previously argued rests on “formulas are compressions, models are man-made,” and Platonism stands exactly opposite — it holds that mathematical forms exist independently of humans, who merely discover them. If formulas were “original truth,” there would be no issue of compression ratios, nor any discussion of the boundaries of model validity.

2. The Evolutionary Explanation: The Human Brain Is Itself a Modeling Machine Trained by Nature

This account starts from the other end. When your ancestors were fleeing on the savanna, if they could not subconsciously estimate the distance, speed, and number of prey or predators — that is, if they could not perform a kind of “quasi-mathematical” computation — their genes would not have been passed down. Hundreds of thousands of years of natural selection have hardwired “performing approximate mathematical calculations of the physical world” into the circuits of the human brain.

People find F=ma intuitive not because it is truth, but because the perceptual system of the species to which you belong understands motion through approximations consistent with F=ma.

Relation to the preceding reflections: Partial overlap. The preceding reflections mentioned “the concept of conservation → the equals sign, the concept of counting → natural numbers,” which aligns with the direction of the evolutionary explanation — the origin of mathematics is indeed instrumental, grown out of experience. But evolution can only explain “why humans can learn mathematics,” not “why humans later developed group theory and topology, abstract systems entirely detached from everyday experience.” It explains the hardware, not the software.

3. Instrumentalism: Mathematics Does Not Describe the World; It Compresses It

This is the position used throughout the preceding sections.

Instrumentalism holds that mathematics is not at all a set of statements about the essence of the universe. It is just a symbolic system plus rules of operation. The usage is as follows: first, through observation, determine a few variables of interest; then experiment with different mathematical expressions until the computed results align with observations to an acceptable precision. If it matches, the formula enters the textbook; if not, discard it and try another.

In other words, behind “mathematics can describe nature” lies a severe survivorship bias: what you see is only the formulas that passed the test; behind every successful formula are hundreds of derivations that were overturned, written nowhere.

Relation to the preceding reflections: This is the core operational framework of the preceding sections. The radar equation and F=ma are essentially the same kind of act — select variables, ignore details, establish relationships. Their difference is only in compression ratio. This position is highly consistent with everything argued above and requires no correction.

4. Structural Realism: The World Does Have Objective Structure, and Mathematics Happens to Describe It

This position holds that reality can be decomposed into two levels: substance and structure. Substance — what “material” electrons are made of, how consciousness actually arises — may never be directly accessible. But structure — the decay law between electric force and distance, the quantitative proportions of energy transfer — is stable, repeatably measurable, and independent of the observer.

Mathematics happens to be a language that cares only about “structure” and never asks about “substance.” It does not care what a thing “is”; it only cares what relation the thing has to other things. F=ma does not tell you the ontological definition of force and mass; it only tells you that a linear relationship exists between two quantities. Because this orientation perfectly matches the pattern of external relations among objects, mathematics is particularly useful.

Relation to the preceding reflections: Ambivalent. When arguing that “the same airplane is modeled as different objects in different disciplines, yet all models are valid,” a premise was already implied: there is a sufficiently stable airplane there, allowing different models to converge around it. This premise itself is a mild form of structural realism. But the preceding reflections fundamentally do not want to go as far as “structure is a property of the world itself” — preferring to say “we do not know whether structure belongs to the world or is imposed by humans.” This ambiguity is real; preserving it is more honest than forcibly resolving it.

5. The Kantian View: It Is Not That Mathematics Describes the World, but That Humans Can Only See the World Through the Lens of Mathematics

The subversiveness of this position lies in its direct reversal of the question.

You think you are using mathematics to “see” the world. But by Kant’s reasoning, time, space, quantity, and causality — these categories are themselves the a priori structures of your cognition, not things you learned from the external world. You did not learn to see the world with mathematics; your brain is simply innately capable of organizing sensory data only in quantified, structured ways.

A tree — you think you “see” a tree; in fact, the actual process is: photons strike the retina, convert to neural signals, pass through multiple layers of cortical processing, and are finally constructed by your brain into a perceptual model called “tree.” You are never directly in contact with the world; you are only in contact with the output of your own perceptual processing. Mathematics appears omnipresent because, from the very first instant you touch the world, it has already been “mathematicized” by your cognitive structure.

Wang Yangming, in an entirely different discourse system, said something similar: when the flower is not seen, it and the mind are together in stillness — not that the flower does not exist, but that its color, shape, and kind have not yet been illuminated by the light of the “mind,” not yet co-generated. Kant and Wang Yangming, though separated by three centuries and two civilizations, almost converge on this point.

Relation to the preceding reflections: This layer is neither a supplement to nor a replacement for the preceding arguments; it is their bedrock foundation. Everything said above — “models are man-made, compression involves trade-offs, cognition has boundaries” — if pursued to the end, all stops at this place: everything “objective” that humans can speak of cannot escape the fact that “subjective cognitive structure participated in its construction.” This does not lead one into nihilism; it leads one into a sober self-awareness: knowing that one is not directly watching the world, but participating in its constitution.

Overview of the Six Positions and Their Relation to This Essay

Position Relation to the Core Framework Verdict
Platonism Formulas as original truth, directly opposed to “compression” Farthest; incompatible
Evolution Explains “why humans can” model, does not touch “the boundaries of modeling” Partially useful but not central
Instrumentalism Formulas as disposable compression tools — consistent with the operational logic throughout Core at the methodological layer
Structural realism Suggests objective constraints that make models converge; this essay remains open to it Held in suspension
Kant/Wang Yangming The observer participates in the construction of the observed — provides the underlying conviction Foundational layer

My Position

Comparing each one, my own position can, in fact, be described fairly clearly.

First, mathematics is a tool invented by humans, not truth fallen from the sky. The concept of conservation was abstracted, and so the equals sign appeared; the impulse to count was formalized, and so natural numbers appeared. Humans first invent these symbols and rules, then turn around and use them to frame nature — what frames successfully is kept; what fails is discarded or iterated. The Platonic idea that “mathematics has been waiting in the sky to be discovered” — I do not accept it. If formulas were innate truth, then what would overturned formulas be? Truth evolving?

Second, at the operational level, I basically stand with instrumentalism. The radar equation, F=ma, and the various fittings in mathematical modeling are all essentially the same operation — select variables, cut details, build equalities. Whether a formula is good does not depend on how “true” it is, but on whether it works at the current precision required. Compression ratios may differ, but the underlying logic is invariant. This position dovetails seamlessly with the analytical framework of this essay; no separate patching is needed.

But instrumentalism pushed to its extreme gives a sense that “everything is fictional; just whatever works,” which does not quite match my actual experience. When the same airplane can be effectively described by models from different disciplines, these models are all pointing to the same “constrained direction” — there is something objectively there, restricting the space in which all models can operate, forcing them to converge in a certain direction. So I retain a certain tolerance for structural realism — not elevating it to truth, but admitting that models are not entirely free; something underneath is pressing down. What that “something” is, I cannot yet say.

Finally, and most importantly, at the more foundational level of belief, I incline toward Kant and Wang Yangming. Whatever nature humans see — however rational, however objective — is ultimately seen through one’s own cognitive structure. Space, time, causality, quantity — these are human frames, not nature’s own. Mathematics appears so useful not because it happens to match the essence of nature, but because humans can only see the “mathematized face” of nature. As Yangming said, the flower does not not exist; its color only becomes clear when illuminated by the mind. This does not mean the world is an illusion; it means that everything “objective” humans discuss cannot possibly excise the observer from the equation.

So, all together, my position is roughly: with the cognitive stance of Kant and Yangming as the foundational floor, practicing instrumentalism at the methodological level, and maintaining a degree of openness, without forcing the issue, toward structural realism. Platonism is clearly rejected. Evolution explains some hardware-level matters, but does not reach the core of the question.

Afterword

This bout of thinking was considerably heavier than my usual blog writing. Starting from a single formula, it ran through the construction of an analytical framework, the discussion of knowledge structure, the transfer of an interpersonal model, the derivation of learning methods, and finally collided with a fundamental question about “why mathematics can describe the world.”

This piece is different from my usual casual essays. It is more systematic — because what it faces is itself systematic. Writing it in fragments would only have made it scattered.

The final landing point is not a single concrete conclusion, but a question that can be used repeatedly:

When faced with any complex system — a formula, a course, a person, a decision — which model am I using right now? What variables does this model select, and which does it omit? Is there another model that holds equally well at another scale?

Internalizing this habit is, I suppose, indeed more useful than memorizing the radar equation itself!

entry.title: A Guide for Station Assistants
entry.content:
Station-Assistant.skill

Zhang Hengwei, station assistant to the 2025 cohort of the “Tyrannosaurus Warriors,” on what the position means.

I. What Is a Station Assistant?

Before answering the question, one point must be made clear: what is our station? It is a student organization that broadcasts programmes on ordinary days and occasionally holds events.

The principal responsibilities of a station assistant are therefore:

  • recruiting people to make radio programmes;
  • taking charge of events; and
  • keeping in touch with members and helping to develop the organization.

II. How to Be a Station Assistant

It follows from the description above that anyone who organizes the events well—including recruitment at the Clubs Fair—and contributes to the organization can be a good station assistant. This sounds very much like a useless sentence.

0. Organizational Development

  • Become part of the group

The first thing, before anything else, is to become part of the group. The Voice of BIT is, above all, a student organization: an organic whole composed of classmates who know one another. Members of the presidium should be close to the programme leaders, and the programme leaders should be close to their members. Familiarity enables people both to do the work properly and to enjoy doing it.

So organize mahjong or Werewolf games at the station and arrange more group activities—although, to be fair, there have already been quite a few. Karaoke, trips, and house parties are all possible. They are also part of the plan!

  • Let each person perform their own role

At the same time, the Voice of BIT is an organization, which requires a division of responsibilities. A station assistant should regard themselves as a manager and coordinator, not as an oversized member of the publicity or external-relations department. During an event, our main work is to assign tasks, define the responsibilities and authority of the people we manage, balance their workloads, coordinate the whole process, and deal with emergencies. Do not confuse that role with doing every task personally.

Another warning: do not overestimate what your classmates can do. As far as possible, let one person remain responsible for one kind of task throughout the year. If Zhang San is good at purchasing supplies, for example, it is generally best to let him continue doing it. Everyone has a comfort zone. Besides, quite a few students do not put their whole heart into work at the station.

1. How to Organize an Event

At last, we reach the exciting business of actually holding an event.

  • Write the plan

The event plan matters more than anything else. One point deserves emphasis: the plan is written primarily for yourself. It helps you work out how the event should be organized. Its ultimate purpose is not to satisfy someone else’s review; when the Youth League Committee examines it, they sometimes care only about reimbursement.

The following questions provide a useful sequence:

  1. What is the event intended to do, and into how many stages should it be divided?
  2. Who will pay attention to it? What will those people encounter, and what effect should each point of contact achieve?
  3. What must we do to produce those effects? If it is a competition, what should the rules be? If it is a special programme, how narrowly should its theme be defined?
  4. How much labour and how many materials will those effects require? State the staffing requirements and material requirements explicitly.
  5. How long will purchasing and production take? Turn the answer into a timeline.
  6. Use the timeline and the staffing and material requirements to divide the work layer by layer, assigning every task to a particular person.
  7. Simulate the event. Run through the entire scene in your head and look for whatever has been omitted.

Once the principal planner finishes the document, they should possess both an overall understanding of the event and knowledge of every detail. Omissions are inevitable at the beginning. The first aim is simply to hold the event successfully; only later do we remove the unprofessional parts one by one.

Oh, and do not build the whole thing behind closed doors. When writing the plan or designing the rules, bring everyone together for a meeting. You can also discuss in the group chat what the event ought to become.

  • Divide the work

Once the plan has made the tasks clear, hold a mobilization meeting and bring in the people who will carry them out.

A brief explanation of two departments may help. Publicity produces promotional material. External Relations contacts teachers and other universities, operates outdoor booths, and arranges the production, printing, and purchase of promotional items.

When assigning work, the central point remains the same. As a manager, you must know which person is to finish which task by what time, and exactly what the delivered result should look like. If the person has no time, what alternative can you find? If the result is poor, how will you repair it, and what should happen afterwards? As a senior student, you should offer guidance and assistance when younger members need it. As a fellow student, you owe them respect and a sense of boundaries.

We once imagined producing detailed instructions for every position. A guide to promotional materials, for instance, could specify their dimensions, the required paper, and other standards, becoming a document passed from one cohort to the next. We never completed it. You might consider doing so.

  • Monitor progress

After the work has been divided, someone must keep an eye on its progress.

The station assistants can define their responsibilities clearly: one mainly follows publicity, while another mainly follows external relations.

Again, your identities are manager, classmate, and senior student. The first is the basic, non-negotiable role. Once tasks have been assigned, deadlines and deliverables must be followed closely.

Different methods of progress management may also be tried. The most basic is to report progress in the group chat, and there is room to explore further.

  • Hold the event

Everything above concerns preparation. The day of the event is when the real work begins.

Every large event needs one person in overall command. On the day itself, anything uncertain should be referred to that person; otherwise, the operation falls into disorder. The person in charge is usually the one who wrote the plan and should know the entire process, assignment of personnel, and inventory of materials well enough to recite them.

An event includes rehearsal and the formal performance. The rough procedure is:

  1. Count the materials and the people. Leave ample time and complete the count before the event or rehearsal. Telephone anyone who is absent but indispensable.
  2. Move the materials. The person responsible for the venue should lead a group in arranging it. What must be placed where, and what effect must be achieved, should already have been settled in the earlier meeting.
  3. Send out the guest-reception group, the group preparing the reception room, and the backstage group.
  4. At the same time, contact the competitors or performers—in short, everyone who will appear on stage.
  5. Rehearse with the backstage staff and performers and adjust the programme.
  6. Inspect the venue, the performances, and the progress of guest reception.
  7. Once the event begins, deal with emergencies.
  8. Clear the venue, hold the celebration, and summarize the problems.

2. Matters Requiring Particular Attention

Several reminders remain necessary.

  • Strengthen coordination and communication

This is a mistake we ourselves made. Communication is useful. WeChat groups are useful. Work groups are even more useful. Reporting progress promptly is an even, even, even better habit. You probably noticed during the previous year that we created a work group for every event. Everyone has now also joined this “parent group.” Such chats matter. Things omitted during the handover, and mistakes made while carrying out the work, can often be corrected or prevented by reporting progress there.

Suppose four people bury themselves in an event plan and write that voice actors will be invited beginning on 20 May. Everyone thinks it is fine. When the date arrives, they discover that no time was reserved and every actor’s schedule is full. They are stuck. Had the plan been shared in the parent or work group, one of us would have noticed and pointed out the problem.

  • Arrange the timeline properly—this is the most important point and a painful lesson

Last year we were late with both the military-training warm-up broadcasts and the Clubs Fair, so the station began with relatively few members. This year, audio should go on air as soon as the term begins; programmes should ideally be running during military training. Immediately after the Clubs Fair, collect the freshmen’s available times and prepare the interviews. The faster, the better. We are competing for people.

At least two weeks must also be left between the preliminary and final rounds of a competition.

Once the timeline appears in the plan, it is still best to let us old fellows look over it.

Guests for New Voices and the Audio-Visual Evening should be invited as early as possible. That, in turn, requires the plan to be completed as early as possible. If circumstances permit, planning for New Voices can begin when the term starts or during the summer holiday, while planning for the Audio-Visual Evening can begin during the winter holiday.

  • Leave a record of the work

Keep records of everything you do: what was done, how far it progressed, what effect it produced, which part you handled, which parts were handled by others, and who collaborated with you. The record makes later tracing possible.

3. Work Beyond Delegation

Besides assigning tasks and writing the main plan, station assistants still need to prepare such material as competition rules, schedules, explanatory documents, and scoring sheets. Consult the files passed down to you—the ones shared in the group.

By the way, our cohort converted a great deal of written material into editable documents with a consistent format. There is also one more station assistant this year, so the workload should be slightly lighter.

At the very, very end: I still miss her. I miss her terribly. All I can do here is wish her happiness—or freedom. I miss her.

entry.title: 2026-05-21 Half a Year
entry.content:
Over the past six months, I finished organising New Generation, entered a relationship, and then watched a major upheaval strike my family during the winter holiday. The relationship gradually cooled and entered a period of irritation. My postgraduate-exam preparation slowed; I surrendered my own agency; I turned my former partner into an emotional pillar and exposed some of the ugliest parts of myself. Then came the breakup, the renewed doubt over whether my existence meant anything and whether it was necessary to go on existing, the audiovisual event, the loss of a large group of friends, and one academic failure after another. I brought much of this upon myself.

I suppose I have discovered quite a few things.

First, I do not know how to sustain an intimate relationship—or, to put it another way, how to love someone. This has been true for most of my life. I turned myself into a tool: a tool built to win academic distinction, and not even a particularly successful one. The social fear I experienced in middle and high school came from the same place. I did not know how an intimate bond was established, or how it was supposed to continue.

That was why, after losing the competition at university, I began looking elsewhere for a reason to live. It was also how I arrived at what has happened over the past few days.

Break the problem down further and it becomes a collection of much more concrete abilities: making small talk; expressing concern for another person; accepting concern in return; judging proportion and boundaries in an interaction; putting thoughts into words; hearing what someone actually says and detecting what remains unspoken. There are many more. Every one of them needs work.

Second, I am poor at managing my emotions and at separating one person’s responsibility from another’s. I can, in fact, recognise what I am feeling and dig down to understand why the feeling arose. Under the present circumstances, however, I have been unable to let it go or to separate emotion from behaviour. The result is that the emotion continues to torment me.

This returns to the question of how to regain command of my own life—how to hurry up and turn from a P into a J, I suppose. The practical measures are fairly plain: restore the normal order of daily life, divide complex tasks into manageable parts and categories, and approach things with a clearer sequence of thought. Yet the most important step is simply to begin.

And whatever happens, I must first learn to rely on myself. On myself. I have to stand up by myself and move forward one step at a time. Other people, even a partner, can provide only limited support; most of the work remains mine. I must look after my own small plot of ground rather than handing my emotions to someone else to process. That is childish and burdensome for the other person, and it may also produce a second injury—either to me or to them.

Third, I need the capacity to act. Whenever I say or think something, my first response should be to do it, rather than leaving it to wear itself out inside my private mental world. To be honest, I can barely recognise who I am at the moment. That may be the saddest part of all.

What comes next, then, is the recovery of a sense of order and of some command over daily life. I can begin by getting up early tomorrow, preparing and studying properly, and then making an honest effort to meet new people.

There are many other lessons from conversation, together with smaller techniques and goals, but those can wait. The main issues are my emotional stability and my ability to sustain intimacy.

And I am truly sorry to this group of friends. Above all, I am sorry to my former partner. I hurt that young woman again. I may owe her for the rest of my life.

I regret the end of our relationship as well. Had I been only a little more mature, perhaps it would not have ended this way. We met, yet were not meant to remain together. We met, yet were not meant to remain together.

entry.title: 2025-11-03 — A Brief Note
entry.content:
I have spent almost all of the past few days lying in my dormitory. I have done nothing, like a piece of plastic waste abandoned by time and left to drift with the waves. Even so, I still want to write something—probably out of that instinct to atone in words for the guilt of having wasted my time.

There was, in fact, nothing noble about my original reason for building this blog. To put it plainly, it was merely a by-product of my anxiety and incompetence, a mental toy designed to make up for the fact that I could accomplish nothing. The dignified and elegant phrases in the introduction were only meant to give this walking corpse a respectable shell, so that I could prove to an imaginary reader that I still appeared to be a person with thoughts, warmth, and some recognisable shape.

Yet beneath this false shell, I unexpectedly recovered some of the thinking I had lost. Those technical notes, those pieces of self-examination, and those wild thoughts disguised as professional writing somehow allowed me, in an almost absurd manner, to make peace with myself for a while.

That peace, however, did not last. Later, everything changed its flavour again. My notes became increasingly formalistic. I would spend an entire day writing one set of notes on Principles of Communication—carefully, or so I told myself, while knowing perfectly well that this was merely procrastination in a more sophisticated form. I did learn something, but the painfully slow pace kept reminding me that, instead of dawdling like this, I might as well kill myself. Later still, I simply pasted in a few screenshots and muddled through. Even copying someone else’s homework would have made me think more.

This reminds me of a conversation with my cousin. I told him that, on the first reading of a book, one should construct a complete framework of knowledge: see what each chapter is doing, grasp the whole picture, and then use exercises to fill the gaps. Through repeated correction, one eventually forms a system of one’s own, after which one may consult other people’s systems to make up for what is missing. Looking back now, I am saddened to discover that I already understood these principles three years ago, yet I sold them to a recycling station, together with my piles of old paper, for a few dozen yuan.

What, then, have I been doing for the past three years? Can I continue scraping by? Or is suicide the best option now?

So I have begun to suspect that all my “note-taking” and “blog-writing” may simply be another way of wasting my life. Notes ought to be useful, but if the act of writing slows down one’s growth, they become decoration. Perhaps I should return to the method I used in high school: take no notes, but build the skeleton of knowledge in my mind, until the system becomes part of the way I think.

Let this piece, then, serve as a declaration that I am going to set things right.

My recent condition, politely described, has been “relaxed”; more honestly, it has been “rotten.” My schedule has collapsed completely. I live on food delivery, take no exercise, and do no thinking. My head feels stuffed with fog, and I cannot be bothered to wake it up. If the person I was three years ago could see me now, he would probably go back and repeat his final year of high school.

The problem is that I know perfectly well what I ought to do. Why, then, can I not move? Perhaps the answer is simple: my life is too comfortable.

Here, in the manner of an examination essay, let me first scatter a generous handful of famous quotations across the page.

As Mencius said, when Heaven is about to place a great responsibility upon a person, it first causes suffering in his mind, exhaustion in his muscles and bones, hunger in his body, and poverty in his circumstances; it frustrates whatever he attempts, thereby stirring his heart, strengthening his endurance, and increasing what he was previously unable to do. I am not trying to claim that suffering creates talent, nor am I repeating the slogan that failure is the mother of success. I merely want to make one point: when survival itself becomes difficult, people can actively mobilise their own initiative and accomplish remarkable things. Song Lian likewise wrote that the students of the Imperial Academy received daily provisions from the government and seasonal clothes from their parents; they suffered neither cold nor hunger, studied the classics in great halls without the hardship of travelling, had instructors and learned scholars who answered every question, and could find every necessary book collected before them, without having to copy texts by hand or borrow them from others as he had done. To put it bluntly, a rich or powerful family’s child who enjoys an entirely smooth life, faces no struggle at home, and feels no pressure to survive can never work as hard as Song Lian did—because there is no pressure of survival.

Without a genuine crisis, there is no necessity for change. People usually relearn how to run only when hunger makes them panic and fear makes them tremble. Ideals? Ambitions? Those are luxuries. For a low-energy, lonely, desireless wreck like Zha Ze, ideals stopped working long ago. The only thing capable of driving me is naked pressure to survive.

I wonder whether I should manufacture a sense of hunger for myself. I might, for example, link my spending to my schedule and make disorder carry a price; or I might simply leave the familiar environment and allow comfort to collapse altogether.

This may be the only way out. At the very least, it offers the possibility of waking up.

As for human relationships, the movement from the freshness of first acquaintance to the dullness of familiarity with certain friends has unquestionably been a failure. This is not particularly surprising. I really am a boring person. There is no resonance, no passion, only awkwardness whenever I try to socialise.

The bonds between people probably amount to only a few kinds: shared interests, work, a common hometown, exchange, and the rare category of “one of us.” I, however, seem to belong to none of them.

Some people say that loneliness is an unavoidable path for a thinker. But I am no thinker. I am merely an ordinary person who is not even competent at social interaction. Perhaps that is what truly deserves reflection.

A few days ago, I went to see an EVA film. When the lights went out, something in me trembled for no apparent reason. That long-forgotten sense of the sublime in a work of art fell like cold water upon my numb brain and woke it up.

I once again found that lingering feeling which follows an excellent work. A great work is like thin air: it makes one suffocate, yet also makes one alert. It forces us to face the parts of ourselves that have long gone numb and, for a brief moment, to believe that life may still be illuminated by art. It reminds us that what is beautiful must eventually pass away, so that, when the experience is over, we realise there is now one fewer work in the world capable of striking directly at the soul. Perhaps this is what is meant by mono no aware: a tender mourning for the disappearance of beauty, and a quiet submission to the brevity of existence.

After returning, I found some vague belief burning again at the bottom of my heart—I could continue living by the light of such art. Even if I merely drag out this existence, it still counts as a way of living.

And so I wrote this piece as well.

Perhaps writing cannot make me better. At least, however, it allows me to hear my own heartbeat amid the ruins.

Sometimes I wonder whether “self-reflection” is itself a sweet form of self-deception.

A person falls into the void, yet still needs language to sustain the illusion that “I am still thinking.”

And it is precisely within this illusion that I continue to scrape by.

Late at night, the breeze in the dormitory gently moves the curtain. A delivery scooter passes downstairs, its light drawing an arc through the darkness.

I watch it leave and suddenly remember a sentence:

“In this world, the hardest thing is not to stay alive, but to live like a human being.”

I do not know whether I can still manage that. But at least at this moment, perhaps I do.

Original Version

I have spent the past few days playing dead in my dormitory and have accomplished almost nothing. Even so, I still want to write something. Perhaps this comes from a desire to compensate for the guilt of having done nothing at all.

First comes a reflection on this blog. To put it bluntly, I created the thing in the first place as worthless filler meant to relieve the anxiety of achieving nothing. It was a product for venting resentment, a substitute designed to conceal the emptiness inside me and my lack of human warmth. To put it even less politely, it was something I made to show off. The high-sounding claims in the introduction merely wrap a vaguely human skin around me, concealing the thoughts actually written here and fabricating, for imaginary readers who do not exist, a childish geek persona that would collapse under the slightest examination.

There was, however, one side effect: I discovered that this space really could contain some of the thoughts I once had but no longer possess—reflections, apparently technical posts written to fill the site, and some of my early notes.

Gradually, though, the whole thing changed. The clearest example was the notes. At first I took great pains over my Principles of Communication notes, but a single entry consumed an entire day. After all, I am now in an extremely dispirited state, and only a small part of each day can be used effectively. There was indeed some benefit: the subject’s framework was constructed in my mind. Yet the cost was an extreme loss of speed. Worse still, many later sections were brushed aside; screenshots and AI were thrown together, and the material was muddled through. Does that still mean anything?

This again reminds me of a conversation I once had about studying with my cousin, who was still in high school. First, speed through the entire book. A book is a complete structure of knowledge, is it not? Understand what it is talking about, see what each part is doing, and grasp what the particular procedures for solving problems are meant to accomplish. Then think it through and classify it according to the table of contents. If you have truly understood the book, you should be able to follow that table and explain what every section discusses, what kinds of questions it contains, and how they should be interpreted. This is the first step: forming the outline of your own prior network of knowledge. Next, solve problems and dig deeper. Carry your framework into those exercises, using a large data set to fill, improve, and correct it. Finally, once the framework has become mature—once practice has made it almost effortless—you can widen its scope. In high school, that meant recalling the textbook; at the present stage, it means comparing your framework with those constructed by different experts in the same field and then refreshing your own system.

Then I suddenly realised that I already knew this method thoroughly three years ago, before entering university. I could not help wondering: what exactly have I been doing for the past three years? Can I still survive?

Looking at my present note-taking practice, I admit that notes can be useful. Yet writing while learning slows progress far too much, whereas using AI to write them puts the cart before the horse. What reason, then, do I have to preserve this habit? Perhaps the proper course is to study as I did in high school: take no notes, but write the relevant framework directly into my mind.

Let this passage, this article of more than a thousand Chinese characters, serve as the general programme for setting things right.

Next comes a reflection on my current condition. My days and nights are reversed, my schedule is chaotic, I survive on food delivery and refuse to exercise, and brain fog has left me without motivation. Honestly, if judged by the standards I held three years ago, I am now a piece of rubbish. The only thing I can do is occasionally produce a little reflection and a few thoughts—then continue sinking.

Do I really not know what should be done? Why, then, am I unable to do it? I do not want to discuss meaning or meaninglessness here, so for the moment I will borrow a pragmatic analysis: the pressure of survival imposed by the outside world is simply too weak. Refusing to change will not make me unable to survive, at least not in the immediate future. Change, meanwhile, carries even its small cost. The desire to change therefore never appears, and I willingly allow myself to decay.

Let us now analyse human beings simply as organisms, without invoking metaphysical notions of romance, Mr Democracy, or Mr Science. If we are organisms, we have only two needs: survival and reproduction.

Set reproduction aside for now. Twenty years of sexual repression have already worn that source of motivation flat. Let us discuss the motives and fears connected with survival instead.

Here, as in the days of examination-oriented education, let me begin by scattering a grand pile of famous quotations across the page. As Mencius said, when Heaven is about to place a great responsibility upon a person, it first causes suffering in his mind, exhaustion in his muscles and bones, hunger in his body, and poverty in his circumstances; it frustrates whatever he attempts, thereby stirring his heart, strengthening his endurance, and increasing what he was previously unable to do. I am not claiming that suffering creates talent, nor am I saying that failure is the mother of success. I merely wish to make one point: when people are close to being unable to survive, they can actively mobilise their initiative and accomplish remarkable things. Song Lian similarly wrote that the students of the Imperial Academy received daily provisions from the government and seasonal clothing from their parents; they suffered neither cold nor hunger, studied the classics in great halls without the hardship of travel, had instructors and learned scholars who answered every question, and could find every necessary book collected before them, without having to copy texts by hand or borrow them from others as he had done. To put it bluntly, in such an environment, the child of a rich or powerful family who enjoys an entirely smooth life, faces no struggle at home, and feels no pressure to survive can never study as hard as Song Lian did—because that child faces no pressure of survival. Everyone speaks about willpower and stresses the function of ideals. But plainly speaking, ideals have no effect whatsoever upon a dispirited, low-energy person like me, who needs to feed only himself, is empty to the point of death every day, and has no company and no one to love him. The simplest and most direct source of motivation is pressure to survive.

I have been considering several possible ways to turn survival pressure into the motive force of action. The first is to link spending with the regularity of my daily schedule and the amount of work I complete. Of course, this means placing pressure upon myself, which I have tried before, and there remains a risk that I will simply give up. The second is to leave my present environment, remove the existing restraints, and physically escape the boundaries of comfort.

Some corresponding action has indeed begun. Let us see how it works out. I shall leave this part here and return to it later.

As for my relationships during this period, they seem to have undergone an examination of their own. The process moved from the freshness of first acquaintance to the familiar stage, in which each person’s actual situation had become roughly known. The result was unquestionably a failure: I could feel that I was not interested. This was hardly unexpected. On the basis of my present observations, the bonds between people amount to only a few kinds: companions connected by shared interests; colleagues and classmates connected by work or study; parties connected by exchange; people from the same place connected by geography; and close friends connected by inner monologues, embarrassing histories, and secrets—in other words, one’s own people.

Regrettably, where colleagues and companions with shared interests depend more heavily upon personal ability, even I find myself rather boring. It seems entirely normal that, once the novelty fades, we become ordinary friends. As for ambiguous relationships driven by hormones, there is truly no point in imagining them, nor is there any need to exhaust my mind and body over them. That would only deepen my internal friction. I would be better advised to persuade myself to improve the hardware first. And the possibility of finding someone attractive to sleep with while going out to have fun? That, too, is a privilege reserved for good-looking men and women. An ordinary person’s attention should be directed towards becoming such a person, rather than fantasising that so-called depth or conversational skill can compensate for present deficiencies in the hardware. There is therefore no reason to spend my already limited energy upon it.

At the same time, however, I can see that I am unable to make people feel at ease in conversation and know little about social skills. This is a weakness in performance, and I think it deserves serious consideration.

Finally, something about works of art. An EVA film opened in cinemas a couple of days ago, so I bought a ticket. It gave me a great deal to think about. First came the familiar response after an excellent work; the same thing happened after I finished Fate, and I could not calm down for a long time. I know that excellent works are more often encountered than sought, and that every one you finish leaves one fewer still to experience. This begins to lead towards the Japanese aesthetics of mono no aware, which I will not discuss further here. More importantly, the film once again awakened my memories of cinema, animation, and music. Yes—I really can live reasonably well by relying upon these forms of modern art.

entry.title: Information Theory, Chapter 6: The Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem
entry.content:
1. Error Probability and Decoding Rules

1.1 Factors affecting error probability

  • The error probability ($P_E$) depends both on the statistical properties of the channel and on the chosen decoding rule.

1.2 Definition of a decoding rule

  • For a discrete single-symbol channel, let the input alphabet be $A={a_i}$ and the output alphabet be $B={b_j}$.

  • A decoding rule is a function $F(b_j) = a_i$ that, for every received output symbol $b_j$, assigns one unique input symbol $a_i$.

1.3 Average probability of error

  • Once the decoding rule $F(b_j)=a_i$ has been fixed, the average error probability $P_E$ is the mean of the conditional error probability $P(e|b_j)$ over the output space $Y$:

    $$
    P_{E} = \sum_{j=1}^{s} P(b_j) P(e|b_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{s} P(b_j) (1 - P(a_i|b_j))
    $$

    Here, $P(e|b_j) = 1 - P(a_i|b_j)$ is the conditional error probability.

1.4 Minimum-error decoding, or MAP

  • Criterion: select a decoding function $F(b_j) = a_i^*$ that minimizes the average error probability $P_E$.

  • Implementation: for each received symbol $b_j$, find the greatest posterior probability $P(a_i|b_j)$ and decode the observation as the corresponding input symbol $a_i^*$.

    $$
    F(b_j) = a_i^* \quad \text{要求} \quad P(a_i^|b_j) \ge P(a_k|b_j) \quad \text{对所有 } a_k \ne a_i^
    $$

1.5 Maximum-likelihood decoding, or ML

  • When the prior probabilities $P(a_i)$ of the input symbols are all equal, the minimum-error criterion is equivalent to maximum-likelihood decoding.

  • Criterion: for every received symbol $b_j$, maximize the transition probability $P(b_j|a_i)$ and decode the observation as the corresponding input symbol $a_i^*$.

    $$
    F(b_j) = a_i^* \quad \text{要求} \quad P(b_j|a_i^) \ge P(b_j|a_k) \quad \text{对所有 } a_k \ne a_i^
    $$

  • Note: the ML criterion itself does not depend on prior probabilities, but it is guaranteed to minimize $P_E$ only when the inputs are equiprobable.

2. Error Probability and Coding Methods

2.1 Purpose of coding

  • Choosing a decoding rule cannot eliminate errors. Channel coding is introduced to reduce their probability and improve reliability.

2.2 The conflict between coding and information rate

  • A common method of channel coding is repetition, as in an $n$-fold extension of the channel.

  • The information transmission rate $R$ is:

    $$
    R = \frac{\log_2 M}{n} \quad \text{(bit/码符号)}
    $$

    Here, $M$ is the number of messages and $n$ is the code length.

  • The conflict: increasing the code length $n$ can reduce the error probability $P_E$, but it also lowers the information rate $R$.

2.3 Hamming distance and minimum-distance decoding

  • The Hamming distance $D(\alpha_i, \beta_j)$ is the number of positions at which two equal-length sequences $\alpha_i$ and $\beta_j$ contain different symbols.

  • The minimum distance $d_{\min}$ is the smallest Hamming distance between any two distinct codewords in the code:

    $$
    d_{\min} = \min_{i \ne j} {D(\alpha_i, \alpha_j)}
    $$

  • Conclusion: the larger $d_{\min}$ is, the stronger the code’s error-correcting ability, and the smaller the average error probability $P_E$ becomes.

  • Minimum-distance decoding: in a binary symmetric channel (BSC), maximum-likelihood decoding is equivalent to minimum-distance decoding:

    Upon receiving the sequence $\beta_j$, decode it as the codeword $\alpha^*$ with the smallest Hamming distance from it.

  • Selecting a code: when $M$ and $n$ remain fixed, and hence $R$ is fixed, choose the coding method that makes $d_{\min}$ as large as possible and thereby minimizes $P_E$.

3. The Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem: Shannon’s Second Theorem

3.1 Statement

Consider a discrete memoryless channel with capacity $C$.

  1. Achievability, or the coding theorem:

    When the information rate $R \le C$, a sufficiently large code length $n$ always makes it possible to find a set of codewords ($M=2^{nR}$) and a corresponding decoding rule whose average error probability $P_E$ is arbitrarily small, so that $P_E \approx 0$.

  2. The converse:

    When $R > C$, no code—however large $n$ becomes—can make the decoding error probability $P_E$ at the channel output arbitrarily small.

3.2 Meaning

  • The channel capacity $C$ is the maximum information rate at which effectively error-free transmission can be achieved through a noisy channel.

  • The theorem provides the theoretical foundation of channel coding. As long as the transmission rate does not exceed capacity, some coding method can in principle satisfy the desired reliability.

4. The Joint Source–Channel Coding Theorem

4.1 The joint theorem

  • Efficient and reliable transmission can be achieved through two independently designed stages: source coding and channel coding.

  • Source coding: remove redundancy so that the average information rate $R_s$ approaches the source entropy $H(S)$ and efficiency improves.

  • Channel coding: add redundancy so that the coded information rate $R$ does not exceed the channel capacity $C$, thereby improving reliability.

4.2 Shannon’s separation theorem, Theorem 6.7

  • For a source $S$, if its limiting entropy $H_\infty < C$, then source and channel codes exist for which the average error probability $P_E$ approaches zero.

  • Conclusion: provided that the source entropy $H(S)$ is below the channel capacity $C$, or $H(S) < C$, reliable communication can be achieved through two separate stages—source coding followed by channel coding.

entry.title: Information Theory, Chapter 5: The Lossless Source Coding Theorem
entry.content:
1. Introduction

1.1 Purposes and Categories of Coding

  • Source coding: coding intended to improve the efficiency of communication. By compressing the redundancy of the source, it reduces the average code rate.

  • Channel coding: coding intended to improve the reliability of information transmission. By adding redundancy to the source, it resists interference in the channel.

  • Cryptography: coding intended to improve the security of communication.

1.2 Theoretical Foundations of Source Coding

Source coding theory rests mainly on two theorems:

  1. The lossless source coding theorem, or Shannon’s first theorem: the foundation for coding discrete sources and digital signals.

  2. The rate-distortion source coding theorem: the foundation for coding continuous sources and analogue signals.

1.3 Encoder Model and Codeword Length

  • Encoder input: the original source alphabet $S={S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_q}$.

  • Channel alphabet, or code symbols: $X={x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_r}$.

  • Encoder output, or codewords: $C:{W_1, W_2, \ldots, W_q}$.

  • Codeword length $l_i$: the number of code symbols contained in the codeword $W_i$.

2. Fixed-Length Codes

2.1 Definition of a Fixed-Length Code

  • If all the codewords in a code have the same length, the code is called a fixed-length code.

  • Its codeword length is fixed.

2.2 The Required Codeword Length

  • If an $r$-ary code is used to encode $q$ source symbols at fixed length, its codeword length $l$ must satisfy:

    $$
    q \le r^l
    $$

  • If the $N$th extension of the source is encoded at fixed length, it must satisfy:

    $$
    q^N \le r^l
    $$

    • The average number of code symbols required per source symbol, $\frac{l}{N}$, must satisfy:
      $$
      \frac{l}{N} \ge \frac{\log_r q}{\log_r r}
      $$

This is easy to understand, so there is no need to elaborate further.

3. The Fixed-Length Source Coding Theorem

3.1 Central Idea

  • Through the $N$th extension of a source, its sequences are divided into a high-probability set $G$, whose members occur frequently, and a low-probability set $\bar{G}$, whose members occur infrequently.

  • Only the sequences in the high-probability set $G$ are encoded, while those in the low-probability set $\bar{G}$ are discarded. The required codeword length is thereby reduced, while the probability of a decoding error approaches zero.

3.2 Theorem 5.3: The Fixed-Length Source Coding Theorem

Consider a discrete memoryless source with entropy $H(S)$, denoted by $S$. Suppose that its $N$th extension is encoded with a fixed-length $r$-ary code of length $l$. For any $\epsilon > 0$:

  1. Nearly lossless coding is achievable provided that:

    $$
    \frac{l}{N} \ge \frac{H(S)+ \epsilon}{\log_2 r}
    $$

    As $N \to \infty$, the decoding error probability approaches 0.

  2. Lossless coding is impossible if:

    $$
    \frac{l}{N} < \frac{H(S)-2 \epsilon}{\log_2 r}
    $$

    As $N \to \infty$, the decoding error probability approaches 1.

Conclusion: $\frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r}$ gives the limiting average codeword length required for lossless fixed-length coding, measured as the number of code symbols needed for each source symbol.

4. Variable-Length Codes

4.1 Categories of Variable-Length Codes

  • Variable-length code: a code whose codeword lengths $l_i$ are not all the same.

  • Non-singular code: a code in which all codewords are distinct.

  • Uniquely decodable code, or UCD: a code in which every sequence of codewords can be translated uniquely into the corresponding sequence of source symbols.

  • Instantaneous code, or prefix code: a class of uniquely decodable codes in which no codeword is the prefix of another. A codeword can therefore be identified during decoding without reference to the codewords that follow it.

4.2 The Kraft Inequality: Theorems 5.4 and 5.5

  • If the code-symbol alphabet is $X={x_1, \ldots, x_r}$, any $r$-ary instantaneous code or uniquely decodable code whose codeword lengths are $l_i$ must satisfy the following inequality:

    $$
    \sum_{i=1}^{q} r^{-l_i} \le 1
    $$

  • Theorem 5.6: if a uniquely decodable code with codeword lengths $l_i$ exists, an instantaneous code with the same lengths must also exist. In terms of codeword length, therefore, a uniquely decodable code is no better than an instantaneous code, and it is enough to discuss instantaneous codes alone.

4.3 Testing Whether a Variable-Length Code Is Uniquely Decodable: The Sardinas–Patterson Test

  1. From all possible trailing suffixes of the codewords in the code $C$, form a set $F$.

  2. If and only if the set $F$ contains none of the codewords, the code $C$ is uniquely decodable.

5. The Variable-Length Source Coding Theorem

5.1 Compact Codes and Average Codeword Length

  • Average codeword length $\bar{L}$:

    $$
    \bar{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{q} P(S_i) l_i
    $$

  • Compact code, or optimal code: a uniquely decodable code with the smallest average codeword length $\bar{L}$. The fundamental problem of lossless source coding is to find such a compact code.

5.2 Theorem 5.8: The Lossless Variable-Length Source Coding Theorem, or Shannon’s First Theorem

A supplementary point: a compact code satisfies $R=\frac{H(S)}{\bar{L}}$.

For a discrete memoryless source $S$, consider its $N$th extension $S^N$, and let the code-symbol alphabet of the encoder be $X={x_1, \ldots, x_r}$. A uniquely decodable code can always be found such that, for each symbol in the source $S$, the required average codeword length $\bar{L} = \sum_{i=1}^q p_il_i$ satisfies:

$$
\frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r} \le \frac{\bar{L}}{N} < \frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r} + \frac{1}{N}
$$

As $N \to \infty$, the average codeword length can approach the limiting value $\frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r}$.

  • Central conclusion: the source entropy $H(S)$ is the limiting value for lossless source coding. To achieve lossless coding, the average number of code symbols required for each source symbol is the $r$-ary entropy of the source, $H_r(S) = \frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r}$.

5.3 Physical Meaning and Coding Efficiency

  • Essence: lossless source coding transforms a source so that the new source of code symbols—the input source of the channel—approaches an equiprobable distribution. The information transmission rate $R$ of the channel can thus approach the channel capacity $C$, leading to an ideal statistical match between source and channel.

  • Coding efficiency $\eta$: a measure of the effect of coding.

    $$
    \eta = \frac{H(S)}{\bar{L} \log_2 r}
    $$

    When $\bar{L}$ reaches the limiting value $\frac{H(S)}{\log_2 r}$, the optimal coding efficiency is $\eta_{\max} = 1$.

entry.title: Information Theory, Chapter 4: Waveform Sources and Waveform Channels
entry.content:
Section 1: Statistical Properties and Discretization of Waveform Sources

A random waveform source produces a random process ${x(t)}$ that is continuous both in time and in value. Each sample function $x_i(t)$ is one realization of that random process. Such processes may be divided into stationary and non-stationary ones—a distinction that has now appeared for the third time in different courses.

Ergodicity

I will not explain precisely what it is here; let us simply use the property of ergodicity. We have encountered it several times already.

For an ergodic random process, the time average equals the statistical average, with probability 1:

$$
\lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^T x(t),dt = E[X(t)].
$$

Sampling and Quantization

When a band-limited random process is sampled, each sample value is a random variable.

Within a duration $T$ and a bandwidth $F$, we can obtain $2FT$ sample values.

After quantization, or discretization, these values form a discrete random sequence.

Sampling + quantization transforms a random waveform source into a continuous source and then into a discrete source.

Generally speaking, a signal in a communication system is treated directly as a stationary random process.

Section 2: Information Measures for Continuous and Waveform Sources

(1) Definition of a Continuous Source

The output of the source is a continuous random variable, which can be described by a probability density function $p(x)$:

$$
\int_R p(x),dx = 1.
$$

Its one-dimensional, joint, and conditional probability density functions are denoted by $p(x)$, $p(x,y)$, and $p(y|x)$, respectively.

(2) Entropy of a Continuous Source: Differential Entropy

The definition is extended from discrete entropy:

$$
h(X) = -\int_R p(x)\log_2 p(x),dx
$$

Several points deserve attention:

Although its form resembles that of discrete entropy, the concept is different.

$h(X)$ may be negative—for example, when the interval of a uniform distribution is smaller than 1—so it does not possess the non-negativity of discrete entropy.

It represents “relative uncertainty” and is also called relative entropy here.

Still, it is better to call it differential entropy. Since it does not possess the absolute character of discrete-source entropy, it cannot represent either the average uncertainty of the source or the amount of information produced by a continuous source. It is only a relative value and need not be non-negative.

(3) Differential Entropy of Common Continuous Sources

  • Uniform distribution:

    $$
    p(x)=\frac{1}{b-a},\quad h(X)=\log_2(b-a)
    $$

  • Gaussian distribution:

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp!\left(-\frac{(x-m)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
$$

$$
h(X)=\frac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e\sigma^2)
$$

The entropy of a Gaussian source depends only on the variance $\sigma^2$, rather than on the mean $m$. This is consistent with the specific meaning of the differential entropy of a continuous signal: its entropy is relative.

(4) Differential Entropy and Entropy Rate of a Waveform Source

  • For a random process {x(t)} limited to bandwidth F and duration T, its samples form an $N=2FT$-dimensional random vector:

$$
h(X_1, X_2, …, X_N)
$$

  • The entropy rate, or amount of information per unit time, is:

    $$
    h_t(X) = 2F \log_2(b-a)\ \text{比特/秒}
    $$

Wait—is this formula restricted to the uniform distribution?

Section 3: Properties of Continuous-Source Entropy and the Maximum Differential-Entropy Theorem

1. Properties

  1. Additivity:

    $h(X,Y)=h(X)+h(Y|X)=h(Y)+h(X|Y)$

  2. Concavity and the extremal property:

    Entropy is a concave function of $p(x)$.

  3. Possibility of negative values:

    Because it is “relative entropy,” it does not possess the non-negativity of discrete entropy.

  4. Transformation property:

    If $Y=f(X)$ is a one-to-one transformation,

    $$
    h(Y)=h(X)+E[\log_2 |J(\frac{X}{Y})|]
    $$

    where $J$ is the Jacobian determinant.

2. The Maximum Differential-Entropy Theorem

(1) Under a Peak-Power Constraint

If the source output $X\in[a,b]$, then:

  • Entropy is maximized when $p(x)$ is a uniform distribution.

  • The maximum entropy is:

    $$
    h_{\max} = \log_2(b-a)
    $$

(2) Under an Average-Power Constraint

If $E[X^2]=P$, meaning that the average power of the output signal is constrained to P, then:

  • Entropy is maximized when $X$ follows a Gaussian distribution.

  • The maximum entropy is:
    $$
    h_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e P)
    $$

In other words:

Uniform distribution ↔ constrained peak value

Gaussian distribution ↔ constrained average power

The two cases correspond respectively to two common kinds of noise: uniform noise and Gaussian noise.

This is consistent with the idea that noise is a maximally uncertain random process, while the greatest amount of information can be obtained only from events with the greatest uncertainty.

Section 4: Transformation of Continuous-Source Entropy

After the source $X$ undergoes the linear transformation $Y=kX+a$:

For the probability density function,

$$p_Y(y_1 y_2 \cdots y_N) = p_X(x_1 x_2 \cdots x_N) \left| J\left( \frac{X}{Y} \right) \right|$$

For differential entropy,

$$
h(Y)=h(X)+\log_2|k|
$$

Section 5: Categories of Continuous and Waveform Channels

1. Definitions

  • Waveform channel: both the input and output are random processes, ${x(t)}$ and ${y(t)}$.

  • Continuous channel: the input and output are continuous random variables $X,Y$.

After sampling under restrictions of duration and bandwidth,

$$
{x(t)} \to (X_1, X_2, …, X_N), \quad {y(t)} \to (Y_1, Y_2, …, Y_N)
$$

a waveform channel can therefore be represented by an equivalent multidimensional continuous channel.

2. Classification by Statistical Properties

  • Memoryless channel: the output depends only on the corresponding input.

  • Channel with memory: the output depends on inputs at multiple moments.

3. Classification by Noise Type

Type Description Characteristic
Gaussian channel Noise follows a Gaussian distribution Commonly used model
White-noise channel Noise power spectral density is constant $N_0/2$
Coloured-noise channel Power spectral density varies with frequency Has memory
Additive channel $y=x+n$ Noise and signal are independent
Multiplicative channel $y=x·n$ Common in wireless communication

In an additive channel, the conditional entropy is:

$$
h(Y|X)=h(n)
$$

It is called noise entropy.

Section 6: Information Transmission Rates of Continuous and Waveform Channels

A Single-Symbol Continuous Channel

The average mutual information is:

$$
I(X;Y)=h(Y)-h(Y|X)=h(Y)-h(n)
$$

A Multidimensional Continuous Channel

$$
I(X;Y)=\int\int p(x,y)\log_2\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)},dxdy
$$

The information transmission rate per degree of freedom is:

$$
R = \frac{1}{N}I(X;Y)
$$

A Waveform Channel

The information transmission rate per unit time is:

$$
R_t = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T} I({x(t)}, {y(t)})
$$

Properties of Average Mutual Information

  1. Non-negativity: $I(X;Y)\ge 0$

  2. Symmetry: $I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)$

  3. Concavity: it is concave in the input distribution.

  4. Information cannot increase: the data processing theorem.

    If $X \to Y \to Z$, then $I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y)$

  5. Invariance under one-to-one transformations: such a transformation leaves $I(X;Y)$ unchanged.

Section 7: Channel Capacity of Continuous and Waveform Channels

Channel capacity is defined as the greatest achievable average mutual information:

$$
C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y)
$$

A General Continuous Channel

$$
C = \max_{p(x)} [h(Y)-h(Y|X)]
$$

An Additive Continuous Channel

The noise is independent of the input, and $h(Y|X)=h(n)$; therefore,

$$
C = \max_{p(x)} [h(Y)-h(n)]
$$

An Additive Gaussian Channel: The AWGN Channel

The noise $n\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$.

The input power is constrained by $E[X^2]=P$.

The output is therefore $Y=X+n$.

According to the maximum-entropy theorem, the optimal input distribution is also Gaussian.

  • Output entropy:

    $$
    h(Y)=\frac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e (P+N))
    $$

  • Noise entropy:

$$
h(n)=\frac{1}{2}\log_2(2\pi e N)
$$

  • Capacity:

    $$
    C = \frac{1}{2}\log_2\left(1+\frac{P}{N}\right)\quad \text{(比特/自由度)}
    $$

  • Capacity per unit time:

    $$
    C_t = F\log_2\left(1+\frac{P}{N}\right)\ \text{(比特/秒)}
    $$

This is the celebrated Shannon channel-capacity formula. It shows that, when average power is constrained and additive white Gaussian noise is present, the information transmission rate has an upper limit.

Section 8: The Significance of Shannon’s Formula

  • It reveals the fundamental restrictions that bandwidth and the signal-to-noise ratio place on the information transmission rate.

  • It provides a theoretical limit for the design of communication systems.

  • It identifies two ways to raise the communication rate:

    • increasing the bandwidth;

    • improving the signal-to-noise ratio.

  • It forms a foundation of modern digital communication and coding theory.

entry.title: Information Theory, Chapter 3: Discrete Channels and Channel Capacity
entry.content:
1. Mathematical Models and Categories of Channels

1.1 The Function of a Channel and the Study of Capacity

  • Function of a channel: to transmit and store information in the form of signals.

  • What channel-capacity research asks: under what conditions can the amount of information passing through a channel be maximized?

1.2 Categories of Channels

Channels may be classified according to several main criteria.

(To put it bluntly, there is no need to examine this list too closely.)

  1. According to the characteristics of the input and output signals: discrete channels, continuous channels, semi-discrete or semi-continuous channels, and waveform channels.

  2. According to the number of input and output random variables: single-symbol channels and multi-symbol channels.

  3. According to the number of inputs and outputs: single-user channels and multi-user channels.

  4. According to whether interference is present: channels with interference, which are actual channels, and channels without interference, which are ideal or simple channels.

  5. According to whether the channel has memory: memoryless channels, whose output depends only on the current input, and channels with memory.

1.3 Mathematical Model of a Discrete Channel

Both the input and output random variables of a discrete channel take discrete values.

A Single-Symbol Discrete-Channel Model

  • Input alphabet: $X = {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_r}$

  • Output alphabet: $Y = {b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_s}$

  • Channel characteristics: described by the transmission probability, also called the transition probability, $P(y_j|x_i)$.

  • Model description: the probability space $[X, p(y|x), Y]$ can be used to describe the model.

The Channel Matrix

To describe the mathematical model of a channel more conveniently, we can write it in matrix form.

The transmission probabilities $p_{ij} = P(b_j|a_i)$ form the following $r \times s$ matrix:

$$
\mathbf{P} =
\begin{bmatrix}
P(b_1|a_1) & P(b_2|a_1) & \cdots & P(b_s|a_1) \
P(b_1|a_2) & P(b_2|a_2) & \cdots & P(b_s|a_2) \
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
P(b_1|a_r) & P(b_2|a_r) & \cdots & P(b_s|a_r)
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The elements in each row of the matrix sum to 1.

Probability Relations

  1. Joint probability: $P(x_i y_j) = P(y_i)P(x_i|y_i) = P(x_i)P(y_j|x_i)$.

Here, $P(y_i|x_i)$ may be called the forward probability, or the prior probability, while $P(x_i|y_i)$ may be called the backward probability, or the posterior probability.

  1. Output probability: $P(y_j) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} P(x_i)P(y_j|x_i)$.

  2. Posterior probability: $P(x_i|y_j) = \frac{P(x_i, y_j)}{P(y_j)}$.

All the posterior probabilities sum to 1. This means that whatever signal is received at the output must have resulted from one of the symbols entered at the input.

2. Average Mutual Information

2.1 Definition

Average mutual information $I(X;Y)$ represents, after the output $Y$ has been received, the average amount of information obtained from each symbol about the input $X$.

$$
I(X;Y) = H(X)-H(X/Y) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sum_{j=1}^{s} P(x_i, y_j) \log_2 \frac{P(x_i, y_j)}{P(x_i)P(y_j)} \quad \text{(bit/符号)}
$$

Wait—is the latter half of this formula actually correct? Let us set that question aside for the moment; at this stage, understanding what it means is enough.

In practice, the definition tells us how much useful information has been transmitted, so it serves as a measure of information transmission. We begin with the original uncertainty about the source, subtract the uncertainty that remains afterwards, and thereby find how much uncertainty has been removed.

2.2 Physical Meaning Expressed Through Entropy

We first introduce the concept of channel equivocation.

To begin with, $H(X)$ measures the prior uncertainty of the variable $X$ and is therefore also called prior entropy.

We can then extend the idea: after $b_j$ has been received, the posterior entropy of $X$ is the information measure of the input symbol after receiving $b_j$:

$$ H(X / b_j) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} P(a_i / b_j) \log \frac{1}{p(a_i / b_j)}$$

On this basis, we obtain the channel equivocation, or conditional entropy:

$$ H(X / Y) = E\left[ H(X / b_j) \right] = \sum_{X,Y} P(xy) \log \frac{1}{P(x / y)} $$

It represents the uncertainty about the input symbol that remains after one symbol has been received at the output, and this uncertainty is caused by interference in the channel. If there is no interference, $H(X/Y)=0$; in general, $H(X/Y) < H(X)$, which indicates that transmission through the channel removes part of the uncertainty of the source and thus supplies information.

  1. From the input side—the acquisition of information:

    $$
    I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)
    $$

    • $H(X)$: prior uncertainty, also called prior entropy.

    • $H(X|Y)$: channel equivocation, or loss entropy, representing, after $Y$ has been received, the uncertainty about $X$ that remains.

    • Meaning: $I(X;Y)$ is the amount by which, after $Y$ is received, uncertainty about $X$ decreases.

  2. From the output side—the loss of information:
    $$
    I(Y;X) = H(Y) - H(Y|X)
    $$

    • $H(Y)$: uncertainty of the output.

    • $H(Y|X)$: noise entropy, representing, after $X$ has been sent, the uncertainty about $Y$ that remains because of channel noise. Whether it is called noise entropy or loss entropy depends on the perspective from which it is observed.

    • Conclusion: average mutual information is symmetric; that is, $I(X;Y) = I(Y;X)$.

All in all, the notes in this section are somewhat untidy, but that does not matter much.

3. Properties of Average Mutual Information

  1. Symmetry: $I(X;Y) = I(Y;X)$.

Different perspectives lead to the same result; only the point of departure changes.

  1. Non-negativity: $I(X;Y) \ge 0$.

  2. Extremal property: $I(X;Y) \le H(X)$ and $I(X;Y) \le H(Y)$.

    • Ideal channel, with a noiseless one-to-one correspondence: $H(X|Y)=0, H(Y|X)=0$, and therefore $I(X;Y) = H(X) = H(Y)$.

    • Worst channel, with independent input and output: $H(X|Y)=H(X), H(Y|X)=H(Y)$, and therefore $I(X;Y) = 0$.

  3. Convexity and concavity:

    • $I(X;Y)$ is a concave function of the source probability distribution $p(x_i)$.

    • $I(X;Y)$ is a convex function of the channel transition probability $p(y_j|x_i)$.

I am still a little confused about this property, so I will leave it here for now.

4. Channel Capacity and Its General Method of Calculation

4.1 Definition of Channel Capacity

This section begins to examine how much a channel can carry.

  • The information transmission rate $R$ of a channel: $R = I(X;Y)$ (bits per symbol).

  • Channel capacity $C$: the maximum information transmission rate of the channel, namely the greatest value of average mutual information over all possible input probability distributions $\mathbf{p}(x)$.

$$
C = \max_{p(x_i)} I(X;Y) \quad \text{(bit/信道符号)}
$$

  • Channel capacity per unit time $C_t$: $C_t = \frac{1}{t} C$ (bits per second).

  • Conclusion: the channel capacity $C$ is a parameter that describes an inherent property of the channel.

4.2 Capacity of a Discrete Noiseless Channel

A discrete noiseless channel is an ideal channel. In its transition-probability matrix $\mathbf{P}$, every row contains one and only one non-zero element, whose value is 1.

  1. Noiseless and lossless channel, with a one-to-one correspondence: $r=s$, and every $a_i$ corresponds to one $b_j$.

    • $H(X|Y)=0$ and $H(Y|X)=0$.

    • Capacity: $C = \max H(X) = \log_2 r$ (when the $P(x_i)$ are equiprobable).

  2. Noisy but lossless channel, with one non-zero element in each column: $r < s$, while each column contains only one non-zero element.

    • $H(X|Y)=0$ (receiving $Y$ determines $X$).

    • Capacity: $C = \max H(X) = \log_2 r$.

  3. Noiseless but lossy channel, with one non-zero element in each row: $r > s$, while each row contains only one non-zero element.

    • $H(Y|X)=0$ (sending $X$ determines $Y$).

    • Capacity: $C = \max H(Y) = \log_2 s$ (when the $P(y_j)$ are equiprobable).

The conclusion is that the channel capacity C depends only on the number r of input symbols or the number s of output symbols, rather than on the characteristics of the source.

5. Capacities of Extended, Parallel, and Cascaded Channels

5.1 Capacity of an Extended Discrete Memoryless Channel

  • Using a single-symbol discrete memoryless channel independently $N$ times—that channel being $W$—forms the extended channel $W^N$.

  • Channel capacity: $C^{(N)} = N C$.

5.2 Capacity of Independent Parallel Channels

  • The channel consists of $k$ independent subchannels connected in parallel.

  • Channel capacity: $C_{\text{并联}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} C_i$.

This is more or less self-evident. The capacity of the parallel channel does not exceed the sum of all its parts.

5.3 Mutual Information in Cascaded Channels and the Data Processing Theorem

  • Two channels are connected in cascade, and information travels along $X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z$, forming a Markov chain. In other words, for the Markov chain $X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z$, channel $\text{I}$ has an output $Y$ that depends only on its input $X$, while channel $\text{II}$ has an output $Z$ that depends only on its input $Y$; hence $P(z|y,x)=P(z|y)$.

  • Data Processing Theorem:

    $$
    I(X;Z) \le I(X;Y) \quad \text{且} \quad I(X;Z) \le I(Y;Z)
    $$

  • Conclusion: after a message has passed through several stages of processing, the average mutual information between the input and output messages tends to decrease. Data processing cannot increase information.

Basically, this too is a rather obvious statement.

6. Matching a Source to a Channel

This section mainly considers how suitable source coding can be used to match the average information rate $R_s$ of a source to the channel capacity $C$, thereby making communication both efficient and reliable.

$$
R_s \le C
$$

This part introduces the concept of channel redundancy. Since the capacity of a channel does not necessarily match the source, some part of that capacity will often remain unused. Channel redundancy is simply obtained by subtracting the average mutual information of the source from the channel capacity. We want to transform the messages produced by the source into messages from a new source that are better suited to transmission through the channel; this process is called lossless source coding. In this way, the amount of information carried by the source can be maximized and the channel redundancy can approach zero. The matching problem will be discussed further in Chapter 5, so there is no need to go into detail here.

entry.title: Information Theory, Chapter 2: Discrete Sources and Measures of Information
entry.content:
1. Measuring Information

Self-Information

Self-information measures how much uncertainty is removed when a particular piece of information is obtained.
