Histogram: displays the frequency distribution of grouped data.

P-P and Q-Q plots: test whether data follow a specified theoretical distribution, such as the normal distribution.

2.5 Exploratory Data Analysis, EDA

Introduction

EDA is a method of statistical analysis that uses visual charts and tables of statistics to explore the internal structure and patterns of data and extract key information without imposing many prior assumptions.

Purposes

  • Data understanding and preprocessing: clarify the meaning and structure of the data and discover outliers, missing values, and duplicates so that the dataset can be cleaned and organized.

  • Description and relationship analysis: understand important features, including the distributions of variables and the relationships among them.

  • Preparation for later analysis: decide whether transformations, non-parametric methods, or linear regression are needed, thereby translating a practical question into a feasible data-analysis problem.

Content

  1. Data screening: check for missing values, outliers, and duplicates; determine whether the sample is balanced; and decide whether sampling, new variables, or variable transformations are required.

  2. Description of data characteristics:

  • Continuous variables: use statistics such as the mean, median, and standard deviation and charts such as histograms and box plots.

  • Discrete variables, nominal or ordinal: use frequencies and proportions, together with frequency tables, bar charts, and pie charts.

  1. Relationships among variables:

Continuous versus continuous variables

This belongs to correlation analysis.

Charts: scatter plots, correlation matrices, and heat maps.

Measures: Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation coefficients. See the related articles on this site for details.

Discrete versus discrete variables

Charts: pairwise cross-tabulations and grouped bar charts; grid charts for several discrete variables.

Ordinal discrete variables use correlation analysis and the correlation coefficients just mentioned.

Nominal discrete variables use contingency analysis, with the $\varphi$ coefficient, the $V$ coefficient, and the contingency coefficient as quantitative measures.

Discrete versus continuous variables

Charts: histograms, box plots, and violin plots.

Quantitative analysis: t-tests, analysis of variance, and similar methods.

Measures: the t statistic and corresponding p-value in an independent-samples t-test, and the statistics used in one-way and multifactor analysis of variance.

  1. Testing data for normality

Histogram: examine how closely its shape matches a bell curve.

Box plot: examine whether the distribution is symmetrical.

P-P plot: under normality, the cumulative proportion of the data remains broadly consistent with that of the normal distribution. Place the cumulative proportion of the data on the X-axis and the corresponding normal cumulative proportion on the Y-axis. If the points lie approximately along a straight line, the data follow the specified distribution.

Q-Q plot: compare the quantiles of the data with those of a theoretical distribution.

  1. Testing the type of distribution

The Shapiro–Wilk test.

The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.

  1. Data transformation

The Box–Cox transformation.

Descriptive Statistics

  • Central tendency:

    • Mean: the most frequently used measure, but easily affected by extreme values.

    • Median: the middle value after ordering the data. It is not affected by extremes and is suitable for all distributions.

    • Mode: the most frequent value. It is not affected by extremes, and several modes may exist.

  • Dispersion:

    • Measures such as standard deviation, variance, and range describe how widely data are spread.

Visualization Charts

  • Bar chart: represents categorical frequencies by the length of bars and is suitable for discrete variables.

  • Line chart: uses rising and falling lines to show how a variable changes over time and is suitable for continuous variables.

  • Box plot: uses a box and line segments to display the maximum, minimum, median, and quartiles, making symmetry visible at a glance.

3. Principal Methods of Analysis

3.1 Hypothesis Testing

We may have a suspicion or claim, such as “this new drug is effective,” but cannot draw a conclusion directly. We must first establish a null hypothesis H0, which usually represents “no effect” or “no change,” and presume it innocent. We then collect sample data and ask whether the evidence is strong enough to overturn that innocent assumption beyond reasonable doubt—at a specified probability level.

The Steps of the Trial

  1. State the hypotheses

The null hypothesis, H0, represents the status quo or absence of an effect and always contains equality (=, ≤, or ≥). In court, it is the claim that the defendant is innocent. For example: H0: the mean effect of the new drug = the mean effect of the placebo.

The alternative hypothesis, H1 or Ha, is the opposing claim that we hope to establish and always contains an inequality (≠, <, or >). In court, it is the claim that the defendant is guilty. For example: H1: the mean effect of the new drug ≠ the mean effect of the placebo.

  1. Set the significance level α

Before the trial begins, we set a standard for conviction. This is the significance level α, commonly 0.05. It is the maximum risk of a mistaken judgement that we are willing to bear. An α of 0.05 means accepting a five-per-cent probability of condemning an innocent person—in statistical terms, wrongly rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.

  1. Calculate the test statistic

This step reduces the evidence, or sample data, to a single numerical value. The statistic measures how far the sample result lies from what H0 predicts. Different problems require different statistics, including Z, t, χ², and F.

  1. Make the statistical decision

This is the final verdict. Two methods are available.

Critical-value method: compare the calculated statistic with a critical value obtained from a table according to α. If the statistic falls in the rejection region, reject H0.

P-value approach: this is the method most commonly used by modern statistical software. Calculate the p-value, which is the probability, if H0 is true, of observing the present sample result or one still more extreme. Compare it with α:

If p ≤ α, the observed event is unlikely under H0. We have reason to question H0 and therefore reject the null hypothesis.

If p > α, the sample result is ordinary under H0 and gives no cause for alarm. We do not have sufficient evidence to reject H0.

Two types of error:

A Type I error, or rejecting a true hypothesis, occurs when H0 is true but we reject it. Its probability is the chosen α.

A Type II error, or accepting a false hypothesis, occurs when H0 is false but the evidence is insufficient to reject it. Its probability is denoted by β.

Common Tests

1. Tests of Parameters in One Normal Population

Test of a mean with known σ: the Z-test

Question: “The national mean height of men is known to be 175 cm, with a standard deviation σ of 5 cm. A random sample of 100 men from our university has a mean height of 177 cm. Are men at our university taller than the national population?”

Test statistic:

$$ Z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} $$

Here, $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean, $\mu_0$ the hypothesized population mean, and $\sigma$ the population standard deviation; n is the sample size.

Test of a mean with unknown σ: the t-test

Question: this is the more common situation. “I want to know whether the mean lifetime of a new batch of light bulbs is 800 hours. I sample 25 bulbs and obtain a mean lifetime of 790 hours and a sample standard deviation s of 30 hours.”

Test statistic:

$$ t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} $$

The sample standard deviation s is used here. The t distribution has heavier tails than the Z distribution because it allows for the additional uncertainty introduced when s estimates σ.

Test of a variance: the chi-squared test

Question: “A manufacturing standard requires that the variance in the length of a component not exceed 0.01 mm². A sample of 30 components has a variance of 0.015 mm². Is the production line insufficiently stable?”

Test statistic:

$$ \chi^2 = \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} $$

Here, $s^2$ is the sample variance and $\sigma_0^2$ is the hypothesized population variance.

Test of a proportion: the Z-test

Question: “Our product had a market share of 20 per cent last year. After a promotional campaign this year, 230 of 1,000 new users chose it. Has the market share increased significantly?”

Test statistic:

$$ Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} $$

Here, $\hat{p}$ is the sample proportion and p₀ is the hypothesized population proportion.

2. Tests of Parameters in Two Normal Populations

The independent-samples t-test for means

Question: “Which of two teaching methods, A and B, is more effective? Students are randomly divided into two groups, one taught with A and the other with B, and their mean final-examination scores are compared.”

Test statistic, assuming equal variances:

$$ t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)_0}{\sqrt{s_p^2 (\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2})}} \quad , \quad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2} $$

Here, $s_p^2$ is the pooled variance.

The F-test for two independent-sample variances

Question: “Before carrying out the preceding t-test, I need to decide whether the variances of the two groups are equal. Group A has a score variance of 100 and Group B one of 120. Do the variances differ significantly?”

Test statistic:

$$ F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} $$

By convention, the larger sample variance is placed in the numerator.

The paired-samples t-test

Question: “I want to know whether a weight-loss drug works. I record the weight of a group of people before they take it and again after one month, then compare the two sets of measurements.”

Approach: these are not independent samples because the observations occur in pairs, comparing the same person before and after treatment. First calculate each person’s weight difference d. The problem then becomes a one-sample t-test on these differences, asking whether their mean $\bar{d}$ differs significantly from zero.

Test statistic:

$$ t = \frac{\bar{d} - D_0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} $$

Here, D₀ is normally 0, and s_d is the standard deviation of the differences d.

3.2 Contingency Analysis

Purpose: to determine whether qualitative, or categorical, variables are associated.

  • Approach—the chi-squared test:

    • Its central idea is a comparison between expectation and reality.

    1. State H0: first assume that the two variables are completely independent and unrelated.

    2. Calculate expected frequencies: under independence, calculate how many observations should theoretically appear in each cell of the contingency table.

      • Formula: expected frequency in a cell = (total of its row × total of its column) / total number of observations

    3. Calculate the chi-squared statistic: compare expectation with reality, meaning the observed frequency. The chi-squared value measures their overall difference.

      • Formula:
        $$ \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{观测频数} - \text{期望频数})^2}{\text{期望频数}} $$

      • Interpretation: if reality differs greatly from expectation, χ² becomes large, suggesting that independence may be untenable.

    4. Make the statistical decision: compare χ² with a critical value, or inspect the p-value. If p is below α, reject the null and conclude that a significant association exists.

  • Measures of association in a contingency table:

    • The chi-squared test tells us whether an association exists but not how strong it is. The following coefficients measure its strength.

    • The φ, or Phi, coefficient is designed for a 2x2 contingency table.

      • Formula: $\phi = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n}}$ (n is the total sample size)

      • Interpretation: values range from 0 to 1, and a value closer to 1 indicates a stronger association.

    • Cramér’s V is more general and can be applied to a contingency table of any size.

      • Formula: $V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n \cdot (\min(r, c) - 1)}}$ (r is the number of rows and c the number of columns)

      • Interpretation: it likewise ranges from 0 to 1, with values nearer 1 indicating stronger association. Because it can be compared across tables of different sizes, it is one of the most common measures in practice.

3.3 Correlation Analysis

  • Purpose: to determine whether quantitative data, or continuous variables, are associated and to measure the strength and direction of that association.

  • How does correlation differ from a functional relationship?

    • A functional relationship is deterministic: one value of X corresponds exactly to one value of Y. In y = 2x + 1, once x is fixed, y is fixed with no deviation, and the graph is a perfect line.

    • A correlation is non-deterministic and random. Variables follow a general tendency but not a strict rule. Taller people, for example, tend to weigh more, but not without exception. Their observations form a cloud of points around a trend line. Regression finds the average trend line behind that cloud, whereas correlation measures how tightly the points gather around it.

  • Measuring correlation:

    • The scatter plot is the most intuitive tool. Its pattern reveals:

      • direction—from lower left to upper right for positive correlation and from upper left to lower right for negative correlation;

      • form—a straight line or a curve;

      • strength—the more tightly points cluster around a line, the stronger the relationship.

    • A correlation coefficient turns the visual relationship into a number.

      • Pearson’s simple correlation coefficient, r:

        • Use: the most common coefficient, measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two continuous variables.

        • Formula:
          $$ r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}} $$

        • Interpretation:

          • Values range from -1 to +1.

          • r > 0 indicates positive correlation; r < 0 indicates negative correlation.

          • The larger the absolute value |r|, the stronger the linear relationship. |r| = 1 means perfect linear correlation, with every point on one line. r = 0 means no linear relationship.

        • Important assumption: the variables should be normally distributed, and the coefficient is highly sensitive to outliers.

      • Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, ρ or rs:

        • Use: appropriate when data are not normally distributed or are ordinal variables, such as the relationship between a ranking of product preference and a ranking of advertising expenditure.

        • Procedure: rather than use the raw values, order each variable from smallest to largest and replace every observation by its rank. Then calculate Pearson’s coefficient for the two rank sequences.

        • Interpretation: it measures the strength of a monotonic relationship—whether the two variables tend to rise and fall together.

      • Kendall’s Tau, τ:

        • Use: another non-parametric rank coefficient suitable for ordinal variables.

        • Procedure: its calculation is more involved and compares the number of all concordant pairs, whose variables are ordered in the same direction, with discordant pairs, whose ordering is reversed.

        • Interpretation: compared with Spearman’s coefficient, Kendall’s Tau may be more robust with small samples or many tied ranks.

      • Significance test for a correlation coefficient, using a t-test:

        • A sample correlation r may differ from zero merely by chance. We must test whether correlation also exists in the population.

        • Test statistic:

          $$ t = \frac{r\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} $$

        • Compare the calculated t with a critical value from the t distribution, or inspect the p-value, to determine whether the correlation differs significantly from zero.

  • Partial correlation:

    • Purpose: in multivariate analysis, identify the “pure” relationship between X1 and Y after removing the influence of another variable, such as X2.

    • In plain language: suppose ice-cream sales, X1, are strongly positively correlated with the number of drownings, Y. This is probably spurious because both are influenced by temperature, X2. Partial correlation measures what remains of the relationship between ice-cream sales and drownings when temperature is held constant. The remaining correlation will probably be nearly zero.

  • 3.4 Regression Analysis

    • Purpose: construct a quantitative relationship of dependence among variables for prediction or control.

    • Categories: univariate or multivariate, simple or multiple, and linear or nonlinear regression.

    • Linear regression analysis:

      • Model assumptions:

        1. Linearity: the relationship between independent and dependent variables must be linear.

        2. Independence: error terms for different observations must be independent. The error in predicting today’s share price, for example, should not influence the error in predicting tomorrow’s.

        3. Homoscedasticity: the variance of the error term should remain constant rather than changing with the independent variable. In plain language, the degree to which predictions miss the mark should be uniform; the model should not be accurate at small values of the independent variable and wildly inaccurate at large ones.

        4. Normality: the error terms must follow a normal distribution.

      • Least-squares estimation of regression coefficients.

      • Goodness of fit of the regression equation:

        Coefficient of determination, R²:

        $$
        R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{Res}}{SS_{Total}}
        $$

        Multiple correlation coefficient:

        $$R = \sqrt{R^2}$$

        Adjusted coefficient of determination:

        $$R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \cdot \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1}$$

        • Ordinary R² has a weakness: adding independent variables can only increase it or leave it unchanged, even if the added variable is irrelevant—using a zodiac sign to predict house prices, for example. This can mislead us into believing that a more complicated model is always better.

        • Interpretation: adjusted R² patches this defect by accounting for the number of independent variables. If a new variable makes no meaningful contribution, adjusted R² falls. When models containing different numbers of variables are compared, adjusted R² is more trustworthy than ordinary R². In the formula, n is the sample size and p the number of independent variables.

      • Standard error of regression

      • Significance tests

        • Are the model and its variables genuinely meaningful, or are they merely accidents of the data? Significance tests answer this question.

        • Overall significance of the regression: the F-test

        • Purpose: test the overall significance of the entire model. Is the regression equation useful as a whole?

        • How to judge: inspect the p-value of the F-test. If it is small, below 0.05 for example, we can reject the null that none of the independent variables is related to the dependent variable and conclude that the model as a whole is valid.

        • Significance of individual regression coefficients: the t-test

        • Purpose: test the individual significance of each independent variable. Does this particular variable have a significant influence on the dependent variable?

        • How to judge: inspect the t-test p-value for each coefficient. A small value, below 0.05, identifies a useful predictor. A large value suggests that the variable may contribute little and might be removed.

    • Residual analysis:

      • Concept: a residual is actual value minus predicted value—the unexpected part that the model fails to explain.

      • Purpose: analyse these surprises to determine whether the theory is defective.

      • Residual plot: the most important diagnostic tool is usually a scatter plot of residual versus predicted value. A good residual plot resembles loose sand: its points are distributed randomly and evenly above and below zero with no visible pattern.

        • A trumpet or funnel shape indicates heteroscedasticity.

        • A clear curved pattern suggests a nonlinear relationship.

      • P-P and Q-Q plots: these specifically test the normality of residuals. If the points lie broadly along the diagonal, the residuals are approximately normal.

    • Other issues:

      • Methods of selecting independent variables

      • When many independent variables are available, we want to select the best combination. Manual screening is cumbersome, so automatic methods have been developed.

        • Forward selection: like building with blocks. Begin with an empty model and add, at each step, the variable that produces the greatest significant improvement. Stop when no variable can improve the model significantly.

        • Backward elimination: like pruning a tree. Begin with a full model containing every variable and remove, at each step, the least useful one—the variable with the largest p-value—until every remaining variable is significant.

        • Stepwise regression: a more flexible combination of forward and backward methods. Whenever a variable enters, reconsider all existing variables. If the newcomer makes one of them less important, remove it.

      • Multicollinearity

        • Concept: a high degree of correlation among independent variables in multiple regression.

        • In plain language: several independent variables in the model are saying almost the same thing, so their information overlaps. Using both usable floor area and gross floor area to predict a house price, for example, may produce multicollinearity because the variables are highly correlated.

        • Harm: estimates of regression coefficients become unstable, their signs may contradict expectations, and t-tests may be insignificant, preventing us from identifying the separate contribution of each variable.

        • Diagnosis: the most common measure is the variance inflation factor, VIF. A large VIF, commonly above 5 or 10, indicates serious multicollinearity with other independent variables.

  • 3.5 Analysis of Variance, ANOVA: Outline

    • Introduction:

      • Purpose: test whether several population means are equal and study the effect of a categorical independent variable on a numerical dependent variable.

      • Relevant terminology.

      • Central idea: compare between-group variance, which contains systematic and random error, with within-group variance, which contains random error, and use their F ratio to decide whether the differences among means are significant.

      • Fundamental assumptions: normality, homogeneity of variance, and independence.

    • One-way analysis of variance:

      • Data structure.

      • Steps: state hypotheses; construct test statistics, including SST, SSA, SSE and their degrees of freedom and the mean squares MSA and MSE; calculate F; and make the statistical decision.

      • Measure the strength of the relationship with R².

      • Multiple comparisons: after rejecting the null, test which particular means differ, using the LSD method for example.

    • Two-way analysis of variance:

      • Types: without interaction and with interaction.

      • Purpose: analyse the effects of two factors, represented as row and column factors, and their interaction on the experimental result.

      • Data structure.

      • Steps: state hypotheses for the row factor, column factor, and their interaction; calculate sums of squares—SST, SSR, SSC, SSinteract, and SSE; calculate mean squares and F values; and make the statistical decision.

      • Measure the strength of the relationship.

3.4 Analysis of Variance, ANOVA: Detailed Account

  • Introduction

    • Purpose: ANOVA is mainly used to test whether the means of two or more populations or groups are equal. In essence, it studies the influence of one or more categorical independent variables on a numerical dependent variable.

      • In plain language: when more than two groups must be compared—for example, the mean student scores produced by teaching methods A, B, and C—performing many t-tests increases the risk of a Type I error. ANOVA provides an all-at-once solution that determines whether all group means are equal.

    • Terminology:

      • A factor is the categorical independent variable under study, such as teaching method.

      • A level is one possible value of that factor, such as methods A, B, and C.

    • Central idea:

      • The essence of ANOVA is to decompose total variation into two parts.

        1. Between-group variance: systematic differences caused by different groups, or levels of the factor—for instance, genuine differences in the effects of teaching methods A, B, and C. It contains both systematic error and random error.

        2. Within-group variance: variation within the same group caused by individual differences and other random factors. Even when every student is taught with method A, their scores will not be identical. This part is treated as pure random error.

      • The F ratio: comparing these variances permits a decision.
        $$ F = \frac{\text{组间方差}}{\text{组内方差}} = \frac{MSA}{MSE} $$

        • Logic: if the null that all group means are equal is true, no systematic error exists, and between- and within-group variances should be similar; F will be close to 1. If group means genuinely differ, between-group variance will be much larger and F will be large.

    • Assumptions: like linear regression, ANOVA has foundations that must hold.

      1. Normality: each group is sampled from a normal population.

      2. Homogeneity of variance: population variances are equal across groups, an especially important condition for ANOVA.

      3. Independence: the observations are mutually independent.

One-Way ANOVA

  • It studies the influence of one categorical independent variable on one numerical dependent variable.

  • Steps:

    1. State the hypotheses:

      • H0: $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$ (all population group means are equal)

      • H1: at least two group means are unequal.

    2. Construct the test statistic: the central task is to decompose the sum of squares.

      • Total sum of squares, SST: the sum of squared deviations between every observation and the grand mean, representing total variation.

      • Between-group sum of squares, SSA: also called the treatment sum of squares, representing variation caused by differences among groups.

        $$ SSA = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i (\bar{x}_i - \bar{\bar{x}})^2 $$

        ($k$ is the number of groups, $n_i$ the sample size of group i, $\bar{x}_i$ its mean, and $\bar{\bar{x}}$ the grand mean)

      • Within-group sum of squares, SSE: also called the error sum of squares, representing variation caused by random error.

        $$ SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2 $$

      • Relationship: $SST = SSA + SSE$

    3. Calculate F:

      • To remove the effect of sample size, divide each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom, df, obtaining a mean square.

        • Between-group mean square, MSA: $MSA = \frac{SSA}{k-1}$

        • Within-group mean square, MSE: $MSE = \frac{SSE}{N-k}$ (N is the total sample size)

      • F statistic:

        $$ F = \frac{MSA}{MSE} $$

    4. Make the statistical decision: compare F with a critical value from the F distribution, or inspect the p-value. If p < α, reject H0 and conclude that significant differences exist among the group means.

  • Post-hoc multiple comparisons:

    • Rejecting H0 with the F-test tells us only that the means are not all equal, not which particular groups differ. Is the difference between A and B, or between B and C? Multiple comparisons provide the follow-up investigation.

    • Common methods: LSD, or least significant difference, Tukey HSD, and Bonferroni. They are essentially variants of pairwise t-tests with corrected significance levels that control the overall Type I error rate.

Two-Way ANOVA

  • It studies the influence of two categorical independent variables and their interaction on one numerical dependent variable.

  • Types:

    • Two-way ANOVA without interaction: assumes that the effects of the two factors are independent and additive.

    • Two-way ANOVA with interaction: the more common and realistic case. It considers not only the separate main effect of each factor but also the distinctive “chemical reaction,” or interaction effect, produced when they occur together.

      • Example of interaction: suppose we study the effects of fertilizer type, A or B, and water level, high or low, on crop yield. If fertilizer A works well with little water while B works well with much water, the factors interact. Their effects are not a simple 1+1=2.

  • Steps:

    1. State the hypotheses: three sets must now be tested.

      • For the interaction, H0 states that the two factors do not interact.

      • For the row-factor main effect, H0 states that the means at all levels of the row factor are equal.

      • For the column-factor main effect, H0 states that the means at all levels of the column factor are equal.

    2. Calculate sums of squares: total variation is decomposed more finely.

      • $SST = SSR + SSC + SS_{interaction} + SSE$

        • SST: total sum of squares.

        • SSR, rows: sum of squares caused by the row factor.

        • SSC, columns: sum of squares caused by the column factor.

        • SS_interaction: sum of squares caused by interaction.

        • SSE: sum of squares caused by random error.

    3. Calculate F: three separate F values are required.

      • $F_{interaction} = \frac{MS_{interaction}}{MSE}$

      • $F_{R} = \frac{MSR}{MSE}$

      • $F_{C} = \frac{MSC}{MSE}$

    4. Make the statistical decision:

      • Examine the F-test for interaction first. If interaction is significant, the effects of the two factors are entangled. Analysing either main effect by itself is then of limited value, and attention should turn to the pattern of interaction.

      • If interaction is not significant, inspect the F-tests for the two main effects separately to determine whether each factor independently and significantly influences the dependent variable.

4. Modelling Problems

4.1 Predictive Modelling

Predictive modelling uses existing data to construct a mathematical model that predicts future numerical values.

Regression Analysis

(This subject was developed in detail in an earlier conversation. The following material supplements and improves the discussion of other regression models.)

  • Linear regression: the basic model, which finds the best straight line, or hyperplane, for the data.

  • Ridge regression

    • Purpose: chiefly to address multicollinearity in linear regression. When independent variables are highly correlated, ordinary least squares, or OLS, produces regression coefficients that are extremely unstable and have large variance.

    • In plain language: ridge regression places unstable coefficients in restraints. It adds a penalty term, the L2 norm, to least squares, preventing coefficients from becoming too large. This constraint makes the model more stable and reliable overall, at the cost of a little accuracy on the training set.

  • Lasso regression

    • Purpose: like ridge regression, it addresses multicollinearity, but it possesses the more powerful feature of feature selection.

    • In plain language: Lasso’s L1 penalty is harsher than ridge’s. It not only suppresses large coefficients but compresses the coefficients of independent variables it considers unimportant all the way to zero. It therefore produces a stable model while simultaneously screening variables and identifying those that truly matter.

  • Logistic regression

    • Note: despite the word regression in its name, this is actually a classification model.

    • Purpose: to predict a binary outcome, such as yes/no or 1/0—for example, whether a user will click an advertisement or an email is spam.

    • In plain language: a special sigmoid function maps the continuous output of linear regression, which can range from negative to positive infinity, into the interval (0, 1). The result can be interpreted as the probability of an event. An output of 0.8 means an estimated 80-per-cent probability of a positive case. We then choose a threshold, such as 0.5: values above it become 1 and values below it become 0, completing the classification.

Regression Decision Trees: C&R, Classification and Regression Trees

  • Purpose: to make regression predictions with a tree structure.

  • In plain language: every leaf in a classification tree represents a class, while every leaf in a regression tree represents a particular numerical value. The tree repeatedly asks a question about a feature—“Is the floor area below 80 square metres?”, for example—to split the data. Each split aims to minimize the variance of the dependent variable, such as price, within the resulting nodes or branches. When growth stops and a new sample falls into a leaf, its prediction is the mean of all training observations in that leaf.

XGBoost Regression: eXtreme Gradient Boosting

  • Purpose: an extremely powerful and efficient ensemble-learning algorithm.

  • In plain language: imagine an elite team that continually learns from and repairs its mistakes.

    1. The first learner, a simple decision tree, makes a rough prediction.

    2. The second does not predict the original data. It specifically learns and predicts the portion the first learner got wrong—the residuals.

    3. The third learns and predicts the residuals still left by the second, and so forth.

    The process continues, every new tree compensating for the shortcomings of all its predecessors. XGBoost adds extensive optimization, making the method fast and effective, and includes regularization to prevent overfitting.

Neural Networks

Neural networks imitate connections among neurons in the human brain to learn extremely complex nonlinear relationships in data. I will skip the details.

Support Vector Regression, SVR

  • Purpose: the regression version of support vector machines, or SVMs.

  • In plain language: ordinary linear regression seeks a line that minimizes the sum of squared distances from all observations. SVR instead seeks a tube or street of width 2ε. It tries to place as many points as possible inside the tube while keeping the tube itself narrow. Loss is calculated only for points outside it. The observations defining its boundaries are the support vectors. By refusing to worry about points inside the tube, SVR becomes less sensitive to outliers and more robust.

4.2 Classification Modelling

Classification uses a mathematical model to assign objects to predefined categories. Its dependent variable Y is discrete.

  • Logistic regression and discriminant analysis

  • Classification decision trees

  • Neural networks

  • Support vector classification, SVC:

    Its central idea is to find the widest street, or maximum-margin hyperplane, between samples of different classes. The edges of the street are supported by the nearest observations, the support vectors. This boundary offers the greatest tolerance for error. When the data are not linearly separable, the kernel trick maps them into a higher-dimensional space where they become separable, after which the widest street is found.

  • Random forests:

    A random forest is both an ensemble-learning algorithm and a form of decision tree.

    1. It builds many different decision trees. To ensure their diversity, training introduces two kinds of randomness: randomly sampling observations, or row sampling, and randomly sampling features used in decisions, or column sampling.

    2. For prediction, every tree votes independently. The majority wins, and the class receiving the most votes becomes the final result.

    This mechanism greatly improves accuracy and stability and effectively prevents the overfitting common in a single decision tree.

4.3 Association Analysis

Association analysis searches a collection of apparently unrelated events for patterns of the form “if A occurs, B is also likely to occur.” The classic example is the story of beer and nappies.

  • The Apriori algorithm

    • Central idea: if an itemset is frequent, all its subsets must also be frequent. Conversely, if an itemset is not frequent, none of its supersets can be frequent.

    • Operation: like a sieve, Apriori begins with frequent sets containing one item and moves upwards layer by layer to sets containing two, three, and more items. At every layer, the principle above prunes large numbers of combinations that cannot be frequent, improving efficiency.

  • The FP-growth algorithm

    • Central idea: Apriori repeatedly scans the database and generates many candidate sets, which is inefficient. FP-growth instead compresses the transactions of the entire database into a special tree called an FP tree, or Frequent Pattern Tree.

    • Operation: it scans the database only twice—once to count item frequencies and once to build the tree. All subsequent mining takes place in this compact tree without returning to the original database, greatly increasing speed.

  • The CARMA algorithm

  • Sequential-pattern-mining algorithms

4.4 Cluster Analysis

  • In plain language: clustering means that birds of a feather flock together. The classes are not known in advance, and no standard answer exists. The algorithm must inspect the characteristics of the data, automatically group similar samples, and separate dissimilar ones.

  • Hierarchical clustering

    • Operation: two approaches exist. Agglomerative clustering begins with each point as a separate cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until every point belongs to one large cluster, drawing a dendrogram in the process. Divisive clustering works in the reverse direction.

  • K-Means

    • Operation: one of the classic clustering algorithms.

      1. First specify the desired number of clusters, K.

      2. The algorithm randomly selects K points as the initial cluster centres.

      3. Every remaining point joins the cluster whose centre is nearest.

      4. Recalculate each cluster’s centre as the mean position of all its points.

      5. Repeat Steps 3 and 4 until the centres stop moving.

  • The TwoStep algorithm

4.5 Sequence Analysis

  • Purpose: like association analysis, but with the additional consideration of temporal order. It seeks patterns such as “the customer bought A first and then bought B after some time.”

  • In plain language: association analysis tells us what appears together in a shopping basket, whereas sequence analysis tells us what the customer’s shopping timeline looks like. It may discover that buyers of a new computer usually purchase a printer within a month, or that viewers of film A are likely to watch sequel B the following week.

  • Applications: website clickstream analysis, customer-lifetime-value analysis, and DNA-sequence analysis.

4.6 Web Data Mining

Purpose: a comprehensive field that applies data-mining techniques to vast quantities of Web data—including page content, link structures, and access logs—to discover useful knowledge and patterns.

Principal areas:

  1. Web content mining: extract information from text, images, audio, and video on Web pages. Search-engine indexing belongs to this category.

  2. Web structure mining: analyse links among pages. Google’s PageRank, for example, uses link structure to estimate the importance of a page.

  3. Web usage mining: analyse access logs to discover users’ browsing patterns and habits. This includes the Web applications of association and sequence analysis mentioned above and supports personalized recommendation and website-layout optimization.

entry.title: A Review of Optimization Methods
entry.content:
In essence, an optimization problem is about finding an extreme value—the maximum or minimum of an objective or evaluation function. This simple idea has an extremely wide range of applications.

Practical Solving Tools

  • MATLAB is not recommended, since its optimization support is relatively limited.

  • LINGO is recommended. It is specialized optimization software, although some extreme problems may still be too difficult for it to finish.

  • Gurobi is recommended. It performs very well and can be used directly from Python.

How to Build a Mathematical Model for an Optimization Problem

(1) Decision variables and parameters

Decision variables are unknown quantities whose values are determined by the solution of the mathematical model. Parameters represent the control variables of the system and may be either deterministic or random.

In plain language, identify what is quantitative, what is unknown, and what must be solved for; then distinguish the independent variables from the dependent ones.

(2) Constraints or restrictions

Because a real system is limited by objective material conditions, the model must include constraints that keep decision variables within their feasible values. Such limits are usually expressed as mathematical constraint functions.

In other words, find the constraints and express them in mathematical language.

(3) The objective function

This is a mathematical function of the system’s decision variables that measures its efficiency—in other words, the goal pursued by the system.

Categories of Optimization Models

Optimization models can be divided into several categories according to the nature of their objective functions and constraints. Each category has distinctive features, and the methods and difficulty of solving them vary greatly.

1. Linear Programming, LP

  • Characteristics: this is the most fundamental and classical form of optimization. Its defining feature is linearity:

    1. The objective function is linear, for example $max Z = 2x + 3y$.

    2. Every constraint is also linear, for example $x + y <= 10$ and $x - y >= 0$.

    3. The decision variables x, y are continuous and may take fractional values.

  • Approach:

    • Geometric intuition: when all the linear constraints are drawn in a coordinate system, they enclose a polygon in two dimensions or a polyhedron in higher dimensions. This is called the feasible region. Theory has proved that an optimal solution must occur at one of its vertices.

    • Central algorithm: the simplex method. The method is remarkably ingenious. Beginning at one vertex of the feasible region, it travels along an edge to a better vertex and repeats this process until the optimal vertex is found. Large-scale linear-programming problems are now commonly solved with an interior-point method.

Still, why do I feel that this category would appear at most in the first sub-question? It does not seem particularly useful.

2. Integer Programming, IP

  • Characteristics: integer programming adds to linear programming the requirement that one or more decision variables must be integers.

    • If all decision variables must be integers, the problem is called pure integer programming, or pure IP.

    • If some variables must be integers while others may be continuous, the problem is called mixed-integer linear programming, or MILP.

    • The most special case is 0-1 integer programming, in which a decision variable can only be 0 or 1. It is commonly used to represent such choices as yes or no and select or reject.

  • Approach:

    • Never assume that ordinary rounding will work. Rounding the result of a linear program may produce an infeasible or extremely poor solution.

    • Integer programming is much harder to solve than linear programming and belongs to the class of NP-hard problems.

    • Central algorithms: branch and bound and the cutting-plane method. Branch and bound can be understood as an intelligent form of exhaustive search. It continually divides a problem into smaller subproblems, or branches, and uses solutions of the corresponding linear programs to determine which branches can be abandoned early, or bounded, thereby avoiding pointless search.

3. Nonlinear Programming, NLP

If either the objective function or any constraint is nonlinear, the model falls within nonlinear programming. Its world is far more complicated than that of linear programming.

3.1 Unconstrained Nonlinear Programming

  • Characteristics: the objective function is nonlinear, but there are no constraints. In plain language, the highest or lowest point of a function may be sought freely throughout its domain.

  • Approach:

    • This is where calculus comes into its own. For a differentiable function, we look for points where the gradient is zero, namely points satisfying ∇f(x) = 0. These stationary points are possible extrema.

    • Central algorithms: various iterative descent algorithms. Starting from an initial point, each step moves a short distance in the direction that decreases, or increases, the function most rapidly, and the procedure gradually approaches an optimum. Classical algorithms include:

      • Gradient descent: the simplest method, which moves in the direction opposite to the gradient.

      • Newton’s method: it takes second derivatives, represented by the Hessian matrix, into account. It converges faster but requires more computation.

      • The conjugate-gradient method, among others.

3.2 Constrained Nonlinear Programming

  • Characteristics: at least one objective or constraint function is nonlinear, and constraints are present. This is one of the most common and complicated classes of real-world problems.

  • Approach:

    • Handling constraints is the key. The method of Lagrange multipliers is the classical theoretical basis for equality constraints. It converts a constrained problem into a larger unconstrained one by constructing a Lagrangian function.

    • Inequality constraints require the more complicated Karush–Kuhn–Tucker, or KKT, conditions, which extend the method of Lagrange multipliers.

    • Central algorithms: methods include sequential quadratic programming, or SQP, the interior-point method, and the penalty method. These algorithms are generally complex and depend on mature optimization solvers.

4. Quadratic Programming, QP

  • Characteristics: this is a special and important subclass of nonlinear programming. Its objective function is quadratic, while all constraints remain linear.

  • Approach: because its structure is comparatively well behaved—a quadratic objective and linear constraints—it can be solved by specialized algorithms that are more efficient than general nonlinear-programming methods, such as the active-set method. It is widely applied in finance, including portfolio optimization, and in machine learning, including support vector machines or SVMs.

5. Dynamic Programming, DP

  • Characteristics: strictly speaking, dynamic programming is an approach to problem solving, but it is often used for multistage decision-optimization problems. The decision process can be divided into a series of related stages, and the decision made at one stage affects the state of the next.

  • Approach:

    • Central ideas: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Instead of making all decisions at once, dynamic programming solves the problem stage by stage, either backwards or forwards. It may first find the optimal decision for the final stage and then use that information to solve the penultimate stage, continuing until it returns to the starting point.

    • By recording and reusing the solutions of subproblems, usually in a table, it avoids repeated computation and greatly improves efficiency. The knapsack problem and shortest-path problems are classic applications.

6. Combinatorial Optimization

  • Characteristics: the task is to find the best arrangement among various combinations, such as the land-allocation strategy in Problem C of the 2024 competition. Combinatorial optimization is not a single specific problem but a large family. Its defining feature is that the decision variables are discrete, and the number of feasible solutions is finite, though often astronomical. Rather than locating a minimum on a continuous curve, it must “combine” many possibilities into the best plan.

    • In plain language, this means solving a “multiple-choice problem” or an “ordering problem.” If ten projects must be selected for investment from a hundred, which ten will maximize the return? That is selection. If ten processes in a workshop must be ordered, which order will minimize the total time? That is sequencing.

    • Integer programming, discussed above, and the facility-location problem and TSP, discussed below, all belong to combinatorial optimization.

  • Approach: the methods used to solve a combinatorial problem vary widely according to its particular structure and difficulty.

    • Exact algorithms aim to find the absolute optimum.

      • Some “simple” problems, such as finding a minimum spanning tree in a graph, have polynomial-time algorithms and can be solved rapidly.

      • For most “hard” or NP-hard problems, the time required by exact algorithms, such as dynamic programming and branch and bound, explodes as the scale of the problem grows. They are therefore suitable only for small instances.

    • Approximation algorithms accept a compromise. Instead of seeking the “best” solution, they seek one that is “good enough.” Such algorithms are fast and provide a theoretical guarantee that their result will not differ from the optimum by more than a specified ratio.

    • Heuristics and metaheuristics become useful when a problem is too large for an exact algorithm and no satisfactory approximation algorithm exists. They are intelligent search strategies based on intuition or experience, including simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and ant-colony algorithms. They can usually find a reasonable solution quickly, but cannot guarantee its quality and may become trapped in a local optimum. They are nevertheless used extensively in engineering practice.

6.1 The Facility-Location Problem

  • Characteristics: this is a classic class of combinatorial-optimization problems. A typical setting contains a number of potential facility sites, such as warehouses, base stations, or supermarkets, and a number of customer locations. The aim is to decide where facilities should be built, how many should be built, and which facility should serve each customer, so that total cost, including construction and transportation, is minimized while all customer demand is met.

  • Approach:

    • Facility-location problems are usually formulated as mixed-integer linear programs, or MILPs.

    • Whether a facility is built at a given location can be represented by a 0-1 integer variable, where 1 means build and 0 means do not build.

    • Other variables can represent which facility serves each customer location.

    • Once the model has been built, mature optimization solvers such as Gurobi or CPLEX can be called. Large-scale problems likewise require specialized approximation algorithms or heuristics.

6.2 TSP: The Traveling Salesperson Problem

  • Characteristics: this is the most famous and representative “star problem” in combinatorial optimization.

    • Problem statement: a traveling salesperson must visit n cities. Starting from one city, the salesperson must visit each city exactly once and finally return to the starting city. In what order should the cities be visited to minimize the total distance travelled?

    • In plain language, draw one continuous route through every point and make that route as short as possible. TSP is a prominent NP-hard problem. Once the number of cities becomes even moderately large—several dozen, for example—finding the optimum by enumerating every possible route is already out of the question.

  • Approach:

    • Exact algorithms: when the number of cities is small, for example no more than twenty, dynamic programming, such as the Held–Karp algorithm, or branch and bound can find an optimal solution.

    • Approximation algorithms and heuristics: large TSP instances are almost always addressed through these two classes of method.

      • Approximation algorithm: Christofides’ algorithm, for example, guarantees a route no longer than 1.5 times the length of an optimal route.

      • Heuristics: examples include a greedy strategy that always moves to the nearest unvisited city; 2-opt and 3-opt, which exchange two or three randomly selected edges to see whether the route improves; and more advanced methods such as genetic algorithms and simulated annealing. All can find routes close to the optimum within a reasonable time.

The next two concepts are linked. They classify “algorithmic efficiency” rather than “optimization models,” but they are essential to understanding whether an optimization problem can in fact be “solved.”

7. Polynomial-Time Algorithms and P Problems

  • Characteristics: the upper bound on an algorithm’s running time, or number of computational steps, can be expressed as a polynomial function of the input size n, namely $O(n^k)$, where k is a constant.

    • In plain language, such an algorithm is efficient. As the problem size n increases, its running time grows comparatively “gently” rather than running out of control. Both $O(n^2)$ and $O(n^3)$ are polynomial time, whereas the exponential running time $O(2^n)$ grows with terrifying speed.

    • All decision problems, which have yes-or-no answers, that can be solved by polynomial-time algorithms form a set called the class P, or polynomial time. P problems are generally regarded as “effectively solvable” or computationally tractable.

    • Note: linear programming belongs to P. Although the simplex method takes exponential time in the worst case, interior-point methods run in polynomial time.

8. Nondeterministic Polynomial Time and NP Problems

  • Characteristics: the name sounds mysterious, but its central idea is not complicated. It describes a class of decision problems with two features:

    1. Finding a solution directly may be extremely difficult, and it is not presently known whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists.

    2. If someone gives you an answer claimed to be a solution, however, you can verify in polynomial time whether that answer is correct.

    • In plain language: solving is hard, but checking is easy.

    • The set of such problems is called the class NP, or nondeterministic polynomial time.

  • Example: consider the decision version of TSP: “Does there exist a tour shorter than L?”

    • Hard to solve: finding such a route directly is extremely difficult.

    • Easy to check: if I draw a particular route for you, you need only add the lengths of its edges and see whether the sum is below L. Addition can be performed very quickly, in polynomial time.

    • TSP therefore belongs to NP.

  • Important relationships:

    • Every P problem is an NP problem, because if an answer can be found quickly, it can naturally be checked quickly as well.

    • But is every NP problem also a P problem? In other words, P = NP? This is the central million-dollar question of computer science. The prevailing view is that P ≠ NP, which would mean that many problems can be checked quickly but cannot be solved quickly.

    • The hardest problems in NP are called NP-complete problems. TSP is one such problem. If a polynomial-time solution were found for any NP-complete problem, every problem in NP could be solved in polynomial time.

    • Optimization problems, not merely decision problems, that are at least as difficult as NP-complete problems are called NP-hard problems.

Optimization Methods

Optimization with Calculus

The first topic would be finding extrema of functions of one, two, or three variables by setting their derivatives equal to zero. There is no need to discuss that in detail here.

The next method is the Lagrange multiplier method for extrema subject to constraints, which I will write down once more.

To find possible extrema of the function $z= f(x,y)$ subject to the condition $\phi(x,y)=0$, first construct the function $F(x,y)=f(x,y)+\lambda \phi(x,y)$, where $\lambda$ is a constant.

We then solve

$$
\begin{cases}
f_x(x, y) + \lambda \varphi_x(x, y) = 0, \
f_y(x, y) + \lambda \varphi_y(x, y) = 0, \
\varphi(x, y) = 0.
\end{cases}
$$

for $x,y,\lambda$; the values $x,y$ are the coordinates of possible extrema.

Heuristics

A heuristic is an algorithm constructed from intuition or experience. At an acceptable cost in computing time, storage space, and so forth, it provides a feasible solution for each instance of the combinatorial-optimization problem under consideration. How far that solution may lie from the optimum cannot necessarily be predicted in advance.

In plain language, a heuristic is a set of “rules of thumb” or shortcuts. When a problem is too complicated for us to find a perfect optimum, or when doing so would take too long, a heuristic can rapidly provide a solution that is reasonably good and probably not far off. It pursues efficiency and practical value at the price of some guarantee of optimality.

Explanations of the Algorithms

1. The Greedy Algorithm

  • Concept: an algorithm concerned only with what lies immediately before it. Whenever it makes a decision, it chooses what currently appears best without considering the effect of that choice on the future. It hopes that a sequence of locally optimal decisions will eventually produce a global optimum.

    The algorithm always attempts to obtain a local optimum. For certain specially structured problems, this strategy really is the best. In most complicated settings, however, such short-sightedness can cause it to miss the globally optimal route or even take a large detour.

  • Applications: although greedy algorithms are not always correct, they miraculously yield an optimum in certain problems, including Prim’s and Kruskal’s algorithms for minimum spanning trees and Dijkstra’s algorithm for single-source shortest paths.

2. Neighbourhood Search, or Hill Climbing

  • Find a local optimum -> move to that local optimum -> search for another local optimum. Continue until no better solution can be found nearby.

  • Analogy, from Gemini 2.5 Pro: imagine that you are trying to find the highest summit in a mountain range covered by dense fog. You are dropped at a random location, and all you can do is look around and take one step in the steepest upward direction available from where you stand. You repeat the process and “climb” one step at a time. Eventually, you reach a summit, because movement in every direction would then take you downhill.

  • Central defect: the method easily stops at a local optimum instead of continuing to seek a global one.

3. Simulated Annealing, SA

  • Simulated annealing was designed to overcome the tendency of hill climbing to become trapped in a local optimum. It adds randomness and a probabilistic escape mechanism to neighbourhood search.

  • Analogy: the process imitates annealing in metalworking: a metal is melted at high temperature and then cooled slowly so that its internal molecules can settle into a stable state of minimum energy. Return to the example of climbing through fog. This time, you are not a steady mountaineer but a “slightly drunk mountaineer.” At the beginning, when the temperature is high, you are mildly intoxicated and full of energy. Most of the time you move uphill, but now and then you stagger a few steps downhill. This apparently foolish behaviour gives you a chance to leave the small hill on which you stand and explore other mountains farther away. As time passes and the temperature falls, the effects of the alcohol wear off. You become increasingly sober and steady, eventually choosing only upward steps until you reach what you regard as the highest summit.

4. The Genetic Algorithm, GA

  • A genetic algorithm imitates the biological principle of natural selection and survival of the fittest. Instead of maintaining only one solution, it maintains a large group of solutions at once, called a population. The population evolves through generation after generation of reproduction and elimination, gradually improving in quality until a strong solution is obtained.

  • Imagine it as a breeding farm:

    1. Initial population: you randomly cultivate the first batch of varied seeds, which represent initial solutions.

    2. Fitness evaluation: plant the seeds and observe which grow best, meaning which solutions are superior.

    3. Selection: preferentially choose the best-growing seeds as the “parents” of the next generation.

    4. Crossover or reproduction: cross these excellent parents to produce offspring. The offspring inherit favourable genes, or useful solution features, from both parents.

    5. Mutation: during reproduction, allow a very small probability of genetic mutation. This introduces new diversity and prevents all the seeds from becoming identical. After thousands of generations of selection and reproduction, the farm ultimately develops a superb variety.

Strengths

The methods are simple, practical, and intuitive, and users can accept them readily.

They are fast, which is particularly important in real-time management.

In most cases, the programs are simple and therefore easy to modify.

Weaknesses

They cannot guarantee an optimal solution.

Their performance is unstable. A heuristic may work differently on different instances of the same problem: some solutions are good, while others are poor. In practical applications, such instability can make its results untrustworthy.

The quality of an algorithm depends on the actual problem, experience, and the designer’s skill. General rules are difficult to summarize, and different algorithms are consequently hard to compare.

Modern Optimization Algorithms, or Metaheuristics

When a problem becomes extremely complicated, traditional heuristics such as greedy algorithms and hill climbing may no longer be adequate. Modern optimization algorithms, usually called metaheuristics, provide higher-level strategic frameworks that guide and improve lower-level heuristic search. They are often inspired by natural phenomena and tend to be more powerful and intelligent.

1. Tabu Search

  • Tabu search is an excellent improvement on hill climbing. The greatest weakness of hill climbing is that it can easily be trapped on a “small hill,” or local optimum. The central idea of tabu search is to possess a memory that helps the search escape this trap.

  • Return once again to climbing in fog. Hill climbing stops you at the first summit it finds. A tabu-search mountaineer, however, carries a tabu list, rather like a little black book.

    1. When you move from position A to a better position B, you write in the book: “I have just come from A; returning to A is forbidden for a while.”

    2. Consequently, even if every path around the small hill at B leads downhill, the ban on retracing your steps forces you to explore a different downward path that you have not previously taken.

    3. This forced movement gives you an opportunity to descend first and then climb the possibly higher mountain next to it from the other side.

    By remembering where it has been and refusing for a time to retrace its route, tabu search greatly improves its ability to escape local optima.

2. Artificial Neural Networks, ANN

  • A neural network is not itself an algorithm that directly solves an optimization problem. It is a computational model that imitates the connections among neurons in the human brain. In optimization, however, it plays two important roles.

  • Role one: a neural network is itself an enormous optimization problem.

    • It is an enormous optimization problem in its own right. The various competitions in AI that seek tiny improvements in performance are all attempts to optimize it further.

  • Role two: it can assist in solving an optimization problem.

    • Suppose the objective function or constraints of an optimization problem are too complicated to express mathematically, as when the yield of a chemical process must be predicted. We can first train a neural network to learn the relationship between the inputs, such as the proportions of raw materials, and the output, such as yield. The trained network then becomes a surrogate model. Instead of optimizing the original process directly, we optimize the inputs of the network to obtain the highest predicted yield.

3. Ant Colony Optimization, ACO

  • What it is: an algorithm that simulates the way real ant colonies search for food. It is particularly good at finding optimal routes in graphs, as in the traveling salesperson problem.

  • Analogy: the analogy is unusually direct because it is the origin of the algorithm itself.

    1. Initial exploration: several routes connect the nest and the food. At first, ants explore randomly in different directions.

    2. Pheromone release: ants leave a chemical called pheromone along the routes they travel.

    3. Positive feedback: suppose there are two routes, A and B, and A is shorter. Ants on route A can travel between the nest and food more quickly. In the same period, they therefore complete more journeys, and the pheromone concentration on route A grows higher.

    4. Route selection: later ants detect the pheromone and are more likely to choose the route where its concentration is high. More and more ants are consequently attracted to route A, further strengthening its pheromone trail.

    5. Convergence: through this positive-feedback process, the colony quickly “discovers” and settles on the shortest route. The artificial ants in the algorithm construct good solutions by simulating the same process.

Graph Theory

Many optimization problems can be abstracted as graphs, including urban transport networks, social networks, and dependencies among tasks. Graph theory is the branch of mathematics that studies structures made up of such “points” and “lines.”

Foundations

First, the word graph here does not refer to a bar chart or pie chart. It refers to a mathematical object made up of vertices and the edges that connect them.

  • Undirected graph

    • Definition: the edges have no direction. If an edge joins vertex A and vertex B, one may travel from A to B or from B to A.

    • This is a “two-way relationship.” A WeChat friendship is an example: if you are my friend, I am necessarily yours. The line connecting us has no arrow.

  • Directed graph

    • Definition: the edges have directions shown by arrows. An edge pointing from A to B means that movement from A to B is possible, but movement from B to A is not, unless a reverse edge also exists.

    • This is a “one-way relationship.” Following someone on Weibo is an example: I may follow you even if you do not follow me. The line connecting us requires an arrow to indicate the direction of the relationship. A network of one-way streets in a city is another typical directed graph.

  • Undirected weighted graph

    • Definition: every edge in an undirected graph is assigned a numerical value called its weight or cost.

    • The relationship is not only bidirectional but also measured. On a map of cities, for example, the cities are vertices and the roads connecting them are edges. The roads permit two-way travel and are therefore undirected, while the length of each road in kilometres is its weight.

  • Directed weighted graph

    • Definition: every directed edge in a directed graph is assigned a weight.

    • The relationship is one-way and has a measure. On a map of airfares, for example, cities are vertices, a flight from A to B is a directed edge, and the ticket price is its weight. Notice that the fare from A to B is usually different from the fare from B to A.

  • Adjacency matrix

    • Definition: a matrix representation of a graph. For a graph with n vertices, an n x n matrix can be constructed. The element A[i][j] in row i and column j represents the connection between vertices i and j.

    • Put simply, it is a “table of connections.”

      • For an unweighted graph, if an edge connects vertices i and j, then A[i][j] = 1; otherwise it equals 0.

      • For a weighted graph, if an edge connects i and j, then A[i][j] equals the weight of that edge; otherwise it can be assigned a special value, such as infinity ∞.

    • The matrix is highly intuitive, but if the graph is “sparse,” with few edges, a matrix wastes a large amount of storage space.

Shortest Paths

  • In a weighted graph, directed or undirected, a shortest-path problem asks for the route from a starting vertex to a target vertex whose edge weights have the smallest sum. A “weight” may represent distance, time, cost, or any other additive measure. In plain language, this is navigation.

  • Central algorithms and categories:

    • Single-source shortest path, SSSP: calculate the shortest paths from one fixed starting vertex, or source, to every other vertex in the graph.

      • Dijkstra’s algorithm: the most classical SSSP algorithm. Its strategy is greedy.

        • Idea: imagine that you stand at the starting point and possess a region in which the shortest paths have already been determined; initially, the region contains only you. At each step, the algorithm expands outwards from the boundary of this region. It selects the nearest vertex not yet included, brings that vertex into the region, and updates the distances from the starting point to all its neighbours. Like ripples on water, the process spreads outwards in circles from the source until it covers every vertex you wish to reach.

        • Important restriction: Dijkstra’s algorithm is highly efficient but has a fatal weakness: it cannot process a graph containing negative-weight edges. Once its greedy strategy brings a vertex into the “determined” region, it never revisits it, whereas a negative edge may make that supposed certainty uncertain.

      • The Bellman–Ford algorithm: a more powerful SSSP algorithm capable of processing negative-weight edges.

        • Idea: instead of being greedy, it uses a forceful strategy of repeated relaxation. It repeatedly performs a “relaxation” operation on every edge, checking whether passage along that edge can shorten the distance from the source to its endpoint. The process is repeated V-1 times, where V is the number of vertices. Since a shortest path contains at most V-1 edges, V-1 rounds are sufficient to propagate the shortest distance to the destination.

        • Additional ability: Bellman–Ford has another unique skill: it can detect a negative-weight cycle. If an edge can still be relaxed after V-1 rounds, the graph contains a cycle whose weight becomes smaller each time it is travelled. A shortest path is then meaningless, since its score can be reduced indefinitely.

    • All-pairs shortest path, APSP: calculate the shortest path between every pair of vertices in the graph.

      • The Floyd–Warshall algorithm: the classical solution to APSP, based on dynamic programming.

        • Idea: its reasoning is elegant. It asks, “What is the shortest path from vertex i to vertex j if only vertex 1 may be used as an intermediate?” Then it asks, “What if vertices 1 and 2 may both be used as intermediates?” Through iteration, it gradually enlarges the set of vertices allowed as intermediate points and updates the shortest distance between every i and j. Once every vertex has been considered as a possible intermediate, the shortest paths between all pairs have been obtained. Its implementation in code is remarkably concise and beautiful.

The Traversability Problem

  • This problem considers how every edge or every vertex of a graph can be traversed without repetition. It is not concerned with how “short” a route is, only with whether the traversal can be completed and how to complete it. In other words, it asks whether the graph can be drawn in one stroke.

  • Two classical problems:

    • Eulerian paths and circuits:

      • Problem: can a path be found that traverses every edge in the graph exactly once? If it begins and ends at the same vertex, it is an Eulerian circuit; if the starting and ending vertices differ, it is an Eulerian path.

      • How to decide: thanks to Euler, this problem has a simple and definite criterion. The key is the degree of every vertex, meaning the number of edges incident on it.

        • For an undirected graph:

          • If every vertex has even degree, an Eulerian circuit must exist. It can start at any point and ultimately return there.

          • If exactly two vertices have odd degree, an Eulerian path exists. It must begin at one odd-degree vertex and end at the other.

          • In every other case, where more than two vertices have odd degree, no path can traverse all edges in one stroke.

      • Real-world application: route planning for an urban snowplough or postal worker. The aim is to travel along every street while minimizing the total distance, meaning that no street is repeated. This is a typical Eulerian-circuit problem.

    • Hamiltonian paths and circuits:

      • Problem: can a path be found that visits every vertex in the graph exactly once? If it begins and ends at the same vertex, it is a Hamiltonian circuit.

      • How to decide: although the problem looks similar to the Eulerian one, their difficulty could hardly be more different. The Hamiltonian problem is a celebrated NP-complete problem, and no simple general criterion is presently known. Unlike checking vertex degrees, we cannot quickly determine whether a graph contains a Hamiltonian path.

      • Real-world application: the traveling salesperson problem, or TSP, mentioned earlier, asks for a minimum-weight Hamiltonian circuit in a complete weighted graph. The salesperson must visit each city, or vertex, exactly once and finally return to the starting point.
