entry.title: Jiangxie STM32 Notes (II)
entry.content:
If you are considering reading these notes, I would actually recommend watching Jiangxie’s course instead:

  • STM32 Introductory Tutorial, 2023 Edition—Detailed Explanation with Chinese Subtitles, Bilibili

OLED

OLED stands for Organic Light-Emitting Diode.

Supply voltage: 3–5.5 V; communication protocol: I2C/SPI; resolution: 128*64.

The following library files were provided by Jiangxie. I neither modified nor examined them; I simply used them as they were:


Interrupts

Concepts

An interrupt occurs when a specified trigger condition, or interrupt source, arises while the main program is running. The CPU pauses the program currently being executed, turns to the interrupt service routine, and, once that routine is complete, returns to the point at which the original program was suspended.

Interrupt priority is needed when several interrupt sources request service at the same time. The CPU weighs their urgency and responds first to the more urgent source.

STM32 devices provide several categories of interrupt priority, and the priority of a particular interrupt is configured within this scheme.

Interrupt nesting occurs when a new source of higher priority requests service while an interrupt routine is already running. The CPU suspends the current interrupt routine, handles the new one, and then returns through the suspended routines in order.

Interrupts in STM32

The STM32 includes 68 maskable interrupt channels—interrupt sources, to put it another way. The figure of 68 is the upper limit for the F1 series, while the actual number depends on the device. These channels cover peripherals such as EXTI, which handles external or peripheral-controlled interrupts, as well as TIM, ADC, USART, SPI, I2C, and RTC.



The Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC) manages interrupts in a unified manner. Each interrupt channel possesses 16 programmable priority levels. Priorities can be grouped and then divided further into pre-emption priority and response priority.

An interrupt with a higher pre-emption priority may interrupt another routine. One with a higher response priority is placed earlier in the queue. If both priorities are equal, the interrupt number determines the order.

NVIC interrupt priority is determined by four bits in the priority register, from 0 to 15. The four bits can be divided into the upper n bits for pre-emption priority and the lower 4-n bits for response priority.

EXTI and AFIO

EXTI monitors the level of a specified GPIO port. When the level on that GPIO changes, EXTI immediately submits an interrupt request to the NVIC. After arbitration by the NVIC, the CPU’s main program is interrupted and the CPU executes the corresponding EXTI interrupt routine.

If the CPU is a doctor, the NVIC is the ticket-calling machine, while EXTI is the nurses’ station that watches what is happening and decides when a number should be called and placed in the queue.

Supported trigger modes include rising edge, falling edge, both edges, and software triggering.

All GPIO ports are supported, but pins with the same number cannot trigger interrupts simultaneously. The reason is that AFIO acts as a multiplexer: for a given pin number, it can select only one source from GPIOA, GPIOB, and GPIOC.

AFIO mainly performs two tasks: remapping pins for alternate functions and selecting interrupt pins.

There are 16 GPIO_Pin channels, together with PVD output, the RTC alarm, USB wake-up, and Ethernet wake-up.

The response may take the form of either an interrupt response or an event response.

An interrupt response triggers the CPU to handle the request in the ordinary way, whereas an event response causes another peripheral to respond to the incoming event.

The last four channels were added because EXTI can wake the device from a low-power mode.

The following diagram is the essential reference when configuring an external interrupt. Remember it, and the overall configuration and coding procedure will also become clear:

Hardware Module

Rotary Encoder

A rotary encoder is a device used to measure position, speed, or direction of rotation. As its shaft turns, its output produces a square-wave signal corresponding to the rotational speed and direction. The speed and direction of the shaft can then be determined from the frequency and phase of that signal.

Common types include mechanical-contact, Hall-effect, and optical-grating encoders.

The particular rotary-encoder circuit we use is the rather cursed arrangement shown below:

Introduction to Library Functions

stm32f10x_exti

misc.h

Writing the Program

Initialisation

The task is simply to configure and connect the entire path from the GPIO to the NVIC.

First, configure the external clocks through RCC. Enabling the clocks for AFIO and GPIO is sufficient. We do not need to configure the clocks for NVIC or EXTI. I do not yet know the precise reason in the case of EXTI; the NVIC, however, is a core peripheral and therefore lies beyond the control of the RCC.

Next, configure the AFIO port as follows:

Then initialise and connect EXTI. This function comes from stm32f10x_exti.c.

Configure the priority group:

Initialise the NVIC:

Interrupt Function

More specifically, locate the interrupt vector table in startup_stm32f10x_md.c. The names of the interrupt functions are fixed in advance.

The interrupt vector table is an array located at a fixed address in memory. Each entry, called an interrupt vector, stores the entry address of the interrupt service routine (ISR) associated with a particular interrupt number. When the CPU receives an interrupt request and obtains its number, the hardware automatically uses that number as an index into the table, reads the corresponding ISR address, and jumps to it. This arrangement enables fast and accurate interrupt handling.

entry.title: Jiangxie STM32 Notes I
entry.content:
Rather than reading these notes, I recommend watching Jiangxie’s course:

  • STM32 Introductory Tutorial, 2023 Edition, with Detailed Chinese Explanations—Bilibili

Introduction

  • STM32 is a family of 32-bit microcontrollers developed by ST around ARM Cortex-M cores. Its many applications need not be listed here.
  • ARM can refer either to the company or to an ARM processor core.
  • ARM designs the core; semiconductor manufacturers complete the surrounding circuits and manufacture the chips.

These notes follow Jiangxie’s course and use the STM32F103C8T6.


  • Core: ARM Cortex-M3
  • Clock frequency: 72 MHz
  • RAM (Random Access Memory): 20K SRAM
  • ROM (Read-Only Memory): 64K Flash
  • Supply voltage: 2.0–3.6 V, normally 3.3 V
  • Package: LQFP48

On-chip Resources

Pin Definitions

System Structure

Boot Configuration

Minimum System Circuit

Supplementary C

Data Types

The data types take the following forms. A careful look at the table is enough.

Macros

#define ABC 123 gives a readable name to a number.

typedef unsigned char uint8_t follows a similar idea: it replaces a long type name with a shorter one that is easier to use.

Enumerations

  • Keyword: enum

  • Purpose: define an integer variable whose possible values are restricted; in effect, a collection of named constants.

  • Defining an enumeration variable:

    enum{FALSE = 0, TRUE = 1} EnumName;

    Because enumeration type names may be long, typedef is normally used to rename them.

  • Referring to its members:

    EnumName = FALSE;

    EnumName = TRUE;

Creating a Project

Project Structure

GPIO

Basic Knowledge

A GPIO pin can be configured in eight input and output modes:

See page 110 of the reference manual for details.

Pin voltage ranges from 0 V to 3.3 V, although some pins tolerate 5 V.

In output mode, a port can produce high or low levels to drive an LED, control a buzzer, or generate the timing of a simulated communication protocol.

In input mode, it can read a level or voltage from a button or external module, collect a voltage through the ADC, or receive data through a simulated protocol.

The on-chip resources are shown below:

Library Functions

Consult the PDFs in the reference documentation and the comments in the original library files for details.

To be honest, what Jiangxie’s course really teaches is a way of thinking about this kind of project: where to begin, how to follow the threads through the system, and how to experience a complete development cycle.

I therefore explain only what the functions used here do, not how to use each one. That belongs to development itself.

stm32f10x_gpio.h:

stm32f10x_rcc.:

This file controls reset and clocks. The following call is used here. Most functions in this library follow the same pattern: their names begin with RCC and their arguments are similar. Look them up when needed; advanced use can wait.

Experiments

Components

  • Active buzzer: contains an oscillator and sounds continuously when DC voltage is applied; its frequency is fixed.
  • Passive buzzer: contains no oscillator and requires pulses from the controller. Changing the pulse frequency changes the sound.
  • LED: omitted.
  • Button: a mechanical spring contact opens and closes the circuit and therefore bounces; debouncing is required.
  • Sensor module: a photoresistor, thermistor, infrared receiver, or similar element changes resistance with an external analogue quantity. A divider with a fixed resistor produces an analogue voltage, which a comparator can convert into a binary digital level.

Coding Procedure

  • Configure the clock through RCC.
  • Initialize GPIO.
  • Implement the program logic in the main loop.

entry.title: Patent Writing: First Notes
entry.content:
Overview

We had previously written an initial report. Later, the teacher came back to us and, in rather polite terms, explained that it was a pile of rubbish: it read like a mid-term inspection report and did not satisfy the requirements. He then guided me through part of the proper form by hand—although by now I have forgotten a fair amount—and sent us several granted patents from earlier cohorts to use as models. I spent the following week alternating between fooling around and working, eventually producing a second preliminary version of roughly ten thousand Chinese characters and several diagrams in Word and Visio. These are the lessons I took from that process.

Before anything else, one point must be stated clearly. This article merely explains the reasoning with which I wrote my own draft and my present understanding of patent writing.

Do not rely on these notes alone. Before writing, compare your work against the documents of patents that have actually been granted and examine how they organize their arguments. What I provide here is only one approach that seems reasonable to me.

First, a diagram borrowed from a creator on Bilibili:

I will not discuss the general categories of patents—those for inventions, utility models, and designs—in detail. For students in information-related engineering, invention patents are normally the relevant kind. Utility models are of limited use, while designs are even further from our work.

The following three requirements were copied from another source.

  1. Utility or industrial applicability:

    An invention must be capable of being made or used in industry and must produce a positive effect or solve a particular technical problem. It cannot remain a purely theoretical or abstract concept, still less a fantasy contrary to the laws of nature; it must have practical value. More precisely, a person skilled in the relevant field should be able to implement the technical scheme from the disclosure in the specification, and the invention should produce the anticipated beneficial effect in practice. A perpetual-motion machine, for example, cannot be realized because it violates conservation of energy and therefore lacks utility.

  2. Novelty:

    Before the application date, or priority date, the invention must not form part of the prior art. “Prior art” means technology made publicly known anywhere in the world before that date. Disclosure may occur through publications such as patent documents, academic papers, books, and product manuals; through public sale, display, or use; or through such other means as oral reports, public demonstrations, and online publication. The central question is whether the claimed technical scheme is completely identical to a scheme recorded in any single item of prior art, or constitutes a direct and equivalent substitution. Any such prior disclosure destroys novelty.

  3. Inventive step or non-obviousness:

    Compared with the prior art existing before the application date, an invention must possess prominent substantive features and represent notable progress. A utility model must at least possess substantive features and progress. The creation cannot merely combine existing techniques or make a minor alteration; it must go beyond what an ordinarily skilled person in the field could readily derive through routine reasoning or experimentation. The central question is whether, to a person possessing ordinary knowledge and technical ability in that field, the invention is non-obvious in view of the prior art as a whole, which often requires several documents to be considered together. It should also normally produce a beneficial technical effect.

The Specification

I begin with the specification because my own approach is to write the detailed specification first. It generally contains the title, technical field, background, summary of the invention, explanation of the drawings, and detailed embodiments. The summary of the invention, drawings, and embodiments should occupy most of the document.

Title

The title is simple. A patent normally begins with an idea; take the name of that idea, revise its wording, and something like “A Method for XXX Based on XXX” can serve as the title.

Technical Field

This section also requires little anxiety. State the field to which the patent belongs. A common template is: “The present invention relates to the field of XX and, more particularly, to an XX method.”

Background

The background resembles the review of domestic and international research in a paper. It explains the fundamental reason for making the invention and should describe the defects of existing technology in detail. A typical sequence begins with a broad setting: as some social problem becomes increasingly serious, the demand for something grows; this creates a more specific demand; existing products fail to satisfy it; and a new method, apparatus, or system is therefore required.

Summary of the Invention

This is one of the principal sections.

It can broadly be divided into three parts, although that does not mean three further subheadings must actually be inserted.

Purpose: explain in two sentences which defects and problems in the background the invention is intended to solve.

Technical scheme: describe the actual operating procedure of the invention. In our patent, this meant explaining the relations among its modules and its basic processing flow. Much of my phrasing came from a senior student’s patent: first state the process in broad terms, then place the details beneath expressions such as “Optionally, wherein…”

As far as I can tell, this section should also remain substantially consistent with the claims. That deserves attention.

Beneficial effects: state what the invention achieves. There is plenty of room for generous phrasing here, so I will not dwell upon it.

Explanation of the Drawings

Preparing the drawings remains an important part of the process. For my draft, the teacher pointed out that we lacked a TOC—here meaning an overall diagram rather than a table of contents. Such a figure presents the processing flow or basic structure of the principal functional units.

A flow mentioned in the text needs a flowchart as an accompanying figure. Hardware requires a schematic or structural diagram. These are the most basic means of explaining one’s own patent.

The figures should preferably be vector graphics. Every stage of a process should carry a label such as S1 so that it can be referred to conveniently in the text. We followed the teacher’s recommendation: draw the figures in Visio, convert them to .svg, and then submit them.

The figures themselves are appended at the end. In the written explanation, describe each through a sentence such as “Figure X is an XX diagram of an embodiment of the present invention.”

Detailed Embodiments

My understanding is that this section provides an example based on the technical scheme and includes every technical point and feature needed to implement it. In practice, I further expanded the process given in the summary and explained each stage with reference to the drawings.

Abstract of the Specification

The teacher did not trust us to write the abstract and sent us his own version. It should include:

  • a sentence stating that the invention discloses an XX method and belongs to a particular field;
  • a description of what the method includes; and
  • its advantages and the problem it solves.

One representative figure should also be selected from the drawings as the abstract figure.

Claims

The claims define the scope of protection. They are especially important when a company is using a patent to protect its property.

Claims are divided into independent claims and dependent claims.

If the patent is intended to earn money, its scope should be made as broad as reasonably possible so as to prevent infringement. Think of Russian nesting dolls: the independent claim covers the largest area, thereby protecting the intellectual property effectively, and the dependent claims narrow it step by step. The independent claim might cover a fork; dependent claim 1 a wooden fork; dependent claim 2 a sandalwood fork; and dependent claim 3 a sandalwood fork made in China. If the patent office rejects the first application, move the substance of dependent claim 1 into the independent claim. If it is rejected again, move dependent claim 2 into it, and so forth. The broader the defensible scope, the better.

If the aim is instead to satisfy a professional-title requirement or strengthen a résumé, and the priority is simply to obtain a grant, the independent claim can begin with a detailed description. This sacrifices breadth but may increase the probability of allowance.

More generally, a patent must demonstrate novelty, inventive step, and utility. These three qualities should repeatedly be visible in the claims.

That is roughly all I have for now.

Tutorials:

A University Teacher Shows You, Step by Step, How to Write—or Pad—a Patent—Bilibili

An Introduction to Writing Invention Patents for Beginners—Bilibili

Other references are omitted for the moment.

entry.title: Drawing with Visio
entry.content:
Download and Installation

There is little need to explain the installation procedure in detail. The posts below can serve as references. Anyone who has reached the point of wanting to learn Visio probably does not need yet another tutorial that explains every click.

Install Visio or Access Visio for the Web—Microsoft Support
A Complete Guide from Installing to Using Visio—CSDN
2025 Visio Installation Guide, Including the Installer—CSDN
Visio 2021 Installation Guide for 64-bit and 32-bit Systems

Visio even has a web version. Looking around, I found that the entire Office family now seems to offer something similar. That is rather convenient if one can afford the subscription, although I have not used it myself:

https://visio.office.com/

One peculiar problem arose during installation. With the Office 2021 suite—Word, PowerPoint, and the rest—already installed, I could not install Visio directly. Once Office had been removed, Visio could be installed. Rather strange.

The method I eventually settled on was to uninstall Office, obtain the complete Office disk image from the university’s licensed-software platform, reinstall the suite, and select Visio during setup. What a nuisance.

If you are a BIT student or alumnus, you might as well begin at ca.bit.edu.cn.

A Short Note on the Historical Development

In broad terms, Microsoft first released the Office suite—Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and similar programs. These applications ran locally, and collaboration meant passing files back and forth by hand. In the 2010s, Microsoft introduced Office 365 and added cloud services such as OneDrive and email. In the 2020s, the brand was renamed Microsoft 365, with further collaborative and AI functions.

The appropriate office software therefore depends mainly on how much collaboration is required and how much the user can afford.

The more detailed account below comes from DeepSeek-R1:

A Timeline of Microsoft’s Office Suites

1. The era of perpetual licenses, 1989–2010

  • 1989: Microsoft first proposed the Microsoft Office brand, packaging several previously separate office applications for sale.
  • 19 November 1990: the company released the landmark Office suite for Windows, containing Word 1.0, Excel 2.0, and PowerPoint 2.0. The familiar trio established a standard for document processing that would last for decades.
  • 1995: distributed alongside Windows 95, Office 95 spread rapidly and became the de facto standard for businesses and individuals worldwide, defeating competitors such as WordPerfect and Lotus.
  • The 2000s: Microsoft successively released perpetual-license editions including Office 2000, XP, 2003, 2007, and 2010. Their functions evolved, but they remained locally installed software, and collaboration continued to depend on file transfer.

2. The transition to cloud subscriptions: Office 365, 2011–2019

  • 28 June 2011: Microsoft formally launched Office 365, marking the transition from perpetual licenses to subscription-based cloud services. The first version targeted business and educational users and combined Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Lync Online, later renamed Skype for Business.
  • 2013:
    • A premium subscription was introduced for small businesses.
    • The business-intelligence tool Power BI was integrated with Excel.
  • March 2014: subscription plans for individual consumers, including Personal and Family editions, extended cloud services to the consumer market for the first time.
  • 2017:
    • Office 365 accounted for more than half of Office revenue for the first time, a major milestone in the cloud transition.
    • In July, Microsoft launched Microsoft 365 for enterprise, combining Office 365 Enterprise, Windows 10 Enterprise, and the Enterprise Mobility and Security suite. At this point, however, Office 365 remained the principal consumer brand.

3. A unified brand and an expanded ecosystem: Microsoft 365, 2020 onward

  • 30 March 2020: Microsoft announced that the consumer Office 365 subscriptions, Personal and Family, would be formally renamed Microsoft 365 on 21 April. The change marked the retreat of the “Office” brand and the growing importance of the cloud ecosystem.
    • Principal additions: AI-related functions such as Microsoft Editor, Presenter Coach, and Money in Excel.
    • Prices remained unchanged: 398 yuan per year for the Personal edition and 498 yuan for the Family edition in China.
  • October 2022: at its Ignite conference, Microsoft announced that the Office applications on mobile, web, and desktop platforms would all be renamed the Microsoft 365 App, accompanied by revised interfaces and icons.
  • From 2023 onward:
    • AI integration, including Copilot, cross-platform compatibility, and security updates continued to deepen.
    • Microsoft 365 developed into an integrated platform for office work, collaboration, cloud storage, AI, and security, extending well beyond the role of the traditional Office toolkit.

The Timeline at a Glance

Period Principal product or brand Important events Model and characteristics
1990–2010 Microsoft Office The three core applications appeared in 1990; Office spread with Windows 95; perpetual editions were updated Local installation and largely closed functions
2011–2019 Office 365 Launched for enterprises in 2011; expanded to individuals in 2014; more than half of revenue by 2017 Subscription cloud service with online collaboration tools
2020 onward Microsoft 365 Consumer rebranding in April 2020; application-wide rebranding in 2022; deeper AI integration Cloud, AI, and an ecosystem platform across devices

In any case, for my present self—a university student who does not know much yet—the simple answer is to keep using an educational edition of the Office suite.

Operation

Omitted. Only after opening the program did I discover that it follows essentially the same logic as the other Office applications. There is no need to waste more words on it here.

So, to summarize: this post has said almost nothing.

entry.title: 2025-07-26 Qingdao
entry.content:
I have just returned from Qingdao. I might as well write another monthly note.

This was my second visit to Qingdao and my first trip with university classmates. To be honest, however, these two recent journeys have left me more confused than before. I no longer know what travelling is for. At first, perhaps, it meant seeing more places. Then it became an opportunity to talk with friends, and later a way of experiencing local life and meeting different people. After Dalian and Qingdao, though, I am no longer sure what the purpose is.

The itinerary was simple. On the first day, we walked around Ocean University of China and then watched the sea beside its gate. The second day was the competition; afterward, we sat on the beach for a while and ate seafood. On the third morning, we attended the award ceremony at a hotel. To my surprise, our rubbish project actually won second prize at the provincial level. Then we went to the aquarium and later to the bathing beach, where I nearly drowned. The fourth day is today: we slept until eleven, played some billiards, and then went our separate ways. I had several hours before my train, so I visited the Wine Museum and began writing this on the journey.

At Ocean University on the first day, the difference between the coast and the interior was immediately visible. Even the elderly security guards were tanned a remarkably—what is the word—sexy shade? It was the deep bronze that seems possible only after years of sea wind, a colour I had almost never seen in Xinyang or Beijing.

The university’s West Coast campus has indeed been sent into exile. There is no nearby metro station, the area is rather deserted, and commerce is less developed than in Liangxiang. The natural surroundings, however, are vastly better. Step outside and there is an open beach where one can watch the water and stand in the wind. The day of our visit was cloudy rather than painfully sunny. The sea was clean and blue, with no Ulva bloom in sight. I stood on the sand facing the water, the wind coming in from the sea and a small fishing boat being repaired nearby. It was difficult not to feel content.

“From my house, facing the sea, spring blossoms.” That is roughly the mood.

The blue water extended beyond sight, set beneath a blue sky and white clouds. Consider the joys and sorrows of a person scarcely more than a metre tall and weighing perhaps a hundred jin: what can they amount to before such an expanse? Whatever happens, the sea continues to rise and fall without expression. Day after day, waves strike the shore and wash the golden sand. As far as the water is concerned, nothing has happened at all.

I began to understand how an environment shapes those who inhabit it. People who live beside the sea may indeed acquire a broader heart.

On the second morning, we prepared for the defence. Our team was fourth, which meant we could eat and leave once the morning session ended. Lunch was provided in the canteen. To be honest, the competition taught me quite a lot.

Three teachers questioned us. The first asked about our latency index and the frame rate of the thermal camera. Since our project was a fire-monitoring drone, these were basic measurements. We had not taken them.

The second teacher worked in optoelectronics and on military drones. He began from requirements analysis and challenged the project point by point. Our thermal image, he argued, was of little use; the initial temperature data alone could support automatic judgment, while the image could be displayed on the terminal if necessary. If there was only one ultrasonic obstacle sensor, why not use a laser module costing a few yuan instead? The object-detection component also served little real purpose.

In summary, we had misunderstood the requirements and therefore misunderstood what we were supposed to build. A system intended to deliver genuine value should have emphasised speed and stability, rather than becoming the demonstration-oriented object we had produced.

The performance standards should also have been specified at the beginning. For ultrasonic obstacle avoidance, for example, the required detection and refresh rates ought to be derived from the drone’s maximum turning and flight speeds.

The teacher’s criticism was concrete and useful.

The third teacher asked which dataset we had used, then turned my own words against a claim in the report that the system could recognise building structures. The lesson was that one cannot be lazy with technical indicators.

That was roughly the feedback. The five-minute defence ended before we had finished. That evening, after seeing a senior student’s post about a top conference, I spoke with SC:

Exactly. We never identified the problem we were trying to solve.
Our requirements analysis really was poor.
We also lacked project-management experience.
But it does point toward another question:
how should I decide where my own energy belongs?
Requirements analysis for a project corresponds to the allocation of effort in personal development.
Even now, I have never objectively mapped the career paths available within our major.
I need to work out what preparation each path requires.
Most of the time, I just bury my head and compete without knowing where I am going.
Perhaps that is the next thing I need to do.

Two years spent in busy mediocrity. Is there still time to compete?

After lunch in the university canteen, I lay down at the hotel for a while and then returned to the beach to let the wind blow and play with the sand. It was ordinary enough, and there is little to write. Nothing happened that evening.

The award ceremony on the third day was held in the kind of luxurious hotel where I would never choose to eat on my own.

To my surprise, our pile of rubbish won second prize. We had no answer to question after question. It was more like an advance notice of admission: we did not enter the national competition, but the result was not entirely bad.

Still, at this stage I would probably be better served by placing my feet on the ground and building a few small things properly.

In the afternoon, we visited the aquarium. The exhibits were average and the ticket expensive. I took photographs, looked at jellyfish, fish, seals, sea lions, and specimens. That was about it.

What remains disturbing is what happened next at Qingdao No. 1 Bathing Beach.

I cannot swim, yet somehow charged into the sea with another friend. I assumed that water below my height could do little harm and ignored the force of the current. A wave knocked me over immediately. Fortunately, my friend saw me disappear and pulled me up. I swallowed only a couple of mouthfuls of seawater, which left me badly nauseated.

But what if he had not seen me? What if the water had carried me away? The thought is frightening. Seawater really is both salty and bitter.

I should stop imagining myself as uniquely important, intelligent, or powerful. There are things one must fear and dangers against which one must guard. A prudent person does not stand beneath a collapsing wall.

For a moment, I even seemed to experience the edge of dying—not that I was truly about to die. The mind simply froze: wait, am I actually going to die? Can anyone save me? What am I supposed to do? Wait—

It was a calm sensation of death, as though the person about to die were not me and yet undeniably were. Or perhaps it was numbness. Perhaps relief.

After I was pulled out, a man nearby told me, in a severe voice, not to enter the water if I could not swim. I laughed it off, grinning and saying that I would stop, and the moment passed.

It reminded me of the traveller who died inexplicably in the Lop Nur desert:

To be honest, I agree with the man’s reaction. Anger evolved as a tool of communication—or, for that matter, all emotions are tools of communication. A stern rebuke was one of the best uses to which that tool could have been put. I am grateful to him. I am the one who needs to reflect.

I cannot continue acting like that. A prudent person does not stand beneath a dangerous wall. The external world must not be treated lightly, although neither should it be feared beyond reason. Some things are to be done; others are not.

The fourth day is today. I slept until eleven, played billiards with Dingding for an hour, and took a taxi into the city. We have spent a ridiculous amount on taxis over the past few days. I wrote the paragraphs above while travelling.

I first visited the Wine Museum. Afterward, I had intended simply to walk toward the railway station. It was only a few kilometres and I still had two hours; I was alone and free to decide. Then I somehow reached a metro station, looked again at the map, and realised how close I was to the old streets around Zhongshan Road. So I went to Qianhaichao for sea-cucumber fried rice.

The Beer Museum was honestly overpriced. Fortunately, I bought my ticket online. Beside me, a young Korean couple with a child purchased theirs on site and paid considerably more.

The encounter made me conscious of deficiencies in both communication and foreign-language ability. The museum employee’s English was poor, so communication was difficult. I used my own half-finished foreign language to explain the situation. The man spoke some Chinese, though not fluently. I then offered to translate the museum text for them and was refused.

The sea-cucumber rice at Qianhaichao really was delicious, but painfully expensive: more than seventy yuan for a bowl that was not enough to make me full. I added a plate of fried clams and a serving of dumplings, spending one hundred and fifty yuan in total. Still, the rice really was good.

Leaving the Wine Museum and walking toward the metro, I suddenly realised that I was about to depart and might never see the street before me again. A strange sadness arrived.

It should have been a beautiful departure. Why could I not leave without hesitation? Was I still unable to let go? Perhaps my friend was right: you do not love beautiful scenery; you love the self who is looking at it.

I think I may nevertheless have found a meaning for travel. Within China, however, the experience does not feel unfamiliar enough. I still want to enter a foreign country, experience an environment that is wholly strange, meet people I have never known, communicate with them, and understand their thoughts and positions.

Before that, I must learn a foreign language properly and change the part of my character that does not know how to live among other people.

I am nearly back at university. It is 23:23, so I will stop here.

Again

I have experienced much more during this period than I would have by remaining in the dormitory, and I have also thought a great deal. Why do I keep this blog? Why place it somewhere most people will never see—somewhere equivalent to remaining undiscovered? And if I do not want it discovered, why put it on the public internet at all?

I do not know.

entry.title: 2025-07-12 Monthly Notes
entry.content:
The last time I wrote a blog post was, indeed, the last time. I have just returned to Beijing after going home from a trip to Dalian. Tomorrow I become a beast of burden again, so I may as well use these two days to take stock of the period just passed.

I

My previous post was written before the examinations. There were only three major courses this semester: Digital Electronics, Signals and Systems, and Electromagnetic Fields. I did reasonably well in Digital Electronics and could solve the problems. Electromagnetics was slightly worse, although fortunately the exam consisted largely of standard question types. My fluency in Signals and Systems was still insufficient, so that exam did not go particularly well.

From the standpoint of the subjects themselves, however, all three were genuinely interesting. Digital electronics uses abstract circuits to process discrete signals and implement logical functions. Signals and Systems develops mathematical models, then applies several transforms to analyse the frequency-domain properties of different signals. Philosophically speaking, it is an attempt to describe and analyse reality in mathematical language. The derivations possess a kind of beauty. I simply did not solve enough problems to become good at them.

I have been wondering whether I should speed-run next semester’s courses during the summer—not for the purpose of drilling exercises, but simply to understand what each subject is trying to do. I have long disliked my present method: study almost nothing during the semester, rush through the material at the end, glimpse the beauty of the course just as the examination arrives, and then move immediately to the next thing once it is over. It is a dreadful way to learn, almost a waste of something precious.

Then another thought occurred to me. Apart from reading under pressure before final examinations and occasionally discovering that a subject is rather interesting, what excites me now? This came up in a conversation with a friend. At first there were figurines, merchandise, and games, which began to feel pointless and expensive. Then came photography, cycling, and an entire wallet-destroying collection of computer peripherals, which were more expensive still. After that came music—mainly Vocaloid with some J-pop—and light novels. Those were comparatively modest interests, yet even my enthusiasm for them now seems to be declining. I have no idea what will interest me next.

I do not know.

Perhaps it will always be like this: the original enthusiasm disappears after a while, or is displaced by one interruption after another.

I was also speaking with Brother RD just now, telling him that I constantly feel lost, unsure what to do or why I am doing any of it. He pointed out something rather accurate: learning without thought leads to confusion, while thought without learning leads to peril. I bury my head in activity when it is time to act, then possess no power to act after I reflect. What should this be called? The separation of learning and thought, perhaps.

II

Another event during finals week was the handover at the radio station. The station has indeed declined over the past two years: one carrot, several holes, and not enough people to fill them. Still, I managed to remain and take on work there. That counts as one of the relatively few moments at university that has felt meaningful.

Remaining at the station means meeting more capable students and talking to people with strong organisational skills. I genuinely enjoy that. Much of their practical intelligence could never be obtained through the kind of closed-door self-instruction I have practised since childhood. Meals, meetings, and work done together may provide a little comfort even to a gloomy shut-in like me.

III

After the exams, I went home to help with university admissions. Two impressions stayed with me: information gaps are genuinely valuable, and outgoing people who know how to deal with others are more likely to secure a better share of what is available.

What do I mean? A high-school student who concentrates exclusively on study may emerge from the entrance examination knowing almost nothing about the choices that follow. I know this from experience. I selected a major almost at random and somehow arrived where I am. Fortunately, the direction I stumbled into happens to suit me, but that was luck and nothing more. Many younger students I met were much the same. My accidental choice turned out well; theirs may not. Students like that are extremely easy to mislead. I therefore still hold the same view: make more friends, open more channels of information, and interpret what someone says in light of their position. A student may retain more of a conscience than some other adviser, for example, but one should also ask whether their interests conflict with yours.

As for extroversion, two parents came to speak with me and added me on WeChat. I knew both of them. One took the initiative to ask further questions, discussed possible choices, and therefore received more information from me. I casually asked the other whether anything remained unclear; they asked only about the admission score and left. Leaving aside whether my advice was correct or personally biased, the first parent almost certainly spoke not only to me but to members of the other admissions groups as well. The amount of information available to that parent was bound to exceed what the second obtained.

There are other examples, but they are inconvenient to record. Perhaps when I return to this post I will remember them; perhaps I will not. It hardly matters.

But have I actually followed this advice myself? I do not know.

IV

Then I went home. Every return produces the same feeling: the place differs slightly from the version preserved in memory. Perhaps it will eventually become the most familiar of strange places. Each time I come back, the older members of my family seem visibly older than I remember. And what, meanwhile, have I made of myself? Neither properly human nor properly ghost, drifting through one confused day after another. If the person I was upon graduating from high school could see me now, what would he think?

That reminds me of the high-school students I met during admissions. They were still so young: energetic, full of expectation, looking toward the future. After talking to them, I could not help asking myself:

“Answer me. Are you truly satisfied with the person you have become?”

Two summers ago, a boy likewise held his examination score and searched through admissions information, full of hope and unaware that he might drown in autumn.

I was twenty-one that day, in the golden age of my life. I had so many extravagant hopes. I wanted to love, to eat, and to become in an instant a cloud in the sky, half bright and half dark. Only later did I learn that life is a slow process of being hammered: people grow older day by day, their hopes disappear one by one, and eventually they become like an ox under the mallet. Yet on my twenty-first birthday I foresaw none of this. I thought I would remain fierce forever, and that nothing could hammer me down.

V

After the admissions work, I went to Dalian. Tourist attractions are much the same everywhere: drivers soliciting passengers, people selling one thing after another. A trip is supposed to offer rest and pleasure, yet the constant sales pitches made the experience irritating.

I also spent two days in the hotel catching up on assignments. Once again, I had left all the work until the end. Next time I should finish it earlier. As things stood, I neither enjoyed the trip fully nor completed the work particularly well.

The main purpose was to travel with friends: climb a mountain, talk, eat together, and settle the accounts afterward. Even so, the experience left me rather lost. Old friends continue moving farther away, while the opportunities to make uncomplicated friendships diminish with age. How many more occasions like this will I have? I do not know.

Taking out the old video camera was a good decision, if only because it encouraged me to record more. Dalian’s coast is beautiful. Unfortunately, the weather was poor on the first day and our stay too short on the second. How pleasant it would be to live like the local students, able to visit the shore whenever one wished and let the sea wind blow for a while. It would certainly beat climbing another mountain for no reason.

As for Japanese, that can wait for another post. Still, I do seem to be improving. While watching anime on the journey back to Beijing, I could clearly understand more than before. I might as well keep learning.

The final section has become something of a running account. Perhaps, after I return from the competition in Qingdao, I can write more carefully about how to begin a day’s work and what the two days in Dalian actually taught me.

Next time. Definitely!

entry.title: 06-09 Thinking and Building
entry.content:
This thought probably came to me, for no obvious reason, while I was reading a manga adapted from a novel. The original author likes to work his own experience into the story, so the book reveals something of his views on love, his philosophy of life, and all those small amusements that belong to a relationship.

That sent me down quite a long train of thought. Personally, I do want to meet more people at this stage of my life, and perhaps get into a relationship. Yet the more I think about it, the more I notice a serious problem: whenever I talk to someone, we rarely seem to meet on the same wavelength. Sometimes the conversation becomes nothing more than my one-sided complaining; at other times, we simply sit there in awkward silence. I suspect there are two sides to the problem—conversational skill, and either the breadth of one’s knowledge or the capacity to offer an interesting point of view.

As for conversational skill, I may begin with something I once came across online. Da Bing was speaking to a young man over a livestream, and the man had exactly my problem: he never got to the point, filled his speech with needless words, and expressed himself poorly. The advice he received was to speak less. Before answering, pause for perhaps two or three seconds—no more than five—to organise and pare down what you are about to say. If that is not enough, simply tell the other person that you need a moment to think. Remove what is unnecessary, then offer the shortest statement that still captures the point.

Two ideas lie behind this advice. First, if you already know that speaking is not your strength, then instead of worrying that you may leave something unsaid, you might as well respect your present limitations: the more one talks, the more likely one is to go wrong. Second, refining a sentence is itself a form of intellectual training, through which you learn to explain an idea both briefly and clearly. There is an additional benefit, too. The other person is likely to feel respected, because you are visibly taking their words seriously enough to think before responding.

I can leave the other techniques for another day. This is something for which I should deliberately seek out material, practise more often, hold more worthwhile conversations, discuss subjects with a higher information density, and do some genuine brainstorming.

Then there is the substance of a conversation—the views one holds and the things one can actually talk about. On the one hand, I should waste less time on fragmented entertainment. An hour of short videos is worse than an hour of gaming; at least finishing a game or watching an anime means putting some time into an interest of my own. On the other hand, I should look for material that contains thought: organise some of the highly rated answers on Zhihu, read more books, and learn more skills instead of letting my brain rot all day. I have even considered setting aside some free time each week to trace the underlying logic of those popular Zhihu answers, although that material may no longer be suitable for this blog.

Sleep.

entry.title: An Introduction to Git and Its Use
entry.content:
This post consists of notes taken while reading the official Pro Git Book. Much of it was copied directly. I read only the first two chapters for this post; subjects such as running Git on a server can wait until later.

A Brief History of Git

The Development of Version Control

Local version control → centralised version control → distributed version control.

Git emerged during the development of Linux. After BitKeeper, a distributed version-control system, withdrew the Linux development team’s right to use it free of charge, Linus Torvalds led the creation of a new version-control system. Git was designed to be simple and fast, to support parallel development, to be fully distributed, and to manage projects on an extremely large scale.

Underlying Idea and Advantages

Git records an index of file snapshots. Whenever an update is committed, it takes a snapshot and stores an index pointing to that snapshot. For efficiency, if a file has not changed, Git does not store it again but retains a link to the previously stored file. Most Git operations therefore need access only to local files and resources and generally require no information from other computers on a network.

Earlier systems such as CVS, Subversion, and Perforce instead recorded differences between successive versions in a form resembling patches, an approach usually called delta-based version control. With Perforce, almost nothing can be done without a connection to the server. With Subversion and CVS, files can be modified offline, but the changes cannot be committed to the database because the local machine has no complete offline database.

Git recognises three principal states in which a file may exist: committed, modified, and staged.

  • Modified means that the file has changed but has not yet been stored in the database.
  • Staged means that the current version of a modified file has been marked for inclusion in the next committed snapshot.
  • Committed means that the data has been safely stored in the local database.

A Git project consequently involves three areas: the working tree, which is an independent copy of one version that can be edited; the staging area, a file in the Git repository directory that records what the next commit will contain; and the Git directory, .git.

Installing Git

  • Linux, using a Debian-based distribution as an example: sudo apt install git-all
  • macOS: run git --version and follow the system prompts. For direct installation with a binary installer, see the Git website: Git—Downloading
  • Windows: use the binary installer described at Git—Downloading Package
  • Compilation from source: see Git—Installing Git. I do not think this is necessary, and it consumes additional time, though anyone interested may try it.

Configuring Git

Git provides the git config tool. Configuration variables may be stored in three locations:

  1. For every user on the system: /etc/gitconfig. If git config is run with the --system option, Git reads from and writes to this file. Note that it is a system configuration file and requires sudo privileges.

  2. For the current user: ~/.gitconfig or ~/.config/git/config. Passing the --global option causes Git to read from and write to this file, affecting every repository belonging to the user.

  3. For the current repository: .git/config. Within that repository, the --local option forces Git to read and write this file, although this is already the default behaviour.

A setting at each more specific level overrides the corresponding setting at the broader level above it.

On Windows, Git looks for a .gitconfig file under the $HOME directory, generally C:\Users\$USER. It also looks for /etc/gitconfig, but only under the root directory of MSys—that is, the destination selected when Git was installed. If Git 2.x or later is used on Windows, another system-level configuration file exists: C:\Documents and Settings\All Users\Application Data\Git\config on Windows XP, or C:\ProgramData\Git\config on Windows Vista and later. This file can be modified only with administrator privileges by running git config -f <file>.

User Information

The first thing to do after installing Git is to set a user name and email address. This is important because every Git commit uses this information, which is written permanently into each commit:

As the preceding section shows, --global configures the current user. To use different information for a particular project, enter that project and run the same command without --global.

IDE Configuration

On Linux, the default system text editor is generally used. The editor can be changed with the following command, using Emacs as an example:

On Windows, specify the full path to the executable.

Git Help

Obtaining a Git Repository

Initialising a Repository in an Existing Directory

In the current directory:

Cloning an Existing Repository

Git clones almost all the data available from the repository server. By default, every version is downloaded.

From the target directory:

This creates a directory named “libgit2” in the current directory and initialises a .git folder inside it. Git retrieves all data from the remote repository and places it in .git, then checks out a copy of the latest version. Enter the newly created libgit2 folder and every project file will be ready for subsequent development and use.

The transmission protocols can wait for another post.

Uploading with Git (zzzz)

The cycle through which file states change is:

![[file-20250604000404216.png]]

The following sections are organised around this cycle.

Tracking New Files and Staging Changes

A file cannot be placed under version control until it has been added to the update. A newly created file remains untracked, and git add <文件> must be run to stage it. Every subsequent commit includes only the contents of the staging area. git add can also accept a directory path and recursively track every file beneath it.

One detail deserves attention. If a new file is added halfway through the work, the version eventually uploaded is the version that existed when git add was last run. Any modifications made afterwards remain unstaged, so the file must be added again.

Ignoring Files That Do Not Need Version Control

Create a .gitignore file in the project root, or in a subdirectory, and list the patterns to be ignored. Glob syntax is supported.

Inspecting File Status

  • git status displays the current branch, its relationship with the remote branch, staged and unstaged changes, and untracked files.
  • git status -s, or --short, displays the same status in a compact form.

Inspecting the Details of Changes

Before committing, use git status to confirm that every required change has been staged, and then inspect the differences.

One distinction is important. To view only unstaged changes, run git diff. To inspect changes that are staged and waiting to be committed, use git diff --cached, or --staged.

Removing Files

1. Complete Removal from Both the Working Directory and Git Repository

git rm <file>:

  • Deletes the file from the working directory.
  • Stages the deletion by recording it in the staging area.
  • After the commit, the file is no longer tracked by Git and has disappeared from the disk.

2. Removal from Git Tracking Only, while Retaining the Working-Tree File

git rm --cached <file>:

  • Removes the file from Git’s tracking list and staging area.
  • Retains the file in the working directory, where it becomes untracked.
  • This is useful when a file was added accidentally but must remain locally, as with a log or build artefact.

3. Forced Removal with -f

  • If a file has been modified and staged, git rm -f <file> is required to force its deletion.
  • This requirement helps prevent accidental deletion of modifications for which no committed snapshot exists and which Git therefore cannot restore.

4. Removing Files That Match a Pattern

  • Use git rm with a glob pattern; for example, git rm log/\*.log deletes every .log file under log/.
  • Note: special characters such as * generally need to be escaped, as in \*.

Moving or Renaming Files

Git infers intelligently from changes in content whether a file has been moved or renamed. The command git mv <old_name> <new_name> can perform either operation and is equivalent to the following three commands:

After the commit, Git recognises the operation as a rename, and git status displays renamed.

If a file is moved or renamed in some other way, such as through a system command or file manager, the following commands must be run manually:

Complete both steps before committing, and Git will still recognise the operation as a rename.

Committing Changes

Running git commit opens the default text editor with a comment template for the commit, resembling the commented lines shown by git status. Enter the commit message on the first line. Alternatively, git commit -m "提交信息" places the message directly on the command line. Each git commit should implement one feature or fix one bug. The message must be clear—must be, must be.

After the commit, Git reports the current branch, the SHA-1 generated for the commit, and statistics such as the number of files and lines involved.

Each commit records only a snapshot of the staging area. Unstaged changes are not included and remain in the working directory; git add must be run again before they can enter a later commit.

Advanced Shortcut: Skipping an Explicit Add

For convenience, it is possible to run:

This skips an explicit git add and staging step, but it stages all previously tracked files together for the commit and is consequently less precise.

Reviewing Git History

Viewing Commit History

This command displays the commit history, with the newest commit at the top and older ones below. It includes information such as the author’s name, the committer, and the summary.

Many options provide more detailed views. Since I still lack experience with large-project development, I will omit them for now and return when I actually need them.

Undoing Changes in Git

If used carelessly, these operations may cause work to be lost.

I will stop here for the moment and continue after the final examinations.

Chinese language pack for Git GUI: stayor/git-gui-zh

References:

  • stayor/git-gui-zh
  • Chinese Localisation of Git—Zhihu
  • Git

entry.title: CMake, Static Libraries, and Dynamic Libraries
entry.content:
CMake

This post originated in the time I spent not paying attention during Signals and Systems.

Basic Concepts

CMake automatically generates build files for different platforms from CMakeLists.txt; it is therefore a tool for generating build systems.

It sits slightly above manual configuration at the basic level, defining project structure, dependencies, and compilation options without requiring each tool to be configured manually.

Configuration

  • CMakeLists.txt
  • A build directory created with mkdir build, which keeps the source tree clean.

(Perhaps the next post could discuss PATH. And the registry?)

CMakeLists.txt Syntax

  • CMake Tutorial — RUNOOB

(And what, exactly, are static and dynamic libraries?)

Workflow

  • Create the build directory → generate the build files (.../build # Cmake...).
  • Compile and build (make ...).
  • Clean the build files (make clean or delete Cmakecache.txt).

As one layer of the compilation process, CMake has build tools such as Make, Ninja, and Visual Studio beneath it. These deserve further study.

Static and Dynamic Libraries

The basic material comes from a RUNOOB blog post.

  • C++ Static and Dynamic Libraries — RUNOOB

As before, this note does not discuss their underlying formats or memory layouts.

What Is a Library?

A library is a toolkit of lower-level components that saves later programmers from reinventing the wheel. At bottom, it is a binary form of visible source code that can be loaded into memory and used.

  • Static libraries (.a, .lib)
  • Dynamic libraries (.so, .dll)

Source file → compilation → linking → execution

Both static and dynamic libraries enter during linking. The distinction lies in how that linking is handled.

Static Libraries

A static library is compiled into the program.

Advantages

  • Convenient when moving the program to another computer, because no environment needs to be configured
  • Convenient to update

Disadvantages

  • Occupies more space
  • Inconvenient to update

Building

  • On Linux, use the ar tool
  • On Windows, use lib.exe

Dynamic Libraries

Advantages

  • Loaded when the program runs
  • Convenient to update

Disadvantages

  • DLL Hell: the environment must repeatedly be configured

entry.title: Interstellar
entry.content:
Let me once again thank my partner for completing this programme with me. What follows is the part I wrote.

Introduction and Background

Interstellar is an original science-fiction adventure directed by Christopher Nolan. It was released on 5 November 2014 and has a Douban rating of 9.4.

Nolan explained his original impulse in roughly these terms: when he was a child, becoming an astronaut represented the noblest dream and the highest ambition. He missed the determination to keep exploring and to advance into the furthest reaches of the galaxy, and hoped that the film might begin a new age of outward expansion. Interstellar is both a tribute to the classic space film and a continuation of that childhood dream. As usual, Nolan favoured physical sets and IMAX film over complete dependence on computer-generated imagery, seeking a stronger sense of reality and immersion.

To keep the scientific theories in the film credible, Nolan invited Nobel laureate and theoretical physicist Kip Thorne to serve as scientific adviser, giving the wormholes, black holes, and other astrophysical phenomena a rigorous foundation. Thorne’s team used thousands of computers to solve simulations based on Einstein’s equations. The resulting image of the black hole also contributed positively to astrophysical research. Thorne later examined the principles behind the film one by one in his book The Science of Interstellar.

Reflections After Watching

The narrative structure of Interstellar is carefully designed and can broadly be understood as containing one visible line and one concealed line. In the visible story, Cooper saves his daughter and the human race by transmitting information from within the tesseract. Gravity is the medium of the message, while love is the motive for his action. Beneath it lies another story: humanity in higher dimensions saves its present-day ancestors by creating the wormhole and the tesseract.

The film’s foreshadowing is as rigorous and precise as a formula. At the beginning, books fall mysteriously from the study shelves, Murph speaks of a “ghost,” and patterns in the dust conceal the coordinates of the NASA base. What appear to be supernatural signs are all recovered at the end, when Cooper moves the world lines along the surface of the tesseract and Murph deciphers the trembling hands of the watch. The circuit closes. Nolan makes the five-dimensional bookshelf both a carrier of paternal love and a time capsule buried by humanity for its own rescue. In the spirit of Murphy’s law, every accident drawn together by gravity eventually becomes a necessary point of starlight.

The film also deserves attention for its handling of detail and its secondary characters. Consider Cooper’s two children. Murph is the pioneer who looks toward the stars and eventually receives the admiration of millions. His son, by contrast, is the guardian whose feet remain in the soil—indispensable, yet easily forgotten. Even his name is the thoroughly ordinary Tom. When their father leaves him the promise of “protecting the home,” this sole ordinary figure in the story carries humanity upon his back. His trust in his father is unconditional. Cooper asks only that he look after the family, and Tom remains with the old house and the fields for decades. Because of that persistence, Murph can return home and still find the watch her father gave her many years before, then decode his hidden message. The father’s spacesuit and the son’s plough shine with equal force: one brings data out of the black hole, while the other preserves the bridge across which that information can pass. Humanity cannot be saved by a handful of extraordinary heroes alone. It also depends upon countless ordinary people who stay at their posts, as Tom does.

After the film ended, I found myself returning to another question: why are people so fascinated by science fiction? Perhaps it is because such works act as prisms, refracting the deepest contradiction in the human soul. We are products of immense clouds of stardust, children of reason; yet among that dust, we are also the only beings moved to tears by starlight. In The Three-Body Problem, the Singer flattens the Solar System with a dual-vector foil and turns it into a flowing galaxy that might have come from Van Gogh. Cold reason and burning compassion meet for an instant in a brilliant final song. In Foundation, people living beneath the structure of psychohistory compose, through their own lives, an epic of faith and betrayal, power and feeling. Science fiction is never merely a fantasy about the future. It examines the reason and emotion within us. Reflected in its mirror, somewhere between the operation of a formula and the radiance of human character, we can finally see ourselves more clearly.

I think Interstellar is so powerful precisely because it sees that contradiction and writes it as an epic beneath the stars. Cooper floats against the surface of the tesseract and moves the world lines of the books with his fingers; suddenly, the cold formulas and the data from a black-hole singularity acquire bodily warmth. Every ray from the accretion disk becomes an echo of longing that crosses dimensions. Through this story, Nolan and Thorne show that science and technology, our strongest weapons in confronting nature, can also carve the shape of love when they turn toward humanity itself. As Carl Sagan wrote in Cosmos, the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, and the iron in our blood were all formed from ancient stars. Technology and human feeling have never been opposites. Like the wave–particle duality of light, they are projections of the same substance in different dimensions.

As the credits rise into darkness with the roar of the organ, we beyond the screen remain trapped in the predicament called “humanity.” We are dust among the stars, yet also the only gods within that dust who attempt to understand it. Nolan tells us that when ripples of gravity spread through spacetime, only love can turn noise into a messenger; when molecules wander without direction through the void, only fingers interlocked beside a fire can define the temperature of existence. Perhaps the universe does not care how humanity opens a path for its species through a wormhole, or how line after line of equations and symbols is written upon a blackboard. Yet this romance, futile in the eyes of the universe, is exactly what enables us to cultivate an oasis called civilization in the desert of endless entropy. Let us raise our heads and look into the night. Every ancient patch of light seems to whisper: calculate the light-years, laugh, weep, and become the gentlest stardust in the universe.

Do not go gentle into that good night.

Old age should burn and rave at close of day.

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

entry.title: 05-28 Twenty
entry.content:
Today is the second day of the fifth lunar month, three days before the Dragon Boat Festival, and my twentieth birthday.

That sentence alone is probably enough for my imagined readers to understand the title. Yes: the twentieth year of my life is about to arrive, and so is its twentieth summer.

On a day like this, I have begun tapping at the keyboard again, perhaps in order to pretend that I am writing something down, as anyone might who wishes to lend life a little ceremony.

Where should the account begin? With my frantic rush to the General Teaching Building for Signals and Systems this morning, or with finishing the homework last night? Perhaps it should begin with lying in bed, scrolling through my phone until four before I finally fell asleep. I have indeed been busy lately. The preliminary round of the Integrated Circuit Innovation Competition ended last week, immediately followed by the China Electrical Engineering Cup mathematical-modelling contest and work at the audiovisual event. I thought this week might offer a little room to breathe. Instead, my teacher began pressing us for progress in the circuit competition; I still had to edit and complete post-production on the Light and Shadow Group’s final programme; and both the municipal and university innovation projects had reached their mid-term deadlines.

Is this work I enjoy? It seems to be. Then why does finishing it leave me so tired? Is this truly the life I want? Am I willing to support myself through these things? Am I even capable of supporting myself through them? Or, pushing the question further, why should I remain alive, and what is remaining alive for? I do not know. I cannot find a reason to go on living; I merely have reasons why I cannot delete my account on Earth Online. Thus, even after reviewing the Z-transform late at night, even beneath a waning moon hanging over sparse paulownia branches, cheap little videos on an electronic screen remain beside me until the rooster announces dawn and the red sun rises.

The phoenix flute stirs the air, yet no graceful brow appears where the lights grow dim; the jade lantern turns, but for whom do fish and dragons dance?

There it is again—that awful habit from high school. Why am I still composing these sour little lines?

In ordinary language: perhaps I genuinely cannot find comfort elsewhere. Or perhaps Douyin offers me at least one guarantee—as long as I have electricity and an internet connection, it will continue recommending videos I may find interesting. And so, on the first day of my twentieth year, entertainment kept me awake until dawn.

Then I slept for three hours and went to Signals and Systems. The lecture concerned the Z-transform, and the course will finish in two weeks before the examination. To be honest, I do find the subject interesting. At the very least, it has taught me what signals and systems are, and how different transforms and analyses in the time and frequency domains can be used to process them. It creates the false yet strangely convincing sensation that, once I finish the course, I will be able to handle signals with ease—as though I had acquired some command over the fate of a thing.

Here I should thank my friend SC, who reminded me during the lecture that today was my birthday. Deeply moving, darling. I had almost forgotten it myself.

Perhaps this is also a place to say something about the meaning of anniversaries. I used to dismiss birthdays, graduations, and other supposedly special days; only holidays capable of giving me time off attracted much attention. Today, however, I might offer this apparently pointless observation: if you pay no attention to a commemorative day and assign it no meaning, then it truly has none. If you do attend to it and find it meaningful, then it becomes meaningful to you. Such a date resembles a mile marker in a marathon. You can ignore it and keep running without difficulty. Yet if you notice it, you realise how far you have already travelled, look back over what was gained and lost along the way, adjust your state of mind, and—whether the judgment is good or bad—continue forward.

The afternoon consisted of the thoroughly absurd classroom component of our social-practice course. The teacher was mostly filling time; I listened to the arrangements, signed in, and left. Nothing more needs to be said.

After dinner, I went to the engineering-training building to work on the drone. The situation was fairly abstract: “Your ministers have only just taken one city—why does Your Majesty press the army onward? How could we dare settle down? Three victories in a month!” When we finished, the senior student left to eat barbecue. The restaurant was decent. Then the two of us suddenly decided to fly the drone on our own; the moment we reached the field and tried, we packed up again. In truth, Brother Ding is usually reliable. This time, I was the unreliable one.

Afterward, Brother Ding and I rode our bicycles along the tree-lined central road of the south campus. The summer evening breeze carried not the slightest trace of coolness, while shouts from the men playing football on the field reached us from the side. Why, in memory, do the stadium lights still seem to have been on? The moment felt inexplicably youthful. On the first day of being twenty—twenty already exhausted, like an office worker or an old man—I felt, for a little while after ten at night, the freedom and vigour of youth from the seat of a bicycle. Perhaps that was the finest twentieth-birthday present the world could have given me.

Do not say the twilight comes too late; the evening sky is still filled with glowing clouds. I should catch the tail of youth and try to form, somewhere in the brain, a few synaptic connections worth remembering.

May we both take courage from this.

entry.title: The Pursuit of Happyness
entry.content:
(Piano version of A Father’s Way)

【Plot Summary】

Hello, listeners. Welcome to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. I am your host, xxx.

Today, I would like to talk about an old film released in 2006: The Pursuit of Happyness, starring Will Smith.

The story takes place in San Francisco in 1981. Its protagonist, Chris Gardner, is a medical-equipment salesman who has invested all his savings in a portable bone-density scanner. The device is slightly more accurate than an X-ray machine, but it costs twice as much. The doctors’ response is simple: unnecessary and too expensive.

He therefore has no choice but to carry the forty-pound machine around every day, facing rejection again and again while continuing to try. His wife works two jobs to support the family, but eventually she can bear the situation no longer and leaves. Three months behind on the rent, he is evicted by his landlord. He and his son sleep in a toilet at a subway station, wait in long queues outside shelters, and even sell blood.

During that period, his only opportunity is an unpaid internship as a stockbroker. He works at the firm during the day and rushes to a shelter at night, while using whatever spare time remains to sell the scanners and obtain money for daily life.

In the end, he is hired and later establishes his own company. To be honest, when I watched this film in the past, I regarded it as a standard inspirational story: a poor man reverses his fate; a father’s love is as firm as a mountain; relentless effort finally carries him to Wall Street. Watching it now, however, I am most deeply impressed not by that “success,” but by the hands with which he covers his son’s ears in the toilet, and by the moment when he walks out of the office building, his eyes red, and applauds himself.

【Artistic Techniques】

The film’s director, Gabriele Muccino, is Italian and previously directed The Last Kiss. He brings traces of Italian neorealism into this film. Handheld cameras are used extensively, giving the images a slightly unsteady quality. The film was shot directly on the streets of San Francisco, and Will Smith was even asked to interact with homeless people there.

The young actor who plays the son is Jaden Smith, Will Smith’s own son. Many of the looks and physical gestures between them are not so much “acted” as genuine responses between father and son. This approach to casting is typical of the neorealist desire to “move life onto the screen”: the suffering in the film appears less like a performance and more like a record of reality.

【Thematic Analysis】

Why has this film remained popular for so long? I think it is because the film does not beautify suffering. It is not a bowl of chicken soup telling us that “effort always leads to success.” Instead, it presents the living and truthful story of a man who repeatedly fails, repeatedly loses what he has, and is repeatedly forced back into his original condition by life.

Chris loses a scanner, a shoe, and a place to live; he nearly loses custody of his son. To reach the queue outside the shelter, he runs wildly through the streets with the machine in his arms. To meet his targets, he gives up his breaks and spends two more hours on the telephone than everyone else each day.

Even the film’s title contains a hidden point: the word Happyness in The Pursuit of Happyness is misspelled; the correct spelling is Happiness. The error is said to come from a piece of graffiti mentioned in the real protagonist’s memoir. It seems to suggest that the “happiness” we pursue is itself imperfect. It is not a standard answer, but the trail of footprints left behind as we make mistakes and continue moving forward.

In other words, happiness is not the sound of a knock for which we wait. It is the road we see behind us when, after running until we are breathless, we finally turn around.

In the eyes of others, Chris is also a man of almost complete “disrepute”: a “deadbeat” who cannot pay his rent, an “incompetent husband” abandoned by his wife, a “madman” who chases swindlers and scanner thieves through the streets, and a person “not worth knowing well.”

Nor does the film give him a single person who is truly his “friend.” He does not even have the chance to ruin a friendship, because he does not qualify to be judged by friends in the first place.

Yet at the moment when his reputation is at its worst, he does not stop and beg anyone to change their view of him. Silently and stubbornly, he simply continues knocking on that door and fulfilling his responsibility as a father.

Perhaps we do not need to be declared “innocent” before we are allowed to live. Perhaps, when the entire world attaches the label “unworthy” to us, the only thing left for us to do is stop begging the world for a judgement that calls us “worthy.” We must move forward with all the charges laid upon us and all those labels marked “unworthy.” Only after we have travelled far enough can the labels be blown away by the wind.

【Reading the Details】

There is a shot in the film which many people have discussed, but which is worth mentioning again.

Chris cannot afford a hotel, so he hides with his son in a subway-station toilet. He holds the boy in his arms and braces the door with his foot while someone outside pounds upon it. He reaches out, covers his son’s ears, and cries without making a sound.

He could have broken down. He could have put his son aside, opened the door, and argued with the person outside, or simply walked out by himself. But he does not. He covers his son’s ears not because the boy might hear the abuse outside, but because he does not want his son to hear his fear. He must still fulfil a father’s responsibility.

At that moment, no one will applaud him. No one will tell him, “You are a good father.” No one even knows. He does all this simply because he is a father. In that toilet, he decides to reserve the last of his dignity for his son.

Many of our decisions are made in order to be seen. We lose weight so that we will look good in photographs, revise so that we will not be mocked, and apologise so that we will be forgiven. But what if no one sees?
