entry.title: Your Lie in April
entry.content:
Your Lie in April: A Programme by the Light and Shadow Group

—The April when I met you is coming. The April without you is coming.

Let me once again thank my partner for this programme. She recommended the anime to me, and she also worked with me to complete both the script and the broadcast. In fact, it would be more accurate to say that, as a senior member, she guided a newcomer like me—boo-hoo. Her contribution to the programme was far greater than mine.

Dramatic Excerpt I

Source: Your Lie in April (Chinese Dub)

Kousei: A melodica? Not bad. (The tone is slightly questioning; pause between the two sentences.)

Tsubaki: (Background voice; a sound effect can be added in post-production.) Miwa told me that the moment she met him, her life changed. (Speak with a smile; let the final sentence fade.) Everything she saw, heard, and felt—everything within her sight—began to fill with brilliant colours. (Pause after “everything within her sight”; strengthen the second half.) The whole world began to shine. (Strengthen the second half.)

(The sound of the melodica continues…)

Main Programme

Hello, everyone. Welcome to today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow on the Voice of BIT. I am your host, Zhang Hengwei, and I am your host, Wang Yiru. (Introduction.) At a time when the animation market is crowded with adaptations of light novels and fast-food series appear one after another, there is an anime that was released eleven years ago but still ranks second in an online Japanese poll of the most moving animated works. It has also become, for countless viewers, a masterpiece that every newcomer to anime ought to watch. More than ten years after its release, many people still commemorate it in their own ways every April. || If you are interested in stories of pure love and curious about a classic anime with such an enduring reputation, Your Lie in April may be exactly the work you have been expecting. In today’s edition of The Age of Light and Shadow, let us enter that April of falling cherry blossoms and listen to the symphony of music and love within Your Lie in April.

This story of music and love begins with an unexpected encounter. The protagonist, Kousei Arima, has studied the piano since childhood under his mother’s strict instruction and has repeatedly won first prize in competitions large and small. An unquestionably gifted young pianist, Kousei is, in almost everyone’s eyes, closely associated with the title of a rising star in the world of piano. Yet an unforeseen change destroys those hopes and breaks apart the musical dream he has always pursued. His mother, severe in her teaching and seldom given to smiles, dies suddenly after suffering from cancer. Faced with this disaster and overwhelmed by grief, Kousei becomes unable to hear the sound of his own piano, and his life loses all light. Then another unexpected encounter completely transforms that dim existence. While waiting for a friend, Kousei happens to meet Kaori Miyazono beneath a cherry tree, playing a melodica. He is drawn towards Kaori, a free and uninhibited violinist, and through a series of accidents the two become friends. Beneath Kaori’s bright and cheerful appearance, however, lies a shadow unknown to others. As an accomplished violinist, she began learning the instrument as a child because she wished to perform with the gifted Kousei Arima. To fulfil that childhood promise, Kaori creates their meeting through the lie that she “likes their mutual friend,” concealing the cruel fact that she is terminally ill. Yet this unexpected encounter not only restores music to Kousei’s world, in which only monotonous black and white keys remained, but also allows Kaori’s meteor-bright life to release its fiercest light during its final countdown. In the time left to her, Kaori uses her music and love to teach Kousei that music is not a chain, but a language through which he can speak to the world. She also teaches him how to face loss. Finally, in the spring when Kaori Miyazono departs, he performs the eternal composition that belongs to them both.

Dramatic Excerpt II

Source: Your Lie in April — Excerpt 2 — Bilibili

Kaori: Are you still playing the piano?

Kousei: I don’t play any more.

I knew it. You are sinking into despair alone again.

Kousei: I can’t do it any more. Everyone important to me has left before my eyes. Music took the people who truly mattered away, until I was the only one left.

Kaori: But you still have me, don’t you? Arima, I am going to have an operation on 18 February. I will give everything I have and struggle until the final moment. It is your fault—all of it. The reason I am struggling so awkwardly and chasing the hope of staying alive is you. The time I spent with you made me unwilling to leave. Won’t you try once more? Aren’t we best at fighting with everything we have? Aren’t we performers who struggle as if our lives depend upon it?

Kousei: But I haven’t touched the piano for a week.

Kaori: You hadn’t touched it when you accompanied me either.

Kousei: I occasionally played while working part-time then. There is no way I can perform well now. It would take a miracle to play in this condition…

Kaori: You are looking down again.

(Kaori plays the violin.)

Kaori: You wanted a miracle? There it is.

Main Programme

As a classic of Japanese animation, Your Lie in April is not merely a story of youth. It is also an anime about music, a classic whose flesh and blood are musical. From Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata in the first episode to Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 in G Minor in the last; from Saint-Saëns’s Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso, with which the two protagonists first perform together, to Kreisler’s Liebesleid, which they never manage to complete together, every piece of classical music corresponds precisely with the plot and becomes a bridge along which emotion can flow. As Kousei breaks free from his mother’s shadow amid the torrent of the Revolutionary Étude, and as Kaori interprets the final blaze of life through the wild freedom of Introduction and Rondo Capriccioso, the notes and the narrative have already become one, producing an almost fated resonance.

The film allows music and narrative to grow together, going far beyond the simple use of “music as background.” With notes as its bricks and tiles, it constructs a city that remains forever in April. As Kaori says, “Music is freedom!” The creators weave that freedom together with the solemnity of classical music, arranging a magnificent concert for the transience of youth. When, ten years later, we still hear news of this concert being performed again and again in the words of so many people, we know that the concert of that April has long since been engraved upon their hearts and entered eternity.

Zhu Guangqian once wrote that, although the contents of tragedy mostly appear frightening on the surface, tragedy is by no means limited to terror. Terror merely causes pain and finally leaves people gloomy and discouraged, whereas tragedy inspires and strengthens them. Your Lie in April is a fine work that carries this principle through. It takes a tragedy in April as its foundation, yet releases an astonishing vitality that urges people to grow and move forward.

The so-called “lie” of the plot is the most beautiful lie woven by a girl who, as her life enters its final countdown, wants to save the person she loves. With the lie that she “likes Watari,” Kaori Miyazono enters the life of Kousei, the former child prodigy, knocks upon the door of his heart, and helps him overcome his inner demon. Through this apparently light and conventional device, the author offers a delicate interpretation of the Japanese aesthetics of mono no aware. In The Tale of Genji, the evening face blooms in the morning and withers by evening; similarly, behind Kaori’s gentle “lie” lies endless sorrow. In the last part of her life, she chooses to build a bridge towards their meeting out of a lie, solely so that, before she disappears, she can use the final vitality within her to save the gifted performer she loves. Like a cherry blossom whose fall is already determined at the instant of its full flowering, this countdown narrative casts a reflected sorrow over every warm scene, producing a tragic aesthetic space with a profoundly Eastern quality.

Just as every cherry blossom that opens in April must return to dust, and just as every performance must eventually end, Kaori—who brings hope and vitality to Kousei—still falls before that April of cherry blossoms arrives. The ending reveals the existential nature of life as “being towards death”: every apparently eternal beauty is, in essence, merely a suspension granted by death. Such recognition of life’s meaninglessness ought to lead towards nihilism. In this work, however, the author completes the turn from nothingness to existence through the characters’ devotion to and love for music. In the last days of her life, Kaori continues her final struggle so that she might perform on the same stage as the person she loves. Even after both his mother and his beloved have left him, Arima continues to play Bach and Chopin for the world, still carrying hope for life. These moments of earnest living constitute defiance against an absurd world. Like Camus’s Sisyphus, who knows the boulder will roll down again but continues climbing, Kousei defies his fate. Likewise, in that final April, Kaori smiles and says, “Even if grief is impossible to restrain, even if we lie wounded at the bottom of the valley, we must not stop playing. Only in this way are we truly alive.” This is her defiance against her terminal illness. Only now do we suddenly understand: life conceals the essence of disappearance beneath the appearance of existence, while human beings, fully aware of the ending, still choose to live with passion. As Romain Rolland wrote, “There is only one heroism in the world: to see the world as it is and to love it.” Yes—the most magnificent heroism of life does not lie in avoiding the inevitability of disappearance, but in turning the final scene into a splendid movement in full bloom. Even if I am to disappear tomorrow, today I will still straighten my tie and go out to greet the final evening glow and the rising sun.

Today, ten years later, Japan’s cherry-blossom front still moves northwards at seventeen kilometres per day. Petals still fall at five centimetres per second, and a pink glow once again rises upon Tokyo Tower. When real visitors lift their heads towards that fleeting splendour on the branches and reach out to catch petals falling at five centimetres per second, perhaps they do not know that Chopin’s Ballade No. 1 in G Minor from ten years ago remains condensed within those blossoms. Perhaps they do not know that the cherry blossoms once contained the harmonics of the young girl’s violin. Yet perhaps, as people already understand, the greatest beauty of cherry blossoms lies in the rain of petals that fills the sky as they fall. This happens to echo the final lie Kaori leaves to the world: although the words written upon it are “farewell forever,” what we hear is “I will wait for you in the future.”

The April when I met you is coming. The April without you is coming.

Closing Song

光るなら

entry.title: An Introduction to Batch Files (.bat)
entry.content:
An Introduction to Batch Files (.bat)

A batch file, whose extension is .bat, is a script file used in Windows to execute a sequence of commands automatically. By writing such a file, one can automate routine tasks, administer the system, and perform file operations with relatively little effort.

How to Write and Use a .bat File

Writing one

Create a new file in Notepad or another text editor, enter the required commands and script logic, save it, and finally change its filename extension.

Running one

  • Double-click the .bat file to run it directly.
  • Alternatively, enter the path to the file at the Command Prompt.
  • A batch file may also be combined with Windows Task Scheduler so that it runs automatically at a specified time.

Common Syntax

  • Comments: explain the script without being executed.

  • Turn off command echoing: prevent commands themselves from being displayed during execution.

  • Display information: print text on the screen.

  • Pause the script: wait for the user to press a key before continuing.

  • Conditional statements: execute different commands according to whether a condition is satisfied.

  • Loops: iterate over files or a list of variables.

  • Variables: define and refer to variables; command-line arguments can also be received through %1, %2, and so forth.

  • Labels and jumps: use goto to control the flow of the script, loosely imitating a function.

Example

The following script checks whether a file exists and prints the corresponding message:

Other Points to Note

  • Debugging: add pause to the script when you need to inspect its output or debug it step by step.

  • Compatibility: batch files are designed specifically for Windows. Other systems, such as Linux, usually employ shell scripts with the .sh extension.

  • Security: do not store sensitive information in a script, and exercise particular care with dangerous commands involving deletion or formatting.

  • Extended use: batch files can work together with PowerShell, VBScript, and other automation tools to handle more complicated tasks.

References:
An Introduction to Windows Office Batch Files
A CSDN Tutorial on Batch Files
Baidu Baike: bat

entry.title: Building and Optimising a Hexo + Fluid + Obsidian Blog
entry.content:
1. Preface

The immediate reason I built this blog was that, while having dinner with a senior student some time ago, I saw the personal site he had made. I already knew that the relevant open-source projects were mature, so a thought struck me and I simply started working—not quite as dramatic as that, perhaps.

It also solved a problem that had troubled me for a long time: I had nowhere suitable to share things. I genuinely wanted to write more—to record the curious little projects I had experimented with, the works of art I had appreciated, and my own thoughts and feelings. While I still had time, I wanted to write longer essays that might protect my ability to think and express myself, rather than letting it disappear in the storm of short videos. But where could I write? Posting on Tieba, Zhihu, or Xiaohongshu did not appeal to me: I disliked the atmosphere of those platforms and had no desire to cover every statement in defensive disclaimers merely to suit it. QQ Space and WeChat Moments were not designed for long arguments; a short paragraph could neither satisfy my wish to express myself nor explain what I meant, and my WeChat contacts might not want to read it anyway. Making videos would be even worse: it would consume still more time and bring the culture of another online community into the calculation.

A personal blog meets these needs rather well. Here I can say whatever I want, describe what I think, and record what I wish to remember. After all, I am largely writing for myself, and almost nobody visits this site to read these articles. Besides, it is an amusing small project, is it not? The underlying software may be open source, but that does not prevent me from using the opportunity to learn something about front-end development.

The final paragraph of this preface is for any reader who happens to arrive. If you also want to build a personal blog of this kind, read on: I will record part of the construction process and the writing workflow I currently recommend.

2. Construction

Tools Used

  • Hexo: the blog framework, which may be understood as the skeleton of the site.
  • Fluid: the site’s theme. Its official documentation is detailed, so the configuration can simply follow that guide and needs no repetition here.
  • GitHub Pages: a convenient, free service for hosting static websites; one GitHub account can have one such site.
  • Obsidian: a text editor that becomes extremely convenient once configured. Its rich plugin system supports such tasks as importing templates and organising files through a directory structure.
  • Typora: a lightweight Markdown editor that adds rendering and keyboard shortcuts to what would otherwise be little more than Notepad.

Installation

Prerequisites

  • Node.js: a program capable of executing JavaScript code; more precisely, it is a JavaScript runtime.
  • Git: the well-known open-source distributed version-control system, designed to handle projects of any size efficiently. It is the Git underlying GitHub and can be regarded as a steward of file versions, supporting the storage, rollback, and upload of different revisions.

Installing Hexo

All the following steps should be carried out from Git Bash in the folder where the blog is to be stored.

The site can then be previewed locally at http://localhost:4000

Changing the Theme

This site uses Fluid:

3. Writing

At first, I used Typora. Yet every image insertion and every item of note metadata had to be handled manually, which felt like a disgrace to the entire business of writing code. I therefore moved to Obsidian, and this article became the first one I wrote with it.

Installing Obsidian needs no explanation here; consult its official site and the relevant articles:

  • Home—Obsidian Help
  • Obsidian Chinese Forum—Knowledge Management and Notes

If you do not yet know how to write Markdown, learn that first. It is useful, and anyone in an information-related field is unlikely to avoid it:

  • Basic Markdown Syntax—Markdown Tutorial

In practice, the syntax works best when combined with keyboard shortcuts.

4. Publishing

First configure hexo-deployer-git:

Then edit the _config.yml file:

5. Workflow, for Now

  • Create a new post with the new command:
  • Open Obsidian and begin writing.
  • After writing, preview the site locally from the terminal:
  • If the preview looks correct, publish it:

6. Optimisation

Folder-Based Category Trees through Automatic Classification

No project is perfect, and the workflow described above still felt awkward in several places. Categories were one example. Logically, when posts are written locally, their categories ought to follow the containment relationships among folders. Hexo’s native approach, however, requires the following metadata at the beginning of every post:

How am I supposed to manage this? Must I remember exactly where every file belongs in the directory tree, without getting a single character wrong? That merely creates more work. Categories are meant to make management easier; this reverses the whole purpose.

I therefore searched for another solution and found an open-source project:

  • xu-song/hexo-auto-category: Generate Categories Automatically for Each Post in Hexo

Installation and configuration can follow its official documentation. One point deserves attention: peculiar things may happen when a file has no category group—or so it appears.

Automatic Git Pushes

After writing the first few posts, I had to enter Git Bash and run hexo clean, hexo g, and hexo d manually every time. This soon became tiresome, which raised an obvious question: why not use an automation plugin?

The original documentation for the method is:

  • Maintaining a Hexo Blog Perfectly with Obsidian + Git—Zhihu

Importing Templates

Obsidian supports templates natively. Configure the path in Settings and create a template file; that is essentially all that is required.

7. Postscript

Image insertion while writing on this site still needs further improvement. For more detail, consult the following expert’s blog, from which much of this article was drawn:

  • My Process for Deploying a Personal Blog with Obsidian and Hexo—SagiRastar’s Blog
  • Obsidian2Hexo—Zhipeng’s Personal Blog

entry.title: Understanding Monitor Specifications and the Principles behind Them
entry.content:
Monitor Specifications and Their Underlying Principles

I recently bought a secondary monitor and decided to organise the relevant knowledge into an article that might make future purchases easier.

How a Colour Display Works

Prerequisite Knowledge

  • Liquid crystal is a synthetic organic material whose state lies between a solid and a liquid. Without an electric field, its molecules may be arranged irregularly and block light; under voltage, they become ordered and transmit light. The reverse arrangement also exists, in which voltage blocks rather than transmits light.
  • Polarisation is the selection of the vibration direction of a transverse wave. By controlling light with polarising filters and observing changes in intensity, one can verify both the transverse nature of light and the selectivity of its vibration direction. A high-school physics textbook gives the details.

Central Idea

Colours are produced by controlling and mixing RGB values.

Technical Approaches

LCD

Conventional LCD

This remains a mainstream, if relatively old, approach. At the bottom is a backlight emitting white light. Above it lies a liquid-crystal layer between two mutually perpendicular polarisers. The liquid crystal rotates the direction of polarisation and thereby controls how much light can pass, which controls brightness. A colour filter outside the liquid-crystal layer produces colour. A conventional backlight usually consists of an LED strip between a reflector and a diffusion plate. When the monitor displays black while switched on, the backlight is still active; moreover, even an unpowered liquid-crystal layer rotates part of the light. The result differs from the pure black of a powered-off screen and reduces contrast.

According to the default state of the liquid-crystal layer, panels can be divided into three types:

  • A VA panel is vertically aligned by default and twists under voltage to transmit light. It offers high contrast, average viewing angles, and a relatively slow response. Inferior panels may smear. It suits films and AAA games.
  • An IPS panel is horizontally aligned by default and rotates in the horizontal plane under voltage. It provides average contrast, broad viewing angles, and a moderate response. It is the balanced choice for most situations.
  • A TN panel twists horizontally by default and turns vertical under voltage to block light. Its contrast and viewing angles are poor, but its response is fast, making it suitable for Counter-Strike veterans and Valorant juniors.
QLED

QLED modifies an LCD by using a blue backlight and coating the substrate with quantum dots. A quantum dot is an extremely small compound that absorbs blue light and emits light at another wavelength—rather like an electron being excited and then returning to its ground state. This approach addresses the limited saturation of an ordinary LCD, but remains an LCD.

Mini-LED

Mini-LED divides the backlight into zones and switches off those behind black regions; everything else resembles an LCD. This supports advanced HDR, although poor tuning can produce smearing or halos.

LED

OLED

OLED stands for Organic Light-Emitting Diode. Conventional diodes work well, but placing three diodes in every pixel and integrating them into a large panel is difficult, which led to OLED technology. Electricity directly excites fluorescent materials to emit coloured light, and three emitters form one pixel. This can also be understood as pixel-level local dimming: it produces no halo, high saturation, a thin panel, fast response, a broad colour gamut, low power consumption without a backlight, and even flexible displays. Its disadvantages arise partly because the three fluorescent materials age at different rates, making burn-in, retained colour, and colour shifts more likely. Other limitations include low peak brightness, PWM dimming, and reduced effective resolution.

W-OLED

W-OLED replaces the three coloured fluorescent materials with white emitters and places an RGBW filter above them. The white subpixel compensates for brightness, but its white light also interferes with the red, green, and blue subpixels, taking us back towards the problem faced by LCDs.

QD-OLED

QD-OLED replaces the QLED backlight with blue fluorescent material and remains within the LED family. It addresses the problem of W-OLED, although external light may excite the quantum-dot material and contaminate the signal.

Micro-OLED

This uses microscopic light-emitting diodes and solves the problem of integrating three conventional diodes into every pixel of a large display. Massive-transfer technology is still immature, however, so a panel may cost hundreds of thousands.

Specifications

Screen Size

Screen size is the diagonal length, usually measured in inches. Ordinary mainstream monitors commonly measure 24, 27, or 32 inches. The portable monitors I have seen—not many—are often around 14 inches. A 24- or 27-inch display is the usual choice and resembles what one finds in an internet café. Anyone wanting more space can choose a larger or ultrawide panel; wealthy buyers may proceed as they please.

Resolution

The most familiar resolutions are probably 1080p (1920*1080), 2K (2560*1440, or 16:9), and 4K (3840*2160). One also encounters names such as 2.5K, commonly used for a 16:10 resolution, although some people call 2560*1440 2.5K. These are only common examples, and labels such as 2K and 2.5K are often used rather casually. The following table, sourced from HeyBox, gives others.

The terminology is so inconsistent that it should not be examined too literally. Gamers, monitor manufacturers, film studios, and television companies all follow different conventions. A few examples:

  • On common video platforms, standard definition means 480p, high definition 720p, ultra-high definition 1080p, Blu-ray 1080p at 60 frames per second, and 4K 2160p; the bit rates remain unknown.
  • According to an editor at a Shanghai television station, 1080p at 10 Mbit/s is HD, 2560*1440 is 2K, and 3840*2160 or 4096*2160 is 4K. Blu-ray refers specifically to an optical disc, a physical storage medium like magnetic tape.
  • According to a worker at a Shandong television station, 480p is standard, 720p is HD, 1080p is ultra-HD, and 4K is simply 4K. Bit rate is calculated from MXF.

For video, resolution alone is insufficient; bit rate is equally important. A 4K video at 5 Mbit/s may look less clear than a 1080p video at 10 Mbit/s. Likewise, a monitor should not be judged by resolution alone, since PPI also matters. Domestic streaming video often looks less clear than locally downloaded material because its bit rate is too low. Perhaps I will organise some sites for finding BitTorrent resources when time permits.

Some serious film enthusiasts even use PotPlayer to adjust colour balance and decoding methods. I came across that practice while browsing forums.

Another issue is scaling. Displaying a 1080p photograph on a 2K screen can make it appear blurrier because the source lacks enough exact pixels and the 2K panel must approximate them, though the difference may not be very noticeable.

Some users point out that the advertised resolution of an OLED should be discounted by about twenty per cent because its pixels operate differently.

Basic Units

  • px, or pixel: the smallest display unit and the basic component of an image.
  • pt, or point: a unit for font size. On digital devices, conversion between pt and px usually depends on resolution or PPI, such as 72 or 96 PPI.
  • PPI, pixels per inch: a measure of pixel density. It is calculated as:

$$
PPI = \frac{\sqrt{(宽度像素数)^2 + (高度像素数)^2}}{屏幕对角线长度（英寸）}
$$

  • DPI, dots per inch, describes the precision of printer output. DPI and PPI are sometimes confused, but strictly speaking DPI belongs mainly to printing, while PPI describes display devices.

Choosing a Panel

See the preceding discussion of light-emission principles. In general, choose IPS or OLED directly. VA is worth considering for AAA games and films, while TN serves high-end competitive FPS play.

Refresh Rate

This is effectively the frame rate: the higher it is, the smoother motion appears. There is little else to say. For someone like me who mainly types and plays visual novels, 60 Hz is enough. Gamers, especially FPS players, benefit from higher rates.

Brightness

Units

Monitor brightness is generally measured in nits, which describe luminous intensity per unit area. Elsewhere, one may also encounter:

  • Candela: one of the seven SI base units and a measure of luminous intensity in a specified direction. It can be understood roughly as the luminous intensity of a point source divided by the solid angle of a sphere centred on that source. One candela is the intensity produced when a source emits radiation of 1/683 watt per steradian in a given direction at a frequency of 540×10¹² Hz, corresponding to green light.
  • Candlepower: an older unit, slightly smaller than a candela but often treated as approximately equal; it is now largely obsolete.
  • Lumen: the total quantity of visible light emitted in all directions. 1 lumen = 1 candela × 1 steradian (lm = cd·sr).
  • Nit: luminous intensity emitted or reflected per unit area. 1 nit = 1 candela per square metre (nt = cd/m²).
  • Lux: illuminance, or incident luminous flux per unit area. 1 lux = 1 lumen per square metre (lx = lm/m²).

In summary, luminous flux in lumens describes the ability of a source to emit light in all directions; luminous intensity in candelas describes its ability in a particular direction; luminance in nits describes emitted or reflected intensity per unit area; and illuminance in lux describes incident light per unit area.

Examples

A cinema screen is roughly 50 nits, while a phone used outdoors generally reaches at least 300 nits. This is why one should not look at a phone in a cinema. In total lumens, of course, the cinema screen far exceeds the phone.

Sony HDR televisions can reach 10,000 nits. Most HDR devices peak near 2,000 nits; anything higher becomes an instrument for blinding people.

Smartphones and tablets range from 200 to more than 1,000 nits. A 400–500-nit screen remains visible during the day, whereas 200 nits is difficult to see in sunlight.

Laptops and monitors range from 200 to more than 600 nits. Excessive brightness is not recommended: a 200-nit maximum is low-end, while 400 is sufficient. If the display remains hard to see, close the curtains instead of raising the brightness. The secondary display I just bought reaches 400 nits.

Contrast Ratio

Contrast is the ratio between the brightest white and darkest black in an image. A greater range means greater contrast. High contrast reveals more detail in both highlights and shadows and gives the picture a stronger sense of depth.

Contrast can be evaluated with the tools at this link. I will not include an image here, since unexplained compression could make the result inaccurate.

Interfaces

  • VGA: an ancient analogue interface. The last one I saw belonged to an antique family computer. It carries video only, is vulnerable to interference and distortion, often produces blurry text, and supports only relatively low resolutions such as 1080p@60Hz. It is disappearing, though it was glorious several decades ago.
  • DVI: introduced to remedy VGA’s limitations, DVI can carry both analogue and digital video and reach 1080p@144Hz, but does not support audio. It has also become rare and needs no detailed treatment.
  • HDMI: the mainstream digital interface, carrying synchronised audio and video. HDMI 2.0 provides 18 Gbit/s for 1440p@144Hz, 1080p@240Hz, or 4K@60Hz. HDMI 2.1 provides 48 Gbit/s, supports 4K@120Hz or 8K@60Hz, and adds dynamic HDR, making it suitable for game consoles and high-end graphics cards.
  • DisplayPort (DP): a professional PC interface. DP 1.4 supports 4K@120Hz HDR or 8K@60Hz HDR and 3:1 DSC compression. DP 2.0 raises bandwidth to 80 Gbit/s and natively supports 8K@60Hz.
  • USB-C: a multifunction interface supporting video through DP Alt Mode, data, and charging through USB Power Delivery. Some monitors connect to laptops with a single USB-C cable, though bandwidth limitations must be considered; USB 3.2 Gen 2, for example, supports only 4K@60Hz.

Competitive gamers should prefer DP 1.4 or HDMI 2.1 and above. Users of thin laptops may consider a single USB-C connection. Anyone switching among several devices should check whether the monitor includes KVM functionality.

The supported resolution can be estimated from interface bandwidth:
$$
总像素子像素色深刷新率 = 总带宽
$$
where:
$$
总像素=横向分辨率纵向分辨率
$$

$$
子像素=RGB色素数=3
$$

For a 4K, 10-bit image at 144 Hz:
$$
38402160310bit144 = 35.8Gbps。
$$

Colour Gamut

Overview

Colour gamut is the range of colours a monitor can display; broader coverage generally means richer performance. Common standards include NTSC, now rather old, sRGB, P3, and Adobe RGB. For ordinary use, sRGB is usually enough: at least 95% for daily work and 99% or 100% for design or stronger preferences. Continue reading if more detail is required.

Further Detail

  • sRGB: developed by Microsoft and HP, it is the default gamut for Windows interfaces and much software, as well as the standard colour space for online graphics. Its coverage within CIE 1931 is limited, especially in green, but most current monitors easily exceed 96% sRGB.
  • Adobe RGB: created by Adobe when sRGB proved insufficient. It is familiar to photographers and editors using products such as Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere. Its broader gamut produces richer colour and is used mainly in expensive professional art and design monitors.
  • DCI-P3: proposed mainly by the American film industry, this relatively new digital-imaging standard emphasises realistic human visual experience and meets cinematic colour requirements. It covers more red and green than sRGB, though I have encountered it less often.
  • Rec.2020: the International Telecommunication Union treats it as a reference standard for high-quality projectors, televisions, and broadcasting equipment. It specifies resolution, frame rate, bit depth, colour gamut, and other parameters.
  • P3: broadly includes DCI-P3 and Display P3. The former is a film-industry standard; the latter is Apple’s revision of DCI-P3 with reference to sRGB. Their white points and gamma differ, but they cover the same colours and both expand substantially beyond sRGB except in blue.
  • NTSC: established by the US National Television System Committee in 1953 for the then-new CRT colour television. It is far too old for modern displays—Apple DOS 3.1 appeared in 1978 and MS-DOS in 1980—and almost no creator working for PCs or mobile devices uses NTSC as a workspace. Its main surviving purpose is comparison with other colour spaces.
  • Rec.709: the film and high-definition television counterpart of sRGB. It began as a colour-gamut standard for early colour television and remains the most widely used standard, including in China’s film and television industry.

Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 are much broader than sRGB and are called wide gamuts. A screen covering about 92% of DCI-P3 can generally be called wide-gamut.

Several Misconceptions

  • Monitors supporting multiple gamuts

Some professional monitors support different gamuts. A wide-gamut display usually exceeds sRGB, but showing sRGB material without management may produce colour shifts and distortion despite impressive saturation. The gamut must therefore be restricted to sRGB for ordinary use. Monitors with gamut-clamping functions explicitly advertise several modes: sRGB for everyday work and Adobe RGB for photographic editing or print proofing, where reliable colour matters.

  • Gamut volume above 100%

A manufacturer may advertise a figure such as 130%, meaning that the covered area extends beyond sRGB and reaches 130% of its nominal area. One trap is that shifting the gamut can improve the numerical value while distorting the actual picture.

  • 72% NTSC

Many irresponsible manufacturers and media outlets have promoted the equation “72% NTSC = 100% sRGB” to present an ordinary panel as suitable for professional work and equal to an older MacBook Pro with 100% sRGB, arguing that the MacBook also measured 72% NTSC. This exploits an information gap in consumers’ knowledge; the claim deserves scepticism.

Colour Depth

Colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of one pixel in a bitmap or video frame buffer, also expressed as bits per pixel (bpp). Greater depth provides more available colours and smoother transitions.

For each colour channel, 8 bit provides 256 grey levels, or 16.7 million colours across RGB, while 10 bit provides 1,024 levels, or 1.07 billion colours. Greater depth reduces banding and produces more natural gradients in skies and shadows.

Most mainstream monitors use native 8-bit panels. Some IPS panels simulate 10-bit output through frame-rate control and are labelled 8 bit + FRC. Native 10-bit panels cost more and appear mainly in professional design monitors and high-end OLED displays. Eight bits is sufficient for most people.

Note: some manufacturers advertise “1.07 billion colours” without making clear that dithering produces them.

Colour Accuracy

Colour accuracy measures whether a monitor displays the colour it is asked to display. It is usually expressed as ΔE, the deviation between displayed and standard colours; lower is better.

The same parameter is also written Delta E or △E.

  • △E ≤ 1: the difference is almost imperceptible and suitable for professional photography and print calibration.
  • △E ≤ 2: sufficient for design and film post-production.
  • △E > 3: colour shifts are visible and calibration is needed.

Professional monitors are calibrated before leaving the factory and include a ΔE report. Some support hardware calibration, such as writing a LUT. Ambient-light changes and panel ageing may cause accuracy to drift, so periodic recalibration with a device such as a Datacolor SpyderX or X-Rite i1Display Pro is recommended. During calibration:

  • Warm up the monitor for at least 30 minutes.
  • Disable dynamic contrast and HDR.
  • Select a gamut that matches the workflow.

HDR

HDR, High Dynamic Range, has become popular in recent years. Put simply, switching it on can make the image more impressive; the certification indicates its level.

By expanding brightness range and contrast, HDR reproduces highlight and shadow detail and colour levels closer to the physical world. Compared with standard dynamic range, it can preserve both textures in bright clouds and details in shadowed rocks, strengthening depth and immersion.

Standards

No single standard governs the whole industry.

  • HDR10: the basic standard, using static metadata with one brightness setting for an entire film. It supports 10-bit colour and usually requires peak brightness of at least 1,000 nits. It is widely used for games and video.
  • HDR10+: an upgraded form using dynamic metadata to optimise brightness frame by frame, with relatively broad compatibility.
  • Dolby Vision: a high-end Dolby Laboratories standard supporting 12-bit colour and dynamic metadata. It demands more capable hardware and appears mainly on premium televisions and streaming services such as Netflix.
  • DisplayHDR: a VESA certification system based on HDR10, with levels such as DisplayHDR 400, 600, and 1000. It specifies peak brightness, gamut coverage, and other parameters. DisplayHDR 1000, for example, requires 1,000-nit peak brightness and 99% DCI-P3 coverage.

Points to Note

  • Some monitors accept an HDR input signal but lack enough brightness or local dimming, so their actual result differs little from SDR.
  • HDR works better in a dark room; intense ambient light reduces the benefit of high brightness.
  • The source material, playback device, and display must all support HDR.
  • HDR is less necessary for games because games possess an inherent advantage at the signal source.
  • A television or monitor advertised as HDR-compatible may mean one of two things. First, both its display controller and panel satisfy an HDR standard. Second, the controller can decode HDR while the panel cannot necessarily pass certification. SDR is commonly based around 100 nits and the lowest HDR certification around 400 nits. A panel between those values can use controller-level HDR support to provide a wider range than SDR and an experience approaching HDR without meeting the full certification.

Weight

Weight matters for a portable monitor, unless one enjoys carrying a brick around. The acceptable value depends on the individual.

Stand and Wall-Mount Support

This depends entirely on personal requirements and is omitted here.

Tools

  • Contrast testing: Pingmudiy Screen Test.
  • The small DisplayHDR application; search for it as needed.

References

What Is Screen Brightness in Nits, and How Many Nits Do You Need?

Television and Monitor Colour Gamuts: sRGB, DCI-P3, Adobe RGB, Rec.2020, and Wide Gamut

Popular Science Series 155: The Structure of a Colour LCD

Polarisation of Light—Baidu Baike

A Detailed Video Explaining LCD, OLED, QLED, Mini-LED, and Other Display Technologies—Bilibili

How Are Lumens, Nits, Lux, Candlepower, and Candelas Related, and Why Are Screens Measured in Nits?

A Detailed Explanation of VGA, DVI, HDMI, DP, and Other Monitor Interfaces—CSDN

Understanding the Differences among VGA, HDMI, DVI, DisplayPort, Thunderbolt, and Type-C

Which Monitor Interfaces Exist?

Monitor Fundamentals 6: Contrast Ratio

What Is HDR? Why Does Everyone Want HDR Mode?

Foundations of px, pt, and ppi

Colour Depth—Wikipedia

[Do You Understand Colour Depth, Gamut, Accuracy, HDR, and Anti-Tearing?](https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/259139655#:~:text=色深代表着画面颜色的「细腻程度」，也以简单理解为颜色数量的多少。 并且，数值越大就越细腻，同时色彩过渡就更加平滑自然。 目前主流显示器的色深一般是6 bit、8bit和10bit。 具体而言，色深8bit指的是红（R）、绿（G）、蓝（B）这三原色，在显示颜色时各有2的 8次方种（即 256 种）。,种不同的绿、256种不同的蓝，这三种原色组合起来，总的颜色数量就是256×256×256%3D16.7 百万。 以此类推，10bit的色数就是 10.7 亿，而6bit的色数是 0.26 百万。 由此可见6bit的色数是相对偏少的，因此色彩显示效果就比较差。)

entry.title: Fall Detection Based on Human Keypoint Recognition
entry.content:
Fall Detection Based on Human Keypoint Recognition

When we first worked on fall detection, we used conventional object-detection algorithms such as YOLO. Discussion soon exposed a problem: a traditional detector finds it difficult to distinguish falling from running, jumping, sitting, or squatting. In other words, the difficulty lies in classification between closely related actions. Then came the rather abrupt thought that fall detection might instead be based on human keypoints, which would make it easier to separate a fall from other movements. The approach is already fairly mature, as the references below indicate. For the moment, this article records an initial investigation of the algorithms. A detailed account of our particular model can wait until the project is completed.

Existing Algorithms

Conventional spatiotemporal analysis

This approach tracks skeletal keypoints—the head, shoulders, knees, ankles, and so forth—in real time and determines whether a fall has occurred by analysing changes in their positions. It is intuitive and readily interpretable, which makes it suitable for real-time detection. Its weakness is that missing data may lead to errors, although there is room to improve its ability to withstand such disturbances.

flowchart LR
    A[视频/图像输入] --> B[关键点提取]
    B --> C[动态特征计算]
    C --> D[分类决策]
    D --> E{{跌倒判定结果}}

    %% 关键点提取模块
    subgraph keypoint_extract [关键点提取]
        direction TB
        B1[OpenPose] -->|输出关键点| B2[BlazePose]
    end

    %% 动态特征计算模块
    subgraph feature_cal [动态特征计算]
        direction TB
        C1[质心高度<br>（头部/躯干骤降）]:::feature
        C2[关节角度<br>（躯干-地面夹角）]:::feature
        C3[运动速度<br>（垂直加速度突增）]:::feature
    end

    %% 分类决策模块
    subgraph decision [分类决策]
        direction TB
        D1[阈值法]:::decision -->|"高度 < 阈值?"| D1a[报警]
        D2[机器学习模型]:::decision --> D2a[SVM] & D2b[随机森林]
    end

    %% 应用样式
    class A input;
    class B,B1,B2 process;
    class C,C1,C2,C3 feature;
    class D,D1,D2 decision;
    class E result;

  • Keypoint extraction:

    A human-keypoint model such as OpenPose or BlazePose obtains the coordinates of body keypoints from a video.

  • Dynamic-feature calculation:

    Height of the centre of mass: a sudden drop in the height of the head or torso may signal a fall.

    Joint angles: the angle between the shoulder–knee line and the ground may decrease sharply, for instance from 90° while standing to nearly 0° after a fall.

    Motion speed: the vertical acceleration of the head or torso may rise suddenly, as in the brief sensation of “weightlessness” during a fall.

  • Classification decision:

    Manually chosen thresholds: define a feature threshold—for example, classify the action as a fall when the centre of mass drops below the knees.

    Machine-learning models: use an SVM or random forest to classify combinations of features. Frankly, we might as well go straight to machine learning.

Deep-learning models of temporal sequences

These methods demand more computing power and more data.

  • LSTM: analyse temporal changes in a sequence of keypoints and capture the dynamic process before, during, and after a fall.
    • Patent CN112163564A, for example, divides the body into the head, torso, and legs, and uses an LSTM to retain motion trajectories and anticipate the risk of a fall.
  • 3D CNN: accept video clips as direct input and extract spatial features of posture together with temporal features of motion. It just about counts, though getting it built would be painful.
  • Graph convolutional networks (GCNs): regard the skeleton as a graph and analyse relations among joints, making them suitable for complex actions. I am still not especially familiar with this architecture; that can be learned when the time comes.

Target-skeleton extraction based on CLAHE and morphology

This is primarily a method of skeleton extraction. It does not require a deep-learning model and therefore consumes fewer computing resources, but its performance may be less stable in complicated backgrounds.

  • Image enhancement: use contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) to improve image contrast and emphasise the human outline.
  • Skeleton extraction:
    1. Separate the moving target through background subtraction and fill holes through morphological closing.
    2. Extract the body contour with an edge detector such as the Sobel operator and remove noise with median filtering.
    3. Apply a thinning algorithm to generate the body skeleton and identify approximate keypoints such as the head and the ends of the limbs.

Extensions

Occlusion:

Use spatiotemporal filtering, such as a sliding-window filter, to fill in keypoints lost through occlusion.

Real-time optimisation:

  • Apply model distillation to transfer knowledge from a large model to a smaller one.

  • Deploy the model on an edge device through tools such as OpenVINO™, thereby reducing reliance on the cloud.

Improving robustness—and yes, I still dislike this translation of robust every time I see it:

  • Fuse data from several sensors. One might, for example, put an accelerometer in a wristband, although that immediately drives up the cost.

entry.title: Standard Score — Z-Score
entry.content:
Z-Score

1. Introduction

A z-score measures the position of a data point relative to the population mean. It can transform data with different units or distributions onto the same standard—namely, the standard normal distribution—thereby making comparison easier. A positive value indicates that the data point lies above the mean, whereas a negative value indicates that it lies below the mean.

2. Formula

$$
\frac{X-\bar{X} }{s}
$$

That is, the difference from the mean divided by the standard deviation. In MATLAB, the zscore() function can be used directly.

3. Applications

  • Outlier detection
    A z-score can be used to identify a possible outlier. A threshold, commonly 2 or 3, is selected; if the absolute z-score exceeds that threshold, the data point may be abnormal. For example, when |z| > 3, a value is usually regarded as being unusually far from the mean and therefore worthy of further inspection. The rule can be understood through the normal distribution: approximately 68% of observations fall within [-1, 1], about 95% within [-2, 2], and about 99.7% within [-3, 3].
  • Data standardisation
    In machine learning or data mining, z-score standardisation removes the influence of measurement units and therefore supports modelling.
  • Comparison across datasets
    Because a z-score removes the influence of the original mean and standard deviation, values drawn from different datasets can be compared directly.

4. Limitations

The usefulness of a z-score depends to some extent on the distribution of the data. It generally works better when the distribution is closer to normal.

Z-score standardisation removes the original practical meaning of a value and therefore reduces interpretability. The result can be used for comparison, but the original value must be restored if its real-world meaning needs to be explained.

References

Explanation of the Z-Score Method for Data Standardisation in MATLAB — CSDN

Z-Score — Baidu Baike

Data Standardisation (I): Z-Score Standardisation — Zhihu

Z-Score: Definition, Formula, and Data Standardisation — CSDN

entry.title: TOPSIS: The Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to an Ideal Solution
entry.content:
TOPSIS: Distance from Ideal and Worst Solutions

I. Modeling

A TOPSIS model can be constructed in roughly three stages:

  1. Convert the original matrix into a benefit-oriented matrix.
  2. Standardize the converted matrix.
  3. Calculate the scores and normalize them.

To my mind, this procedure has much in common with the entropy weight method. The two should, in fact, be capable of being used together.

Converting the matrix into benefit-type indicators

Four kinds of indicators frequently occur in practice:

Type of indicator Principal feature Examples
Benefit-type The larger the value, the better Examination scores, GDP growth, corporate profit
Cost-type The smaller the value, the better Expense, defect rate, pollution
Intermediate-type The nearer the value is to a specified point, the better pH in water-quality assessment
Interval-type A value within a specified interval is best Body temperature, plant nutrients in water

TOPSIS requires all indicators to point in the same favourable direction. In other words, every indicator must be converted into a benefit-type indicator. Cost-type, intermediate-type, and interval-type indicators must therefore be transformed.

Converting a cost-type indicator into a benefit-type indicator:
$$
x_{new}= \frac{\max - x_i}{\max - \min}
$$
If all elements are positive, the following expression may also be used:

$$
x_{new}=\frac{1}{x_i}
$$

Converting an intermediate-type indicator: Such a value should be neither too large nor too small; a particular value is best, as with pH in water-quality assessment. Suppose that ${x_i}$ is a sequence of intermediate-type indicators and that the optimal value is $x_{best}$. The transformation is:
$$
M = \max{|x_i - x_{best}|}
$$
$$
\bar{x}i = 1 - \frac{|x_i - x{best}|}{M}
$$
Converting an interval-type indicator: A value within a particular interval is best. Human body temperature, for instance, is generally preferable when it lies between 36°C and 37°C. Suppose that ${x_i}$ is a sequence of interval-type indicators and that the optimal interval is $[a,b]$. The transformation is:
$$
M = \max{a - \min{x_i}, \max{x_i} - b},\ \tilde{x}_i =
\begin{cases}
1 - \frac{a - x_i}{M}, & x_i < a \
1, & a \leq x_i \leq b \
1 - \frac{x_i - b}{M}, & x_i > b
\end{cases}
$$
This is essentially the same transformation described for the entropy weight method. For details, see the entropy weight method.

Standardizing the matrix

Standardization removes the influence of different units and dimensions.

Suppose n objects are to be evaluated through m indicators. After all indicators have been converted, the matrix is:

$$
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1m} \
x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2m} \
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{nm}
\end{bmatrix}
$$
Let the standardized matrix be Z. Each of its elements is:

$$
z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}^2}}
$$
Thus:

$$
Z =
\begin{bmatrix}
z_{11} & z_{12} & \cdots & z_{1m} \
z_{21} & z_{22} & \cdots & z_{2m} \
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
z_{n1} & z_{n2} & \cdots & z_{nm}
\end{bmatrix}
$$
There is more than one method of standardization, but every method seeks to remove dimensional effects. The chapter on entropy weighting, for example, gives the following expression for data containing negative values:

$$
z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \min{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}}}{\max{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}} - \min{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}}}
$$

Calculating and normalizing the score

The ideal solution is:

$$
Z^+ = (\max{z_{11},z_{21},\cdots,z_{n1}}, \max{z_{12},z_{22},\cdots,z_{n2}}, \cdots, \max{z_{1m},z_{2m},\cdots,z_{nm}})
$$
The worst solution is:
$$
Z^- = (\min{z_{11},z_{21},\cdots,z_{n1}}, \min{z_{12},z_{22},\cdots,z_{n2}}, \cdots, \min{z_{1m},z_{2m},\cdots,z_{nm}})
$$
Define the distance between the $i(i = 1,2,…,n)$th object and the ideal solution as:
$$
D_i^+ = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(Z_j^+ - z_{ij})^2}
$$
Define the distance between the $i(i = 1,2,…,n)$th object and the worst solution as:

$$
D_i^- = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}(Z_j^- - z_{ij})^2}
$$
The unnormalized score of the $i(i = 1,2,…,n)$th object is then:

$$
S_i = \frac{D_i^-}{D_i^+ + D_i^-}
$$
Clearly, $0 \leq S_i \leq 1$. As $S_i$ increases, $D_i^+$ decreases; the object is therefore closer to the ideal solution.

II. Extensions

Combining TOPSIS with weights

The procedure above assumes that all indicators have equal weights. In an actual evaluation, however, different indicators generally carry different weights. The distance formulas should therefore be revised, with ω representing a weight:
$$
D_i^+ = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\omega_j(Z_j^+ - z_{ij})^2},\ D_i^- = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\omega_j(Z_j^- - z_{ij})^2}
$$
The entropy weight method can be used directly here. Of course, having experts assign scores—more or less by informed guesswork—is also an option.

Where the formula comes from

The formula

$$
S_i = \frac{D_i^-}{D_i^+ + D_i^-}
$$
is essentially:

$$
\frac{x - \min}{\max - \min} \rightarrow \frac{x - \min}{(\max - x) + (x - \min)} \rightarrow \frac{x与最小值的距离}{x与最大值的距离 + x与最小值的距离}
$$
$D_i^+$ and $D_i^-$ are, in fact, Euclidean distances. The underlying idea has a great deal in common with that of the entropy weight method.

References

Qingfeng’s Mathematical Modeling Notes: TOPSIS—CSDN

An Introduction to Common Evaluation Models in Mathematical Modeling—Zhihu

TOPSIS: Principles and Code Implementation—Zhihu

entry.title: Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation (FCE)
entry.content:
Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation

Quantities may be divided into two broad classes: certainty and uncertainty.

  • Certainty is studied by classical mathematics, including geometry and algebra.
  • Uncertainty includes:
    1. Randomness, which is studied through probability theory and stochastic processes. Throwing a die and observing which face appears is a familiar example: probability and statistics are used to describe the regularities behind such phenomena.
    2. Greyness, which is studied through grey system theory.
    3. Fuzziness, which is studied through fuzzy mathematics. Expressions such as “the weather is hot today” and “the young man is handsome” belong to this category.

Fuzzy comprehensive evaluation is an evaluation method grounded in fuzzy mathematics. On the basis of membership theory, it converts qualitative judgments into quantitative ones. In other words, fuzzy mathematics is used to reach an overall assessment of an object constrained by several factors. The method produces relatively clear results and has a strong systematic character. It is particularly useful for vague questions that resist direct quantification and is therefore suitable for many problems involving uncertainty.

Basic Concepts of Classical and Fuzzy Sets

Classical sets and characteristic functions

  • A classical set is a collection of things sharing a common property, such as a colour, a sex, a mobile-phone brand, or membership in the natural numbers.
  • The basic properties of such a set are exclusiveness and certainty—the conception of sets that we have generally accepted since high school.

Fuzzy sets and membership functions

  • A fuzzy set describes a vague concept, such as handsome, tall, fair-skinned, or young.

  • Unlike a classical set, a fuzzy set permits something to belong and not belong at the same time, at least to different degrees. It therefore lacks strict certainty and mutual exclusiveness. Many real situations are of this kind, including Problem B in the first university modeling contest of 2025.

  • In mathematics, a fuzzy set is represented by a membership function:

    $$
    \mathbf{u_A: U \rightarrow [0,1]}
    $$
    The distinction between the binary set ${0, 1}$—that is, ${0, 1}$—and the interval $[0, 1]$ matters here. The former permits only two possibilities, whereas the latter contains infinitely many.

Methods for Determining a Membership Function

Fuzzy statistics

One may construct the values oneself or collect them through a questionnaire.

Existing objective scales

For example, the Engel coefficient may be used to describe a household’s level of wealth.

Assignment methods

Certain distributions are selected directly as membership functions according to the nature of the problem. This approach is highly subjective.

Among these choices, trapezoidal distributions are used relatively often.

Application: Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation

An outline of the evaluation problem

A fuzzy evaluation problem generally attempts to accomplish one of two tasks:

① Assign an object in the universe of discourse to a specified comment in the evaluation set.
② Treat the available schemes as the evaluation set and select the best scheme.

Three sets are introduced in fuzzy comprehensive evaluation. Note that the symbols below do not necessarily carry the same meanings as similar symbols elsewhere.

  • Factor set (evaluation-index set) $U = {u_1,u_2,…,u_n}$
  • Evaluation set (set of possible results) $V = {v_1,v_2,..,v_m}$
  • Weight set (weights of the indicators) $A = {a_1,a_2,…,a_n}$

Single-level fuzzy comprehensive evaluation

  1. Determine the factor set

    In a single-level evaluation, n is usually small, generally no greater than 5, and the indicators are not strongly correlated.

  2. Determine the evaluation set

  3. Determine the weight of each factor

    Weights can be obtained in many ways, including the Delphi method—an expert survey, or, less ceremoniously, an exercise in making up numbers—the weighted-average method, and collective assessment. A practical suggestion is to use the analytic hierarchy process when no data are available and the entropy weight method when data do exist.

  4. Construct the fuzzy comprehensive judgment matrix and evaluate each element

  5. Carry out the fuzzy comprehensive judgment

Multi-level fuzzy comprehensive evaluation

A single-level evaluation forms the basis of a multi-level one. Indicators that are related to one another are first combined within a group. As noted above, the factors directly compared at a single level should not be strongly correlated; within the scope of that level, they may therefore be treated as relatively independent. Each related group is then combined to obtain its degree of membership in the evaluation set. The same operation is repeated at higher levels until an overall result is produced.

Summary

  1. There are three principal ways to determine a membership function, and the choice should depend on the actual problem.
  2. Benefit-type and cost-type indicators are different concepts from the three kinds of fuzzy sets—left-shoulder, intermediate, and right-shoulder—and should not be confused.
  3. The factor indicators in a single fuzzy comprehensive evaluation should not be strongly correlated. Strongly related items require a multi-level evaluation, which usually contains no more than three levels.

entry.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
entry.content:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Principal component analysis is an algorithm for dimensionality reduction. It forms mutually uncorrelated principal components from linear combinations of the original variables, retaining the main information while removing noise and accelerating data processing. PCA is often used to simplify data, support cluster analysis, and address multicollinearity in regression. Since the meaning of a principal component is often ambiguous, however, PCA is not commonly chosen as an evaluation model.

I. Introduction

  • Objective: replace a large number of original variables with a smaller number of new ones while preserving as much information as possible.
  • Applications: dimensionality reduction, noise removal, and faster data processing.
  • Suitable situations: the indicators are highly correlated and reasonably easy to explain, while interpretability is not a major requirement.
  • Limitations: nonlinear relationships are handled poorly, and details may be lost if the retained contribution is insufficient.

II. Central Idea

Suppose there are $n$ samples and $p$ indicators, forming an $ n \times p$ sample matrix:

$$
X = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \
x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p} \
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np} \
\end{bmatrix}
= (x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_p)
$$
The aim is to find new variables $ z_1, z_2, \dots, z_m $, where $ m \leq p $, such that:

$$
\begin{cases}
z_1 = l_{11}x_1 + l_{12}x_2 + \cdots + l_{1p}x_p \
z_2 = l_{21}x_1 + l_{22}x_2 + \cdots + l_{2p}x_p \
\vdots \
z_m = l_{m1}x_1 + l_{m2}x_2 + \cdots + l_{mp}x_p \
\end{cases}
$$
The coefficients $ l_{ij} $ are determined according to the following principles:

  1. Different principal components are mutually uncorrelated.
  2. The first principal component has the greatest variance among all possible linear combinations.
  3. Subject to being uncorrelated with the first, the second principal component has the greatest possible variance.
  4. The process continues until $ m $ principal components have been selected.

III. Calculation

1. Standardize the data

  • Calculate the mean and standard deviation:
    $$
    \bar{x}j = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} x_{ij},\quad S_j = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j)^2}{n-1}}
    $$

  • Standardize each observation:
    $$
    X_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j}{S_j}
    $$

  • The standardized matrix is:
    $$
    X = \begin{bmatrix}
    X_{11} & X_{12} & \cdots & X_{1p} \
    X_{21} & X_{22} & \cdots & X_{2p} \
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
    X_{n1} & X_{n2} & \cdots & X_{np} \
    \end{bmatrix}
    $$

2. Calculate the covariance matrix

  • Definition:
    $$
    R = \begin{bmatrix}
    r_{11} & r_{12} & \cdots & r_{1p} \
    r_{21} & r_{22} & \cdots & r_{2p} \
    \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
    r_{p1} & r_{p2} & \cdots & r_{pp} \
    \end{bmatrix},\quad r_{ij} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n} X_{ki} X_{kj}
    $$

3. Solve for eigenvalues and eigenvectors

  • Eigenvalues:
    $$
    \lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_p \geq 0
    $$
    Here, $ R $ is a positive semidefinite matrix.

  • Corresponding eigenvectors:
    $$
    a_1 = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} \ a_{21} \ \vdots \ a_{p1} \end{bmatrix},\quad
    a_2 = \begin{bmatrix} a_{12} \ a_{22} \ \vdots \ a_{p2} \end{bmatrix},\quad \dots,\quad
    a_p = \begin{bmatrix} a_{1p} \ a_{2p} \ \vdots \ a_{pp} \end{bmatrix}
    $$

4. Calculate the contribution and cumulative contribution

  • Contribution:
    $$
    \text{贡献率} = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_k}
    $$

  • Cumulative contribution:
    $$
    \text{累计贡献率} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{i}\lambda_k}{\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_k}\quad (i=1,2,\dots,p)
    $$

5. Write the principal components

In general, the first ( m ) components whose cumulative contribution exceeds 80 percent are selected:

$$
F_i = a_{1i}X_1 + a_{2i}X_2 + \cdots + a_{pi}X_p,\quad (i=1,2,\dots,m)
$$

6. Interpret the components

The meaning of a component is judged from the loading of each indicator upon it. An indicator with a larger loading has a greater influence on that component.

IV. Extensions

  1. Cluster analysis: dimensionality reduction simplifies the independent variables and makes graphical presentation easier.
  2. Regression analysis: PCA may alleviate multicollinearity.
  3. Factor analysis: PCA is, in effect, a special case of factor analysis. Since factor analysis is generally easier to interpret, it is often the better choice when interpretation matters.

References

Qingfeng’s Mathematical Modeling Notes: The Principles and a Case Study of PCA—CSDN

Principal Component Analysis in Mathematical Modeling: Explanation and Applications—Baidu Developer Center

Modeling Encyclopedia: PCA Explained, with Python Code—Zhihu

entry.title: Pearson Correlation Coefficient
entry.content:
Pearson Correlation Coefficient

Variance describes the degree to which a single variable is dispersed. Covariance replaces the squared term $(X - E[X])^2$ in variance with the product $(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])$. It therefore measures the average product of the deviations of two variables from their respective means and reflects the tendency of the variables to change together. Covariance, however, is affected by the units in which the variables are measured and is consequently difficult to compare directly. The natural solution is to make it dimensionless by dividing it by the two standard deviations.

Definition

The Pearson correlation coefficient, commonly known as the linear correlation coefficient, describes the linear relationship between variables X and Y. It is defined as follows:
$$
\rho_{X, Y} = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} = \frac{E\left[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])\right]}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} = \frac{E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)}{\sqrt{E\left(X^2\right) - [E(X)]^2} \sqrt{E\left(Y^2\right) - [E(Y)]^2}}
$$

Note: When X and Y are connected by some nonlinear relationship, the Pearson coefficient may fail to represent that relationship properly.

Properties of the Correlation Coefficient

  1. Independence and lack of correlation:

    If X and Y are independent, then $\rho_{X,Y} = 0$. The converse is not generally true: $\rho_{X,Y} = 0$ does not necessarily imply independence, unless X and Y follow a bivariate normal distribution.

  2. Range:

$$
-1 \leq \rho_{X,Y} \leq 1
$$

Calculating the Coefficient for Two Sets of Indicators

Means

$$
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i,\quad \bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i
$$

Variances (unbiased estimates)

$$
\sigma_X^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2,\quad \sigma_Y^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2
$$

Sample covariance

$$
\operatorname{cov}(X,Y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})
$$

Correlation coefficient

$$
r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}
$$

Explanation: The denominator contains the respective standard deviations so that covariance becomes dimensionless. This removes the influence of different units and scales and standardizes the result within ([-1, 1]).

Guidelines for Interpretation

The strength of the relationship between two variables may be judged from the absolute value of the calculated coefficient (r):

|r| Strength of correlation
0.8-1.0 Extremely strong
0.6-0.8 Strong
0.4-0.6 Moderate
0.2-0.4 Weak
0.0-0.2 Extremely weak or nonexistent

Further Reading

  • An In-Depth Explanation of Expectation, Variance, and Covariance
  • Zhihu: How Should We Understand the Pearson Correlation Coefficient?
  • Correlation Coefficients: The Formula and Meaning of Pearson’s Coefficient—CSDN Blog

entry.title: Entropy Weight Method (EWM)
entry.content:
Entropy Weight Method (EWM)

Background

This is a more objective method for assigning weights that appears frequently in mathematical modeling. Because the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) is too subjective—expert scoring is essentially making things up arbitrarily—the entropy weight method is introduced as an alternative.

Intuition

For a set of data indicators, the larger the variance, the smaller the similarity among the data, and thus the greater its contribution. To take an extreme case: if for a given indicator all of its values are identical, then its similarity is maximal, and the weight assigned to this indicator for the purpose of discrimination can be set directly to zero. Entropy is a measure of uncertainty: the greater the uncertainty, the larger the entropy, and the more information it contains. Consequently, the weight of its influence on the final decision should be set higher.

To illustrate with an example from Qingfeng’s mathematical modeling course: suppose Xiao Zhang and Xiao Wang are two high school students. Xiao Zhang is a good student who always gets full marks on final exams, whereas Xiao Wang is a poor student who often fails. In one particular exam, Xiao Zhang again gets full marks—but Xiao Wang also gets full marks. That is highly unusual. Xiao Wang’s result carries a great deal of information, and the corresponding weight should therefore be higher.

Definitions

  • Information Content

    The amount of information is defined as:
    $$
    I(x) = -\ln(p(x))
    $$

  • Information Entropy
    Information entropy is defined as the expected value of the information content:
    $$
    H(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i)\ln(p(x_i))
    $$
    When all events are equally likely, entropy reaches its maximum:
    $$
    H(X) = \ln(n)
    $$

Calculation Procedure

The entropy weight method mainly consists of the following three steps:

Data Standardization

Suppose there are objects and indicators, and the raw data form a matrix (which must first be positively oriented):

$$
X = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1m} \
x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2m} \
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \
x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{nm}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Positive Orientation

  • Requirement: When computing probabilities in the subsequent steps, every element must be non-negative.
  • Treatment: If any negative values are present, a specific method must be applied to standardize them into the [0,1] interval.
Indicator Type Characteristic Example
Benefit indicator (positive) The larger, the better Grades, profit, GDP growth rate
Cost indicator (negative) The smaller, the better Expenses, pollution level, unemployment rate
Intermediate indicator The closer to a certain value, the better PH value in water quality assessment
Interval indicator Best when falling within an interval Body temperature, the content of a certain substance in water
  • Converting cost indicators to benefit indicators:

$$
x_i = \max{x_1, x_2, …, x_i} - x_i
$$

Note: If all elements are positive, the reciprocal can be taken directly.

  • Converting intermediate indicators to benefit indicators:

For an intermediate indicator sequence with the optimal value being $x_{best}$, and $x_{new}$ being the positively oriented benefit indicator, the orientation formula is:

$$
M = \max{|x_i - x_{best}|}
$$

$$
x_{new} = 1 - \frac{|x_i - x_{best}|}{M}
$$

  • Converting interval indicators to benefit indicators:

For an interval indicator sequence with the optimal interval being $x_{best}$, and $x_{new}$ being the positively oriented benefit indicator, the orientation formula is:
$$
M = \max{a - \min{x_i}, \max{x_i} - b}
$$

$$
x_{new} =
\begin{cases}
1 - \frac{a - x}{M}, & x < a \
1, & a \leq x \leq b \
1 - \frac{x - b}{M}, & x > b
\end{cases}
$$

Standardization Methods

  • Method 1 (applicable when there are no negative values):
    $$
    z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{ij}^2}}
    $$

  • Method 2 (when negative values exist):
    $$
    z_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \min{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}}}{\max{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}} - \min{x_{1j}, x_{2j}, \ldots, x_{nj}}}
    $$

Calculating the Probability Matrix

Starting from the standardized matrix, calculate the proportion of each sample under each indicator to form the probability matrix:

$$
p_{ij} = \frac{z_{ij}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{ij}}
$$
This ensures that the probabilities in each column (for each indicator) sum to 1.

Calculating Information Entropy and Entropy Weights

Calculating Information Entropy

Compute the information entropy:

$$
e_j = -\frac{1}{\ln n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_{ij}\ln(p_{ij}) \quad (j=1,2,\ldots,m)
$$
Note: When $p_{ij}=0$, it is stipulated that $\ln(0)=0$.

Here, dividing by $\ln n$ normalizes $e_j$ to the $[0,1]$ interval.

Calculating the Information Utility Value

The information utility value $d_j$ is defined as:
$$
d_j = 1 - e_j
$$
The larger the information utility value, the more information the indicator contains.

Normalizing to Obtain Entropy Weights

Finally, the information utility values for all indicators are normalized to obtain the entropy weights $\omega_j$:
$$
\omega_j = \frac{d_j}{\sum_{j=1}^{m} d_j} \quad (j=1,2,\ldots,m)
$$

Score

$$
score_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_{j}z_{ij} \quad (i=1,2,\ldots,n)
$$

Example Code

(Taken from this post)

Extensions

  1. Modified TOPSIS Method: The entropy weight method can be used to modify the TOPSIS method, making the decision-making process more objective.
  2. Combining Subjective and Objective Weights: Combining objective weighting (entropy weight method) with subjective weighting can yield a more reasonable weight allocation.
  3. Other Objective Weighting Methods: For example, grey relational analysis can also serve as a method for calculating weights.
  4. Choice of Standardization Method: Different standardization methods will produce different (Z) matrices, so the appropriate method should be chosen according to the specific situation.

Model Summary

  • Step 1: Check whether the input matrix contains negative values and perform any necessary standardization to ensure the data are non-negative.
  • Step 2: Calculate the proportion of each sample under each indicator to construct the probability matrix.
  • Step 3: Use the probability matrix to compute the information entropy for each indicator, then calculate the information utility value, and finally normalize to obtain the weight for each indicator.

entry.title: XGBoost Formula Notes
entry.content:
XGBoost Technical Notes

Parameter Settings

See the code.

Relevant Mathematical Formulas

  • Objective function of the model:

$$
\text{Obj}(\theta)^{(t)} = \sum_{i=1}^n L(y_i, \hat{y}i) + \sum{k=1}^K \Omega(f_k)
$$

  • Regularisation term

$$
\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2} \lambda \sum_{j=1}^T w_j^2
$$

  • Approximation of the objective function

$$
\text{Obj}(\theta)^{(t)} \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ g_i f_t(x_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i f_t^2(x_i) \right] + \Omega(f_t)
$$

  • Gain

$$
\text{Gain} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(\sum_{i \in I_L} g_i)^2}{\sum_{i \in I_L} h_i + \lambda} + \frac{(\sum_{i \in I_R} g_i)^2}{\sum_{i \in I_R} h_i + \lambda} - \frac{(\sum_{i \in I} g_i)^2}{\sum_{i \in I} h_i + \lambda} \right] - \gamma
$$

  • Log loss

$$
\text{LogLoss} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i) \log(1-p_i) \right]
$$

  • Classification error rate

$$
\text{Error} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i \neq y_i)
$$
